The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (﴿فَالتَّالِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا﴾ is a verbal noun (masdar) derived from the meaning of at-talliyat). So the author, may Allah have mercy on him, parsed ﴿ذِكْرًا﴾ as a verbal noun derived from the meaning of ﴿التَّالِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا﴾. From this we benefit a grammatical point: that the verbal noun may be from the wording or from the meaning. If it is from the meaning, it is a semantic verbal noun (masdar ma'nawi); if it is from the wording, it is a verbal noun of the same root (masdar lafzi). So when you say: "I sat sitting (qa'adtu julusan)", then "julusan" is a semantic verbal noun, while "qa'adtu qu'udan" is a verbal noun of the same root.
﴿At-talliyat dhikran﴾: the author says that at-talliyat originally means adh-dhakirat dhikran, so at-talliyat in his view means adh-dhakirat, and ﴿dhikran﴾ is its verbal noun derived from its meaning. But what appears is contrary to the author's statement: that ﴿dhikran﴾ is the object of at-talliyat, because ﴿at-talliyat﴾ is an active participle that has fulfilled the conditions of governing, being definite with (al), and ﴿dhikran﴾ is its direct object; i.e., "fa-at-talliyat" means "fa-allati yatlina adh-dhikr", and the intended dhikr is the Qur'an. It is called dhikr because it is a remembrance of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, for it is among the best of remembrance; because it reminds a person of his Lord; because it reminds a person of his Lord's rulings; because it reminds a person of his Lord's blessings; and because it is a dhikr (honor and elevation) for the one who acts upon it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 44], and because it admonishes its possessor and reminds him, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿A Book We have revealed to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that those of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Sad 29]. So the Qur'an is a dhikr in these five respects. Will you repeat them?
* A student: Yes. First: because it is a reminder for a person to be mindful by, and it reminds you of Allah, glorified and exalted, and that it raises his status, and that it reminds you of the rulings of Allah, glorified and exalted, and that it reminds you of morals (...).
* The Shaykh: Of those who passed away, and of Allah's blessing, and it is also itself a dhikr of Allah, among the best kinds of dhikr.
﴿So those who recite the reminder (3). Indeed, your God is One﴾: this sentence is the answer to the oath; therefore the nun in ﴿inna﴾ is kasra here, because it falls in the answer to the oath and because its predicate is connected with the lam, ﴿la-wahid﴾. When inna is the answer to an oath, its kasra is obligatory; and when its predicate is connected with the lam, or its postponed subject, or a complement of one of them is connected with the lam, its kasra is obligatory.
﴿Inna ilahakum﴾: the address. The author says: (O people of Makkah). But the correct view is that it is general, including everyone addressed. However, what led the author to restrict it to the people of Makkah is that this verse is Meccan and the polytheists were the people of Makkah. But the general meaning should not be restricted by the place of its revelation, and if the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the occasion, then the consideration is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the place. So the correct reading is ﴿Inna ilahakum﴾, meaning: O people, ﴿la-wahid﴾, one, meaning: there is no partner for Him. "Wahid" and "Ahad" and what resembles them indicate singularity, i.e., that He, the Mighty and Majestic, has no partner.
﴿Ilahakum﴾ is on the pattern fa'al in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., "ma'lukum" (the one you worship), and the one worshipped (ma'luh) is the one who is served out of love and exaltation. By His love a person carries out the commands, and by His exaltation a person refrains from the prohibitions. So, O people, your worshipped is truly One with no partner. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has no partner in His lordship, no partner in His divinity, and no partner in His names and attributes. So who will bring evidence that He has no partner in His lordship?
* A student: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 9].
* Another student: (Indeed your Lord is One).
* The Shaykh: Where is "Indeed your Lord is One"? I don't know a verse with this wording.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: We are talking about lordship.
* The student: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 16].
* The Shaykh: Yes. Good. As for divinity: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾ [Muhammad 19]. As for names and attributes: ﴿There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [Ash-Shura 11]. So Allah, the Exalted, is One in His divinity, His lordship, His names and His attributes, glorified and exalted.
Then he said: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [As-Saffat 5]. ﴿Rabb﴾ here is either an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan), or the predicate of a deleted subject, the estimate being: He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. And "rabb" means creator, owner, and manager. He is the One who created the heavens and the earth, the One who owns the heavens and the earth, and the One who manages the heavens and the earth. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command﴾ [Al-A'raf 54]. This is His singularity in creation and management. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran 189], and this is His singularity in dominion.
"As-samawat" is the plural of "sama'", which is well known, and its number is seven heavens by the text of the Qur'an: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 86]; ﴿Allah is the One who created seven heavens and of the earth their like﴾ [At-Talaq 12]. The earth is likewise seven, according to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the explicit Sunnah. As for the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, in His saying... does the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicate that they are seven earths?
* A student: ﴿and of the earth their like﴾ [At-Talaq 12].
* The Shaykh: His saying: ﴿and of the earth their like﴾. The likeness here is in number, because it is impossible for the earth to be like the heaven in its essence, or in its vastness and greatness; the heaven is wider and greater, and its substance differs from the substance of the earth. So it must be that the likeness is in number. As for the Sunnah, it is explicit, such as his saying ﷺ: "Whoever takes a span of land unjustly, Allah will encircle him with it from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (1610) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, may Allah be pleased with him.]]
﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ [As-Saffat 5]: meaning, and the Lord of what is between them. What is between them? Undoubtedly what is between them are great creations, as evidenced by their being placed as a counterpart and equal to the heavens and the earth, so they must be a great thing. It is not merely the clouds we see subjected between the sky and the earth; rather there are great things between the sky and the earth among the signs of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We know some of them: the clouds, for they are between the sky and the earth; the stars are between the sky and the earth; the sun is between the sky and the earth; the moon is between the sky and the earth; because of Allah's saying: ﴿Each in an orbit they swim﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 33].
As for what was famous among the astronomers of the past, that the sun is in the fourth heaven, the moon in the lowest heaven, and Mercury, Saturn and Jupiter in the other heavens, in this order:
Zuhal sharā mirrīkhahu min shamsihi, fa-tazāharat bi-'Uṭārid al-aqmār
How many is this? Seven, arranged from highest to lowest.
Zuhal sharā mirrīkhahu min shamsihi, fa-tazāharat bi-'Uṭārid al-aqmār
The highest is (Zuhal) Saturn in the seventh heaven; (sharā) Jupiter in the sixth; (mirrīkhahu) Mars in the fifth heaven; (min shamsihi) the sun in the fourth; (fa-tazāharat) Venus in the third; (bi-'Uṭārid) Mercury in the second heaven; (al-aqmār) the moon in the lowest heaven. This is what is famous among the astronomers of the past, but it is contrary to the correct view, because the apparent meaning of the texts is that the sun, moon and stars are all below the heaven; they are not fixed in the heavens, but are in an orbit that moves between the sky and the earth, and the moon is the nearest of them to the earth. The evidence is that it eclipses what is above it, as we have witnessed and others have witnessed at times; you find it passing beneath a star, and the star is hidden by it, and this indicates that it is below the stars.
In any case, we say: between the seven heavens are the clouds, the sun, the moon, the stars, the planets, and other matters we do not know. We may not know these matters, and perhaps later knowledge will reveal to us much of them.
He said: ﴿And Lord of the easts﴾ (i.e., and of the wests, for the sun has an east and a west each day). He said: ﴿al-mashariq﴾ and then said: (i.e., and the wests). So it is as if this is the method of mentioning one of two opposites while omitting the other, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And He made for you garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [An-Nahl 81], meaning: and the cold, for the garments, which are shirts and the like, protect from heat and cold.
Here He said: ﴿And Lord of the easts﴾, and the author said: meaning (and the wests).
In any case, ﴿al-mashariq﴾ is the plural of mashriq. So what is meant by the easts? Is what is meant, as the author said, the sun's risings, because each day it has a rising? Or should we say that al-mashariq is more general, including the risings of the sun, the risings of the moon, the risings of the stars, and the risings of everything that rises? Which of these? The second is more general. So we say: ﴿Lord of the easts﴾, meaning: the risings of the sun, the risings of the moon, the risings of the stars, and the risings of everything that rises. Allah mentioned the easts without the wests because the easts are more indicative of power than the wests, since rising is a beginning and setting is an end; and in rising, especially the sunrise, there is illumination and light in which the completeness of blessing clearly appears.
His saying ﴿al-mashariq﴾ here is in the plural. In some verses it comes in the dual, such as His saying: ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [Ar-Rahman 17], and in some verses it comes in the singular: ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾, as Allah said: ﴿Lord of the east and the west; there is no deity except Him, so take Him as Disposer of affairs﴾ [Al-Muzzammil 9]. So is this a contradiction or what?
The answer: No, and there is nothing in the Qur'an that contradicts: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction﴾ [An-Nisa' 82]. The Qur'an cannot contradict itself, nor can it contradict authentic Sunnah; for a weak Sunnah may contradict the Qur'an, and its contradiction of the Qur'an indicates its weakness, but with authentic Sunnah it is impossible.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verses 1–17 (part 3 of 7):**

If there is something whose apparent meaning is contradictory, there must be a way to resolve the contradiction. This is either by reconciling the texts (*al-jam'*), which is the first level for acting on texts whose apparent meanings conflict, or by abrogation (*naskh*, the annulment of an earlier ruling by a later one), provided the chronology is known and the text is of a kind that admits abrogation, or by preference (*tarjih*), where one of the two is preferred over the other. All three levels are necessary. Sometimes, however, the examiner may not find any of these ways. He may be unable to reconcile the texts, he may not know of any abrogation, and he may be unable to establish a preference. What then is his position? *Tawaqquf* (suspension of judgment): he says, "God knows best." It is not permissible under any circumstances to believe that there is any contradiction in the Qur'an or in authentic Sunnah. But is he allowed to try to know these levels? Or, if it is difficult for him the first time, should he stop? He must try to examine the matter again and again until it becomes clear, so that doubt does not enter his heart and he does not deviate, and we seek refuge with God.

This point has come incidentally: there is no contradiction in the Qur'an, either within itself or with authentic Sunnah. If there is something whose apparent meaning is contradictory, we must use the three levels: first, reconciliation (*al-jam'*). If that is not possible, then abrogation. If that is not possible, then preference. If we cannot reach any of these, then suspension of judgment, but with an effort to reach one of these levels.

So, based on this principle, we can apply the difference found concerning the East and the West. We say: "the East" in terms of direction, meaning the direction of the east. ﴿Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but Him﴾ means the direction of the east and the direction of the west. The evidence for this is the Almighty's saying: ﴿To God belong the East and the West; wherever you turn, there is the Face of God﴾ [al-Baqarah 115], meaning the direction of God, according to one of the two interpretations.

As for "the two easts" and "the two wests," ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman 17], what is meant is the easts of summer and winter and the wests of summer and winter. The sun has a limit in its rising in summer, which is the Tropic of Cancer, and it has a limit in its course in winter, which is the Tropic of Capricorn. The difference between the two easts is great, and none of the created beings can move the sun from the Tropic of Cancer to the Tropic of Capricorn, nor shift it by a single hair's breadth. The same applies to the moon, since it moves between the two easts and the two wests.

If someone says: In which place in the Qur'an does "Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests" occur in the dual?

Student: Surah al-Rahman.

Shaykh: In surah al-Rahman. Elsewhere?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, this is not in al-Isra'; this is in surah (al-Muzzammil). I want the dual: has it occurred anywhere other than (al-Rahman)? In any case, the reason it is mentioned in the dual in (al-Rahman) is that this surah addresses two categories: humankind and jinn. So this is a meaningful correspondence with the context of the whole surah.

(The easts and the wests): the plural here is clear. It may be in terms of the easts of everything that rises and the wests of everything that sets, from the sun, the moon, the stars and the planets. Or it may be that the easts of the sun are daily, since each day it has a rising point. Which level is this? It is the level of... what? The three levels? It is the level of reconciliation. So the reconciliation between them is that we say: "the easts" (*al-mashariq*) refers to the easts of everything that rises, or to the easts of the sun each day. "The two easts" (*al-mashriqayn*) refers to the easts of summer and winter and their two wests. "The east and the west" (*al-mashriq wal-maghrib*) refers to the direction. He said: (﴿and Lord of the easts﴾ means "and of the wests").

﴿Indeed, We have adorned the lowest heaven with an adornment of the planets﴾ [al-Saffat 6]. The pronoun in ﴿Indeed, We﴾ refers to God, the Mighty and Majestic. He used the plural pronoun referring to God as a mark of glorification, not as an indication of plurality, because the verse says: ﴿Indeed, your God is one﴾ [al-Saffat 4]. This is an expression of glorification. His saying ﴿We have adorned the lowest heaven with an adornment﴾ means: We have placed upon it what adorns it, namely the planets. For this reason He said: ﴿with an adornment of the planets﴾. In another reading it is ﴿with an adornment, the planets﴾, and both are correct. ﴿With an adornment of the planets﴾ means: with the planets that adorn the heaven, as He said: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾ [al-Mulk 5]. The word ﴿the planets﴾ in the reading mentioned by the author is in the genitive as a second term of a construct phrase (*mudaf ilayh*), and "adornment" is the first term of the construct, not nunated. ﴿with an adornment of the planets﴾, because the planets themselves are an adornment with which the lowest heaven is adorned.

If someone asks: Why was the lowest heaven called "lowest" (*dunya*)? Because it is nearer to the earth than what is above it, so it is "lowest." And perhaps we may also say: it is lower than what is above it in extent and strength, because the higher you go the more the space expands. The heavens around the earth are circular like a sphere, and it is known that as you ascend it will widen, and as it widens it will be stronger, because if what is widened were not as strong as what is beneath it, it would weaken. As a building widens, it must become stronger.

Let us give you an example. If you brought a reinforced slab five meters wide that needs, say, ten centimeters of thickness, but then you made it twenty meters, it would need more: that is, it would need to be thicker, because if it kept the same thickness as the first while being wider, it would (...). And the wider it is, the stronger and more firmly built it must be.

His saying ﴿with an adornment of the planets﴾ means that the planets adorn the heaven. We will raise an objection to this: we mentioned just now that the stars and planets are in an orbit between the heaven and the earth, and the apparent meaning of the verse is that the lowest heaven is adorned with something attached to it. The answer to this is that a thing may be adorned by something even if the latter is separate from it. Have you seen that if you place chandeliers outside a palace, for example, around a palace, then when you look at the palace with the chandeliers between you and it, these chandeliers will appear as an adornment of the palace, even though in reality they are not attached to it? Everything that comes between you and another thing will be attributed to the second thing and will appear to you as attached to it. Even when we were children, one of us would say: "I touch the sky," and stretch out his finger; the onlooker sees it as though it touched the sky, but that is not so.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, nearness and strength.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, this is about the lower world, the lowest heaven (...).

* * *

Student: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the lowest heaven with an adornment of the planets (6), and as a protection from every rebellious devil (7). They cannot listen to the exalted assembly, and they are pelted from every side (8), repelled, and for them is a perpetual punishment (9). Except one who snatches a fragment, and a piercing flame pursues him (10). So ask them: are they more difficult to create, or those We have created? Indeed, We created them from sticky clay (11). Rather, you marvel, and they mock (12). And when they are reminded, they do not remember (13). And when they see a sign, they ridicule it﴾ [al-Saffat 6–14].

Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God the Exalted said: ﴿By those ranged in ranks (1), and those who drive away with a driving (2), and those who recite the remembrance (3): indeed, your God is one﴾ [al-Saffat 1–4]. What is the grammatical position of this sentence ﴿indeed, your God is one﴾ in relation to what precedes it?

Student: It is the answer to the oath (*jawab al-qasam*).

Shaykh: The answer to the oath. The breaking of ﴿inna﴾ here has two reasons.

Student: First: because it begins the sentence.

Shaykh: No.

Student: Second: because the answer is accompanied by the particle of emphasis *lam*.

Shaykh: That is one. And the first?

Student: That it is the answer to an oath.

Shaykh: That it is the answer to an oath. Correct. ﴿Your God (*ilahakum*)﴾: *ilah* means?

Student: Worshipped (*ma'luh*).

Shaykh: Worshipped, that is, the one who is worshipped. Good. The saying ﴿is one﴾: the objection to this is that the polytheists have many gods.

Student: Yes, they have gods, but they are false gods.

Shaykh: We say: yes, they have gods, but they are false gods. What is the evidence?

Student: ﴿There is no god except One God﴾ [al-Ma'idah 73].

Shaykh: No, the evidence that they are false?

Student: That they neither benefit them nor harm them.

Another student: ﴿That is because God is the Truth, and what they call upon besides Him is falsehood﴾ [Luqman 30].

Shaykh: Yes, correct. And His saying: ﴿They are only names you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority﴾. The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ uses the plural for the heavens and the singular for the earth. Is that because the earth is one, or what?

Student: The earth is not one; it is multiple.

Shaykh: The evidence?

Student: ﴿And of the earth, the like of them﴾.

Shaykh: What is ﴿and of the earth, the like of them﴾?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: (...), otherwise we have learned nothing.

Student: ﴿God is He who created seven heavens, and of the earth the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq 12].

Shaykh: Why did you say that "the like" here means equal in number? Could it not mean like them in attribute?

Student: Because it cannot be like them in attribute, since the earth is smaller than the heaven, so it must be equal in number.

Shaykh: Yes indeed. That is why God describes the heaven as strong: ﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾ [al-Naba' 12], ﴿And We made the heaven a protected ceiling﴾ [al-Anbiya' 32], ﴿And the heaven We built with might﴾ [al-Dhariyat 47]. Such descriptions do not occur for the earth.

His saying ﴿and what is between them﴾: what does making it a counterpart to the heavens and the earth indicate?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: It is clear that the heavens are great, and so is the earth. ﴿And what is between them﴾: why did God make it a counterpart and equal to these two, although it appears to us to be far less?

Student: That is, what is between the heaven and the earth is anything (...).

Shaykh: Like what?

Student: That is, what is between the heaven and the earth, like clouds, stars, the sun, the moon and other things we have not been informed of.

Shaykh: Well done. So this indicates that what is between the heavens and the earth consists of great creations.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿and Lord of the easts﴾. What is meant by "the easts"?

Student: According to the author's view: the easts of the sun.

Shaykh: Because each day it has a...?

Student: Rising point.

Shaykh: So its easts would be three hundred and sixty easts. And according to the second view?

Student: The easts of the stars, the moon and the sun.

Shaykh: And everything that rises or sets.

In this verse the plural "easts" is used. In another verse also: ﴿So I swear by the Lord of the easts and the wests﴾ [al-Ma'arij 40]. In some verses the dual is used, and in some verses the singular. How do you reconcile these aspects?

Student: As for the dual (...), the east of summer and the east of winter; as for the singular, the direction of the east and the direction of the west; and as for the plural, the east of each day according to its own.

Shaykh: Each day and its west, or the east of everything that rises and sets.

What is our position if the Noble Qur'an or authentic Prophetic Sunnah contains something whose apparent meaning is contradictory?

Student: First, reconciling the texts.

Shaykh: The first position is reconciliation. Is this obligatory?

Student: Yes.

Shaykh: Why is it obligatory if it is possible?

Student: Because by reconciliation both texts are acted upon.

Shaykh: Because both pieces of evidence are acted upon. Well done. If it is not possible?

Student: Then abrogation.

Shaykh: Then abrogation, on what condition?

Student: That the conditions of abrogation are met, and the absence of (...).

Shaykh: Among them is knowledge that the abrogating text came later.

Student: Knowledge of the chronology.

Shaykh: Knowledge of the chronology. If there is no abrogation?

Student: Then preference.

Shaykh: Then preference. The grounds for preference are many. If there is none?

Student: Then suspension.

Suspension. Is this possible in reality?

Student: In reality, no.

Shaykh: In reality, no. That is, it is not possible for a contradiction to arise in which these three things are absent. But from the viewpoint of the one deriving the ruling it is possible, either because of his deficiency or his negligence. Good.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have adorned the lowest heaven with an adornment of the planets﴾ [al-Saffat 6]. What is meant by "the lowest heaven"?

Student: The heaven we see (...).

Shaykh: Correct, the one that is next to the earth. Why was it described as "lowest"?

Student: Because the one who looks at the heaven thinks it is near.

Shaykh: Because of its nearness, that is one. The second?

Student: Because it is less than the other heavens in strength (...).

Shaykh: Correct, and in extent, because the more the circle widens the greater it becomes. How is it said "We adorned the lowest heaven," when we established that the stars are in an orbit between the heaven and the earth?

Student: Because it is possible to adorn a thing with something that is not part of it.

Shaykh: Yes indeed, separate from it. Can you give us an example?

Student: A palace, for example (...), and the entrance is not part of the palace.

Shaykh: That is, he adorns it with chandeliers and the like, although they are separate from it.

His saying: ﴿with an adornment of the planets﴾: there are two readings?

Student: ﴿with an adornment of the planets﴾ and ﴿with an adornment, the planets﴾.

Shaykh: That is, with the genitive construction and with nunation. According to the reading of the construct, what is the meaning?

Student: The planets themselves.

Shaykh: "With the adornment of the planet," that is, with the adornment that the planets produce. And according to the nunated reading?

Student: It is not the planets themselves.

Shaykh: No.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: In the explanation. That is, its meaning is that it is with an adornment in general; what is this adornment? He explained it by His saying: ﴿the planets﴾.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: In the detail, or the explanation after the general statement, there is a benefit. What is it?

Student: That the soul is eager for the explanation (...).

Shaykh: So the explanation or detail falls upon a soul that is eager, and that is more eloquent and more likely to be accepted. That is, when something comes in general and then comes in detail or explanation, it is more eloquent, because when it reaches the soul in general, the soul seeks the explanation of this general matter, so it reaches an eager soul, and that is more eloquent and more firmly established in the heart.

Student: (...) it was divided, it would have been more inviting (...).

Shaykh: That is about divisions. ﴿with an adornment of the planets﴾, ﴿and as a protection﴾: we have stopped at them now.

Student: The third reading is also like that (...).

Shaykh: What is the third reading?

Student: With nunation and the accusative for "the planets." That is, as an apposition (*badal al-ishtimal*) for "the heaven." "The planets" is an appositive of the heaven.

Shaykh: We do not have this reading here.

Student: It is canonical (*sab'iyya*).

Shaykh: But we do not have it present.

Student: No, he mentioned it in the commentary.

Shaykh: In the commentary. ﴿with an adornment, the planets (accusative)﴾: according to this reading, the planets are an appositive of the heaven. Is it like this in your copy? (...) What does the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) say?

Student: It says: (...) ﴿with an adornment﴾, "the planets" is an explanatory appositive (*ataf bayan*) to it, and there remains a third reading, which is nunating "adornment" and making "the planets" accusative. The three are canonical readings. And His saying ﴿with an adornment, the planets (accusative)﴾: Abu Bakr read ﴿with an adornment﴾ with nunation and ﴿the planets﴾ in the accusative. There are two possibilities: one is that the adornment is a verbal noun (*masdar*) whose agent is omitted, its estimated meaning being that God adorned the planets by making them shining and beautiful in themselves. The second is that "adornment" is a name for what is adorned with, like *liqa* is a name for what the inkwell is struck with. So according to this, "the planets" is accusative by an implied verb "I mean," or it is in apposition (*badal al-ishtimal*) to "the lowest heaven," that is, "its planets," or to "adorned with an adornment." Hamzah and Hafs read it likewise, except that they put "the planets" in the genitive, meaning by "adornment" what is adorned with, and "the planets" is an apposition or explanation of the adornment. The rest read "adornment" in construct with "the planets," which admits three possibilities...

Shaykh: The accusative reading is in fact better because its accusative is by an implied verb, "with an adornment, I mean the planets," which is better than its being an appositive of the heaven: "We have adorned the heaven, the planets."

He says: (﴿وَحِفْظًا﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, meaning: We guarded it with the shooting stars.) ﴿حِفْظًا﴾: this means that ﴿حِفْظًا﴾ is in the accusative governed by a deleted verb, the sense being "We guarded it," i.e., We guarded the lowest heaven. ﴿حِفْظًا﴾ by what? By the shooting stars, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We have adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and made them missiles against the devils.﴾ [al-Mulk 5].

And here He says: ﴿And as a guard against every rebellious devil.﴾ [as-Saffat 7]. ﴿مِنْ كُلِّ﴾ ("against every") is connected to an implied verb, which is "We guarded it."

And his saying: (﴿شَيْطَانٍ مَارِدٍ﴾ "rebellious devil": obstinate, going beyond obedience). ﴿شَيْطَانٍ﴾ is indefinite, as you can see, and so it includes every devil. It is indefinite and is also the object of the genitive ﴿كُلِّ﴾ (every), so there are two sources of generality in it: indefiniteness, and the fact that (كل) "every" is attached to it. The word shaytan (devil) is said to derive from (shaṭa yashīṭu, "to burn/rage"), in which case the nūn is extra. It is also said to derive from (shaṭana), meaning "to be far away," in which case the nūn is original. The apparent view is that the nūn is original, and the word derives from (shaṭana) meaning "to be distant," because the devil has been distanced from the mercy of Allah. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And upon you is the curse until the Day of Recompense.﴾ [al-Hijr 35].

And his saying: ﴿مَارِدٍ﴾ (mārid) is the one who is obstinate and very strong in transgression, and we seek refuge in Allah.

And his saying: (﴿لَا يَسْمَعُونَ﴾ "they do not listen," i.e., the devils, is a new sentence, and their hearing is in the meaning of what was guarded against.) ﴿لَا يَسْمَعُونَ﴾: the clause, as the author said, is a resumptive sentence (istinaf). That is, the rebellious devils do not listen to the Highest Assembly. This resumed clause is in meaning what was guarded against in His saying: ﴿And as a guard against every rebellious devil.﴾ Guarded against what? Against their listening to the Highest Assembly. That is, the heaven was guarded from the devils so that they would not listen to the Highest Assembly.

He said: (﴿إِلَى الْمَلَإِ الْأَعْلَى﴾ "to the Highest Assembly" [as-Saffat 8]: the angels in the heaven. Listening is construed with (إلى "to") because it implies the sense of giving ear.) Al-mala' originally means a group, and it is generally used for the notables, as is frequently found in the stories of the messengers' deniers, where Allah says: ﴿The chiefs said﴾. Generally, al-mala' are the notable and prominent group among their people. There is no doubt that the angels, peace be upon them, are noble, because they are servants made subservient to worship Allah; they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded. So they are among the most upright of Allah's servants in obedience. Later, Allah willing, in the benefits section we will see whether they are better than humans or humans are better than them.

Here He says: ﴿الْأَعْلَى﴾ (the Highest). Is it highest in rank or highest in attribute? There is no doubt that they are highest in place, since the heaven is above the earth. It may also be meant as highest in attribute, so both meanings are combined, just as when Allah the Exalted is described as the Highest, He is highest in place and highest in attribute.

He said: (And listening is construed with "to" because it implies giving ear.) This is an answer to an implied question, namely that (سَمِعَ "heard") in Arabic takes its object directly, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the speech of she who pleads with you﴾ [al-Mujadilah 1]. Here He said: ﴿they do not listen to the Assembly﴾ and did not say: "they do not hear the Assembly." The author answered it by saying the verb is construed with the meaning of giving ear. Construal (tadmin) means that the verb carries a meaning appropriate to its object or complement, whether it is a direct object or a genitive. The question is: when such an expression comes, is the figurative extension in the verb, meaning the verb is construed with a meaning suited to the complement it takes, or is the figurative extension in the particle?

The grammarians mention two views on this. The first view, held by the Kufans, is that the figurative extension is in the particle. The second view is that the verb is construed with a meaning suited to the particle that follows it. The clearest example is His saying: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [al-Insan 6]. If we took the apparent wording, the meaning would be that this spring is drunk "with" (بها). It is known that one cannot drink with a spring, since one drinks only from it, using a vessel. So the spring is not drunk with, but drunk from. Shall we say the (ب "with") here means (مِن "from"), so the figurative extension is in the particle; or shall we say that (يشرب "drinks") is construed with the meaning of (يَرْوَى "quench thirst"), so that the sense is: "a spring by which the servants of Allah quench their thirst, after they have drunk from it"?

We have mentioned two views of the scholars on this. There is no doubt that placing the construal in the verb is better than placing it in the complement, because when you place the construal in the verb you gain two benefits:

The first benefit: what the wording of the verb indicates.

The second: what the meaning of the construed verb indicates.

But if you make the figurative extension in the particle, you gain only one meaning, which is removing the particle and substituting another particle in its place, and you have gained nothing; the verb remains as it is according to what the wording indicates. The conclusion is that saying the verb is construed with a meaning suited to the particle or to the complement is better than saying that the complement is where the figurative extension lies.

Here, ﴿they do not listen to the Assembly﴾ [as-Saffat 8]: we say here that the verb is construed with the meaning of giving ear; that is, they do not give ear to them as listeners.

(And in one reading, with the letters mīm and sīn doubled.) That is, ﴿لَا يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾ (lā yassammaʿūn), originally yatasammaʿūn, with the tāʾ assimilated into the sīn, so it became yassammaʿūn. Is this reading canonical (sabʿiyyah) or irregular (shādhdhah)? It is canonical, because in the author's terminology when he says (وفي قراءة "and in a reading") it is canonical, and when he says (قُرِئ "it was read") it is irregular, or is it the other way?

He said: (﴿وَيُقْذَفُونَ﴾ "and they are pelted," i.e., the devils are pelted with the shooting stars ﴿from every side﴾ from the horizons of the heaven ﴿repulsed﴾ [as-Saffat 9]: a verbal noun from (dahara), meaning he drove him away and far off, and it is an object of purpose. ﴿وَلَهُمْ﴾ "and for them" in the Hereafter ﴿is a punishment, constant﴾: perpetual.)

The pronoun in ﴿وَيُقْذَفُونَ﴾ refers to the devils. If someone says that the devils have not been mentioned before, the answer is: yes, they have been mentioned in His saying ﴿every devil﴾, because "every devil" is general and thus indicates the plural. Yes or no? It indicates the plural. So ﴿يُقْذَفُونَ﴾ means the devils whose plurality is known from ﴿كُلِّ شَيْطَانٍ﴾. And they are pelted from every side. Who pelts them? Allah the Mighty and Majestic pelts them, commanding these shooting stars, so they pelt them. Qadhf (pelting) means throwing with force. ﴿مِنْ كُلِّ جَانِبٍ﴾ "from every side": from the sides from which they are struck, ("from the horizons of the heaven") as the author said.

﴿دُحُورًا﴾ means driving away and banishing. As the author said, it is an object of purpose: that is, for the sake of the repulsion. How many objects are there? Five: the absolute object, the direct object, the object of place/time, the object of purpose, and the object accompanying (the verb). These are five. Here are examples:

I struck a strike, Abū ʿAmr, the morning he came, and I walked along with the Nile out of fear of your punishment for me.

This gives five examples: (ضربت ضربًا "I struck a strike") is the absolute object. (أبا عمرو "Abū ʿAmr") is the direct object. (غداة أتى "the morning he came") is the object of time. (وسرت والنيل "and I walked along with the Nile") is the accompanying object. (خوفا من عقابك لي "out of fear of your punishment for me") is the object of purpose.

He says: ﴿دُحُورًا﴾, ﴿وَلَهُمْ﴾ "and for them" in the Hereafter ﴿عَذَابٌ وَاصِبٌ﴾ "a punishment, constant": that is, perpetual. They are punished in this world with these shooting stars, and punished in the Hereafter with lasting punishment, because the devils are among the people of the Fire.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿إِلَّا مَنْ خَطِفَ الْخَطْفَةَ﴾ "except one who snatches a snatching" [as-Saffat 10]: a verbal noun, meaning the single instance. The exception is from the pronoun in ﴿يَسْمَعُونَ﴾: that is, only the devil who heard a word from the angels listens, and he takes it quickly, so a piercing shooting star, a bright meteor, pursues him, piercing him, or burning him, or disabling him.)

When He said ﴿they do not listen﴾, and this negation was general, meaning none of these devils listens to the Highest Assembly, He made an exception for the rebellious devils who snatch a snatching; so He said: ﴿except one who snatches a snatching﴾, meaning one who takes a thing swiftly.

Is ﴿خَطْفَةَ﴾ a verbal noun indicating a single instance? That is, "except a devil who snatches a snatch." Such a one is safe. But if he snatches the snatch, is he saved? Allah the Exalted said: ﴿then a piercing shooting star pursues him﴾. Here He made an exception from the negation of their listening to the heaven: the one who snatches a snatch. He does hear, but does he escape before reaching the earth? No: ﴿then pursues him﴾, that is, a piercing shooting star follows him; a bright piercing meteor, that is, one which penetrates him, so it pierces him or burns him or disables him: it pierces, burns, or disables. Perhaps he escapes this shooting star, if Allah the Mighty and Majestic wills, and reaches the soothsayer and inspires him with what he heard. Then the soothsayer lies, adding to what he heard many lies, a hundred or more or fewer. Then the soothsayer informs people of what will happen; if it occurs he says: "He knows the unseen," and he uses this as propaganda for himself. For this reason soothsayers among the Arabs in the pre-Islamic era were held in great honor, and people went to them for judgment, because when they reported such matters of the unseen and what they reported came to pass, they gained great standing among people.

So the devils became three categories:

A category that is never able to listen at all.

Another category that may listen by snatching, and is burned by the shooting star.

A third category that listens by snatching and escapes. All this is by Allah's permission and will, in accordance with His wisdom: ﴿except one who snatches a snatching, then a piercing shooting star pursues him﴾. All these verses are about showing the greatness of the heaven, and that the heaven is protected and guarded, so no one can reach it.

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: (﴿فَاسْتَفْتِهِمْ﴾ "so ask them for a ruling": inquire of the disbelievers of Makkah, either to establish or to rebuke. ﴿أَهُمْ أَشَدُّ خَلْقًا أَمْ مَنْ خَلَقْنَا﴾ "are they stronger in creation, or those whom We created?" [as-Saffat 11]: from the angels and the heavens.)

*The student: (...).

*The teacher: (﴿إِلَّا مَنْ خَطِفَ الْخَطْفَةَ﴾ a verbal noun, meaning the single instance, and the exception is from the pronoun in ﴿يَسْمَعُونَ﴾: that is, only the devil who hears the word from the angels listens, and snatches it swiftly, so a piercing shooting star follows him.)

He said: (﴿فَاسْتَفْتِهِمْ﴾ inquire of all the disbelievers of Makkah, either to establish or to rebuke ﴿أَهُمْ أَشَدُّ خَلْقًا أَمْ مَنْ خَلَقْنَا﴾ "are they stronger in creation, or those whom We created?": from the angels and the lands and what is in them. And using (مَنْ "who") is taghlib, giving precedence to rational beings.)

"Istaftihim" means ask them for a verdict. Fatwa (verdict) originally means reporting a matter, but in the terminology of jurists it means reporting a legal ruling. Here the intended meaning is not the legal verdict but the linguistic one: that is, ask them and inquire of them: ﴿are they stronger in creation, or those whom We created?﴾ They will say: are they stronger, or is the one created by Allah stronger? Those created by Allah are stronger. Everyone knows that the creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of people. Likewise, those who believe in the unseen acknowledge that what is hidden from us of Allah's creatures is greater than what we witness. Except for someone who wants to be obstinate and says: "I am stronger in creation," as the devil said to Allah the Exalted: ﴿I am better than him: You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ [al-Araf 12]; and as Pharaoh said to his people: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly speak clearly?﴾ [az-Zukhruf 52], and he said: ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [an-Naziat 24]. Otherwise, everyone knows that the great creatures such as the heavens, the earth, the sun and the moon are greater than the creation of man. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, We created them﴾.

The author said: "And using (مَن "who") is taghlib (giving precedence to rational beings)." How? The use of (مَن) in His saying ﴿or those whom We created?﴾, and He did not say (ما "what"), giving precedence to rational beings. That is because among what Allah the Mighty and Majestic created there are rational beings and non-rational beings. Among them are those who reason and those who do not: the angels and jinn reason, while beasts and inanimate things do not reason, although beasts are closer to reason than inanimate things. Nevertheless, all these things have a kind of perception by which they recognize their Creator, the Mighty and Majestic, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Him; there is not a thing except that it glorifies Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra 44]. And the Prophet ﷺ informed that Uhud loves the Prophet ﷺ and the Prophet ﷺ loves it.[[Al-Bukhari, whose wording this is (1481), and Muslim (1392/503), from the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Saʿidi, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: We approached with the Prophet ﷺ from the expedition of Tabuk, until when we came in sight of Madinah he said: "This is Taba, and this is Uhud, a mountain which loves us and which we love."]]

He said: ﴿Indeed, We created them﴾ (that is, their origin is from sticky clay that clings to the hand; the meaning is that their creation is weak, so let them not be arrogant by denying the Prophet and the Qur'an, which leads to their easy destruction).

When He said ﴿are they stronger in creation, or those whom We created?﴾, He explained the origin of their creation, so that it would be clear whether they are stronger or those whom Allah created. The truth is that the sentence ﴿are they stronger in creation, or those whom We created?﴾ needs a pause in terms of grammar. So who will parse it?

*A student: The hamzah is an interrogative particle, (هم "they") is the subject, and (أشد "stronger") is the predicate.

*The teacher: Yes, the hamzah is interrogative, (هم) is the subject, and (أشد) is the predicate.

*The student: (خلقًا "in creation") is an exception.

*The teacher: No.

*A student: An object.

*The teacher: No.

*A student: A specification (tamyiz).

*The teacher: A specification, because when (أفعل "more/most") is followed by a noun in the accusative, that noun is a specification (tamyīz).

﴿أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنْكَ مَالًا﴾ [al-Kahf 34] ﴿مَالًا﴾ "in wealth": we say it is a specification. ﴿وَأَعَزُّ نَفَرًا﴾ "and mightier in followers": we say it is also a specification. So when a noun in the accusative follows a comparative adjective, it is a specification. As for ﴿أَمْ مَنْ خَلَقْنَا﴾, this is the counterpart (muʿādil); therefore the hamzah here is for equalization: that is, "Are they and those whom We created equal?" The answer: No, they are not equal; rather, the one whom Allah created is greater. And Allah knows best.

* * *

*The student: ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock. And they say: This is nothing but obvious magic. When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers too? Say: Yes, and you will be humbled.﴾ [as-Saffat 14–18].

*The teacher: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed devil. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Indeed, We adorned the nearest heaven with the adornment of the stars [6], and as a guard against every rebellious devil [7], they do not listen﴾ [as-Saffat 6–8], and so on to the end.

First: what is the position of the clause ﴿they do not listen﴾ relative to what precedes it?

*The student: It is a resumptive sentence.

*The teacher: A resumptive sentence.

*The student: (...).

*The teacher: (...) in His saying ﴿and as a guard﴾; that is, a guard against their listening to the Highest Assembly. Now, in ﴿يَسْمَعُونَ﴾ are there two readings?

*The student: ﴿يَسْمَعُونَ﴾...

*Another student: ﴿يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 37, verses 1–17 (part 5 of 7):**

* The Shaykh: ﴿يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾ (*yassammaʿūn*). Alright. On the reading ﴿يَسْمَعُونَ﴾ (*yasmaʿūn*), how is it followed by (إلى) *ilā* ("to"), when the verb takes its object directly? Because (سمع) *samiʿa* ("to hear") is transitive without a preposition, and here he said ﴿لَا يَسْمَعُونَ إِلَى﴾ (they do not listen to).
* A student: He means: they cannot (...) hearing from a higher angel.
* The Shaykh: But he said (إلى) *ilā*, and did not say (لا يسمعون الملأ).
* A student: So this is transitive by means of a particle.
* The Shaykh: Yes. Why, although (سمع) takes its object directly?
* A student: Some of them say it does not take its object directly.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: Because it is used with the meaning of ﴿يُصْغُون﴾ (*yuṣghūn*, they lend an ear).
* The Shaykh: Because it is used with the meaning of ﴿يُصْغُون﴾, (they do not lend an ear to the assembly on high). ﴿يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾: what is its original form?
* A student: ﴿يَتَسَمَّعُونَ﴾ (*yatasammaʿūn*).
* The Shaykh: ﴿يَتَسَمَّعُونَ﴾, then the *tāʾ* was assimilated?
* A student: Into the *sīn*.
* The Shaykh: And it became?
* The student: ﴿يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾
* The Shaykh: ﴿لَا يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾. Alright, what is meant by ﴿الْمَلَإِ الْأَعْلَى﴾ (*al-malaʾ al-aʿlā*, the exalted assembly)?
* A student: The angels.
* The Shaykh: The angels. And what is the original meaning of (الملأ) *al-malaʾ* in the language?
* A student: The group.
* The Shaykh: Any group whatsoever?
* A student: No, a strong group.
* The Shaykh: The nobles of a people are called *malaʾ*. His words: ﴿دُحُورًا﴾ (*duḥūran*, as a repulsion). What is its *iʿrāb* (grammatical analysis)?
* A student: Absolute.
* The Shaykh: How "absolute"? What does it mean?
* A student: It is one of the five objects.
* The Shaykh: (...) an eye. You want to count us (...) because you know one of them. We will accept from you only one word.
* A student: An absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*).
* The Shaykh: An absolute object!
* A student: An object of purpose (*mafʿūl li-ajlihi*).
* The Shaykh: An object of purpose. And what is the meaning of ﴿دُحُورًا﴾?
* A student: It means: they are driven away.
* The Shaykh: It means expulsion and removal. That is: (...) for the sake of driving them away from the sky. Alright, his words: ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ خَطِفَ الْخَطْفَةَ﴾ (*except one who snatches a snatching*). Of what is this exception?
* A student: I say: ﴿لَا يَسَّمَّعُونَ إِلَى الْمَلَإِ الْأَعْلَى﴾.
* The Shaykh: Of what? Look, ﴿لَا يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾ contains ﴿لَا﴾ and contains ﴿يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾, and contains the *wāw*.
* The student: From ﴿لَا يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾, from ﴿لَا﴾.
* The Shaykh: From ﴿لَا﴾?! The meaning does not hold.
* A student: They do not listen except (...).
My question is: where is the exception's antecedent (*mustathnā minhu*)?
* A student: The *mustathnā minhu* is ﴿لَا يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾.
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: The *wāw* of the plural in ﴿يَسَّمَّعُونَ﴾.
* The Shaykh: From the plural *wāw* in *yasammaʿūn* (they do not listen except one who snatches). Alright, on this reckoning its position is nominative, as a substitute for the *wāw*, and the accusative is also permissible. His words: ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ خَطِفَ الْخَطْفَةَ فَأَتْبَعَهُ شِهَابٌ﴾ (*except one who snatches a snatching, and a bright flame pursues him*). What is the meaning of ﴿فَأَتْبَعَهُ شِهَابٌ﴾?
* A student: A flame overtook him.
* The Shaykh: A flame overtook him. Alright, where does the flame come from?
* A student: From the stars.
* The Shaykh: From the stars. His words: ﴿ثَاقِبٌ﴾ (*thāqib*) mean?
* A student: Piercing, burning, and stunning.
* The Shaykh: Yes, well done.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿فَاسْتَفْتِهِمْ أَهُمْ أَشَدُّ خَلْقًا أَمْ مَنْ خَلَقْنَا﴾ (*So ask them: are they stronger in creation, or those whom We have created?*). ﴿أَمْ مَنْ خَلَقْنَا﴾: what is meant by ﴿مَنْ خَلَقْنَا﴾?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: The heavens and the earth and whatever is in them.
* The Shaykh: The heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, because He said: ﴿رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا وَرَبُّ الْمَشَارِقِ﴾ (*Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the easts*), then He said: ﴿فَاسْتَفْتِهِمْ أَهُمْ أَشَدُّ خَلْقًا أَمْ مَنْ خَلَقْنَا﴾, from the heavens and the earth and what is between them. Clear? Here there is a difficulty: He used (من) *man*, which denotes rational beings, although most of them are not rational. Why is the minority given precedence?
* A student: Because it is more excellent.
* The Shaykh: Because it is more excellent and more noble.
His words: ﴿إِنَّا خَلَقْنَاهُمْ مِنْ طِينٍ لَازِبٍ﴾ (*Indeed We created them from sticky clay*). What is the grammatical position of the sentence?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, my brother, may Allah bless you. The testimony of some of you for others is not accepted, because you are defending yourselves against harm.
* The student: We did not complete it.
* The Shaykh: You did not complete it, but we mentioned it. In any case, do not defend him; perhaps he knows it himself.
* A student: Resumptive (*istiʾnāfiyya*).
* The Shaykh: Resumptive for what?
* A student: For the answer.
* The Shaykh: For what thing? What is its purpose?
* A student: That they are not able to do that.
* The Shaykh: No. How are they not able to do that? What does "they are not able" mean?
* A student: ﴿فَاسْتَفْتِهِمْ أَهُمْ أَشَدُّ خَلْقًا أَمْ مَنْ خَلَقْنَا﴾ makes clear to them that they are not able to do that.
* The Shaykh: They are not able to do what?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They did not claim that they create.
* A student: (...) their weakness (...).
* The Shaykh: Their weakness. Correct, to demonstrate their weakness. When He said ﴿أَمْ مَنْ خَلَقْنَا﴾, it is as if someone asks: "Of what were they created?" He said: ﴿إِنَّا خَلَقْنَاهُمْ مِنْ طِينٍ لَازِبٍ﴾, so they are weak in origin.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَالصَّافَّاتِ صَفًّا (١) فَالزَّاجِرَاتِ زَجْرًا﴾ (*By those who range in ranks, then those who drive with a driving*), to the end.
In these three verses Allah, Mighty and Majestic, swears by the angels with regard to their attributes: those who range in rows, those who drive, and those who recite; because each attribute of them indicates the greatness of the Creator, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the excellence of the angels in their three states: the ranking, the driving, and the reciting (*tilāwa*). For one swears only by what is worthy of being sworn by. If someone says: how did Allah swear by a created thing, since the angels are created, and swearing by a created thing is *shirk*?
The answer to this is that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, may swear by whatever He wills of His creation, because He is the Owner, just as He, Glorified and Exalted, may command whatever He wills, even if it is *shirk*, and even if it is injustice and transgression. Have you considered Allah's command to the angels to prostrate to Adam, when prostration to other than Allah is *shirk*? Yet He may command what He wills. Have you considered His command to Abraham the Friend (*al-Khalīl*) to slaughter his son, when slaughtering a son is among the greatest major sins, and by Allah's command it became an act of obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic? Likewise, swearing by other than Allah is *shirk*, but nonetheless Allah may swear by whatever He wills of His creation.
But we must know that Allah does not swear by any of His creation except that this thing is among His greatest signs, so swearing by this created thing includes swearing by the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which are His acts; for the greatness of the created thing indicates the greatness of the Creator.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that one of the attributes of the angels is the ranking. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَإِنَّا لَنَحْنُ الصَّافُّونَ﴾ (*And indeed we are those who range in ranks*) [al-Ṣāffāt 165], and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Will you not form ranks as the angels form ranks before their Lord?"[[Reported by Muslim (430/119) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Samura, may Allah be pleased with him.]]
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the angels are entrusted with executing commands through driving, like the driving of clouds and the driving of disbelievers at the time of their death; based on His words: ﴿فَالزَّاجِرَاتِ زَجْرًا﴾.
* Among the benefits of these noble verses: that the angels recite the Remembrance, that is, they recite the Qur'an. This indicates the angels' worship of Allah, and the excellence of the Qur'an, since the angels recite it; based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿فَالتَّالِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا﴾ (*then those who recite a reminder*).
Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿إِنَّ إِلَهَكُمْ لَوَاحِدٌ﴾ (*Indeed your God is One*) [al-Ṣāffāt 4], to the end of the verses.
* Among the benefits of these verses: the oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in His divinity; based on His words: ﴿إِنَّ إِلَهَكُمْ لَوَاحِدٌ﴾.
* Among their benefits: the invalidity of the divinity of anything other than Allah; based on His words: ﴿إِنَّ إِلَهَكُمْ لَوَاحِدٌ﴾. For if He is One, then whatever else is other than Him is false.
* Among their benefits: the importance of *tawḥīd* (monotheism); because Allah, the Exalted, swore to establish it. He swore by the angels to establish this *tawḥīd*; and because Allah, the Exalted, emphasized it with three emphatics: the oath, the second (*inna*), and the third, the *lām* in ﴿إِنَّ إِلَهَكُمْ لَوَاحِدٌ﴾.
* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the correspondence between what is sworn by and what is sworn to. What is sworn by? The angels in the state of those attributes: the ranking, the driving, and the reciting. What is sworn to? The oneness of Allah. The correspondence between them is that the angels do this only out of *tawḥīd* for Allah, Glorified and Exalted, and out of glorifying Him.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's lordship (*rubūbiyya*), Glorified and Exalted; based on His words: ﴿رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾ (*Lord of the heavens*).
* Among its benefits: the comprehensiveness of His lordship in His words: ﴿السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا وَرَبُّ الْمَشَارِقِ﴾.
* Among its benefits: the necessary connection between *tawḥīd al-uluhiyya* (oneness of divinity) and *tawḥīd al-rububiyya* (oneness of lordship). His words: ﴿رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا﴾, after His words ﴿إِنَّ إِلَهَكُمْ لَوَاحِدٌ﴾, serve as evidence for His oneness in divinity. This is because if He is singular in lordship, it necessarily follows that He is singular in divinity; as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ﴾ (*O people, worship your Lord who created you and those before you*) [al-Baqara 21]. How then do you worship other than Him, who did not create you and did not create anyone? ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ ضُرِبَ مَثَلٌ فَاسْتَمِعُوا لَهُ إِنَّ الَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ لَنْ يَخْلُقُوا ذُبَابًا وَلَوِ اجْتَمَعُوا لَهُ﴾ (*O people, a parable is given, so listen to it: indeed those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gather together for it*) [al-Ḥajj 73]. For this reason the scholars said: whoever acknowledges *tawḥīd al-rububiyya* must also acknowledge *tawḥīd al-uluhiyya*, or else he is contradictory; for it is said to him: how do you acknowledge that Allah alone is the Lord and Creator, and then worship with Him one who creates nothing? Is this anything but contradiction?
This verse and similar verses of the Mighty Book indicate the necessary connection between? I say: this verse and its like indicate the necessary connection between the oneness of lordship and the oneness of divinity. What is the basis of that?
* A student: Whoever acknowledges the oneness of lordship must acknowledge the oneness of divinity.
* The Shaykh: He is obliged to acknowledge the oneness of divinity. And how do we oblige him?
* A student: Because if he says that Allah the Exalted is One, it must be that he does not (...).
* The Shaykh: One in creation, so it is obligatory that he not worship other than Him. Yes.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation that the heavens are plural; based on His words: ﴿رَبُّ السَّمَاوَاتِ﴾, and it has been explained in several places that they are seven, and likewise the earth.
* Among its benefits: an indication of the greatness of the heavens and the earth and what is between them; because Allah attributed lordship to them in the context of establishing proof, and this indicates their greatness, and that because of their greatness they became like a binding evidence for the oneness of divinity.
* Among its benefits: that between the heavens and the earth there are great created things that required that what lies between the sky and the earth be a counterpart to the heavens and the earth.
* Among the benefits of the verses: the complete power of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in directing the easts and the wests; based on His words: ﴿وَرَبُّ الْمَشَارِقِ﴾. No one is able to direct these easts and wests, neither by advancing, nor by delaying, nor by shifting, meaning changing their place. Even if all creation gathered to advance the rising of the sun by one minute, or to delay it, or to move it from its place, they would not be able to. Rather, that belongs to whom? To Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He is the One who directs it, and He has commanded it to proceed by His wisdom, so it proceeds to a set term. If Allah wills to change it, He changes it; He returns it from whence it came, so it rises from where it set.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّا زَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا بِزِينَةٍ الْكَوَاكِبِ﴾ (*Indeed We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of stars*), to the end of the verses.
* Among the benefits of these verses: an explanation that Allah, the Exalted, adorned the sky with these stars. For if you see in the sky, on a clear night with no moon and no light around you, you will find in it a beauty you cannot imagine, from the beauty of these stars: some shining, some faint, some close to one another, some far apart, and differing in their shapes, which indicates the greatness of the Creator, Mighty and Majestic; and that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, made these stars an adornment for the sky. In them there is also a benefit other than adornment, which He indicated by His words: ﴿وَحِفْظًا﴾ (*and as protection*). And there is a third benefit besides protection and adornment: guidance; ﴿وَعَلَامَاتٍ وَبِالنَّجْمِ هُمْ يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ (*and landmarks; and by the stars they find their way*) [al-Naḥl 16]. These stars therefore have these three benefits.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the heavens are layered, one lower than another; based on His words: ﴿إِنَّا زَيَّنَّا السَّمَاءَ الدُّنْيَا﴾ (*the nearest heaven*), which indicates that there are heavens above it, and so it is.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah's care for His creation; in that He adorned for them the canopy above their heads. For if it were pitch dark, with nothing luminous in it that they could see, there would be some desolation in that. But Allah, the Exalted, cared for this and adorned it for them. In it there is also care from another aspect: that He guarded the nearest heaven with these stars.
If someone says: what is the benefit of this protection? We say: the benefit is so that the devils do not tamper with what is sent down from the sky of revelation, or so that the devils do not deceive creation through soothsayers, claiming that they know the unseen.
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: that the devils are rebellious; based on His words: ﴿مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْطَانٍ مَارِدٍ﴾ (*from every rebellious devil*), on the basis that the word (مارد) *māridin* is a descriptive qualifier that clarifies. But if it is made a restrictive qualifier, then it indicates that some devils are rebellious and others are not. The verse allows both: it may be that *mārid* is an attribute of every devil, and it may be that it is an attribute of some devils, with others not rebellious.
* Among the benefits of the verses: that these devils do not listen to the exalted assembly with complete hearing by which they attain their aim. And by what? By these meteors that burn them. None of them can listen with complete attention, as a person listens to his shaykh and to the one speaking to him. Rather, you find them coming to the sky snatching, so they snatch what they hear without any pause or deliberation, because they fear the meteors.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the devils are bodies; based on His words: ﴿فَأَتْبَعَهُ شِهَابٌ ثَاقِبٌ﴾, for only a body can be pierced or burned. And so it is: the devils are bodies, but they are subtle bodies that penetrate dense human bodies. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Satan flows through the son of Adam as blood flows."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3281) and Muslim (2175/24) from the hadith of Safiyya bint Huyayy, may Allah be pleased with her.]] Just as the soul flows through the body as blood flows, and the soul is a subtle body, so the devils are subtle bodies that penetrate dense or heavy bodies.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, may give these subtle bodies the power by which they reach the sky, is it not so? Based on His words: ﴿لَا يَسْمَعُونَ إِلَى الْمَلَإِ الْأَعْلَى﴾ (*they cannot listen to the exalted assembly*), ﴿إِلَّا مَنْ خَطِفَ الْخَطْفَةَ﴾, and there is no doubt that they may reach the sky, and that they have a strength greater than the strength of humans with dense bodies. Have you considered when Solomon said: ﴿أَيُّكُمْ يَأْتِينِي بِعَرْشِهَا قَبْلَ أَنْ يَأْتُونِي مُسْلِمِينَ (٣٨) قَالَ عِفْرِيتٌ مِنَ الْجِنِّ أَنَا آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَقُومَ مِنْ مَقَامِكَ﴾ (*Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission? A powerful one of the jinn said: I will bring it to you before you rise from your place*) [al-Naml 38–39]. He had a set time at which he would rise from his place, so he said: ﴿أَنَا آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَقُومَ مِنْ مَقَامِكَ﴾, meaning: before the time comes when you rise. Solomon was in the Levant (al-Shām) and the throne of the Queen of Sheba was in Yemen. And he says: ﴿آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَقُومَ مِنْ مَقَامِكَ وَإِنِّي عَلَيْهِ لَقَوِيٌّ أَمِينٌ (٣٩) قَالَ الَّذِي عِنْدَهُ عِلْمٌ مِنَ الْكِتَابِ﴾ (*I will bring it to you before you rise from your place; indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it. Said one who had knowledge from the Book*) [al-Naml 39–40]. And the one who had knowledge of the Book, who invoked Allah with what he invoked: ﴿أَنَا آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَرْتَدَّ إِلَيْكَ طَرْفُكَ﴾ (*I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you*), meaning: before you send your glance and then return it. For what he brought was brought by the angels, and the angels are stronger than the devils. Therefore he saw it immediately; and when he saw it settled before him, ﴿قَالَ هَذَا مِنْ فَضْلِ رَبِّي﴾ (*he said: this is of the bounty of my Lord*), to the end of the verses.
The point is that the devils have a capacity and strength that bring them to the sky, and the One who gave them this capacity and strength is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the excellence of the angels, in that they are described as the exalted assembly (*al-malaʾ al-aʿlā*), because of the height of their place and rank. In this there is both physical height and moral height.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verses 1–17 (part 6 of 7):**

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the meteors with which the devils are pelted come at them from every direction. Wherever they try to flee, they find the meteors. It does not necessarily follow that these meteors gather upon them all at once. One meteor may come at them from one direction, but if they try to flee, a second meteor comes at them, and so on. Whichever direction they try to flee from, they will find a meteor. He said: ﴿and they are pelted from every side﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the devils are not fit to dwell in the heavens, to sit in them, or to draw near to them. Therefore they are pelted to keep them away: ﴿repulsion﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the devils are accountable, and punishment falls upon them and reward is attained by them. Lasting punishment falls upon them, as shown by His words: ﴿and for them is a lasting punishment﴾, meaning: perpetual.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the devils may bring news of the heavens, as shown by His words: ﴿except one who snatches a fragment, and he is pursued by a piercing flame﴾. But someone may say: Allah said ﴿except one who snatches a fragment﴾ and then said ﴿and he is pursued by a piercing flame﴾, so at that point he does not reach his goal. The answer is that other texts indicate that he may reach his goal: he reaches the soothsayer before the flame overtakes him.

He said: ﴿So ask them: are they harder to create, or those We have created? Indeed We created them from sticky clay﴾ [al-Saffat 11].

* In this noble verse there is an indication that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is charged with conveying the message and with debating, as shown by His words: ﴿So ask them﴾. And this is so, for Allah commanded him to convey what was revealed to him from his Lord: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah 67]. He commanded him to argue with his people: ﴿and argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl 125]. And He informed that he would argue with them, as shown by His words: ﴿If they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to Allah, and so have those who follow me﴾ [Al 'Imran 20].
* Following from this benefit: the duty of the people of knowledge, who have inherited his knowledge, is like his duty in this matter. They are obliged to argue with the people of falsehood and to confront them. From this it is clear that knowledge is a kind of jihad in the way of Allah, because the seeker of knowledge argues with the enemies of the Shariah with truth, so that their falsehood may be repelled by it. Sometimes intellectual invasion is more destructive than armed invasion, as you witness. Intellectual invasion enters every house with the consent of its owner, without meeting any opposition or resistance. Military invasion, however, does not enter the house, nor even the country, except after bitter fighting and fierce resistance. The enemies of the Muslims sometimes dominate them through armed invasion by fighting, and this can be guarded against. Sometimes they do so through intellectual invasion, which is more severe and more harmful than armed invasion, because it strikes the Muslims in the depths of their homes without their knowing it. They may leave Islam, and Islam may be wiped completely from their hearts while they do not perceive it, because they entice the Muslims with desires. When the heart is immersed in desires, it forgets what it was created for. It forgets the worship of Allah, and there is no attachment to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in its heart. So you find a person, in his standing, sitting, going and coming, thinking of nothing but these desires and striving for nothing but these desires, as if he was created for nothing else. Likewise, they instill in the hearts of the weak the glorification of these disbelievers, and the belief that they are more advanced, more civilized, more upright in their way, and so on. Thus the Muslim becomes weak and melts away in the flames of these people. This undoubtedly exists, and many Islamic lands have lost their morale and their identity because of this intellectual invasion.

If they invaded the Islamic lands with a military invasion, they would occupy the lands with their bodies, but people's hearts would recoil from them and hate them. The real problem is that they invade people with their qualities, their morals and their beliefs while they sit in their homes, having opened the hearts to them. This is the problem, and this is the ruin. For this reason, invasion with scientific weapons drawn from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger is equal to, if not more beneficial and more effective than, military invasion. So I urge you, may Allah bless you, and I urge myself, to prepare the means to confront our enemies who want to invade us in our homes with their corrupt ideas and their polluted morals, indeed with their deviant ideas and their polluted morals, so that we may protect the Muslims from the evil of these people. For their weapon is more destructive and more severe than the weapon of iron and fire, as is evident. Perhaps some of you who have gone to other lands have come to know more than I do, which has led to deviation in belief and to being swept away by desires, until some Islamic lands have become as if they were disbelieving lands.

Now they are trying to invade this land by every means they can. Indeed, we sometimes find in the newspapers the call for the decline of the morals and customs of the Muslims. Sometimes advertisements appear for European and Western fashions, with such wording as: (an exhibition of Western fashions, or European fashions, or European trends will open), or what is similar to this. All of this is so that they may corrupt our morals. When morals are corrupted, belief is corrupted. When belief is corrupted, the Muslims' attachment to their Lord disappears, and then they become the weakest of nations. We ask Allah for protection and safety.

Now, ﹙﻿So ask them: are they harder to create﹚ — let us stop here.

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﹙﻿Nay, you wonder, and they mock. And when they are reminded, they do not remember. And when they see a sign, they mock. It will be but a single shout, and at once they will be looking. And they will say, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Judgement." This is the Day of Decision, which you used to deny. Gather those who did wrong, their companions, and what they used to worship besides Allah, and lead them to the path of Hellfire. Halt them, for they are to be questioned. What is wrong with you that you do not help one another? Rather, today they are submissive﹚ [al-Saffat 12–26].

* Student: (...).

* Student: Wonder has three types: wonder of approval, wonder of (...), and wonder of (...). This does not apply to Allah, glorified and exalted.
* Shaykh: We say: this is a type of wonder that you have mentioned, and it does not apply to Allah. What is the evidence that it is impossible in relation to Allah?

* Shaykh: Good. Give an example of wonder in the sense of approval, of wonder that is produced by approval.

* Student: The example does not come to mind.

His words: ﹙﻿And when they see a sign, they mock﹚. What is meant by "sign"?

* Student: (...).

He said: ﹙﻿yastaskhirun﹚ and did not say "yaskharun."

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, mockery with arrogance and haughtiness. Good. Is there a rule among the grammarians that conveys what you said, namely that when the form is increased, the meaning is increased?
* Student: When the form increases, the meaning increases.

* Student: (...).

* Student: (...).

When what precedes "illa" requires what follows it, it is called an emptied exception.
What is the meaning of "mubin"?
