In these verses there are the following benefits:
* First: the disavowal, on the Day of Resurrection, of both the follower and the leader from these misguided ones. The followers place the blame on the leaders, and the leaders place the blame on the followers.
* Also among its benefits: the leaders have no authority by which they compel the followers; rather, the followers are the ones who chose error for themselves.
* In it is also evidence that these polytheists and disbelievers have a better grasp of reality than the Jabriyyah and their like, who say that a person is compelled in his deeds, for these people acknowledge that a person acts by his own choice, as in His saying: ﴿And we had no authority over you; rather, you were a transgressing people﴾ [al-Saffat 30].
* Among its benefits: the followers on the Day of Resurrection gain nothing from following the leaders; rather, the leaders rebuke them for their transgression, saying: "You are the ones who exceeded the limit by abandoning the following of the messengers and then following us."
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He speaks, as in His saying: ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us, indeed we are tasters﴾ [al-Saffat 31], and speech is that which conveys a meaning.
  From this it follows, or is derived, that the speech of Allah consists of letters and sound, as is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah, contrary to the Ash'aris, who say that the speech of Allah is the meaning subsisting in the self, and that what is heard of these letters and sound is only a created thing which Allah created to express what is in His self.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the acknowledgment by the deniers of the messengers of Lordship, as in their saying: ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us﴾.
  It follows from this that there is a refutation of most of the theologians who define tawhid as tawhid al-rububiyyah only. They say that tawhid is to believe that Allah, the Exalted, is one in His essence, having no counterpart; one in His acts, having no partner; and one in His attributes, having no likeness. In these three statements they do not mention tawhid al-uluhiyyah, that is, they do not say: one in His divinity, having no partner. Rather, they make tawhid consist only of tawhid al-rububiyyah and tawhid al-sifat. Though there is in this statement a generality that requires specification, it omits tawhid al-uluhiyyah.
  This tawhid, which most theologians claim is the tawhid the messengers brought, the polytheists undoubtedly acknowledged and did not deny. Yet despite this, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, judged them to be polytheists and made lawful their blood, their property, their women and their lands.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that these deniers, followers and leaders alike, all receive the punishment; as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, we are tasters﴾ [al-Saffat 31], meaning: tasters of the punishment of our Lord which became due against us.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a warning against keeping company with people of misguidance, as in His saying: ﴿So we misled you; indeed we were misguided﴾ [al-Saffat 32]. The Prophet ﷺ warned against keeping company with a bad companion, saying: "The likeness of the good companion is like the carrier of musk: either he will give you some, or you will buy from him, or you will find a pleasant fragrance from him. And the likeness of the bad companion is like the bellows-blower: either he will burn your clothes, or you will find a foul smell from him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2101), and Muslim (2628/146), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.]]
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: attributing a thing to its cause, as in His saying: ﴿so we misled you﴾; for they were not the ones who actually misled them, but rather they were the cause of their misguidance. Guidance and misguidance are in whose hand?
* The students: In the hand of Allah.
* The Shaykh: In the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. But these people were a cause of the misguidance of those, so they attributed the act to themselves in His saying: ﴿so we misled you; indeed we were misguided﴾.

* * *

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿Indeed, they that Day﴾, the Day of Resurrection, ﴿will be sharers in the punishment﴾ [al-Saffat 33]). His saying: ﴿Indeed, they that Day will be sharers in the punishment﴾: (Inna) and its subject in (innahum), and (mushtarikun) is its predicate.

In these verses there are several benefits:
* First: the disavowal, on the Day of Resurrection, of both the follower and the leader from these misguided ones. The followers, or those who follow, place the blame on the leaders, and the leaders place the blame on the followers.
* Also among its benefits: the leaders have no authority by which they compel the followers; rather, the followers are the ones who chose error for themselves.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 30–63 (part 2 of 7):

This verse is evidence that these polytheists and disbelievers know the reality better than the Jabriyyah (determinists, the school holding that man is compelled in his actions) and those like them who say that man is compelled in his deeds. For these people acknowledge that man acts by his own choice, as shown by His saying: ﴿And we had no authority over you; rather, you were a transgressing people.﴾ [Al-Saffat 30]

* Among its benefits: on the Day of Resurrection, the followers gain nothing from following their leaders. Rather, the leaders rebuke them for their transgression and say: "It is you who exceeded the limit by abandoning the following of the Messengers, and then following us."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He speaks, as in His saying: ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us; indeed, we are to taste [the punishment].﴾ [Al-Saffat 31] Speech (qawl) is words that convey a meaning. It follows from this that the speech of Allah consists of letters and sound, as is the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community), unlike the Ash'ariyyah, who say that the speech of Allah is the meaning subsisting in the self, and that what is heard of these letters and sounds is merely a created thing which Allah created to express what is in His self.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the acknowledgment by those who denied the Messengers of Lordship (rububiyyah), as shown by His saying: ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us﴾ [Al-Saffat 31].
It follows from this a refutation of the majority of the theologians (mutakallimun) who define tawhid (monotheism) as tawhid al-rububiyyah only. They say that tawhid is to believe that Allah, the Exalted, is one in His essence, with no equal; one in His actions, with no partner; and one in His attributes, with no likeness. In these three statements they do not mention tawhid al-uluhiyyah (monotheism of worship), meaning they do not say "one in His divinity, with no partner." Instead, they made tawhid consist only of tawhid al-rububiyyah and tawhid al-sifat (monotheism of the attributes). Yet this speech contains a generality that requires clarification, but in it tawhid al-uluhiyyah is omitted.
This tawhid, which the majority of the theologians claimed is the tawhid that the Messengers brought, the polytheists undoubtedly acknowledged and did not deny. Despite this, the Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ) ruled that they were polytheists, and made lawful their blood, their property, their women, and their lands.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these deniers, followers and leaders alike, will all receive punishment, as shown by His saying: ﴿indeed, we are to taste [the punishment]﴾ [Al-Saffat 31], meaning: we are to taste the punishment of our Lord which has come into effect against us.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: warning against keeping company with people of misguidance, as shown by His saying: ﴿So we led you astray; indeed, we were ourselves astray﴾ [Al-Saffat 32]. The Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ) warned against keeping company with bad companions, saying: "The likeness of the good companion and the bad companion is like the bearer of musk and the blower of the bellows. The bearer of musk will either give you some, or you will buy some from him, or you will get a pleasant scent from him. As for the blower of the bellows, he will either burn your clothes, or you will get a foul smell from him."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5534) and Muslim (2628/146), from the hadith of Abu Musa.]]

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: attributing a thing to its cause, as shown by His saying: ﴿So we led you astray﴾ [Al-Saffat 32]. This is because they were not the ones who actually led them astray; rather, they were the cause of their being led astray. For guidance and misguidance are in whose hand? In the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But these people were a cause of the misguidance of those others, so they attributed the act to themselves in their saying: ﴿So we led you astray; indeed, we were ourselves astray﴾ [Al-Saffat 32].
* * *

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿Indeed, they, that Day﴾ meaning the Day of Resurrection ﴿will be sharers in the punishment﴾ [Al-Saffat 33]). His saying: ﴿Indeed, they, that Day, will be sharers in the punishment﴾: inna (indeed) and its noun is in (innahum) and mushtarikun (sharers) is its predicate. Fi al-'adhab (in the punishment) is linked to mushtarikun, and yawma'idhin (that Day) may be linked to mushtarikun, or it may be linked to a circumstantial element from the pronoun in (innahum). His saying: ﴿that Day﴾ means: the day when the Resurrection takes place. The tanwin (nunation) in yawma'idhin is a substitute for an omitted clause.
His saying: ﴿Indeed, they, that Day, will be sharers in the punishment﴾: the pronoun refers to the followers and the leaders. They will share in the punishment on the Day of Resurrection, that is, in its basic nature, even if some of them are more severely punished than others, as shown by the saying of the Most High: ﴿And for each there are degrees according to what they did﴾ [Al-An'am 132].
Does their sharing in the punishment lighten it for them? No, as shown by the saying of the Most High: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong, that you will be sharers in the punishment﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 39]. Whereas people in this world, when they share in punishment or calamities, some of them console and strengthen others. But in the Hereafter this does not benefit, for each of them sees himself as the one most severely punished, and we seek refuge in Allah. The sharing of another with him does not benefit him.
(﴿Indeed, they, that Day, will be sharers in the punishment﴾, that is: because of their sharing in misguidance) The author's explanation here is a rationale for the cause of their sharing in the punishment, since they shared in misguidance.
(﴿Indeed, that is how﴾ as We deal with these, ﴿We deal with the criminals﴾ [Al-Saffat 34]).
The author estimated it thus: as We deal with these, We deal with the criminals. It is also possible that the meaning is: such an act We perform upon the criminals, while they are criminals.
His saying: ﴿kadhalika﴾ (that is how): its grammatical analysis is that we say: the kaf (like) is a noun meaning "like," and it is in the accusative position as an absolute object, meaning: such an act We perform.
His saying: ﴿Indeed We, that is how We do﴾: Allah described Himself with the verb as a form of exaltation, since He referred the pronoun to Himself in the plural form. It is known that He, glorified and exalted, is One, but He described Himself with this out of exaltation.
His saying: ﴿with the criminals﴾: al-mujrim (the criminal) is one who has acquired a crime, which is sin. Every criminal, Allah, the Exalted, deals with in this manner. But crime is of two kinds: a crime that is not accompanied by any righteous deed, and this one is dealt with in this way definitely, and is not deserving of pardon. And a crime accompanied by a righteous deed, and this is subject to His will: if Allah wills, He punishes him, and if He wills, He forgives him, as the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners should be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa' 48].

The author said: (﴿Indeed, that is how﴾ as We deal with these ﴿We deal with the criminals﴾ other than these, that is: We punish them, the follower among them and the leader ﴿Indeed, they﴾ [Al-Saffat 35], that is: these people, as indicated by what follows it). ﴿Indeed, they﴾ means these people, namely the followers and the leaders.
﴿Indeed, they, when it was said to them, "There is no deity except Allah," were arrogant﴾ [Al-Saffat 35]. ﴿When it was said to them: "There is no deity except Allah"﴾: who said it? The Messengers said it, as shown by His saying: ﴿And they say, "Are we to forsake our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ [Al-Saffat 36]. Perhaps we choose the generality: that is, if the Messengers or others said to them, even other than the Messengers, it may be correct that they say: "Say: there is no deity except Allah," but they respond with this false answer.
His saying: ﴿When it was said to them: "There is no deity except Allah"﴾: this sentence is the word of tawhid to which all the Messengers called. Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 25]. Its grammatical analysis: we say: la (no) is a negation of the genus, ilaha (deity) is its noun, and its predicate is omitted, its estimation being: "true." Illa (except) is a particle of exception, and Allah is a substitute (badal), or the word of majesty (Allah) is a substitute for the omitted predicate.
His saying: ﴿There is no deity except Allah﴾ [Al-Saffat 35]: ilah means ma'luh (one who is worshipped), and al-ma'luh is the one worshipped out of love and exaltation, the one whom hearts worship, incline toward, and humble themselves before. And ilah, I mean this form (fa'al), is in the sense of maf'ul (object), and it occurs frequently in the Arabic language, like al-ghiras (the planted), al-bina' (the built), and al-firash (the spread), meaning: al-maghrus (the planted), al-mabni (the built), and al-mafrush (the spread).
His saying: ﴿There is no deity except Allah﴾: Allah is a proper name for the Holy Essence, which no other is named by. It is the origin of the names. For this reason, the names of Allah, the Most High, usually come as attributes of Him, and He Himself comes as an attribute of others only rarely. Most often all names come as attributes of Allah: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Sovereign of the Day of Recompense﴾ [Al-Fatihah 2–4]. In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Sometimes He comes as a follower of something else, as in His saying: ﴿To the path of the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy. [It is] Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ [Ibrahim 1–2]. Here this great word (Allah) comes as a follower of what precedes it.
Where is the response of idha (when)? The response of idha is "they were arrogant" (yastakbirun). But someone may say: why did you not put it in the jussive mood? How did you make it the response of idha without putting it in the jussive, even though it is a present-tense verb? The answer is that idha is a conditional particle that does not put the verb in the jussive mood.
His saying: ﴿yastakbirun﴾ [Al-Saffat 35] means: they exalt themselves with arrogance and pride. They consider themselves too great to be told: "There is no deity except Allah," and they disdain that, that is, disdain saying this word, because they see in themselves that they are greater and more exalted. For this reason He said: ﴿yastakbirun﴾, that is: they are arrogant toward saying it, so they do not say it; and they are arrogant toward whoever says it, so they do not respond to him. Their pride, we seek refuge in Allah, is from two directions: the first direction is arrogance toward saying this word; the second is arrogance toward responding to the one who calls them to it.
And with their inner arrogance they say with their tongues: (﴿Are we﴾ [Al-Saffat 36] concerning its two hamzas, what has preceded applies). What has preceded? Four readings or six? Four, according to what the author said: to pronounce both hamzas fully; to soften the second; to insert an alif between them in the case of full pronunciation and softening. That is, we say ﴿a'innā﴾ [Al-Saffat 36] is full pronunciation; ﴿ain-na﴾ is softening; ﴿a'a-inna﴾ is full pronunciation with an inserted alif; and ﴿a'a-in-na﴾ is softening with an inserted alif.
﴿Are we indeed to forsake our gods for a mad poet?﴾ [Al-Saffat 36]. The interrogative here is for negation, and they confirmed this negation by His saying: ﴿a'innā latārikū﴾, they confirmed it with inna (indeed) and the lam (la). That is: is it possible that we forsake our gods for this speaker whom they described with these two things: a poet and mad (that is, because of the saying of Muhammad ﷺ)? It means it is impossible for us to forsake our gods for the speech of this mad poet.
The poet: he is one who composes poetry. The mad: is the opposite of the sane. It is known that their saying is false, and besides being false, it is self-contradictory. The contradiction lies in: how can a poet be mad, or how can a madman be a poet? A madman cannot produce well-ordered prose, so how could he produce poetry that stirs the emotions and is said to have come from a poet? But, we seek refuge in Allah from blindness: when it takes hold of the heart, a person no longer knows what he says, and may say something self-contradictory without knowing it. It is known that Allah refuted them in this claim, so He said: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him. It is not but a reminder and a clear Quran﴾ [Ya-Sin 69]. And He said: ﴿Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe, you are not, by the favor of your Lord, a madman﴾ [Al-Qalam 1–2]. Rather, you are the most intelligent of the intelligent. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, refuted them in this claim of theirs, and they are undoubtedly liars. The Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ) was the most intelligent of people, and the Prophet ﷺ brought a speech that is not poetry, but rather the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
﴿Are we indeed to forsake our gods for a mad poet?﴾ [Al-Saffat 36]. For this reason Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿Rather, he came with the truth﴾ [Al-Saffat 37]. Bal (rather) here is for an annulling reversal (al-idrab al-ibtali), meaning: rather, you lied in what you said, and he, that is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, came with the truth. The ba' here is for accompaniment, meaning he came accompanied by the truth. So his speech is true, and what he brought is also true. That the Prophet, peace be upon him, says this from Allah, we say: this is true, he is truthful, and what the Quran contains is true, and its opposite is falsehood. So al-haqq (the truth) here is a description of the Prophet's ﷺ speech that he is the Messenger of Allah, and a description of what he brought. It is thus a description of both the report and the one reported. So the Prophet's ﷺ report that this Quran is from Allah, we say: it is true; and what he brought is also true. This is because the Quran contains perfect justice and perfect truthfulness, as Allah the Most High said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [Al-An'am 115].
So the quality of being true (al-ahaqqiyyah) here is from two aspects: from the aspect of the report and from the aspect of what is reported. The report, that the speech of the Prophet ﷺ is from Allah, is true, with no falsehood in it. What is reported, that what the Messenger ﷺ brought is entirely true and contains no falsehood, is shown by His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [Al-An'am 115].
So sidq (truthfulness) is a description of reports, and 'adl (justice) is a description of rulings. The whole Quran is either a report or a ruling. Its reports are true, and its rulings are just.
(﴿Rather, he came with the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ [Al-Saffat 37], those who came with it, which is: there is no deity except Allah).
Sadda'a (confirmed) means: the Prophet ﷺ confirmed the messengers who were sent before him. And how did he confirm them? We say: his confirmation of the messengers has two aspects:
The first aspect: his coming corresponds to what they reported, and so this is a confirmation. Like this? What did you say?
* Student: That what he brought corresponds to what the Messengers brought.
* The Shaykh: What they reported, so he is confirming. As if you said: Zayd will arrive tomorrow; when he arrives, his arrival becomes a confirmation of your saying, and his coming becomes the fulfilment of your saying.
Also ﴿and confirmed the messengers﴾ [Al-Saffat 37], meaning: he said that the Messengers are truthful. We all know that it is part of the religion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that a person says: "We believe in Allah and in the messengers of Allah. ﴿Each believes in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers. We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [Al-Baqarah 285]." So the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ confirmation of those who came before him is in these two aspects:
First: his coming is a confirmation of what they reported, that he would be sent. And who was the last of them? Jesus. He said to his people: ﴿Indeed, I am the Messenger of Allah to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah and bringing good tidings of a Messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾ [As-Saff 6].
The second: that he described what the earlier Messengers brought as what? As truthful.
﴿He came with the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ [Al-Saffat 37]. He said: (those who came with it, which is: there is no deity except Allah).
In truth, the author's explanation of this contains some deficiency. Why? Because he confirmed the messengers in this and in other matters. It seems that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, restricted it to the saying: there is no deity except Allah, based on the context, since the context was speaking about: there is no deity except Allah ﴿Indeed, they, when it was said to them, "There is no deity except Allah," were arrogant (35). And they say, "Are we to forsake our gods for a mad poet?" (36). Rather, he came with the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ [Al-Saffat 35–37], that is: he confirmed them that there is no deity except Allah. But it is better to take the general meaning: he confirmed them in this and in other matters.
* * *
Then He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿Indeed, you﴾ [Al-Saffat 38] contains an iltifat (shift)). ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾ [Al-Saffat 38]. He says: it contains an iltifat. The iltifat is that the context requires him to say: "Indeed, they will taste the punishment," because the whole discourse has been about the absent third person: ﴿Indeed, they, when it was said to them, "There is no deity except Allah," were arrogant (35). And they say, "Are we to forsake our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ [Al-Saffat 35–36]. So the context required that He say: "Indeed, they will taste the painful punishment." But there was a shift in the context from the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab). So what is the benefit of this shift?

Earlier we mentioned that every *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person within a passage) has a common benefit, which is to alert the addressee. When speech stays in one pattern, the listener or reader becomes inattentive. When the style changes, he pays attention and asks: why did it change, and what is the purpose of the change? So all shifts share the purpose of alerting, and each one has its own particular function. Here there is a shift from the third person to the second person, because direct address is more forceful in warning: ﴿إِنَّكُمْ لَذَائِقُو الْعَذَابِ الْأَلِيمِ﴾ ("Indeed you will taste the painful punishment") is stronger than "Indeed they will taste the painful punishment." This is why, when we reflect on the story of al-Khidr with Musa (ﷺ), he first rebuked him saying: ﴿أَلَمْ أَقُلْ إِنَّكَ لَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبْرًا﴾ ("Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?") [al-Kahf 72]. The second time he said: ﴿أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكَ إِنَّكَ لَنْ تَسْتَطِيعَ مَعِيَ صَبْرًا﴾ ("Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?") [al-Kahf 75]. Without doubt, direct address strikes the mind more immediately, so it has a greater impact than the third-person pronoun. The rest, God willing, will follow.

* Shaykh: And what is it?
* Student: (...) It removes weariness from being in one uniform style; the *iltifat* keeps away boredom by changing the wording.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, this may be said. It may be one of the benefits, or it may be included within the alerting, because when a person is alerted, his energy is renewed.
* Student: (...) I say, O Shaykh (...) in a situation where a person is sincere about it, unlike the Jabriyya (...) he is called to account in this way and so he admits...
* Shaykh: But who said that these people held the view of the Jabriyya during their lifetime?
* Student: I mean, not all of them said it, but it is also not far-fetched that the Jabriyya...
* Shaykh: The basic principle is that their saying this was out of conviction even during their lives. This is the basic principle.
