Benefits:
God the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿فَإِنَّهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ فِي الْعَذَابِ مُشْتَرِكُونَ﴾ [al-Saffat 33].
* From this verse and what follows, we learn first: that the followers and the leaders are each sharers in the punishment, as He says: ﴿فَإِنَّهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ فِي الْعَذَابِ مُشْتَرِكُونَ﴾. The benefit of this is that neither the followers nor the leaders will escape. If someone asks: does sharing imply equality? The answer is no; rather, each has degrees according to what they did.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the humbling of these leaders who used to exalt themselves over people in this world, because He has brought them together with those they enslaved in this world: ﴿فَإِنَّهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ فِي الْعَذَابِ مُشْتَرِكُونَ﴾, because the Hereafter is a house of justice in which there is no favoritism.
* From the benefits of these verses: God, the Exalted, did not wrong them with this punishment, as He says: ﴿إِنَّا كَذَلِكَ نَفْعَلُ بِالْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾. They were punished only for their crime.
* Also among its benefits: people are equal before God; whoever deserves punishment or reward receives it, as He says: ﴿إِنَّا كَذَلِكَ نَفْعَلُ بِالْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾. That is, We did not do this to these alone; rather, this ruling applies to every criminal. The same applies to reward: God, the Exalted, rewards every doer according to his deed, in line with the qualities by which he deserves that reward.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of God's action, the Mighty and Majestic, as He says: ﴿إِنَّا كَذَلِكَ نَفْعَلُ﴾. God, the Exalted, is the doer of what He wills. An action implies renewal according to its object: God's creation of the heavens and the earth was not eternal; rather, it began when He created the heavens and the earth. And God's creation of the fetus in its mother's womb was not eternal; rather, it is newly occurring at the time this fetus comes into being.
We move from this benefit to one that branches from it: the affirmation of God's voluntary actions, against those who deny this and say that no voluntary action subsists in God, and justify this with a false reason. They said: a voluntary action implies coming into being, and what comes into being can only be caused by something that came into being, while God is eternal and everlasting. There is no doubt that this view is false. Something that comes into being can be caused by something that does not come into being, as in God's actions. Did God not create the heavens and the earth and then establish Himself upon the Throne, so that the establishment came after the creation of the heavens and the earth? Does God not descend every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains? So the descent occurs after two-thirds of the night have passed, yet God has always been and always will be existent. Moreover, a person himself finds that actions of his are renewed while he precedes them, is that not so? A person's action today is not his action of yesterday, yet he precedes his actions, so actions subsist in him while he precedes them. If this is permissible in the created, it is even more so in the Creator, because it is a perfection.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the complete power and authority of God, the Mighty and Majestic. The reason is that these criminals are known for their arrogance, pride and haughtiness, as with Pharaoh and other chieftains; yet God overpowers them, punishing them and doing with them what He wills, in line with His wisdom.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: ﴿إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا إِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ﴾ [al-Saffat 35]: these criminals are at the extreme of arrogance. When this mighty declaration is said to them, a declaration that, if the heavens and earth were weighed against it, it would outweigh them, they become arrogant toward it, considering themselves too great to say it or to believe the one who says it. This is because we have already said: arrogant toward what? Toward the speaker and the one spoken about, that is, toward the report and the one reported.
* From the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation to submit to what this declaration requires, because God related it in the context of people who were arrogant toward it, in the manner of blame. Accordingly, whoever accepts it and submits to it has removed blame from himself and fulfilled what is obligatory upon him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: whoever says "la ilaha illa Allah" sincerely must submit to God's commands and not be arrogant. For this reason, many texts link entry into Paradise to saying "la ilaha illa Allah." It is well known that entry into Paradise does not follow from merely uttering it, since the hypocrites say it too, yet they do not enter Paradise. Rather, what is meant is one who says it while submitting to what this great declaration requires: following God's commands and avoiding His prohibitions.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is not permissible to direct any kind of worship to anyone other than God, as He says: ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ﴾ [al-Saffat 35]. So no kind of worship may be directed to other than God: not prayer, nor vow, nor prostration, nor bowing, nor pilgrimage. All of it must be directed to God, the Mighty and Majestic, because He alone is the one truly worshipped.
* Among the benefits of the verse: in His saying: ﴿وَيَقُولُونَ أَئِنَّا لَتَارِكُو آلِهَتِنَا لِشَاعِرٍ مَجْنُونٍ﴾ [al-Saffat 36], these people denied what the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God requires. The first is: ﴿كَانُوا إِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ﴾ [al-Saffat 35]; the second is that when they were told: believe in Muhammad, they said: ﴿أَئِنَّا لَتَارِكُو آلِهَتِنَا لِشَاعِرٍ مَجْنُونٍ﴾. So they did not uphold "there is no god but God," nor did they uphold "Muhammad is the Messenger of God." Is that not so?
* Students: Indeed.
* Shaykh: God, the Mighty and Majestic, constantly links these two declarations in many verses. Consider His saying: ﴿أَفَلَمْ يَدَّبَّرُوا الْقَوْلَ أَمْ جَاءَهُمْ مَا لَمْ يَأْتِ آبَاءَهُمُ الْأَوَّلِينَ (68) أَمْ لَمْ يَعْرِفُوا رَسُولَهُمْ﴾ ("Have they not contemplated the word, or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old? Or have they not recognized their Messenger?") [al-Mu'minun 68–69]. In the first, there is an allusion to the testimony that there is no god but God; in the second, "Or have they not recognized their Messenger," is the testimony that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.

Therefore the Prophet ﷺ also made these two testimonies a single pillar among the pillars of Islam, saying: "Islam is built upon five: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, the establishment of prayer, the giving of zakat..." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (8), and Muslim (16/21) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar.] and so on, because these two testimonies are inseparable, and because the foundation of all worship rests on belief in these two testimonies; for the foundation of worship is sincerity (ikhlas) and following the Prophet's example (mutaba'ah), and through these two the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah is realized.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these arrogant people were not content with their arrogance toward the truth; they went further and disparaged the one who brought the truth. From where is this derived? From His saying: ﴿Are we really going to abandon our gods for a mad poet?﴾ [as-Saffat 36]. So it was not enough for them to abandon the truth; they attacked and disparaged those who brought it.
Has this method been inherited, I mean disparaging the one who brings the truth? Yes, it has been inherited. The people of innovation (ahl al-bid'ah) label the people of the Sunnah with every defect and ugly description: they called them "al-Mushabbihah" (the anthropomorphists), "al-Mujassimah" (the corporealists), "al-Hashawiyyah" (the literalist filler), "al-Ghuthaa'" (scum), "al-Nawabit" (the upstarts), and "al-'Ammah" (the common folk), and similar words that convey disparagement. But Allah, glory be to Him, has appointed for every prophet an enemy among the criminals, and for every follower of a prophet an enemy among the criminals. Those chosen ones inherited the choicest of creation, namely the messengers, and these wretched ones inherited from whom? From the most wretched of creation, those who disparage the messengers.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the intense zeal of these polytheists for their gods. Consider how they said: ﴿Are we really going to abandon our gods﴾ [as-Saffat 36], and this shows the intensity of their partisanship for them and their jahili fanaticism. It has already been mentioned in Surah Ya-Sin that Allah, exalted is He, said of these gods: ﴿They are unable to help them, though they are a host brought forth [for them]﴾ [Ya-Sin 75]. So the idols and gods cannot help them, yet these are a host brought forth to defend these gods.
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ [as-Saffat 37].
Several benefits are derived from it. First: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ brought the truth, so his whole religion includes the truth in what concerns one's dealings with Allah and one's dealings with the servants of Allah. Allah the Exalted said about the Qur'an that the Messenger ﷺ brought: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra' 9]. Volumes could be written on this phrase and still not exhaust its meaning: ﴿guides to that which is most upright﴾ in everything, in beliefs, acts of worship, morals and transactions, in doing and in abstaining. If you were to trace the Shari'ah as far as you can, you would find that this description applies to all the qualities of the Shari'ah; every quality of the Shari'ah is more upright than anything else.
He says: ﴿Rather, he has brought the truth﴾ [as-Saffat 37]. The opposite of truth is falsehood, and falsehood is either lies in reports or injustice in rulings. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truthfulness and justice﴾ [al-An'am 115]. We have mentioned another meaning of His saying "bil-haqq" (with the truth), apart from the meaning that what he brought is true: that he ﷺ is truthful in what he brought, so what he brought is true, and he is truthful in his statement that it is from Allah and that he is not a liar.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of what the Messenger ﷺ brought, from His saying: ﴿Rather, he has brought the truth﴾ [as-Saffat 37]; and also praise of the Messenger ﷺ, in that He described him as having brought the truth. There is no doubt that describing one who brings what is from Allah as having brought the truth is among the greatest virtues and praiseworthy attributes.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that the Prophet ﷺ is the last of the messengers, from His saying: ﴿and confirmed the messengers﴾ [as-Saffat 37]; for the definite article (al) here denotes generality and therefore encompasses every messenger. This indicates, though not explicitly, that he is the Seal of the Messengers, indeed the Seal of the Prophets, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any man among you, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Ahzab 40]. This verse has a great meaning. He said: "but the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets." The context would have led one to expect: "but the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Messengers," or "but the Prophet of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets." Instead He said "the Messenger of Allah," because the description of messengerhood is higher than the description of prophethood. "The Seal of the Prophets" means that after him no messenger or prophet will come, and so it is: he, peace and blessings be upon him, is the best of the messengers, and after him there will come neither prophet nor messenger.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is obligatory upon us to believe in the messengers who came before, because our Prophet ﷺ confirmed the messengers; so it is obligatory upon us to affirm them too, since the follower must follow the imam, and our imam is Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, so it is obligatory upon us to follow him.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication that the earlier messengers gave tidings of him, from His saying: ﴿and confirmed the messengers﴾ [as-Saffat 37]. There is no doubt that the earlier messengers informed of him, and that the last of them, Jesus, gave glad tidings of him. As for the first, the evidence is His saying: ﴿And [recall] when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I give you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him." He said: "Do you affirm and accept My commitment on that?" They said: "We affirm it." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses"﴾ [Ali 'Imran 81]. What is meant by this is Muhammad ﷺ, for he came confirming what they had, so they were obligated to believe in him by the terms of this covenant. Consider also the night of the Mi'raj, when the messengers, indeed the prophets, prayed in congregation; who was their imam? Their imam was Muhammad ﷺ, which shows that he is the best of them, for leadership in prayer implies a leadership that surpasses prayer.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾ [as-Saffat 38].
* Student: There is a benefit here: the self-contradiction of these people, that they called him a poet.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed.
* And there is also in it: the self-contradiction of these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ, in that they described him as a mad poet, for a madman cannot be a poet. They stumble about in confusion. Unless someone claims that the statement is divided, meaning that some of them said "poet" and some said "mad," and the saying is attributed to all of them although not all of them said it, since they were content with it. If someone claims this, it has a basis; but if the speaker himself combined the two descriptions, then he has contradicted himself.
And He said: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾ [as-Saffat 38].
(...).
* Student: ...The theologians (mutakallimun) explain tawhid as: Allah is one, having no equal in His essence, and no likeness. And we have just mentioned that they say: "None is able to originate creation except Allah"?
* Shaykh: That is: they explain "There is no god but Allah" as encompassing all of tawhid.
* Student: (...) they explain "There is no god but Allah."
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Because He has no equal in His essence.
* Shaykh: No. We said: tawhid according to them is that He is one in His essence with no equal, one in His attributes with no likeness, and one in His acts with no partner. This is tawhid according to them. But the specific interpretation of "There is no god but Allah" is "the one able to originate creation."
* Student: Is the phrase "There is no god but Allah" not the statement of tawhid?
* Shaykh: Yes, but what is their tawhid? Their tawhid is these three things, the affirmation of Allah's unity in these three matters. Then they interpreted "There is no god but Allah" with this specific meaning, that He is able to originate creation. They interpreted it in a way that implies its meaning is tawhid of lordship (tawhid al-rububiyyah) only.
* Student: May Allah reward you, O Shaykh. Regarding the statement of these people, "None is able to originate creation except Allah," is this statement in itself not correct? That the one who creates from the beginning is none other than Allah, glory be to Him?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: But we said that it is a false statement (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, the falsehood is their interpretation of "There is no god but Allah" in this way, not their saying "None is able to originate creation except Allah," which is true. But their interpretation of "There is no god but Allah" by this is the falsehood. Do you understand now?
* Student: ﴿Are we﴾ [as-Saffat 36] has four readings (...). What is the tas-hil (easing)?
* Shaykh: Tas-hil means you do not pronounce the second hamza clearly and fully, you do not pronounce it explicitly, so you say: ﴿a-ina﴾.
* Student: That is, (...).
* Shaykh: No, tas-hil means glide quickly: ﴿a-ina﴾. Listen to my words: ﴿a-ina﴾, as if you walked lightly.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, half.
* Student: The polytheists (...) when the Messenger ﷺ said: "There is no god but Allah" (...) ﴿Has he made the gods one God?﴾ [Sad 5]. That is, they were better than these people (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no doubt. There is no doubt that they were better than these, and more understanding of its meaning than them, there is no doubt.
* Student: More understanding of its meaning?
* Shaykh: Yes, correct. And this is among the things that is raised against them: they said that the polytheists whom the Messenger ﷺ fought were more knowledgeable than you, in the sense of "There is no god but Allah."
* Student: What is the difference between "lā ma'būda bi-ḥaqq" and "lā ma'būda ḥaqq"?
* Shaykh: What is the difference? If we say "lā ma'būda bi-ḥaqq," the predicate has not been stated, and "bi-ḥaqq" is attached to "ma'būd," meaning: no one is worshipped in truth except Allah, and on this reading the predicate is Allah. This is problematic according to the rules of grammar, because "lā" of generic negation only governs indefinite nouns. If we say "lā ma'būda ḥaqq," then "ḥaqq" becomes the predicate of "lā," and is not attached to "ma'būd." For this reason some have construed it as: "lā ma'būda mawjūd illā Allāh" (no existing worshipped one except Allah), and this is not correct, why? (...) existing that anything other than Allah be worshipped. But the correct view is to say "lā ma'būda ḥaqq," just as if you said "lā aḥada qā'im illā Zayd," where "qā'im" is the predicate. "Lā ma'būda ḥaqqun illā Allāh": you have understood.

* * *

I seek refuge with Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment (38), and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾ [as-Saffat 38, 39].
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment.﴾ As is well known, this sentence is emphasized with two emphatics: one is "inna," and the second is the lam. His saying "la-dhA'iqu" is the predicate, and the nun was dropped because of the annexation (idafah), since the nun is dropped from a dual or plural noun in annexation, and the tanwin is dropped if it is singular. His saying "al-'adhab al-alim": "alim" here means "mu'lim" (painful), and fa'il may come in the sense of maf'il, as in the poet's saying:

Does the summoner of Rayhanah, the hearer, keep me awake, while my companions sleep?

"Amin rayhanata al-da'i al-sami'" means "al-musmi'" (the one who makes to hear).

His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾ contains the truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin), because these people were warned of this punishment, and being warned of the punishment is the knowledge of certainty ('ilm al-yaqin). Then they saw the Fire, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are about to fall into it, and will find no escape from it﴾ [al-Kahf 53]; this is the eye of certainty ('ayn al-yaqin). Then it was said to them: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾ [as-Saffat 38], and this is the truth of certainty (haqq al-yaqin). Thus the three levels are combined in the threat against these people: knowledge, sight, and truth.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾, the author said that there is an iltifat (shift) in it: from where to where? From the third person (ghaybah) to the second person (khitab), because addressing someone directly with such a thing is more eloquent and more forceful. When you speak about an absent person, it is not like when you address a person directly with what you threaten him.

So the benefit of the iltifat here, in addition to alerting, is the intensity of the impact of this threat on them, because they were addressed with it directly, and it was not spoken of in the manner of speaking about an absent party: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment.﴾ What is meant by it is the punishment of Hell, may Allah protect us, because it is painful; and Allah, mighty and majestic, has informed of the painfulness of this punishment in great varieties, which Allah mentioned in His Book, and the Prophet ﷺ mentioned a great deal of it in the Sunnah.

He said: ﴿and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, meaning: you will not be recompensed with this punishment except for something you yourselves sent forward for your souls, except what you used to do.

Here the author said, in explaining the verse: "(﴿illa﴾ is the recompense of ﴿ma kuntum﴾)." This is a known matter, because what they did existed and passed; the deed was in the world and is over, and the recompense is in the Hereafter. They were not recompensed the deed itself, but they were recompensed the requital of the deed. Hence the author estimated: "(﴿illa﴾ is the recompense of ﴿ma kuntum﴾)."

But if someone asks: what is the benefit of expressing the recompense by the deed? We say: the benefit in that consists of two matters.

The first matter: to know that the recompense is of the same kind as the deed; as you judge, so you will be judged. When the recompense is expressed by the deed, this implies that the recompense is in proportion to the deed.

The second benefit: the strength of the rebuke to these people, because the recompense is the act of others; when it is expressed as "recompense," it is somewhat milder. But when the recompense is expressed by the deed, it becomes sterner in rebuke, as if it were said to them: "This is your own doing, by yourselves." Therefore the recompense was expressed by the deed.

As for His saying: ﴿and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, in terms of grammar we say: the waw is the deputy subject (na'ib fa'il) of "tujzawna," and "ma" is a relative pronoun in the accusative position as the second object, since "jaza" takes two objects. But is it of the type of "zanna," whose two objects originally were a subject and predicate, or of the type of "kasa," whose object did not originally have a subject-predicate structure? The second. Is that so? Because if you estimated that the waw is the subject and "ma" the predicate, the sentence would not be correct.

﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do (39), except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ [as-Saffat 39, 40] (i.e., the believers; an exceptive clause that is disconnected).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿illa ma kuntum﴾ is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), and the disconnected exception is one in which "lakin" (but) can take its place. If it is asked: why was "lakin" not used instead of "illa," since the meaning is one of contrast, being a disconnected exception? Why was the original particle of contrast, "lakin," not used?

We answer: it came to convey the strong connection of what follows with what precedes; the original of the exception is connection, while the original of "lakin" is the opposite, disconnection. When "lakin" comes, it separates what follows from what precedes; but when "illa" comes, it implies a strong connection of what follows with what precedes, and so it is: when He mentioned the recompense of the criminals, He mentioned the recompense of the sincere.

This is one of the aspects of the Glorious Qur'an being "mathani," in which opposite meanings are paired: when the threat is mentioned, the promise is mentioned; when the believer is mentioned, the disbeliever is mentioned; when Paradise is mentioned, the Fire is mentioned, and so on. For if the speech came in one unbroken course in mentioning fear and Fire, the side of fear would dominate the reader, leading to despair of Allah's mercy; and if the speech came in one unbroken course of promise and encouragement, it would lead to hope, so that a person would fall into feeling secure from Allah's plan. So the Qur'an brings this and that side by side, so that a person keeps oscillating between fear and hope.

His saying: ﴿illa 'ibad Allah﴾: "'Ibad Allah" here refers to servitude of the Shari'ah, because servitude is of two kinds: servitude of decree (qadar) and servitude of the Shari'ah. Servitude of decree encompasses everyone, does it not?

Servitude of decree encompasses everyone, meaning believer and disbeliever, righteous and wicked, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93]. All are subject to the decree of Allah, mighty and majestic; they cannot flee from it, nor oppose it, nor be arrogant toward it. As for servitude of the Shari'ah, it is specific to whoever obeys Allah, mighty and majestic, and worships Allah by His law. So who is excluded from it? The disbelievers, because the disbeliever is not a servant of Allah in terms of the Shari'ah; rather he is arrogant toward His law.

This verse, ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾, which of the two types is it? It is the servitude of the Law (sharʿ). That is, except those who worship Allah by His Law, whom Allah has made sincere for His obedience. These are not like those who came before.

He said: ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 40].

The author said: (That is, the believers). However, "sincere" (al-mukhlaṣ) carries a sense of selection. Allah made them sincere for Himself, so they were servants of Allah and not of anyone else, because committing to obedience to Allah is the realization of worshipping Allah. A person who disobeys Allah has in him a measure of worship of other than Allah, according to the extent of the disobedience that has occurred in him. Is that correct? The one who disobeys Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has in him a departure from the worship of Allah in proportion to the disobedience that has occurred in him, because Allah says: ﴿Have you seen one who takes as his god his own desire, and Allah has sent him astray knowingly?﴾ to the end of the verse [al-Jathiyah 23]. This indicates that every person who disobeys Allah... and every disobedient person is only disobeying out of desire within himself, and he has fallen short of the servitude of Allah in proportion to the disobedience he committed.

So, the sincere ones have a kind of selection: Allah made them sincere for Himself, so they became truly servants of Allah, the Exalted. For this reason He said ﴿the sincere﴾. The sincere servants of Allah are those whom Allah made sincere for Himself, so He did not give Satan any authority over them, as Allah said regarding Satan: ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [Sad 82, 83]. The sincere one is enveloped by Allah's care and protected from Satan, the Exalted. The point is that the sincere one has a greater standing than the believer, and for this reason He said here ﴿the sincere﴾, those whom Allah made sincere for Himself, so they were not servants of anyone other than Allah.

Regarding ﴿the sincere﴾, he said: (a disjunctive exception, istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ). Is there an exception that is not disjunctive? Yes, there is the connected exception (al-mutṣil), and its rule is that the excepted item is of the same kind as the item from which it is excepted. That is the connected exception. The disjunctive exception (al-munqaṭiʿ) is where the excepted item is not of the same kind. The grammarians give an example of the disjunctive exception: "The people stood up except a donkey." He says: because the donkey is not of the kind of "the people," so the exception is disjunctive.

Their reward is mentioned: ﴿Except Your sincere servants among them﴾. Their reward is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Those, for them is a known provision﴾ [al-Saffat 41].

(﴿Those, for them﴾ in Paradise ﴿is a known provision﴾ in the morning and the evening).

The pronoun in ﴿Those﴾ refers to the sincere servants of Allah. He used ﴿Those﴾, which indicates distance, even though they were mentioned just before in ﴿the servants of Allah, the sincere﴾. He did not say "these" (hāʾulāʾ) but "those" (ulāʾika), to exalt their status and to show how high their rank is. The demonstrative for the distant is used to elevate and magnify the status, as al-Farazdaq said addressing Jarir:

Those are my fathers, so bring me their like,
When the gatherings bring us together, O Jarir.

He said: (Those are my fathers). He pointed to them with the demonstrative for the distant, to exalt their status and raise them high.

﴿Those, for them is a known provision﴾ [al-Saffat 41], that is, a gift. The author said (in Paradise). It is better to state it as Allah stated it: for them is a known provision in Paradise. It may also be said that they are rewarded in this world too, but the apparent context of the verse, ﴿fruits, and they will be honored, in the Gardens of Bliss﴾ [al-Saffat 42, 43], indicates that what is meant is the provision that they will have in Paradise.

His saying ﴿provision﴾ means a gift, and ﴿known﴾. The author says: (in the morning and the evening). It seems that he is pointing out that what is meant by "known" is known in terms of time. But if it were said that it is more general: known in time, known in kind, known in this world, and known when they encounter it, it would be more comprehensive. This provision is known in this world because Allah has informed us of it, and it is also known in time: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam 62]. It is known in its specific form and kind when they meet it, as Allah said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And they will be given it, resembling one another﴾ [al-Baqarah 25]. So it is known to them in this world, and likewise in the Hereafter.

(﴿Fruits﴾ [al-Saffat 42] is a substitute (badal) or an explanation (bayan) of the provision, and it is what is eaten for pleasure, not to preserve health).

﴿Fruits﴾, in the nominative, is a substitute or explanation of "provision," because the word provision is more general than fruits. So ﴿fruits﴾ is a partial substitute (badal baʿḍ min kull), since provision is more general. Here ﴿fruits﴾ is not given nunation (tanwīn) because it is diptote (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf), the form of the plural of plurals (ṣīghat muntahā al-jumūʿ), and fawākih is on the pattern fawāʿil.

The author said about fruit: it is (what is eaten for pleasure, not to preserve health). That is, fruit is what a person eats for enjoyment, not to sustain himself with it, so it is a luxury consumption. Likewise, the people of Paradise eat what they eat there for the sake of enjoyment, not to preserve health, because their health is guaranteed: "For them is that they will be healthy and never fall ill, and that they will live and never die." [Narrated by Muslim (2837/22) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah.] So everything they eat in Paradise is of the category of fruit, because the people of Paradise, the author says, are free of needing to preserve health, since their bodies were created for eternity. For this reason it came in a hadith that they do not urinate or defecate, but what they eat comes out as perspiration (rashh), meaning sweat that smells like musk. [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3327) and Muslim (2834/15) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] So they enjoy this eating when they eat and when it comes out, because it comes out as perspiration with the scent of musk, just as when a person is anointed with musk he finds pleasure and a pleasant fragrance. I ask Allah to make me and you among them.

﴿Fruits, and they will be honored﴾ [al-Saffat 42] (by the reward of Allah), ﴿in the Gardens of Bliss﴾ [al-Saffat 43]. They are honored. It is a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah), which indicates permanence and continuity. That is, they are honored in this Paradise in every respect by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Allah honors them, so they look upon Him, and He promises them His pleasure, so He never becomes displeased with them. They are honored by the angels: ﴿The angels will enter upon them from every gate, saying, "Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured; how excellent is the final home"﴾ [al-Ra'd 23, 24]. They are honored by the attendants: ﴿There will circulate among them eternal youths with cups and jugs and a cup from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 17, 18]. They are honored in every way; they will not find, on any day or at any moment, any humiliation. Rather, they are in the utmost honor in every respect. Even if there were nothing except that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, honored them and permitted them to look at His Face, and He speaks to them, the Mighty and Majestic, and this is the utmost of joy. Nothing is more delightful, more pleasant, or better than conversing with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, while they look at His Face.

﴿Fruits, and they will be honored (42), in the Gardens of Bliss﴾. "Gardens" is the plural of "garden" (jannah). In the Arabic language, jannah is an orchard with many trees, and it was named so because it covers whoever is in it. Its root letters jīm-nūn mean to cover, and for this reason you find that all its meanings return to this. Al-janan is the heart, which is hidden. Al-junnah is what a fighter covers himself with to shield against arrows. Al-jinn is a hidden unseen world. Al-jannah is an orchard covered by trees. But we do not explain the Garden of Bliss in this way; rather we say: it is the abode that Allah prepared for His friends, and in it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Because if you said that it is an orchard with many trees, the longing for it and the looking toward it would weaken, since the listener would imagine that this Paradise is like the orchards of this world, and he would wander through people's orchards, thinking of any orchard, "the orchard of so-and-so son of so-and-so," so his heart or his imagination would not go beyond this orchard, even though Paradise contains what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. As Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [as-Sajdah 17]. And Allah the Exalted said in a hadith qudsi: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3244) and Muslim (2824/2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] So the better way is to explain the Paradise which is the Garden of Eternity by what? By saying that it is the abode that Allah the Exalted prepared for His friends, and in it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

His saying ﴿the Bliss﴾, ﴿in the Gardens of Bliss﴾, is an idafah of a thing to its type, meaning gardens of bliss in which there is no misery and no hardship, bliss for the heart, which is joy, and bliss for the body, because they ﴿will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein is silk﴾ [al-Hajj 23]. So they are blessed in their bodies and blessed in their hearts. Consider His saying: ﴿And He will reward them for their patience with a garden and silk﴾ [al-Insan 12], and He also said: ﴿And He will give them radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insan 11]. Radiance is in the face, which is beauty, and joy is in the heart. So their beauty is both inward and outward. For this reason it is called the Garden of Bliss, because a person enjoys bliss in it outwardly and inwardly: his heart is blessed with joy, and his body is blessed with the sight and the clothing of silk.

(﴿Upon thrones, facing one another﴾ [al-Saffat 44], none of them sees the back of another). "Thrones" is the plural of "throne" (sarīr), which are the seats on which one sits. But they are not like the thrones of this world; rather they are ﴿upon thrones woven with gold﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 15]. One cannot imagine the beauty of these thrones, because in them is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. What no human heart has conceived, a person cannot imagine, because it is beyond what can be imagined. Whatever you estimate of bliss and beauty, Paradise is higher and greater.

His saying ﴿facing one another﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun implied in ﴿upon thrones﴾, meaning while they are facing one another. This indicates the perfection of their manners and the spaciousness of their gatherings: the perfection of manners, because they face one another and none of them turns his back to the other; and also the spaciousness of their gatherings, because when they are many and face one another, the circle must be wide. Yes? It must be wide. So the gatherings are spacious, however many people come, they are accommodated, and they face one another in them. ﴿Upon thrones facing one another﴾ [al-Saffat 44]. He says (none of them sees the back of another) because of the facing.

(﴿They will be circulated among with a cup﴾, to each of them, ﴿a cup﴾ is the vessel with its drink, ﴿from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Saffat 45], from wine that flows on the surface of the earth like rivers of water).

﴿They will be circulated among﴾: (yuṭāf) is a present passive verb, and it does not mention who circulates among them. But it is mentioned in another verse that ﴿there will circulate among them eternal youths; when you see them you would think them scattered pearls﴾ [al-Insan 19]. "Wildan" means young boys, servants: ﴿as if they were preserved pearls﴾ [at-Tur 24], ﴿when you see them you would think them scattered pearls﴾ [al-Insan 19], because of their beauty (...) and their attractiveness.

"Scattered" (manthūr) is because they are dispersed in serving their masters, and pearls when scattered are spread about on the ground. So they are spread about serving their masters, each has a task. It delights a person to find these servants each in his work, none of them idle and none of them waiting for another, not like the servants of this world who crowd one another, each saying: "Hurry up, so my turn comes." No, each is in a specific service. This is the most delightful thing for the master when he sees these servants standing in his service in this manner that (...) ﴿when you see them you would think them scattered pearls﴾ [al-Insan 19].

His saying ﴿with a cup from a flowing spring﴾: the author said: (it is the vessel with its drink). The cup is well known; it is the vessel with its drink. Allah has explained that this cup is full (dihāq), ﴿and a full cup﴾ [an-Naba' 34], that is, filled. Moreover, it is filled to a known measure: it is not so large that it is filled and then, if a person drinks it, he becomes tired, and if he leaves some remainder it becomes unappetizing; nor is it so small that it does not quench them, while they are not thirsty, but for enjoyment. Rather Allah said: ﴿of silver, which they have measured with measure﴾ [al-Insan 16], meaning it was made to the measure that the drinker enjoys, neither large nor small.

His saying ﴿with a cup from a flowing spring﴾, he said (from wine flowing on the earth). Al-maʿīn originally means flowing water, and what is meant here by ﴿with a cup from a flowing spring﴾ is: from wine that is flowing, like the flowing of a spring of water...

﴿Upon thrones facing one another﴾, he says: (none of them sees the back of another) because of the facing.

(﴿They will be circulated among﴾, to each one of them, ﴿with a cup﴾, which is the vessel with its drink, ﴿from a flowing spring﴾ [al-Saffat 45], from wine flowing on the surface of the earth like rivers of water).

﴿They will be circulated among﴾: (yuṭāf) is a present verb in the passive, and it does not mention who circulates among them. But it is mentioned in another verse that ﴿there will circulate among them eternal youths; when you see them you would think them scattered pearls﴾ [al-Insan 19]. "Wildan" means young boys, servants: ﴿like hidden pearls﴾ [at-Tur 24], ﴿when you see them you would think them scattered pearls﴾ [al-Insan 19], because of their beauty, attractiveness, and handsomeness. "Scattered" is because they are dispersed in serving their masters, and pearls, when scattered, are spread out on the ground. So they are dispersed in serving their masters, each with a task. It delights a person to find these servants each engaged in his work, none idle, none waiting for another, unlike the servants of this world who crowd one another, each saying: "Hurry up, so my turn comes." No, each is in a specific service. This is the most delightful thing for the master when he sees these servants standing in his service in this manner (...); ﴿when you see them you would think them scattered pearls﴾.

His saying ﴿with a cup from a flowing spring﴾: the author said: (it is the vessel with its drink). The cup is well known; it is the vessel with its drink. Allah has explained that this cup is full, ﴿and a full cup﴾ [an-Naba' 34], that is, filled. Moreover, it is filled to a known measure: it is not so large that, if a person drinks it, he becomes tired, and if he leaves some remainder it becomes unappetizing; nor is it so small that it does not quench them, while they are not thirsty but enjoying it. Rather Allah said: ﴿of silver, which they have measured with measure﴾ [al-Insan 16]; meaning it was made to the measure that the drinker enjoys, neither large nor small.

And His saying: ﴿with a cup from a flowing spring﴾. He said: (from wine that flows over the earth). Al-Ma'in (flowing water) originally means running water. The meaning here, ﴿with a cup from a flowing spring﴾, is: from wine, ﴿flowing﴾ like a flowing spring of water. In Surat Muhammad, Allah the Exalted has made clear that the likeness of the Garden promised to the God-fearing is: ﴿therein are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of clarified honey﴾ [Muhammad 15]. These are rivers that flow. He who created, Mighty and Majestic, such great quantities of honey from this insect resembling a fly is able to create rivers of honey in the Garden. This is not strange. These rivers do not come from bees; rather they come by the word of Allah (Be), and it is. It is clarified honey, with no wax or impurities, of the finest kind (...) in taste and fragrance. Ibn al-Qayyim, in his Nuniyya, based on a hadith[[Abu Nu'aym narrated in al-Hilya (6/205) from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Perhaps you think that the rivers of Paradise are a trench in the earth. No, by Allah, they flow over the surface of the earth. Its banks are tents of pearls, and its clay is pure musk (al-Adhfar)." I said: O Messenger of Allah, what is al-Adhfar? He said: "That which is unmixed." It was also narrated by Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Sifat al-Jannah (69) from Anas as a mawquf (companion's) report.]] said concerning this:

Its rivers flow without a trench, glory be to the One who holds them back from overflowing.

That is, the rivers of Paradise are not like the rivers of this world, which need a trench, or boundaries that prevent them from going right or left, or a pit dug for the river. No. They flow on the surface of the earth according to what its people wish, without workers directing them by digging or building a trench. Rather, they flow wherever they wish, without any effort. He said:

.......................Glory be to the One who holds them back from overflowing.

He who holds back the sea from drowning the people of the earth, and that is nothing compared to Paradise, is able to hold these rivers so that they do not turn aside to the right or the left.

* Student: Shaykh, is it better (...) the Makkan (...)? In my view, they cannot at present (...) memorize the Book of Allah (...), meaning we take from the end of the Qur'an (...)?

* The Shaykh: By Allah, what I see is that it is better to begin from the beginning of the Qur'an, because that is more energizing for him. He hopes he will reach the end of the Qur'an. As for if he has memorized (...) of the Qur'an, whatever it is, it is in any case energizing.

* Student: (...) about this mutual facing (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, the apparent meaning is the time of their visiting one another.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: (...) Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned it in Hadi al-Arwah. But whether the visit is with Allah on Friday or their visiting one another, they undoubtedly visit one another. And it appears that even a person sitting with his intimate friends and family, out of the perfection of their manners, they will be facing one another.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, in (...) the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived"[[Narrated by Muslim (2825/5) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi (may Allah be pleased with him).]], the apparent meaning of the hadith is that it has not been seen. So if we say that Adam was expelled from the Garden of Eternity (...), I say: how is the hadith to be interpreted, and likewise the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in the Night Journey and the Ascension?

* The Shaykh: What is meant is the people of this world now. As for the rare case, for example, that the Messenger saw Paradise and entered it and saw what is in it, that is a rare state from among the signs of Allah. Likewise Adam, peace be upon him.

* Student: So what is meant is the people of this world now.

* The Shaykh: What is meant is the people of this world. And you should know that every general statement can be specified.

* * *

* Student: (...) ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers. There is no harm in it, nor are they intoxicated by it. And with them are those of restrained gaze, with large, beautiful eyes. As if they were hidden eggs. Then some of them turn to others, questioning. One of them says: Indeed, I had a companion who used to say, "Are you truly among those who believe? When we die and become dust and bones, will we truly be repaid?" He said: "Would you like to look?" So he looked and saw him in the midst of Hellfire. He said: "By Allah, you almost brought me to ruin. And had it not been for the favor of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth﴾ [al-Saffat 46–57].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 40]. Is this the starting point of the discussion?

* Student: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾ [al-Saffat 38].

* The Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment (38), and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾ [al-Saffat 38, 39]. In this sentence, ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾, there is a shift (iltifat) from where to where?

* Student: (...) The discourse shifted from the third person to the second person.

* The Shaykh: From the third person to the second person. What is its benefit?

* Student: Alerting. (...) The first benefits alerting, and that benefits the severity of the punishment's impact.

* The Shaykh: Alerting. Good, that is one, and the root purpose of alerting applies to every iltifat. The second: he shifted from the third person to the second person?

* Student: For the severity of the punishment's impact.

* The Shaykh: Because it is more forceful in rebuke, since the one being rebuked is addressed directly with it.

Good (...) good. Thrones, but not the thrones of this world, woven (mawdunah) of gold; meaning, stitched and woven of gold.
Good. ﴿facing one another﴾ [al-Saffat 44]?

* Student: They face one another (...).

* The Shaykh: ﴿facing one another﴾ means they face one another, so no one has his back to another.

Good. Now let us take the lesson, the benefits:

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment﴾ [al-Saffat 38].

* In this verse and what follows there are many benefits:
* Among them: that these deniers or those who are arrogant toward the statement "There is no god but Allah" will taste the punishment, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, you will taste﴾. This sentence is emphasized with two things: inna and the lam.
* Among its benefits: that the punishment of these people is direct punishment, just as a person directly eats his food. By His saying: ﴿taste the punishment﴾. The original sense of "dhawq" (tasting) is for food that is eaten, and then it was applied to anything whose occurrence is certain.
* Among its benefits: that the punishment of these people, may Allah protect us, is painful, ﴿painful﴾ meaning causing pain, and it is a pain that the bodies of this world cannot bear even a part of, because they, may Allah protect us, will be punished with a fire sixty-nine times more intense than the fire of this world. Whenever their skins are burned through, they will be replaced with other skins so that they may taste the punishment. The essential point is that it is a painful punishment, with a pain having no equal in this world, and a person cannot imagine it because of its severity. We ask Allah to protect us and you from it.
* Among the benefits of these verses: the perfection of Allah's justice, Mighty and Majestic, in that He made the recompense of the same kind as the deed, by His saying: ﴿and you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾ [al-Saffat 39]. Unlike the kings of this world or the guardians of this world, whose requital for deeds may exceed what is deserved. A person may become angry and punish one under his authority with more than he deserves. But Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not recompense a person except for his deed.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of recompense, and its necessary implication is the affirmation of resurrection, because full recompense for deeds happens only on the Day of Resurrection. So in the verse there is evidence for the affirmation of resurrection and the affirmation of recompense.
* Among its benefits: a refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists), who say that a person does not act, and that a person's deeds are not attributed to him because he is compelled to them. So a person's movement by speech or action is like his involuntary movement, indeed like the movement of a feather by the wind. But this view is refuted by the texts and by reason.
* Among the benefits of the verses: that the Qur'an is mathani (oft-repeated), in which meanings are repeated, so that a person is between fear and hope, when encouragement and warning are repeated together, as in these verses: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 40].
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: the honor of those who uphold the command of Allah, for Allah attributed them to His worship in His saying: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾. There is no doubt that it is a source of pride for a person to be attributed to the worship of Allah. For this reason Allah, glorified and exalted, mentions the description of His Prophet Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, in his most noble stations. He described him as a servant when mentioning the sending down of the Qur'an to him: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾ [al-Furqan 1], ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Baqarah 23]. He described him as a servant in the station of the Night Journey and Ascension: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Isra' 1]. And He said regarding the Ascension: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm 10]. He described him as a servant in the station of defending him: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah 23]. This is a challenge to those who deny the Messenger, peace be upon him, to bring the like of what he brought. Thus servitude to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is without doubt a source of honor for the worshipper, and the poet says:

Do not call me except by "Slave of Her" (ya 'abdaha), for indeed it is the most honorable of my names.

I seek refuge with Allah. This shows that servitude to the Beloved is among the most noble and most delightful states for the worshipper.
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: that Allah, glorified and exalted, bestows His favor upon whom He wills, making them sincere to Himself so that they are not servants of anyone else. In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾. This is more emphatic than ﴿the sincere (mukhlisin)﴾, though each has its merit. But the one made sincere (mukhlas) by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for Himself, so that he has no will except for his Lord, this is more emphatic. He said: ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: that the servants of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are divided into two categories: sincere servants and non-sincere servants. "Servants" in the sense of servitude to decree are non-sincere; they are like cattle, indeed they are more astray. But servants of Allah in the sense of servitude through the Law are the sincere ones.
* Among the benefits of the verses: that these sincere ones have a gift with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, known to Him and to them. ﴿For them is a known provision﴾ [al-Saffat 41], known to Allah and known to them, for Allah the Exalted informed His servants of what they will receive on the Day of Resurrection of various kinds of reward.

Good. If someone asks: is it known in reality or in meaning?

The answer is that it is known in meaning. As for the reality, it is not known; that is, we do not know the true nature of this bounty or this provision, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for the eyes, as a reward for what they used to do﴾ [al-Sajdah 17]. And by His saying in the Hadith Qudsi: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived"[[Agreed upon. Al-Bukhari (3244) and Muslim (2824/2), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).]]. So we know of the bounty of the Hereafter only the names. As for the realities, they are not known, as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "There is nothing in Paradise of what is in this world except the names"[[Narrated by al-Tabari in his Tafsir (1/392).]]. Fruit, palm trees, pomegranates, but the realities differ greatly. So it is known in meaning, not known in reality and essence, because that is not grasped except by certainty of knowledge.
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: that the people of Paradise eat this provision for enjoyment and pleasure, not for sustenance that they need. By His saying: ﴿fruits﴾ [al-Saffat 42]. In this world a person eats food sometimes for sustenance, because he needs it, and sometimes for enjoyment and delight. But in the Hereafter all its food is for delight.
* Among the benefits of the verses: that the people of Paradise are honored. Honored by whom? In three respects, which we mentioned yesterday: from Allah, from the angels, and from the servants, the youths. So they are honored in every respect.
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: that Allah's reward for the doer of good is much greater than his deed. Is that not so? Because our good deeds, if they were attributed to Allah's reward, would be nothing. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The place of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than this world and all that is in it"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (2892) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi (may Allah be pleased with him).]]. Then our good deed, however great it is, has an end: its end is death. But the reward of the Hereafter has no end. So it becomes clear that the grace of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His reward are far greater than the work of the worker. This is the fulfillment of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains, and Allah multiplies for whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah 261].
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: that the Garden has categories and kinds. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿in gardens﴾ [al-Saffat 43], but they all share in being gardens of bliss.
* Among its benefits also: that the whole Garden is bliss, bliss for the body and bliss for the heart. The bliss of the heart is in joy, expansiveness, and constant happiness, which is not touched by any anxiety, grief, or sorrow. And the body: ﴿and He gives them radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insan 11], ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant (8), pleased with their striving﴾ [al-Ghashiyah 8, 9], and other verses indicating the bliss of this body. The body itself is blessed, and what it wears of adornment and jewelry is likewise blessed.
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: the spaciousness of the dwellings of the people of Paradise, since they face one another on couches, for facing one another requires spaciousness of place, especially with their great number.
* Among the benefits of the noble verses also: the perfection of the manners of the people of Paradise, in that they face one another such that none of them turns his back on another, but all of them face one another. There is no doubt that this is the perfection of manners. And manners, in reality, are as good among the people of Paradise as they are good among the people of this world. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam 4]. And there is no doubt that when a person is well-mannered he is beloved among people. Harshness and indifference to people is a blameworthy character.

Therefore let us consider matters we practice. First and foremost, the matter of greeting (salam). We find that many people, although they are keen on worship, do not care about greeting, neither initiating it nor returning it. This is contrary to the state of the believer with his brother. It is among the right of a Muslim over his brother that when he meets him he greets him, and greets him with a sincere greeting accompanied by cheerfulness. As for greeting him with the tip of the nose, such that you would not know he was greeting unless it was for the whistling letter, this is not a greeting.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 30–63 (part 7 of 7):

Worse than that is for a person to greet his brother with a clear voice, with well-articulated sounds, audible, and then return the greeting with a voice that cannot be heard, or return it with his nose, or return it with his hand like this. This is undoubtedly forbidden for him, because Allah says: ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, greet with one better than it or return it﴾ [An-Nisa' 86]. It is known that if he says "(Peace be upon you)" and the other says "(Upon you is peace)," is this better or not? No, it is not better, nor is it equal. So it must be either an equal response, which is the minimum obligation, or a better one, which is the most complete.

Likewise, we find some people turning their backs on their brothers and not caring about them, and this is an error; this should not be. I sometimes see that when I finish the prayer, one of the people comes forward, not feeling that behind him are human beings like himself. Why do you advance over them? This causes divisions of hearts. For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) said to the people when they were forming the rows for prayer: "Do not be at odds, lest your hearts become at odds."[[Narrated by Muslim (432 / 122) from the hadith of Abu Mas'ud al-Badri (may Allah be pleased with him).]] So he made disagreement over advancing and falling back a cause of disagreement of hearts. If I were beside this man, I would feel that this man had insulted me by advancing over me and presenting his back to me.

Some people make excuses, for example, that there is cramping, and that he wants to stretch his legs, so he advances in order to sit cross-legged.

We say: if you are like this, then either advance a great deal, stand up and be far away, or fall back.

He says: "I cannot fall back, because behind me is a row of people completing the prayer."

We say: Then stand up and move far forward so that you do not turn your back on the people. As for turning your back on the servants of Allah after they have finished the prayer and leaving them behind you, this is undoubtedly bad manners, and the one beside you will feel that you have humiliated him.

Likewise, there are some among us who do not honor the elder: the young person advances over the elder. Two people meet at the door of the mosque or the door of a house, and then the younger one hastens forward, perhaps in a hurry, so that he enters before the elder. This is not good. Honoring the elder is one of the good qualities and one of the traits of the believer. So a person's being indifferent and not caring about others is undoubtedly contrary to good manners. The people of Paradise, may Allah make us among them, will be on couches facing one another, arranged in a circle so that each of them faces the others.

* Among the benefits of these verses is also the comfort of the people of Paradise, for they are at leisure on the couches, speaking with one another and enjoying one another's company face to face.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses is also that, while they are seated on the couches, servants circulate among them with various kinds of delights and drinks. Among these is that they circulate among them with a cup from a flowing spring, the cup of pure wine free of impurities. But this cup is measured according to what the drinker needs: not so large that it tires him, nor so small that it diminishes his pleasure, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups which were crystal-clear, crystal of silver, which they have determined in measure﴾ [Al-Insan 15–16].

* Among the benefits of these noble verses is the clarity of this drink that is circulated among them, based on His saying: ﴿white﴾ [As-Saffat 46].

Up to here ends what preceded.

* * *

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿white﴾ [As-Saffat 46] ("whiter than milk"). The author said that it is "whiter than milk." In reality the verse does not indicate that it is whiter. Rather, "whiter than milk" came in the description of the Prophet's (ﷺ) Pool, which will be in the plains of the Resurrection. It was described as being "whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, and more fragrant than musk."[[Ahmad narrated (5913) with his chain from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: When the verse "Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar" was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is a river in Paradise, its banks are of gold, it flows over pebbles of pearls and rubies, its drink is sweeter than honey, whiter than milk, colder than ice, and more fragrant than musk." It was also narrated by Muslim in a similar form (2300 / 36) from Abu Dharr (may Allah be pleased with him).]] As for the wine of Paradise, Allah described it only as white.

He said: ﴿white, delicious﴾ [As-Saffat 46] ("delicious"). Here He expressed "delicious" with the verbal noun (maṣdar) in place of the active participle or the passive participle (ism al-fa'il or ism al-maf'ul). This is because "delicious" (ladhidh) can be used as both the active and passive participle. Describing something with the verbal noun is more emphatic than describing it with a derived noun (mushtaq) from the verbal noun. So when you say "So-and-so is justice (ʿadl)," it is more emphatic than when you say "So-and-so is just (ʿādil)," as if you have made him justice itself. So here He described this wine or this cup as "delicious" (ladhdhah), meaning as if it were pleasure itself and not the thing characterized by pleasure. Expressing the description in place of the described is more emphatic than expressing it with the described thing, because it is an expression of the origin from which something branches off, since the derived noun branches from the noun from which it is derived, the verbal noun.

﴿delicious for the drinkers﴾ [As-Saffat 46]. ﴿For the drinkers﴾ is for emphasis. That is, while they are drinking it they enjoy it, unlike the wine of this world, which, as He says, is repulsive while drinking. As for the wine of the Hereafter, it is a delight for the drinkers. It is also free from bad effects, as He says: ﴿No headache will they get from it, nor will they be intoxicated by it﴾ [As-Saffat 47].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 30–63 (part 1 of 7):

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿They will say, "Rather, you were not believers (29). And we had no authority over you. Rather, you were a transgressing people."﴾ [al-Saffat 29, 30].

﴿And we had no authority over you﴾: The grammatical analysis of this sentence is clear. The particle (ma) is a negation particle, and (kana) is a past-tense verb that puts the subject in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative. (Min sultan) is its postponed noun, governed by the preposition (min), which is grammatically superfluous (za'ida). (Lana) is the fronted predicate. This differs from those who said: (ma) is Hijazi and (kana) is superfluous. This is because if you said: "And we have no authority over you," the sentence would be correct, since (kana) here is intended to indicate existence, as it signifies an action or a past time. By contrast, if it were dropped, it would not indicate past time, and the sentence would not signify past time. It is therefore necessary here that (ma) be a negation particle and (kana) a past-tense verb that is not superfluous.

His saying: ﴿And we had no authority over you﴾. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: that is, (no power or ability that compels you to follow us).

Know that (sultan) means authority (sultah), and in every context it is according to what fits it. At times, (sultan) refers to knowledge, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They are nothing but names you have named, you and your forefathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm 23], meaning: no proof or evidence.

At other times it refers to power, might and dominance, as in this verse, meaning: we had no authority over you by which we could compel you to follow us. Rather, you followed us by your own choice and will. It is as though they are saying: Do not blame us, but blame yourselves, just as Satan said: ﴿When the matter has been decided, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you and failed you. I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾ [Ibrahim 22].

These misguided leaders place all the blame on the followers. Yet when we look at reality, we find that blame falls on both the followers and the leaders. As for the leaders, they adorned their deeds for them, invited them, belittled them, and made them foolish, until they inclined them toward falsehood. As for the followers, they were not forced into this, nor were they compelled to it; rather, they themselves followed this by their own choice. So each one bears the blame that befits his action.

﴿Rather, you were a transgressing people﴾ [al-Saffat 30]: astray like us. ﴿Rather﴾ here is a transitional (idrab intiqali), not one to cancel what came before, but to move from one thing to another. So they repeated their charges against them: first they said: ﴿Rather, you were not believers﴾, and then they said: ﴿Rather, you were a transgressing people﴾. The transgressor (taghi) is one who exceeds his limit, as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose beyond its limit, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah 11], meaning when it exceeded its limit. So they describe them as transgressors, that is, going beyond the limit they should be upon, which is following the messengers, not following these misguiders.

The author's saying (astray) is open to question, because transgression is an additional matter beyond straying. The correct view is that transgression means: what? Those who exceed the limit they ought to be upon, namely following the messengers.

(﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us﴾ [al-Saffat 31], that is: it became due, and it was established and became binding, with no injustice or falsehood in it. ﴿The word of our Lord﴾ means that everyone who departed from obedience to Allah and denied His signs is in the Fire. His saying: (﴿The word of our Lord﴾ concerning the punishment, that is, His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ [Hud 119]) is, according to what the author said, what is meant by their saying: ﴿the word of our Lord﴾. It seems he is pointing to the Exalted's saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾. However, the apparent meaning is that the saying of Allah intended here is His words to Iblis: ﴿Whoever follows you from among them, I will surely fill Hell with you all together﴾ [al-A'raf 18]. This is because the verse the author pointed to contains a statement that Allah, glorified and exalted, decreed by His wisdom to fill the Fire with disbelievers, but it does not contain the direct address to Satan and his followers: ﴿Whoever follows you from among them, I will surely fill Hell with you all together﴾. That is a direct threat to whoever follows Satan. So interpreting our phrase by the second verse is more appropriate than interpreting it as the author did.)

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, we are tasters﴾ [al-Saffat 31] (﴿Indeed, we﴾ all together ﴿are tasters﴾ of the punishment by that saying, and from it arose their saying ﴿so we misled you﴾, which is explained by His saying: ﴿Indeed, we were misguided﴾ [al-Saffat 32]).

They say: ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us﴾ [al-Saffat 31]. The pronoun in ﴿against us﴾ refers to both the followers and the leaders. ﴿Indeed, we are tasters﴾ also: the pronoun refers to both the followers and the leaders. It is as if they are saying: We did not save ourselves, so how can we save you?

Then He said: ﴿so we misled you﴾, that is, we made you among the people of error by turning you away from the path of guidance. ﴿Indeed, we were misguided﴾ is an explanation of ﴿so we misled you﴾. Here, in your text, (the explained by his saying) means: by the saying of Allah the Exalted. It is also correct to say (explained by their saying), that is, by the saying of these people which Allah related from them. The singular pronoun has its justification, and the plural has its justification.

﴿Indeed, they that Day will be sharers in the punishment﴾ [al-Saffat 33]. This is the saying of Allah.

﴿Indeed, they﴾, that is, the followers and the leaders, ﴿that Day﴾ (the Day of Resurrection, ﴿will be sharers in the punishment﴾, that is, because they shared in the misguidance). That is, these people share in the punishment, each being punished according to the measure of his sin, and your Lord does not wrong anyone. It is impossible for the followers to be spared from accountability, or for the leaders to be spared from accountability, because the followers submitted to error by their own choice, while the leaders deceived and deluded them. So each one receives the punishment he deserves, even though they share its origin.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Thus﴾, as We do with these, ﴿We will do to the criminals﴾ [al-Saffat 34]). The analysis of this sentence: (Inna) is the particle with its subject, and the clause (nafʿalu) is its predicate. Likewise, the kaf is a noun meaning (like), in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). That is: indeed We do the like of that action to the criminals. This construction occurs frequently in the Qur'an, but its analysis, as I said, is that you make the kaf a noun meaning "like," and make it accusative as an absolute object, with the verb that follows it, and it usually does follow it.

(﴿Indeed, thus﴾, that is, as We do with these, ﴿We will do to the criminals﴾). This shows that these people were criminals, because they deserved the punishment that others deserved, as He said: (﴿We will do to the criminals﴾ other than these, that is, We will punish them, both the follower and the leader). And Allah knows best.
