If you say: what do we make of His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he spoke, Satan threw into his wish﴾ [al-Hajj 52], where He said: ﴿any messenger or prophet﴾? This also implies that the prophet, who is one to whom a law was revealed but who was not commanded to convey, was sent. The answer: the sense of the verse is "And We did not send before you any messenger, nor did We send any prophet," and it is like the saying of the poet:
*I fed her straw, and cold water* ...........................

Cold water is not fed, but given to drink, so the sense is: "and I gave her cold water to drink." It is known that omitting what is known is permissible, as Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Alfiyya:
*And omitting what is known is permissible, as when you say, "Zayd," after "Who is with you two?"*

﴿And We had already sent among them warners﴾, meaning: frightening ones. Frightening from whom? Frightening those who oppose them with punishment and deprivation of reward, for the disobedient is deprived of the reward of obedience, since if He willed He could replace disobedience with obedience. Likewise he is punished with what this disobedience requires. He says: ﴿among them warners﴾. Is "warners" (mundhirin) here an active participle or a passive participle?

**Students:** Active participle.

**Shaykh:** An active participle from (anzara, yunzir). The warner is the one who frightens. He said: ("mundhirin" from the messengers: those who frighten).

﴿So look, how was the end of those who were warned?﴾ [al-Saffat 73]. "Look" (unzur) is addressed to a single masculine addressee. Who is he? Is it the Messenger ﷺ? Is it proper that the address be directed to him? The second is more general: so look, O addressee, or O listener, how was the end of those who were warned? Here He said: ﴿how was the end of those who were warned﴾ and did not say "what was." That is, look at the manner and the outcome, because whoever looks at the manner has looked at the outcome.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 64–82 (part 3 of 6):

If one were to say: "What was their punishment?" the answer would be: destruction. But look at how their punishment was, at its manner: ﴿So each We seized for his sin. Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and among them were those who were seized by the Blast, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned﴾ [al-'Ankabut 40]. So look at the manner, the manner of the outcome, so that by this contemplation you may benefit from the severity of the punishment and its fitting correspondence to the sin. For Allah said: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾, meaning that His punishment is suited to his sin. And when you reflect on this, you will find the matter as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said. For example, 'Ad used to boast of their strength and say: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15], so they were destroyed by the most gentle of things, which is the wind. Allah sent upon them a wind that destroyed them, ﴿so that none could be seen except their dwellings﴾ [al-Ahqaf 25]. And Pharaoh used to boast of the rivers that flowed beneath him, so he was destroyed by that in which he took pride, which is water. Thus, whenever you contemplate the destruction of the peoples who denied the messengers, you will find that their punishment was entirely fitting to their sins.

Therefore, "Look how" is more eloquent than "Look at what their outcome was." The reason: it indicates the severity of the seizing and its fitting correspondence to the sin. Moreover, when you look at the manner, you will look at the outcome as well; but if we say, "Look at their outcome," you are only commanded to look at the outcome alone.

As for His saying: ﴿How was the end of those who were warned﴾, the clause here is interrogative, but it is in the position of an accusative as the object of ﴿Look﴾. Is this looking with the eye or with the heart? This looking is with the heart. Usually, looking with the eye is followed by (ila) (to), as one says "nazara ilayhi" (he looked at him), whereas looking of the heart is transitive without a preposition, as in ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yunus 101], meaning with the hearts. As for with the eyes, it is of no benefit if the heart is not affected by it.

As for His saying: ﴿How was the end of those who were warned﴾, ﴿those who were warned﴾ here: is it an active or passive participle? It is a passive participle: those who were warned and frightened, but they did not fear, and the warning did not affect them. So how was their end?

The author said: (i.e., their end was punishment). That is, the end was dreadful, and Allah protect us, they were punished with a destructive, annihilating torment.

Then He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ (i.e., the believers). Yes, and for this reason the author explained it with the active participle, to indicate that "al-mukhlisin" here is an active participle, because the explanation corresponds to what is explained. So He says: ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾. The exception here is disjunctive (munqati'), because what follows is not of the same kind as what precedes. When what follows "illa" is not of the same kind as what precedes it, it is a disjunctive exception. The sign of a disjunctive exception is that it can be replaced by (lakin, but). Yet why is "illa" used instead of "lakin"? To indicate the strength of the connection of what follows with what precedes; it conveys the sense of correction (istidrak) while the link between what precedes and what follows is maintained in meaning, though this differs from that.

As for His saying: ﴿Except the servants of Allah﴾, is the servitude meant here special or general? Special, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿the sincere﴾. We previously explained that servitude is divided into general and special; (i.e., the believers, for they were saved from the punishment because of their sincerity in worship), and this is according to the reading with a kasra on the lam, (or because Allah made them sincere for it, according to the reading with a fatha on the lam). So the author, may Allah have mercy on him, informed us that there are two readings in the verse: ﴿al-mukhlisin﴾ and ﴿al-mukhlasin﴾. But he did not state them explicitly; rather, he gave their meaning. So there are two readings: (mukhlisin) because of their sincerity to Allah, for they directed their intention purely to the face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, the Lord of the servants, to whom belong the face and the deed, so they did not turn to anything other than Allah. The person who is sincere to Allah, whose heart is devoted to Him, is granted success, and his habits become acts of worship, because he is always with Allah, always reflects on the signs of Allah, and always loves closeness to Allah, so he strives that his speech, his action, and his abstention are all for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This, in truth, is the winner who gained time and gained life; no moment passes over him except that he is profiting by it. But most people are heedless of this matter; most people are in heedlessness, heedless. They have not made themselves sincere to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Indeed, among people there are those for whom acts of worship are merely habits: he stands, performs ablution, and prays because that is his custom, as if these acts were a daily routine. Therefore we find that they do not affect the heart, due to severe heedlessness of sincerity to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. They are sincere to Allah in worship. Likewise (mukhlasun): Allah made them sincere, and the author said: (for worship).

Yet if a more exalted meaning than this were stated, it would be more fitting: Allah made them sincere for Himself and chose them from among all the servants. ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen﴾ [Sad 47], those whom Allah chose and made the elite of His servants for Himself. This is more eloquent in praise than what the author said, that Allah made them sincere for worship. Rather, we say: He made them sincere to Himself from among all the servants: ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾.

The author says: ﴿And Noah had certainly called Us, and We are the best of responders﴾ [al-Saffat 75]. This sentence is an elaboration of His saying: ﴿And most of the former peoples had already gone astray before them﴾. Here Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, begins to explain how this misguidance was, and when it occurred. It began with the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth, who was Noah, peace be upon him. Noah was the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth, by the evidence of the Book and the Sunnah. As for the Book, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾ [al-Nisa' 163], so He said: ﴿as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him﴾. Therefore there was no sent prophet before Noah. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly sent Noah and Abraham and placed in their descendants prophethood and scripture﴾ [al-Hadid 26].

Since prophethood and scripture were in their descendants, no one before Noah was given prophethood and scripture. By prophethood here is meant the prophethood of messengership; as for the prophethood of revelation and worship, it had already been given to Adam, for Adam was a prophet spoken to, but not a messenger sent.

As for the Sunnah, it is authentically related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the hadith of intercession: "People will come to Noah and say to him: You are the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4476) and Muslim (193 / 322) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik]. So Noah, peace be upon him, is the first of the messengers. He remained among his people nine hundred and fifty years, i.e., a thousand years less fifty, calling them night and day: ﴿He said: My Lord, I have called my people night and day, but my call has only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh 5–6], calling them secretly and openly: ﴿Then indeed I have proclaimed to them, and I have declared to them secretly in private﴾ [Nuh 8–9]. But they, Allah protect us, were not increased by that except in aversion and arrogance, despite the strength of the message and the great signs. Yet they, Allah protect us, turned away and grew arrogant, and none believed with him except a few. When Noah, peace be upon him, saw what had happened from his people and despaired of them, he invoked against them, saying: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant. Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and will not beget except wicked disbelievers﴾ [Nuh 26–27], and he said: ﴿I am overcome, so give help﴾ [al-Qamar 10]. So Allah answered his supplication, and for this He said: (﴿And Noah had certainly called Us, and We are the best of responders﴾ He said, by his saying: My Lord ﴿I am overcome, so give help﴾). ﴿So he called upon his Lord: I am overcome, so help!﴾ Allah gave him victory and answered his supplication. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So We opened the gates of the heaven with water pouring down, and caused the earth to gush forth with springs, and the waters met according to a matter already decreed﴾ [al-Qamar 11–12]: water springing from the earth, and water descending from the sky, the earth boiling with a great boiling that covered all the earth, until the oven, which is the place where fire is kindled, began to gush forth water, and the sky poured down with great torrential water. The waters met until they reached the peaks of the mountains. None was saved from it except those who were believers, for they were with Noah, peace be upon him, in the ship. For this reason, Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And Noah had certainly called Us, and We are the best of responders﴾.

We have mentioned that Noah is the first of the messengers. Who is the last of them? Muhammad ﷺ is the last of the messengers. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Ahzab 40]. He did not say "Seal of the Messengers" together with His saying "but he is the Messenger of Allah," indicating that after him there can come neither a prophet nor a messenger. ﴿So We are the best of responders﴾: the sentence ﴿And Noah had certainly called Us﴾ is emphasized with three emphases, as previously mentioned: the oath, the lam, and qad. In explaining the emphasis here we say what we said before.

As for His saying: ﴿So We are the best of responders﴾ (fa-la-ni'ma), the fa is a conjunction particle indicating sequence and immediacy; the lam is a preparatory lam for the oath; and the sense of the sentence is: "By Allah, how excellent are the responders!" The word "al-mujibun" is the subject (fa'il) of (ni'ma), and (ni'ma) and (bi'sa) and similar words require a subject and a specified term (al-makhsus) which is a subject whose sentence is its predicate. Is that not so? They require a subject and a subject-topic whose clause forms a predicate about it. This subject is called the specified term of praise or blame. So where is the specified term in this verse?

He says: "We," so "how excellent are the responders: We." And our Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, has spoken truly: how excellent is the Responder, Allah, glorified and exalted. His answer is not like the answer of others. Allah's answer, glorified and exalted, is a certain answer, but on condition that the conditions of answering are fulfilled and the impediments are absent. If the conditions of answering are not fulfilled, He, the Mighty and Majestic, does not answer, for His answering, like all His acts, is based on wisdom, and wisdom is placing a thing in its proper place. When the conditions of answering are fulfilled, there is a place for the answer, and the answer is realized; and when they are not fulfilled, there is no place for the answer, and it is not realized. It also requires the absence of impediments, that no impediment to answering exists. The mention of these conditions and impediments will come, Allah willing, when the benefits are mentioned.

In sum, Allah exalted Himself by saying that He is the best of responders, and Allah the Mighty has spoken truly, for He, exalted is He, is the best of responders: He answers His servants when wisdom requires it, with the existence of the conditions and the absence of impediments. ﴿So We are the best of responders﴾ (i.e., He called upon Us against his people, so We destroyed them by drowning). Yes, he called upon Allah against his people, and Allah destroyed them by drowning; they were drowned to the last of them. It is related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "If Allah were to save anyone from drowning, He would have saved the mother of the child" [Mustadrak al-Hakim (3349) from the hadith of 'A'ishah]. Who is the mother of the child? A woman who had a child with her. When she saw the water rising, she feared for herself from drowning, so she took refuge on a mountain, and the water rose until it reached her; then she climbed higher, until the water reached her again, until it reached the summit of the mountain, and the water reached her. When she saw that the water had reached her and overwhelmed her, she lifted the child above her hands, so that she would drown before him. The Prophet ﷺ said, as is reported from him: "If Allah had shown mercy to anyone, He would have shown mercy to the mother of the child" [Mustadrak al-Hakim (3349) from the hadith of 'A'ishah], because this is among the greatest forms of mercy: that she made her death come before his, lifting him upon her hands until the drowning overtook her before him.

The point is that these people, and other nations, are not benefited by faith when they see the severity of punishment. Consider Pharaoh: when drowning overtook him, what did he say? ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel have believed, and I am of the Muslims﴾ [Yunus 90]. But it did not benefit him. It was said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before﴾ [Yunus 91]. No nation was benefited by its faith when it saw the punishment, ﴿except the people of Jonah: when they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the worldly life and gave them enjoyment for a time﴾ [Yunus 98].

The people of knowledge said: the wisdom behind this is that their prophet had left them in anger before he was permitted to, so the word had not come into effect against them, due to the incompleteness of the warning concerning them. Therefore, when they believed, Allah removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the worldly life and gave them enjoyment for a time, and they will find what they deserve of punishment or reward.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And We saved him and his family from the great distress﴾ [al-Saffat 76]. Who are his family? Should we say the intended meaning is the believers? Or should we say that "ahl" (family) means the special household of the man? There is a difference between "al" and "ahl": "al" means followers, while "ahl" means the close ones, the special household of a man, as Allah said: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household﴾ [al-Ahzab 33]; this does not include the whole nation, but the close household. So shall we say that the intended meaning is his family who are his close ones? This is closest to the verse; yet other verses show that those who were saved were he and those who believed with him.

Excepted from "family" is Noah's son, who disbelieved and was overtaken by the drowning. When Noah, peace be upon him, asked his Lord: ﴿He said: My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges. He said: O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose work was other than righteous. So do not ask Me for that about which you have no knowledge. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ [Hud 45–46].

Excepted from that also is his wife, as Allah said in Surat al-Tahrim: ﴿Allah presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot; they were under two of Our righteous servants but betrayed them﴾ [al-Tahrim 10]. They betrayed them by what? By disbelief, not by immorality and adultery; for it is impossible that Allah would make the wife of a prophet commit adultery, since adultery is filth, and Allah said: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men﴾ [al-Nur 26]. So the betrayal of the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot was by disbelief, and disbelief may exist in a prophet's wife while he does not know; therefore He said: ﴿but they betrayed them﴾, meaning they concealed disbelief from Noah and from Lot.

In sum, "ahl" here is not general. Shall we say it is a general term intended for the specific, or a general term that is specified? It is a general term that is specified; for a general term intended for the specific must be known to the addressee from the outset as meaning only the specific. But a matter that is known only through another text is called a specified general term.

He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And We saved him and his family from the great distress﴾ [al-Saffat 76]. "Al-karb" means the opposite of spaciousness, and a person in distress is one who has been struck by what distresses him. There is nothing greater than the distress of death. This distress that befell his people was a great distress, for it is drowning, in which a person dies while watching; that is, a person dying of illness dies from something he knows he has no power to remove, but in drowning he dies while still hoping to be saved, so you find him striving with all his strength to escape, yet it does not happen for him; he is as if dying, and death cuts him off while he looks on. Therefore it became a great distress, because it is death by drowning. Similar is death by burning in fire, for a person dies by a thing he feels he could escape, yet he is powerless, so the impact of death upon him is more severe. Thus He said: ﴿And We saved him and his family from the great distress﴾. The author said: (i.e., the drowning). ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ [al-Saffat 77].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 64–82 (part 4 of 6):

There is a grammatical difficulty in the verse, namely that ﴿al-bāqīn﴾ (الباقين) is in the accusative even though it comes after ﴿hum﴾ (هم), and ﴿hum﴾ would normally be a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is in the nominative. So why does it come in the accusative here?
* A student: It is a separating pronoun (fasl).
* The Shaykh: The brother says it is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl), and a separating pronoun has no place in i'rab. On this basis, ﴿al-bāqīn﴾ is the second object of ﴿ja'alnā﴾, because (ja'alnā) is one of the verbs of transformation (af'āl al-taṣyīr); it means (ṣayyarnā, "we made"), and it takes two objects: the first object is ﴿dhurriyyatahu﴾ and the second object is ﴿al-bāqīn﴾.
As for the phrase ﴿hum al-bāqīn﴾: we have said that it is a separating pronoun, and a separating pronoun has no place in i'rab but it does have a place in meaning. So what is it?
* A student: O Shaykh, it separates the predicate.
* The Shaykh: That is, it distinguishes the predicate from the adjective (ṣifah). That is one. The second?
* The student: Emphasis.
* The Shaykh: It conveys emphasis.
* A student: And it conveys restriction (iḥṣār).
* The Shaykh: And it conveys restriction (ḥaṣr). The benefits of the separating pronoun are three: emphasis, restriction, and separation, meaning distinguishing the predicate from the adjective. As for its effect on i'rab, it has none at all.
﴿dhurriyyatahu﴾: "his offspring," meaning his progeny. God made the progeny of Noah the ones who remain. For this reason it is said that Noah, peace be upon him, is the second father of mankind, and the first father is Adam.
It is said that Ibrahim is the father of the prophets, and it is not said that he is the father of mankind. Why? Because mankind was not confined to the descendants of Ibrahim, but he is the father of the prophets, because all the prophets after him are from his descendants, as God said earlier: ﴿And We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book﴾ [al-Hadid 26]. So the prophets before Ibrahim were from whose descendants? Noah's. And the prophets after Ibrahim were from the descendants of Noah and Ibrahim, because Ibrahim was from the descendants of Noah: ﴿And We made his descendants the ones who remain﴾.
The author said: (So all people are from his offspring, peace be upon him). All people after him are from his offspring.
﴿dhurriyyatahu﴾ [al-Saffat 77]: "his offspring," meaning his progeny. God made the progeny of Noah ﴿hum al-bāqīn﴾ (the ones who remain). For this reason it is said that Noah, peace be upon him, is the second father of mankind, and the first father is Adam. It is said that Ibrahim is the father of the prophets, and it is not said that he is the father of mankind. Why? Because mankind was not confined to the descendants of Ibrahim, but he is the father of the prophets, because all the prophets after him are from his descendants, as God said earlier: ﴿And We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book﴾ [al-Hadid 26]. So the prophets before Ibrahim were from whose descendants? Noah's. And the prophets after Ibrahim were from the descendants of Noah and Ibrahim, because Ibrahim was from the descendants of Noah.
﴿And We made his descendants the ones who remain﴾. The author said: (So all people are from his offspring, peace be upon him). All people after him are from his offspring; as for those before him, they are not from his offspring, that is, from the offspring of Adam. The author said: (He had three sons: Sam, who is the father of the Arabs, Persians and Romans; Ham, who is the father of the Sudanese; and Japheth, the father of the Turks and Khazars; and Gog and Magog and what lies beyond). This is the well-known view among historians, that the sons of Noah, peace be upon him, were three: Sam, Ham and Japheth. But this has not come through an authentic sunnah from the Prophet ﷺ, nor does the Qur'an indicate it. So it is better for us to say that the people after Noah are from his descendants, while this division requires evidence, and there is no evidence for it from the Book of God or the sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ. God, glorified and exalted, mentioned that the earlier nations are known only to God. In which verse? In Surat Ibrahim: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows except God?﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. When God denies that anyone knows them except Him, it is necessary that their knowledge be received from whom? From where? From God, glorified and exalted, from God and not from other than Him. So we return to revelation.
Accordingly, what is in the books of historians about the conditions of past nations, if it is not supported by evidence from the Book and the sunnah, is something to be held in suspension and not asserted with certainty, like the narratives of the Children of Israel. These three sons of Noah are among those about whom we suspend judgment. We do not care whether the rest of his sons were three or thirty. What matters is that we believe in what God's Book indicates, namely that the descendants of Noah are those who remained, and as for those who believed with him, they may have had no descendants? It may be that they had descendants, but they did not persist. God knows best. It is possible for a person to have a son and a grandson and then his line to end, and it is possible that he has a son and grandsons up to five generations and then his line ends. We do not know, but what remained of his line is Noah: ﴿His descendants are the ones who remain﴾.
﴿And We left for him a good mention among the later generations﴾ [al-Saffat 78] ("We preserved for him"). He says: ﴿We left for him﴾ and did not say "We left to him." ﴿We left for him﴾ indicates that "left" (tarakna) is construed with a meaning that fits the preposition mentioned. He says: ﴿We left for him among the later generations﴾, meaning We preserved for him a good praise. I say: He did not say "We left to him among the later generations," but rather he said: ﴿We left for him among the later generations﴾. So "left" must be construed with a meaning appropriate to ("alā, "for"), and the appropriate meaning for ("alā) is praise, that is, We praised him with a praise that was left among the later generations, and this is indeed so; God, glorified and exalted, praised him with one of the finest praises. He said: ﴿The offspring of those whom We carried with Noah; indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾ [al-Isra' 3]. This is the greatest praise and the most honorable distinction: that God, mighty and majestic, describes one of the sons of Adam, saying: ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾, meaning one who fulfilled servitude and gratitude to Him, peace be upon him.
So God preserved for him a good praise among the later generations, until the last of the nations, indeed until the Day of Resurrection, because this Book will remain until God lifts it at the approach of the Hour, and this whole Qur'an contains praise of Noah.
(﴿We left for him﴾: We preserved for him a good praise ﴿among the later generations﴾ of the prophets and nations until the Day of Resurrection.) The apparent meaning of the noble verse is that all the prophets who came after Noah mentioned him with good praise, so all the prophets and nations extol Noah, peace be upon him, with what God praised him by, because he is mentioned in all the books.
﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat 79]: ﴿Peace﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and it is indefinite for the sake of magnification, meaning a great peace, because it is peace from whom? From God. ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds.﴾ This praise means that God safeguarded him from the defects that could tarnish him, and in place of those defects from people, God gave him praise. So God combined two things for him: praise and his safety, or combined his being spared from what would blemish him. For this reason we say that "salām" means "taslīm" (safeguarding), that is, God safeguarded him from everything that could harm him of the defects that could tarnish him among the sons of Adam.
﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾: the intended meaning of ﴿the worlds﴾ here is those after Noah, not those before him, as far as is apparent. On this basis it is a general term used to mean a specific one.
God said: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ [al-Saffat 80]. ﴿Indeed We﴾ (...) but the intended meaning is magnification, for God is one, glorified and exalted, but when His name is mentioned with something indicating plurality, the intended meaning is what? The intended meaning is magnification. ﴿Thus﴾ means such a reward, ﴿We reward the doers of good﴾, meaning everyone who does good, for God, glorified and exalted, rewards him as He rewarded Noah, peace be upon him. God rewarded Noah with two things: what He left for him among the later generations, and what He safeguarded for him among the worlds. Likewise, whoever is a believer in God, mighty and majestic, and does good in his worship and toward His servants, God, exalted, will reward him as He rewarded Noah. For this reason you find the leaders of the Muslims: you find that God placed in the hearts and tongues of people praise of them, despite the fact that some people disparage them, because every person of good must have someone of evil who disparages him: ﴿And thus We made for every prophet an enemy from among the criminals﴾ [al-Furqan 31].
Likewise, whoever holds fast to the guidance of a prophet has an enemy among the criminals without doubt, but God, glorified and exalted, appoints for this believer someone who replaces that disparagement with praise and who defends him against it. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾, those who did good.
Good conduct is divided into two kinds: good conduct in the worship of God, and good conduct toward the servants of God. As for good conduct in the worship of God, we do not explain it better than the explanation of the Messenger of God ﷺ, when he said: "Ihsan is that you worship God as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. What do you understand from this hadith? "That you worship God as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." What do you understand? We understand that worship in the first category is worship of seeking, and worship in the second category is worship of fleeing. Is that known?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: Is it not known? Alright. Worship in the first category is worship of seeking: "as though you see Him." It is known that souls yearn for God, glorified and exalted; so if one worships God as though he sees Him, he persists in worship in order to reach what? To his Beloved, to God, mighty and majestic. "But if you do not see Him," meaning if you do not reach this level, which is worship of desire and seeking, then indeed He sees you, so worship Him in the worship of fleeing and fear of Him. This is not like the first, because this one worships God out of fear of Him, while the first worships Him out of hope. So the first rank is more perfect than the second rank, and for this reason the Prophet ﷺ placed it at the second level. He said: "If you do not see Him," and worship Him as though you see Him, "then indeed He sees you." So beware of opposing Him or falling into disobedience. This is good conduct in the worship of God.
As for good conduct toward the servants of God, it is giving kindness to them with wealth, person and standing. Some of them said: it is giving generosity, withholding harm, and a cheerful countenance. Giving generosity means giving; withholding harm means that you do not harm anyone, neither by your speech nor by your deeds; a cheerful countenance means that you do not meet people with a frowning, scowling face, because whoever he is, if he meets people with a frowning, scowling face, he is not doing good to them. Indeed God, glorified and exalted, rebuked the Prophet ﷺ, the best of creation, when what happened with 'Abd Allah ibn Umm Maktum occurred, though the Messenger ﷺ acted from his own ijtihad. God, exalted, said about that, and what did He say? He said: ﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. And what would make you know? Perhaps he would have purified himself, or be reminded and the reminder would benefit him. As for one who thinks himself self-sufficient, to him you give attention. And not upon you is it that he should not purify himself. But as for one who came to you striving, and he fears [God], from him you are distracted﴾ [Abasa 1–10]. These are mighty words, yet God, mighty and majestic, softened them by beginning with the third-person pronoun, saying ﴿He frowned﴾, as if speaking of another person, not of the Messenger, and He did not say "You frowned and turned away," because, as we have often noted, addressing someone directly is greater and more severe than speaking of them in the third person.
In short, good conduct toward the servants is by giving generosity, withholding harm, and a cheerful countenance. If you wish, say that good conduct toward the servants is giving kindness to them with wealth, person and standing: with wealth, clearly; with person, by serving him; and even so, if you serve a person and help him, you are rewarded, as the Messenger ﷺ said regarding: "and you help a man with his mount, lifting him onto it, or lifting his goods onto it, is charity" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2989), Muslim (1009/56), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. Among the bodily giving is a cheerful countenance; there is no doubt that it is among the bodily kinds of kindness, since it relates to the body. The third, as we said, is standing: by benefiting people through mediation and intercession in what is good for them and for you (...).
* * *
﴿Indeed they will eat from it and fill their bellies from it. Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of boiling water. Then indeed their return is to Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat 66–68].
* Among the lessons of this noble verse and what follows: it shows that these people, namely the people of the Fire, may God protect us, cannot leave the Fire, as indicated by: ﴿Then indeed their return is to Hellfire﴾.
* Among its lessons: its apparent meaning indicates that the Fire is everlasting, since it is the final destination, which implies there is nothing beyond it. This view, namely that the Fire is everlasting, is the definitive view, and it is not permissible to believe otherwise, because God mentioned eternity in three places in the Qur'an: in Surat al-Nisa', in Surat al-Ahzab, and in Surat al-Jinn. In Surat al-Nisa' God, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿God would never forgive them, nor would He guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa' 168–169].
In Surat al-Ahzab God, exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, God has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Ahzab 64–65].
In Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And whoever disobeys God and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 23]. After these three verses, which concern the unseen and the seen, it is not permissible to depart from the meaning they convey. If the dweller abides for an everlasting eternity, then the dwelling must be likewise, meaning everlasting and impossible to perish. The view that the Fire may perish, or that it must perish, is a very weak view. Our Shaykh, may God have mercy on him, commented on Ibn al-Qayyim in his book Shifa' al-'Alil, where he mentioned the disagreement from some of the early scholars, and commented that this is a very weak view, and he found it strange that such a view would come from someone like Ibn al-Qayyim, may God have mercy on him, because it contradicts the Qur'an. But every noble steed stumbles.
* Among the lessons of the noble verse: an indication that these people wish and hope to leave the Fire, but they are returned to it, as indicated by: ﴿Then indeed their return is to Hellfire﴾. We have mentioned during the commentary that a person hoping to leave and then being returned suffers more intensely and more painfully.
Regarding God's words: ﴿Indeed, they found their fathers astray [69]. So they were rushing in their footsteps [70]﴾ [al-Saffat 69–70], among the lessons: these deniers followed their fathers into misguidance, as indicated by: ﴿they found their fathers astray﴾, so they went astray just as they did.
* Among its lessons: an indication of the blameworthiness of imitation that opposes the truth, because God mentioned this as a rebuke against them and a reproach to them for finding their fathers astray and then following them and abandoning the path of truth. So if imitation is necessary, to the point that a person cannot reach a ruling through inference, then imitation is permissible out of necessity, as God, exalted, says: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl 43]. He did not say "so derive from the Qur'an and sunnah if you do not know," because one who has no knowledge cannot derive rulings by himself, and if he tries to derive rulings from the evidences while having no knowledge, he will go astray and stumble blindly. So a person who lacks knowledge is obligated to imitate, and one who has knowledge is obligated to exercise ijtihad. This view is a middle position between those who are strict in denouncing imitation and those who are strict in denouncing the mujtahids. Thus imitation is for necessity.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 37, verses 64–82 (part 5 of 6):**

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Is the term "fathers" (ābāʾ) applied to grandfathers or not? The apparent meaning is that His words, ﴿their fathers﴾, include both the nearer father and the more distant ancestors. Applying the term "father" to a grandfather, even a distant one, is well known in the Book and the Sunnah. Allah the Exalted says, ﴿the religion of your father Abraham﴾ [al-Hajj 78], so Allah called Abraham a father although he was a distant grandfather.

  From this principle follows the preference for the view that a grandfather excludes the siblings absolutely, whether they are full siblings, paternal siblings, or maternal siblings, in matters of inheritance. The stronger view is that if a paternal grandfather is present, he excludes the siblings, even full or paternal siblings, because he is a father. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), which is reported from thirteen Companions. It is also the school of Abu Hanifah and the view chosen by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, and it is the stronger, definitive view.

  The reasoning is that those who hold that the grandfather inherits have produced detailed rules which, if they were part of the Shari'ah, would necessarily have been explained in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ). They say that if the grandfather has no sharer-heir (ṣāḥib farḍ) with him, he is given a choice between a third and the muqāsamah (sharing as a male with the siblings), and if a sharer-heir is present, he is given a choice between a sixth, a third of the remainder, and the muqāsamah. We say: From where do you derive this division? If this division were legislated, it would have to be in the Book and the Sunnah, because Allah, glory be to Him, divided the sharer-heirs with a clear and evident division. He mentioned the mother's shares, and likewise the brothers and sisters: the maternal siblings, and the sisters in general. So where is this division? From where do you have that if the grandfather is not a sharer-heir his inheritance is a third or the muqāsamah, and if he is a sharer-heir his inheritance is a sixth or a third of the remainder or the muqāsamah? The point is that this will come to us, God willing, in the chapter on inheritance (farāʾiḍ) in greater detail than this, but we touched on it here because of His words, ﴿their fathers﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the ugliness of the action of these blind imitators, who rushed to follow the traces of their fathers, while in the matter of the truth they turn back on their heels. From this follows the danger of those people who, when the truth agrees with their desires, hasten to it, but when it does not agree, they draw back from it and become slow to accept it. These people resemble the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿But if the right was with them, they would come to him willingly﴾ [al-Nur 49]. So when the right is in their favour, they come to it submissively, and when the right is against them, they turn away and try to twist the necks of the texts to suit their desires.

  In His words, ﴿And most of the earlier peoples had indeed gone astray before them﴾, there is evidence that most of the earlier nations went astray, and this is so. It has already passed us that the Messenger (ﷺ) saw a prophet with a group, and a prophet with one or two men, and a prophet with no one with him.[[Agreed upon (Bukhari, 5752; Muslim, 220/374), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas.]]

* Among its benefits: consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) by mentioning the like of those who denied him, because a person is consoled and takes comfort from the calamities of others.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the care of Allah the Mighty and Majestic for His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in that He presented to him examples with which he could be consoled, because a person's consolation through others makes the matter easier for him and increases his strength and drive in calling to what he calls to.

* Among its benefits: a warning to these deniers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that there may befall them what befell the earlier nations.

In His words, ﴿And We had certainly sent among them warners﴾ [al-Saffat 72], there is evidence that Allah established the proof against every nation, because of His words, ﴿And We had certainly sent among them﴾, meaning among the earlier ones, ﴿warners﴾. This is confirmed by His words, ﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]. So the proof was established upon every town.

* It is also derived from the verse that whoever the message has not reached, there is no proof against him, because the warning did not reach him. This is so. But what will be the fate of this man, or what is his ruling in this world and the Hereafter? We say: As for this world, he is judged by what he worships and follows in religion. If he follows Judaism, he is a Jew; if Christianity, he is a Christian; if Zoroastrianism, he is a Zoroastrian; if communism, he is a communist. This is in this world, meaning that we do not apply the rulings of the Muslims to him in this state, because he follows a religion other than Islam. As for the Hereafter, his ruling is with Allah the Mighty and Majestic. The soundest view on this is that Allah, glory be to Him, will test them with whatever He wills. Whoever obeys among them enters Paradise, and whoever disobeys enters the Fire (...). Let us restate this issue: What is the ruling on one who has not received the message in this world? His ruling is the ruling of what he follows in religion, because we only have the outward. As for the Hereafter, his affair is with Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Allah will set a test for him on the Day of Resurrection with whatever He wills. If he obeys, he enters Paradise, and if he disobeys, he enters the Fire. If someone says: Is there legal obligation (taklīf) in the Hereafter? Do you not say that legal obligation ends with death?

  The answer: Yes, there is legal obligation in the Hereafter. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said, ﴿On the Day when the shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostrate, but they will not be able﴾ [al-Qalam 42]. Their being called to prostration is legal obligation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: it is fitting in address to mention what suits the situation, and to omit what eloquence requires omitting. Its reasoning: here He mentioned only the warning concerning the messengers, although the state of the messengers, peace be upon them, is both warning and giving glad tidings. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and as warners, so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa' 165].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the mercy of Allah, glory be to Him, toward creation, in that He did not leave them to their own intellects in worshipping their Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. What is its reasoning? He sent messengers to them. And He sent messengers to them not merely to say ﴿Bow and prostrate, and worship your Lord, and do good﴾ [al-Hajj 77]. No, rather He combined their call with what? With warning and giving glad tidings, so that this would be a motivation for them to carry out the commands and avoid the prohibitions.

* Among the benefits of His words, ﴿So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾ [al-Saffat 73]: alerting the intelligent person to reflect on the outcomes of the deniers, and likewise on the outcomes of those who responded. A person is commanded to reflect on the state of both of these groups. If he reflects on the outcome of those who responded, and that it is a praiseworthy outcome, he becomes one of them; and if he reflects on the outcome of the deniers, he is wary of them and keeps away from them, because of Allah's words, ﴿So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah does not punish for a sin except after the proof has been established, because of His words, ﴿the end of those who were warned﴾. They were warned, and so the end came.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that the one who reflects should look at the manner of the punishment, so that it may be greater in his perception in one respect, and so that he may know the wisdom of Allah the Mighty and Majestic in fitting the punishment to the sin. Why? For the sin. So he looks at these two matters to show the punishment and its severity, and to show its fittingness to the sin: ﴿So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾.

In His words, ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 74], there is an indication that the one who is made sincere (mukhlaṣ) and the one who makes sincere (mukhliṣ) are mutually linked: their sincerity and Allah's making them sincere lead to a final outcome of salvation. The reason is the exception, ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾, for these people have the outcome of salvation, and their outcome is praiseworthy.

* Among its benefits: urging a person to be one of these servants so that he may be saved.

* Among its benefits: the virtue of sincerity (ikhlāṣ), because of His words, ﴿except the sincere servants of Allah﴾. Sincerity, as you know, is what we were commanded, ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship Allah, being sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah 5]; ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Ghafir 14]; ﴿So worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [al-Zumar 2]. And sincerity, as has already passed us, is the removal of all impurities from worship.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the honouring of these sincere people, by what? By attributing their servitude to Allah. There is no doubt that whatever is attributed to Allah gains honour. For this reason, Allah honoured His House by attributing it to Himself, saying, ﴿And purify My House﴾ [al-Hajj 26], and He honoured the mosques by attributing them to Himself: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mention of Allah's name in His mosques﴾ [al-Baqarah 114]. The Prophet (ﷺ) also called them the houses of Allah: "No people gather in one of the houses of Allah..."[[Recorded by Muslim (2699/38), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] And this is undoubtedly an honouring of what is attributed.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: explaining the blessing of Allah upon these servants, in that He made them sincere to Himself, so that their only aim was Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

  If someone says: Do these servants not have aims? They eat with intention, drink with intention, and enjoy dwellings and women with intention. So the intention of other than Allah has entered their aims. What is the answer?

  The answer: They draw near to Allah by this intention. For example, in eating, a person eats out of appetite without doubt, and to remove necessity, but this eating can be an act of worship in several ways. First: if he intends by it to carry out the command of Allah, since Allah commanded eating and drinking.

  Second: if he intends by it to preserve his health and the sustaining of his body, because a person is commanded to look after himself. Allah said, ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa' 29], and the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Your self has a right over you."[[Recorded by Bukhari (1968), from the hadith of Abu Juhayfah.]] If they intend by this to seek help from this eating and drinking in obeying Allah, especially when it is a direct aid, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "Take suhoor, for in suhoor there is blessing."[[Agreed upon (Bukhari, 1923; Muslim, 1095/45), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]

  Fourth: if he intends by it to enjoy the blessings of Allah and to spread them out, Allah loves for His servant to enjoy His blessings, because a generous person loves people to enjoy his generosity. The most honourable time for the generous person is when guests knock on his door so that he may honour them, is it not so? But the miser is the opposite: when someone knocks, he says, "He is not here." The other, however, has opened his door to people and rejoices when people come and enjoy his hospitality.

  So a person's intention to enjoy the blessing of Allah and to spread it out is undoubtedly a means of drawing near to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because Allah loves, when He bestows a blessing upon His servant, to see the effect of His blessing upon him.

* Student: (...) Ibn al-Qayyim said in Hadi al-Arwah: "The Fire is two fires: the fire of the disbelievers and the fire of the sinful monotheists. As for the fire of the sinful monotheists, it will perish, but the fire of the disbelievers will not perish." Does not the detail of this rule out that (...) Ibn al-Qayyim did not hold that the Fire perishes?

* Shaykh: No. He mentioned in the book Shifa' al-'Alil the disagreement concerning the Fire of Hell, which is for the disbelievers.

* Student: Is this not a restriction of what he stated without restriction in Shifa' al-'Alil?

* Shaykh: (...) a second view. The discussion concerns our Shaykh's comment on this which he found before him.

* Student: One who has received the message, but he was born in an environment where polytheism is widespread, and they have implanted in his heart enmity between him and those who hold correct belief. What is his ruling?

* Shaykh: Apparently the proof has been established against him, because Allah the Exalted established the proof against the polytheists, although most polytheists, or the common polytheists, do not understand.

* Student: He is a Muslim, but...

* Shaykh: Yes, but he is a polytheistic Muslim. For example, if it is said to him that going to the grave of its occupant and calling upon him is polytheism...

* Student: He does not know...

* Shaykh: (...) If he does not know its meaning, that does not mean the proof has not been established against him. Rather, our statement concerns a man who understands. It is said to him that this is polytheism, and it is said to him that Allah says, ﴿So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾ [Ghafir 14], and they say to him that Allah says, ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated﴾ [Ghafir 60], and the verses are explained to him. But merely that a man comes to him and says, "Do you know that this is polytheism?", this may not be the establishment of proof. Do you understand?

* Student: Some people (...) know of Islam only its name. They do not know what Islam is. Is this sufficient for establishing the proof, that they know that in...?

* Shaykh: This issue is based on a scholarly disagreement: is the excuse the establishment of the proof, or the understanding of the proof? Some scholars say: if the proof is established, whether the one invited understood it or not, he has no excuse. Others say: it is necessary that he understand the proof that is established upon him. As for if a messenger were sent calling to guidance, but this thing was not understood, the proof is not established upon him, because Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And We did not send any messenger except in the language of his people, to make clear to them. Then Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills﴾ [Ibrahim 4]. After the explanation and understanding, people are divided by these messengers into the astray and the guided. The matter requires reflection on reality: is it sufficient that the proof merely be established? And if the proof is established upon him, must he seek the meaning, so that it is said, "You were negligent," and "Why did you not inquire? You are at fault"? Or is it said that if a man has the proof established upon him and it reaches him, but in a confused manner, then he is excused, especially if he dies at a time when he could not investigate and inquire?

  In any case, this is an issue of great depth, and it requires a thorough review of the statements of the scholars on it, because in our present time there is a need to understand it, since many Muslims are in this condition. That is, the truth is presented to them, or presented to them in a confused way, as is found now among the people of innovation. For example, there are groups such as the Rafidah innovation, the Khawarij innovation, the Ash'ari innovation, the Mu'tazilah innovation, and many innovations in which the people are confused, and truth is mixed with falsehood. Many people think the truth is with them while they are upon innovation and misguidance. So the matter truly needs a complete investigation of this subject and a review of the statements of the scholars, especially the scholars who were free in their thinking, such as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and Shaykh Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, and those like them (...).

* Student: ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds. Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was among Our believing servants. Then We drowned the others. And indeed, among his party was Abraham, when he came to his Lord with a sound heart, when he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship? Is it falsehood, gods other than Allah, that you desire? So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?" Then he glanced at the stars, and said, "Indeed, I am ill"﴾ [al-Saffat 79–89].

* Shaykh: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. We have already explained the benefits, and I think we have reached His words, ﴿So see how was the end of those who were warned﴾ [al-Saffat 73]?

  Allah the Mighty and Majestic said, ﴿And Noah had certainly called Us, and excellent were the Responders﴾, and so on to the end.

* From the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of a matter with an oath when the need calls for it, and that this is from eloquent speech, because Allah, glory be to Him, emphasised this with an oath, the lam, and "qad."

* Among its benefits: encouraging the Prophet (ﷺ) and others to call upon Allah, glory be to Him, and that when His servant calls upon Him in supplication, Allah responds.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's hearing, because of His words, ﴿And Noah had certainly called Us, and excellent were the Responders﴾. There is no response except after hearing.

* Among its benefits: praise of Noah, peace be upon him, by his turning to his Lord when difficulties befall him.

Among the benefits of His words, ﴿So excellent are the Answerers﴾, is praise of Allah, the Exalted, for His perfect answering, because praising the one who answers entails praising the answer. The answering of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is not like the answering of others. It is an answer of bounty and kindness, in which He may give a person more than he asked for.

Among its benefits is the demonstration of Allah's mercy, the Exalted, in answering the one who calls upon Him, and of His power to answer supplication, because answering entails the ability to do so, since one who is incapable cannot answer.

Among its benefits is the demonstration of Allah's greatness, through the use of the plural *wāw* in His attribute in His words ﴿al-Mujībūn﴾. This is certainly not a plural of number, since Allah is One, but it is a plural of majesty.

Among the benefits of His words, ﴿And We delivered him and his family from the great distress﴾ [As-Saffat 76], is the demonstration that his people were afflicted by a great distress, namely destruction by drowning, and that Allah, the Exalted, delivered Noah and his family.

Among its benefits too is the demonstration of Allah's power, in that the punishment befell this nation, so some were saved and some were drowned.

Among its benefits, that is, among the benefits of the story, is the perfection of Allah's justice, the Exalted, in that He recompenses each person according to what he deserves: whoever deserves deliverance He delivers, and whoever deserves destruction He destroys.

Among its benefits is the permissibility of using a general term even when it is specific in meaning, because His words ﴿his family﴾ include, what do they include? They include the believers and the disbelievers among them. Other verses have shown that among his family were those who were not saved.

Among the benefits of His words, ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ [As-Saffat 77], is that Noah, peace be upon him, is the one whose offspring of the children of Adam survived, so everyone after Noah is from his progeny. For this reason he is called the second father of mankind. Here a question arises, which is this: it may be said that the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned that Allah distinguished him by sending him to mankind as a whole, whereas a prophet used to be sent only to his own people,[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (438) and Muslim (521/3), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.]] and the apparent meaning of this noble verse is that Noah was sent to all of mankind, because of His words ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾, and his descendants were those who directly descended from him, not those in some other place.

The answer to this is that this verse does not entail what was mentioned. There may have been nations in distant places that perished and did not survive to the descendants of Noah. The distant nations that were not reached by Noah's call may have had their own messengers, and then those nations and the messengers sent to them perished, and nothing remained except the descendants of Noah.

Among the benefits of His words, ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ [As-Saffat 78], is the demonstration of Allah's favour, the Exalted, upon His servant through the praise of later generations for him. When a person dies, people are divided regarding him into two groups: a group that praises him well, and a group that praises him badly. Rarely does the whole community agree upon praising someone, and by "the community" I mean the community of the call (*ummat al-da'wah*, the community addressed by the message). As for the community of response (*ummat al-ijābah*, those who accept the message), they often agree upon praising a particular person. But the community of the call, among whom are the disbeliever, the believer, the sinner and the wrongdoer, does not agree upon praising a single person, because whoever has strong faith and calls to Allah will inevitably find opponents among the enemies of Allah, the Exalted. But the people of goodness and faith love the caller to Allah and praise him as he deserves.

In His words, ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾ [As-Saffat 79], there is evidence that Allah, the Exalted, cleared Noah, peace be upon him, among the later generations, since they speak words that keep him free from defamation. Thus Allah combined for him good praise and the removal of bad praise, by His words ﴿Peace be upon Noah among the worlds﴾.

Among its benefits too, that is, among the benefits of the verse, is the use of a general term while intending a specific meaning, because His words ﴿among the worlds﴾ do not include those who came before Noah, since apparently no mention of them had preceded.

Among the benefits of the story of Noah as a whole is the bringing of good news to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions, since they have an example in Noah and those who were saved with him, and a warning to those who deny him, since there is a warning in what happened to the deniers of Noah, peace be upon him.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed, among those of his party was Abraham﴾ [As-Saffat 83].

Among the benefits of His words, ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ [As-Saffat 80], is that the doer of good is rewarded with the like of what Noah, peace be upon him, was rewarded: being saved from destruction and having his honour kept free from bad mention. The more a person does good, the greater his reward and the safer he is.

Among the benefits of the verse is the establishment of analogical reasoning (*qiyās*), in His words ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾, meaning that We reward every doer of good with the like of this recompense.

Among its benefits is that Allah, the Exalted, attaches reward, punishment, praise and blame to attributes, not to individuals, because He attached the reward to goodness. For this reason, none of Allah's rulings, the Exalted, was ever restricted to a particular person for his own person. Even the special privileges of the messengers are not special privileges of individuals, but of attributes, because they have an added attribute beyond others, namely the attribute of prophethood and messengerhood, so they were singled out with some rulings suited to their station. But that a particular person be singled out simply because he is so-and-so the son of so-and-so, for example, does not exist in the Sharia, because Allah, the Exalted, establishes rulings and attaches them to attributes, not to individuals.

Among the benefits of the verse are His words ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants﴾ [As-Saffat 81]. This points to the perfection of these two attributes, servanthood and faith, and that they are the most noble attributes a person can possess: to be a servant of Allah and a believer in Him. Allah said, "Indeed, he was among Our believing servants," meaning Noah. Noah, peace be upon him, is among the Ulu al-'Azm (the resolute messengers). So if being among Allah's believing servants is among his virtues and excellences, this indicates the excellence of servanthood and faith.

Among the benefits of His words, ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ [As-Saffat 82], is the demonstration of Allah's wisdom, the Exalted, in that He drowned those who denied His messenger, peace be upon him, indeed those who denied His messengers, because Allah said: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 105]. The denial of the people of Noah was not because he was Noah, but because of what he brought. For this reason, denying one messenger is denying all the messengers, because it is a denial of the category of messengerhood, not of the person of the messenger.

Among its benefits too is the establishment of justice by drowning these deniers, because Allah, the Exalted, did not drown them unjustly; rather, they were the ones who wronged themselves.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 64–82 (part 1 of 6):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat 64]. Look at these sentences: is there connection (ittisal) between them or disconnection (inqita')? In rhetoric, is there a rhetorical connection, or is there a disconnection between them?
* Student: Connection.
* The Shaykh: No, disconnection; because connection (ittisal) is conjunction with the letter waw, and here each sentence stands independently. The wisdom in this is so that a person knows about this tree from each verse by a separate attribute, as if each attribute on its own suffices apart from the rest of the attributes. So how many (...) for the wrongdoers. Is this not among the greatest of the descriptions that cause fear when one denies this tree?
﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of Hellfire﴾.
* Student: "From the root of Hellfire."
* The Shaykh: ﴿in the root of Hellfire﴾ this is Qur'an.
* Student: I say: is there not a reading variant here?
* The Shaykh: There is no reading variant at all. ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of Hellfire﴾ (i.e., the bottom of Hell, whose branches rise up to its levels). ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of Hellfire﴾. We have previously discussed whether this tree is one for the individual, or one in kind and genus? And we said: there are two possibilities. It may be that it is a large tree that fills the entire Fire, and branches from it extend through its levels, as is the apparent meaning of the author's words. And it may be that it is a multitude of trees, but it is spoken of in the singular in terms of its type, as when you see a tree in the desert and say: "This tree tastes bitter, its taste is sweet, its taste is such-and-such." You do not mean this one single tree; you mean this kind and this type. So the zaqqum tree may be one tree that has filled the Fire with its branches, and Allah is capable of all things. Otherwise, the Fire is deep in its bottom, as in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) when we heard a crash, and he said: "Do you know what this is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "This is a stone that was thrown into the Fire and it has been falling until it reached its bottom, seventy autumns ago."[[Recorded by Muslim (2844/31) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]
That is, for seventy years it has been falling in the Fire and has not reached its bottom. If we say this tree is one, and that its branches have filled the levels of the Fire, then Allah is capable of all things. And if we say it is one in genus and type, there is no difficulty in that.
He says: ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of Hellfire﴾. And what do you imagine of this fiery tree that springs forth from the root of Hellfire? Its place of growth will have an effect on it, because the place of growth affects what grows in it. Even a single species, if planted in this soil, differs from what it would be if planted in another soil, though it is one species. This tree that springs forth from the root of Hellfire will have the effect of its place of growth upon it. For this reason He said: ﴿in the root of Hellfire﴾, and did not say: "in Hellfire," to show that its roots are deep in the Fire, may Allah protect us.
He says: (﴿Its shoots﴾ likened to the shoots of the palm tree ﴿as if they were the heads of devils﴾ i.e., the ugly-looking serpents).
﴿Its shoots﴾ means the fruit which resembles the spathe of the date palm ﴿as if they were the heads of devils﴾. "Shayatin" is the plural of "shaytan." Is the intended meaning the true devil, or a kind of serpent as the author said? If we look at the apparent wording, we say the intended meaning is the true devil. The possibility that it means a kind of serpent of ugly appearance is valid, because a repulsive animal may be called a shaytan, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The black dog is a shaytan."[[Recorded by Muslim (510/265) from the hadith of Abu Dharr.]]
But our duty, as we have often mentioned, is to keep the Qur'an on its apparent meaning, and to say: the intended meaning of "shayatin" is the well-known devil. The comparison to the heads of devils is made even though people have not seen them, because everyone knows that whatever is attributed to the devil is ugly and repulsive, and no one inclines toward it. So the comparison here is to something imagined in the mind, not to something known through the senses, and on this basis it is among the most eloquent of ugly comparisons. There is no need to say they are serpents; even if we said they are serpents, are these serpents known to everyone? A serpent that only a rare few people know does not repel people. Indeed, when the author said they are serpents, he lowered the sense of ugliness in a person's soul. But with ﴿as if they were the heads of devils﴾, a person's skin crawls and his hair stands on end when he hears this ugly comparison. On this basis, the correct view is that the intended meaning is the real heads of devils, but they are compared to them because it is known to all people that they are ugly and repulsive.
(﴿Then indeed they will eat from it﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿and fill their bellies with it﴾, despite its ugliness, due to the intensity of their hunger.) I seek refuge in Allah. ﴿Then indeed they will eat from it﴾: the sentence here is a nominal sentence emphasized by "inna" and the "lam," is it not? It is to convey that their eating is continuous, because a nominal sentence conveys establishment and continuity, and it is emphasized by "inna" and the "lam" to indicate that they will eat from it with emphatic eating, even though it is ugly in appearance and foul in taste and smell. But, may Allah protect us, the severe hunger compels them to eat from it by force, without desire and without pleasure, only to fill their bellies. Even so, if a person were in this world he might prefer death to eating from this, but in the Fire they are punished by eating from it. For this reason He said: ﴿Then indeed they will eat from it, and fill their bellies with it﴾. We ask Allah for well-being. That is, they will not be satisfied, and they will not limit themselves to necessity. When you are in this world and extremely hungry, and a rotten piece of meat is offered to you, do you fill your stomach with it? You eat only what is necessary. If you tried to fill your stomach, your soul would refuse, and if you did fill it, you would almost vomit it. But in the Fire they are punished by it, so they do not eat only what they need; rather they fill their bellies, eating and saying: "Bring more, bring more." Just as they are compelled to drink boiling water, drinking it like thirsty camels that have gone astray. This is part of the intensity of their punishment, may Allah protect us: their condition reaches such extreme hunger that it compels them to eat this evil tree and fill their bellies with it, and such extreme thirst that it compels them to drink the ḥamīm, which is scalding water from which they gain no benefit. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And they are given boiling water to drink, which cuts their intestines to pieces﴾ [Muhammad 15]. And He, Mighty and Majestic, said of their bathing: ﴿Boiling water will be poured over their heads, by which what is in their bellies and their skins will be melted﴾ [al-Hajj 19-20]. Its heat reaches what is in the bellies, though the rest of the body stands between it and them, yet the heat reaches that, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The fire of Allah, kindled, which rises over the hearts﴾ [al-Humazah 6-7]. It reaches the hearts. We ask Allah for safety. May Allah save us from the Fire. He says: ﴿filling their bellies with it﴾.
As for His words: ﴿al-buṭūn﴾ ("the bellies"), the "al" here is for previous mention (al-'ahd). Which mention? Is it mental (dhihni) knowledge? Can we not say it is mention previously stated (al-'ahd al-dhikri), since something indicating the belly was already mentioned? We say: mention previously stated must have the same word preceding it, and here the word did not precede it, but what indicates it preceded in His words ﴿Then indeed they will eat﴾, because one eats only if he has a belly. ﴿Filling their bellies with it﴾ means the bellies of them.
He says: ﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of boiling water﴾ ("thumma," then, is a conjunction indicating what? Order and delay, which shows that when they eat they become thirsty, and when they are thirsty the water does not come to them immediately, but after a delay that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained in His words: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal that scalds the faces﴾ [al-Kahf 29]). So they are not given water quickly after eating and becoming thirsty. No, they cry for help and call for water to come and cool the blaze of thirst for them. But when this water is given to them, they are given a mixture of boiling water, meaning water of enormous heat. The "shawb" is the blaze of the Fire. This blaze is explained by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in the verse I quoted a moment ago: when the water is brought near their faces to drink, it scalds their faces, may Allah protect us, scalding them until their flesh falls off from its intensity. When they drink it, their intestines receive it, but they are cut to pieces by it: ﴿And they are given boiling water to drink, which cuts their intestines to pieces﴾ [Muhammad 15].
Brothers, we are not speaking of the tales of the ancients; we are speaking of a real matter which, if a person truly imagines it, distresses him in reality. This is not something merely said or reported; it is the truth. The truth concerns these tyrants who denied the messengers of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and exchanged Allah's blessing for disbelief. All of this will happen; it is not the report of the ancients. Therefore, when we recite such verses we must feel that this is the certainty of knowledge (ʿilm al-yaqīn), and that it will be the certainty of sight (ḥaqq al-yaqīn). After they are made thirsty and cry for help, this matter is that they are not relieved with cold water nor with sweet water, but with a mixture of boiling water (i.e., hot water they drink, which mixes with the food from the tree, so that it becomes a mixture for it).
The author explained "shawb" here as "mixing," as in "I mixed the water with milk," meaning I blended it. It fits both this and that: it is a mixture, and it is also the blaze of the heat of this boiling water. All of this will occur: the blaze occurs before drinking, and the mixture occurs after drinking.
﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a mixture of boiling water (67). Then indeed their return is to Hellfire﴾. That is, after that their return will be to Hellfire. The sentence "(what you see)" is a nominal sentence. He did not say "then they will return," but said: ﴿Then indeed their return is to Hellfire﴾, emphasized by what? By two emphases: "inna" and the "lam." This sequence contains a difficulty: is it a sequence of mention (tartib dhikri) or a sequence of meaning (tartib ma'nawi)? The author holds that it is a sequence of meaning, but it may be a sequence of mention; that is, after Allah mentioned the types of punishment they will suffer, He explained that their final destination is Hellfire, meaning this Hellfire in which these punishments are, and they return to nothing other than it. The sequence of mention exists in the Arabic language, as in the poet's saying:

Indeed, whoever rules, then his father rules,
then after that his grandfather rules.

The rule of the father precedes my rule, and the rule of the grandfather precedes the rule of the father. Or it may be said: as Allah said about them: ﴿Every time they wish to come out of it, they are returned into it﴾ [al-Sajdah 20], and that they are brought near its gates and given this boiling water to drink, so that their souls long to come out and they have some hope. When they have that hope and are then returned to the root of Hellfire, this becomes a greater punishment for them, because the arrival of despair after hope is more severe than despair that continues, since hope lifts despair; when they are returned to punishment, despair returns and is more painful.

Have you seen: if a man were shackled before you, and you began trying to unfasten his shackle, he would rejoice, would he not? But if you returned, tightened the bonds on him, and brought another shackle, his despair and grief would increase upon his grief, after he had seen the glimmer of hope and was humiliated again. These people, may Allah protect us, every time they wish to come out and some hope arises for them, they are returned into it. So He says: ﴿Then indeed their return is to Hellfire﴾, that is, to the root of Hellfire, which they had hoped to come out of when they were brought near its gates.

﴿Indeed they found their fathers astray (69). So they hasten onward in their footsteps (70)﴾. ﴿Indeed they﴾: that is, these wrongdoers who are punished with this punishment. ﴿Found﴾: that is (found), ﴿their fathers﴾, and "alfa" here means "found," as in His words: ﴿And they found her master at the door﴾ [Yusuf 25]. And ﴿alfayā﴾ means they found her master.

..................... ∗∗∗ And he found her words to be a lie and a deception.

That is, he found her words. So the meaning of ﴿they found their fathers﴾ is: they found them astray, lost from the truth. He says: ﴿So they hasten onward in their footsteps﴾ [al-Saffat 70]. They found their fathers astray after the proof had been established against them by their fathers' misguidance, but did they follow the proof? No. He said: ﴿So they﴾, meaning after they found their fathers astray, may Allah protect us, they are ﴿hastening in their footsteps﴾, that is, they are driven and urged on, and "hur'a" means to hurry and rush toward something. So they are upon their fathers' footsteps and upon what their fathers were upon of shirk and wrongdoing, hastening; that is, driven hard, rushing to follow their footsteps. The messengers had come to them with the truth, but how did they answer? ﴿They said: We found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf 23], and in another verse: ﴿And we are upon their footsteps guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf 22]; that is, they did not accept from them. They knew their fathers were astray, yet, may Allah protect us, they remained upon what they were upon, and indeed they raced to it and held even more firmly to what their fathers had been upon.

(﴿So they hasten in their footsteps﴾: they are driven and urged on to follow them, so they rush to it.) The whole discussion concerns the polytheists of Quraysh, as evidenced by His words: ﴿And certainly most of the ancients went astray before them﴾. This sentence contains three emphases; can you identify them? ﴿And certainly went astray﴾.
* Student: "Certainly."
* The Shaykh: What is "la-qad"?
* Student: "Laqad," and the conjunction.
* The Shaykh: The "lam" and "qad."
