The author said: (They were astrologers. They went out to a festival of theirs and left their food by their idols, claiming it would be blessed, and when they returned they would eat it. They said to the master Abraham: come out with us. ﴿So he glanced at the stars﴾.) This statement which the author supposes to be omitted for the sake of brevity: by what? By omission, it requires proof that these people prepared food, placed it by these idols for blessing, intended to eat it after their return, and asked Abraham to come out with them. All of this requires evidence. We noted earlier that the stories of the earlier prophets are known only to God: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you, the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows but God?﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. If that is the case, we do not receive the reports of these people except from revelation, either from the Book or from the Sunnah. Whatever reports of them come by another route, namely not the route of revelation, we suspend judgment on, unless we know that they contradict the sharias. If we know they contradict the sharias, we are obliged to reject them.

So in this story we should limit ourselves to what God, Mighty and Majestic, has mentioned: that Abraham, one day, glanced at the stars in order to argue with his people and show their inability. This is like His saying in Surah al-An'am about Abraham's argument with his people: ﴿When the night covered him, he saw a star and said, this is my lord. But when it set, he said, I do not love those that set﴾ [al-An'am 76], that is, that disappeared, ﴿for a lord cannot disappear from what he lords over.﴾ Since this star disappeared, he knew it was not a lord, because a lord must have complete care for those he lords over.

﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said, this is my lord﴾ [al-An'am 77]. The moon is clearer and more evident than the star. ﴿But when it set, he said: unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people﴾ [al-An'am 77]. This is an allusion to his people, saying they are misguided. Notice the progression: first he said ﴿I do not love those that set﴾, meaning he disowned that. The second was an implication that his people were misguided: ﴿unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people﴾ (77). ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said: this is my lord, this is greater﴾ [al-An'am 77–78]. Indeed the sun is greater than the moon. ﴿But when it set, he said: O my people, I am free from what you associate﴾ [al-An'am 78]. He declared their polytheism and his disassociation from them, and this is from the perfection of his argument. So it is not far-fetched that this verse ﴿So he glanced at the stars﴾ [al-Saffat 88] is of the kind of argument mentioned in Surah al-An'am.

* Student: May God be good to you, Shaykh. (...) His Lord's saying, glorified: ﴿came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾, that this is after death (...) In Surah al-Shu'ara: ﴿And do not disgrace me on the day they are resurrected. The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara 87–89]. We say: this supports (...) after death.

* Shaykh: This perhaps supports that it is after death, but ﴿when he said to his father and his people﴾ is in life, and this is what prevents a firm judgment that it is after death. For this reason we leave ﴿came to his Lord﴾ open: God knows best whether it was after death or during life.

* Shaykh: Yes, this must be shown to be false.

* Student: Usually the source of the permission is the Dar al-Ifta.

* Shaykh: Strange, I have not seen this.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, but from Dar al-Ifta (...).

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Show it to me, so we can write to them about the matter.

* Shaykh: In any case, we will look at it and alert them.

* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. May Allah keep you safe. The eclipse now, they know the past and the future. Do they now predict eclipses in the future or not? They predict future eclipses now. They tell you: the eclipse begins at such-and-such minute and ends at such-and-such minute. They know the past just as they know the future. They calculated the eclipse that occurred during the time of the Messenger ﷺ, on that day, Monday, corresponding to the twenty-ninth of the month of Shawwal in the tenth year, at eight-thirty by Cairo time, seven-thirty by the time of the Kingdom. I checked this time against the European timing, I think, I don't know, by Allah, in January, I forgot which day of January, and I found that between its eclipse and the rising of the sun there were forty minutes, that is, two-thirds of an hour. And some of the narrations that came in Musnad Ahmad: "When the sun had risen the height of a spear."[[(20178) from the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub.]]
* Student: It seems they confirm this statement, as if they accept it?
* Shaykh: Yes, because this (...) by calculation, and something past, known by calculation. And in it is evidence that the historians, do you know when the historians say? They say: Ibrahim, may Allah be pleased with him, died on the tenth of Rabi' al-Awwal. Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet ﷺ, on the tenth of Rabi' al-Awwal. And this is not possible, the sun can never be eclipsed on the tenth day.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Because the cause of a solar eclipse is the moon coming between it and the earth. On the tenth of Rabi' it is not possible, this is never possible.
* Student: And the moon, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: And the moon is only in the nights of full moon.
* Student: (...) meaning the fifteenth night.
* Shaykh: The fourteenth, the fifteenth, the sixteenth, meaning the nights of full moon are possible; because the cause of its eclipse, the natural cause, is the earth coming between it and the sun. For this reason, when the scholars assumed: if the sun rises while the moon is eclipsed, the eclipse prayer is not prayed. We say: this is an impossible assumption; because it is not possible for the sun and the moon to meet at a horizon so that an eclipse occurs, ever, or not? Because the eclipse requires that the moon be beneath the earth so that the earth comes between it and the sun.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: I have never heard that (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it was eclipsed, but since it was not clear, what (...) no, it was eclipsed here, how we put a mirror, because you cannot see it with the eye, but we put a mirror and saw it eclipsed, perhaps about between an eighth and a quarter.
* Student: But it was announced many times, Shaykh (...) it was announced more than once (...).
* Shaykh: No, I have no doubt about it, and this is something mentioned by the scholars among the verifiers, such as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and others, and Ibn Hazm (...) it is not possible. This is something known by calculation, it is not knowledge of the unseen.
* Student: The view of the jurists when they said: if an eclipse coincides with a festival.
* Shaykh: It is never possible.
* Student: So they assumed.
* Shaykh: If an eclipse coincided with a festival, we say this in Shawwal, meaning on the Festival of Fitr: if an eclipse coincided with a festival, it is known that the day is not a festival, and that the witnesses erred in their testimony; because the illusion of the observer is a possible matter, but the change of the custom which Allah established is an impossible matter. Even the scholars also said: if an eclipse occurred while he was standing at Arafat (a lunar eclipse), he prays and then departs, so that the prayer is not missed. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah says: this is a hypothetical matter that can never occur. But the scholars, the jurists, assume things for training in the legal rulings, such as when they say: they assumed twenty grandmothers in the wills and inheritances, twenty grandmothers. When are there twenty grandmothers? Setting aside the one connected with two parents, or three, or four, or five, twenty grandmothers, where? Who will have twenty grandmothers inheriting? In any case, these are arithmetical problems with no difficulty in them (...).
* * *

* Another student: The interrogation here is for threat.
* Shaykh: For threat. He threatens them by Allah, mighty and majestic: if they worship other than Him, what do you think He will do to you, will He leave you or not? This, according to the author's view, has another meaning, which we mentioned.

So what is your opinion about your Lord, will He permit you to associate with Him? Because of his saying ﷺ: "I am free of him and his partner."[[Narrated by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] (...) The fourth aspect: So what is your opinion about the greatness of Allah, glorified and exalted.
* Shaykh: These are four aspects, all of which the verse can bear. And it has passed with us that if a verse can bear several aspects that do not contradict one another, it is taken to all of them.
His saying: ﴿about the Lord of the worlds﴾, and He did not say "about Allah, mighty and majestic." Why? We will mention it now, because we did not mention it yesterday. He said: ﴿about the Lord of the worlds﴾ (...) what do you think of Allah? It is an indication that these worshipped gods are themselves created and nurtured by Allah, mighty and majestic, so how can they be worshipped besides Him? For these gods are included within ﴿the worlds﴾, because what is meant by ﴿the worlds﴾ is whatever is other than Allah, mighty and majestic, and among them or among whom are these worshipped gods. So if these worshipped gods are, in your view, included among the things nurtured by Allah, mighty and majestic, how can you worship them alongside Allah? And Allah, glorified, has set forth an example of this in a human slave: would a master be pleased that his slave share with him in what is peculiar to his master? ﴿Allah presents to you an example from yourselves: do you have among your slaves any partners in what We have provided for you, so that you are equal therein?﴾ [Ar-Rum 28] What is the answer?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: ﴿Allah presents to you an example from yourselves: do you have among those your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided for you, so that you are equal therein?﴾
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it is not so: ﴿You fear them as you fear one another﴾ [Ar-Rum 28]. It is not this. So we have no partners among what our right hands possess in what Allah has provided us. Reflect on His saying: ﴿in what We have provided for you﴾, and it becomes clear to you that this is the provision of Allah, and yet the masters monopolize it from whom? From the slaves. ﴿so that you are equal therein﴾. And this is the point of the interrogation and the answer: no. We only said that this is the point of the interrogation because they are partners with them in what Allah has provided them, but only to the measure of sustenance and necessity. The slave shares with his master: he eats, drinks, and dresses as the master does, and all of this is sharing in the provision of Allah. But are they equal to their masters in that? No. If that is so, then why do you make others equal to Allah in worship? The point is that His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ — peace and blessings be upon him, he intended by it to establish proof that these gods cannot be gods. Why? Because they are nurtured by Allah, mighty and majestic, and the nurtured is a slave who cannot be a lord.
(﴿So he glanced a glance at the stars﴾ — deceiving them into thinking he relies upon them, so that they would rely upon him — ﴿and said: Indeed, I am ill﴾ — sick, i.e., I will become sick ﴿So they turned away from him﴾ — to their festival ﴿departing﴾) ... to the end. ﴿He glanced a glance at the stars﴾: this is Ibrahim, peace be upon him. ﴿He glanced a glance at the stars﴾, i.e., he looked at them. He only did that because his people used to worship the stars and set up temples for them on earth, and the origin of worship was for the stars. So he looked at these stars, and when he looked he said: ﴿Indeed, I am ill﴾. He looked at them while not believing in them, peace be upon him, as a matter of tawriyah (equivocation, using an expression that has a double meaning). This is tawriyah by action. Just as tawriyah can be by speech, it can be by action. Tawriyah by speech is common and well known; tawriyah by action is that a person shows another that he sees something when he does not want it, or that he turns away from something while he has set his mind on it. Perhaps you hear two people talking, and you do something as if you are turning away from them, meaning you begin, for example, to occupy yourself with a book or some work, to show them that you are heedless of what they are saying, but you are recording what they say. This is tawriyah by action, because you have shown others something contrary to what he sees.
And tawriyah by speech is that you show another something contrary to what he hears. So Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made tawriyah by looking at the stars, then said: ﴿Indeed, I am ill﴾ [As-Saffat 89]. The author explained "ill" with the meaning "I will become ill." This is also tawriyah, tawriyah by speech; because the apparent meaning of the words ﴿I am ill﴾ is "now, and I cannot go out with you," but he meant "I am ill" as "I will become ill," because the active participle is suitable for the present and future tenses, so it is correct to say: "I am present now," and "I am present tomorrow," is it not so? Since it is suitable for both, and he glanced a glance at the stars and said: "I am ill," they turned away from him and left him, while he, peace and blessings be upon him, by this action intended a matter that would become clear later.
(﴿So they turned away from him, departing﴾ [As-Saffat 90, 91] — i.e., he inclined secretly toward their gods, which were idols, and there was food with them.) He inclined to their gods, which are the idols they worship. He said: (and there was food with them), and the author derived this from His saying: ﴿He said: Will you not eat?﴾, because offering them food indicates that food was present.
(He inclined to their gods) — i.e., he turned secretly and went off secretly. And the "rawagan," as is well known, is speed; the speed of a person, but in a way that no one perceives. He went secretly to these gods, i.e., their worshipped objects. ﴿He said: Will you not eat?﴾ And "alā" here is for offering. Is this statement by way of compulsion? The answer: No, it is not by way of compulsion, and he could not compel them to eat, because he knows they will not eat. But he said it by way of mockery and derision, and to bind these worshippers to the fact that these idols do not deserve worship, not because they are independent of food, but because they do not reason or know. And whoever does not reason or know cannot be worshipped. Then even if the placing of food before them by their people is valid, this is evidence that they are not fit for divinity, because the god is independent of others. For this reason Allah established the proof that Jesus son of Mary and his mother are not two gods, by their eating food, and that He, glorified and exalted, alone is the true God, by His giving food and not being fed. So the need of what is worshipped for food is evidence of its deficiency, and that it is not fit to be a god. But they, out of their foolishness, place food before them as if they need it, eat it, and dispose of it.
He says: ﴿He said: Will you not eat? [91] What is wrong with you that you do not speak?﴾ [As-Saffat 91, 92] ﴿What is wrong with you﴾: the interrogation here is for belittling; i.e., he belittles them by their not speaking. He addressed these idols in the manner of addressing rational beings, in His saying: ﴿What is wrong with you﴾, and did not say "what is wrong with you" in the feminine, descending to the level of their owners who consider them to be beings of knowledge and of acceptance and repulsion for them: ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not speak?﴾ That is: what prevents you from speaking, if you are gods?!
If someone asks: was this address to these idols in the absence of their worshippers? If you say yes, what is the benefit of this address? And if you say no, then how is the answer to His saying: ﴿So they turned away from him, departing﴾ [As-Saffat 90]?
The answer is that we say: their worshippers did not all depart from them, but there were guards with them such that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, speaking to these idols in such words is appropriate. Otherwise, if no one was with them, his words would be idle, with no benefit. But there were guards with them who could learn from them what Ibrahim had learned, by his offering them food and their not speaking. And if they do not speak, and have no will and no awareness, they are not fit for worship.
﴿What is wrong with you that you do not speak? [92] Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾ [As-Saffat 92, 93]. At the beginning of the verses He says: ﴿He inclined to their gods﴾, i.e., he turned secretly. And "ilā" (to) indicates the goal. But here He said: ﴿he turned upon them, striking﴾. He said "upon them" rather than "to them," because the striking fell upon these idols, so that he, peace be upon him, would break them.
﴿Then he turned upon them﴾, i.e., upon these gods. As I pointed out at first, he addressed them in the manner of addressing rational beings, and so he used the plural pronoun of the masculine.
﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand﴾: with force, and so he broke them.
His saying ﴿striking﴾ is a verbal noun in a position of circumstance; i.e., he turned upon them, striking with the right hand. It may also be a verbal noun of a deleted verb, and the estimate is: he turned upon them, striking a strike.
The author's statement "with the right hand, i.e., with force" is not necessarily fixed; it may be that it means with the right hand, i.e., with the right hand, and he struck with it; because the right hand is generally the instrument of work, and because it — the right hand — is generally stronger than the left hand. For this reason you find that it is rare for some people to be left-handed, working with the left hand as they work with the right.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verses 83–96 (part 3 of 4):**

﴿So he turned upon them, striking them with the right hand.﴾ (Striking with force, so he broke them. Then the news reached his people, and those who saw him ﴿came hastening toward him﴾ [al-Saffat 94], meaning they walked quickly. They said to him: "We worship them, and you break them!")

When his people learned what he had done, they came toward him hastening, that is, rushing in groups. The evidence for this is the verb *aqbalu* ("they came") with the conjunction *wa* ("and"). They came to him rushing, to object to him. Why did he break them? Allah the Exalted mentioned in Surah al-Anbiya': ﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is among the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Anbiya' 59]. They regarded this as injustice and aggression, so they came hastening to defend their gods. This is how idol-worshippers are: they defend idols, while the idols cannot help them. Yet they are soldiers mustered for them.

So these people came hastening toward Abraham to defend their gods. But he, upon him be peace, was steadfast for the sake of Allah. He said to them, rebuking them: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ [al-Saffat 95] (idols of stone and other materials?). The interrogative here is for rebuke and denunciation. In reality, it is for rebuke, denunciation and mockery. How can you worship something you carve with your own hands? Is it reasonable for the object of worship to be made by its worshipper?

The answer is: No. It is not reasonable. Only the most foolish of fools would do this: something you make with your own hand, then you worship it, humble yourself before it, turn to it, cling to it, and hope from it for benefit and harm! This is folly. But, may Allah protect us, when Allah blinds a person's insight, the sight of the eye does not benefit him. In the pre-Islamic period (*Jahiliyyah*) they used to do something similar. When they stopped in a land during a journey, they gathered four stones: three for supporting the cooking pot and one to be worshipped. Thus this worshipped stone became equal to the supports of the pots. Some of them say that they used to knead a god from *ajwah*, that is, dates: an image of dates which they worshipped besides Allah. When they got hungry, they ate it. They did not say, "Feed us," or "Prepare food for us." It itself was eaten. This is folly. Likewise were the companions of Abraham, upon him be peace, the people of Abraham: they made gods with their own hands, then they began to worship them.

The author's words *(asnaman)* ("idols") indicate that *tanhitun* ("you carve") takes two objects. The first is the returning pronoun to the relative clause, whose estimated form is *ma tanhitunahu* ("what you carve it"). The second is the omitted word which the author estimated: *a-ta'buduna ma tanhitunahu asnaman?* ("Do you worship what you carve, idols?").

He said: (﴿And Allah created you and what you make﴾ [al-Saffat 96], that is, your carving and what you carved. So worship Him alone. The *ma* is a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*). It is also said to be a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), and it is also said to be a qualifying indefinite (*mawsufah*).)

﴿And Allah created you﴾. If Allah is the Creator, then He is more worthy of worship. Who is more worthy of worship: the one who created you, or the ones you created? The one who created you. For this reason He said: ﴿And Allah created you and what you make﴾. He said: (your carving and what you carved). He, may Allah have mercy on him, gave the verbal noun and the passive participle: (your carving), indicating that *ma* may be a verbal-noun particle, and it may be a relative pronoun. If we make it a verbal-noun particle, the meaning is: "your carving." If we make it a relative pronoun, the meaning becomes: "what you carved."

Listen: "And Allah created you and your work" if we say it this way, *ma* becomes a verbal-noun particle. If we make the meaning "And Allah created you and what you make," *ma* becomes a relative pronoun. If we make *ma* a relative pronoun, a returning pronoun must refer back to it, and in the verse it is omitted, meaning "and what you make it." The necessary implication is one under both interpretations. If we say the meaning is "And Allah created you and your work," then the creator of the work is the creator of the product. If we make the meaning "And Allah created you and what you make," then, since Allah the Exalted created what is made, namely those who performed the work, this indicates the creation of the act and also the creation of the agent. Under either interpretation, the verse establishes the proof that these idols are not fit to be worshipped, because they are made.

﴿You and what you make﴾. They said: (*ma* is a verbal-noun particle; it is also said to be a relative pronoun, and it is also said to be a qualifying indefinite). What is meant by "qualifying"? The qualifying *ma* is that which is expressed by a qualifying indefinite noun. That is, "Allah created you and an idol you make," or "and idols you make." We do not say "and that which you make," but we say "and idols you make." The author has now informed us that *ma* has three meanings: that it may be a verbal-noun particle, a relative pronoun, and a qualifying indefinite. These are three of ten, because *ma* has ten meanings. Who can memorise the verse composed on this?

* Student:
*Mahamil (ma) are ten, if you wish to count them,*
*So keep to a verse free of poetic defect.*
*You will understand the conditional sense of the connective; so wonder*
*At its indefinite use, by a kaff, a negation, and an added* ... *the exaltation of the verbal noun.*

* The Shaykh: (*Ma* is a verbal-noun particle, it is also said to be a relative pronoun, and it is also said to be a qualifying indefinite.)

(*Sa-tafhamu*): the interrogative *ma*, as in: *ma hadha?* ("What is this?")

(*Shart*): the conditional *ma*, as in: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾ [al-Baqarah 197].

(*Al-wasl*): the relative *ma*.

(*Fa-'jab*): the exclamatory *ma*, as in: *ma ahsana hadha!* ("How beautiful this is!")

(*Li-nukriha*): the indefinite qualifying *ma*. You say: "I passed by a *ma* which is wonderful to you," meaning "by a thing which is wonderful to you." You also say: "I knew him a certain type," meaning a little type, so it is a qualifying indefinite.

(*Bi-kaff*): the restrictive (*kaffah*) *ma*, as in: ﴿Allah is only One God﴾ [al-Nisa' 171]. Here *ma* restrains the word from governing.

(*Wa-nafy*): the negative *ma*, as in: *ma hadara Zayd* ("Zayd did not attend").

(*Zid*): the superfluous *ma*, as in *idha ma* and *idha ma*, as in: ﴿When they are angry, they forgive﴾ [al-Shura 37].

*And O seeker, take this benefit: what comes after "idha" is superfluous.*

(*Ta'zim masdar*): meaning that it comes for exaltation. This is different from exclamation. For example, you say: "I passed by a *ma* which is awe-inspiring," meaning "by a great and awe-inspiring thing." Perhaps we also say that the exclamatory *ma* contains a kind of exaltation, since it indicates both exaltation and wonder.

(*Masdar*): the verbal-noun *ma*, and of it is this verse: ﴿And Allah created you and what you make﴾ [al-Saffat 96]. These are the ten meanings of *ma*. The student of grammar should memorise verses like these, because they delimit the meanings for him, just as the author of the poem said about the sentence that needs a *fa'* when it comes as the answer to a condition:

*A nominal sentence, a demanding sentence, a noun that is indeclinable,*
*And with *ma*, *qad*, *lan*, and the future particle (*sa*/*sawfa*).*

* Student: How great is Allah! Is it exclamatory or exaltation?

* The Shaykh: Usually the exclamatory has some kind of exaltation in it.

* Student: The saying: (...) ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾. "Indeed I am sick" of your gods, meaning sick from your worship of them. Is this the far meaning?

* The Shaykh: It is possible, but it is not the apparent one. Is he sick from their worship, an ailment?

* Student: Is this far meaning not the near meaning?

* The Shaykh: No. The near meaning is that he is sick now. This is the near meaning. What supports it is that he looked at the stars, and that he wanted to excuse himself from going with them.

* Student: If that is so, what is the meaning of ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating﴾ [al-Saffat 90]? When he said ﴿I am sick﴾, they turned away from him retreating?

* The Shaykh: They said: "This one cannot possibly go with us," so they took his sickness as an excuse for him.

* Student: If that is so, what is the evidence that when he was alone and addressed the idols, they had all gone away from him?

* The Shaykh: They did not all go away from him. There were people, the guards. It is not possible that they would leave these idols without soldiers. They must have had guards who honour and protect them.

* Student: (...) Is a psychological illness not called "I am sick"?

* The Shaykh: Psychological? Yes.

* Student: (...) a psychologically sick person from their worship..

* The Shaykh: This is what he said, meaning ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾ means that he is sick from the worship.

* Student: (...) in a way (...).

* The Shaykh: By Allah, I do not know.

* Student: O Shaykh, in another verse Allah says: ﴿They said, "Who has done this to our gods?"﴾ [al-Anbiya' 59]. It seems as if they did not know. If it were as we said, that they had guards, (...) this indicates that they did not recognise him. ﴿They said, "We heard a youth mention them, called Abraham"﴾ [al-Anbiya' 60]. That is, we did not see him when he broke them. We only heard him mention them with evil.

* The Shaykh: Do you not know that if they had seized him and said, "You are the one who did it the first time," and brought witnesses from among its keepers, its guards would not have been accepted by the people? But when they searched for him as if they were asking, this became further from accusation, as Joseph, upon him be peace, did when he put the drinking cup in his brother's baggage. When he first searched, he began with their containers before his brother's container. He knew it was in his brother's container, but if he had gone straight to extract it from his brother's container from the first time, they would have doubted that. They say this so that it will not be said that they are accused, so they come to Abraham at the first moment, and perhaps the guards had found out.

As for the benefits, they begin from His saying: ﴿And indeed, among his followers﴾.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham﴾ [al-Saffat 83].

* Among the benefits of this verse and what follows: the origin of the religion of the prophets is one. They are all followers of one another, strengthening each other's call. The evidence for this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya' 25]. ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger﴾, meaning any messenger at all, ﴿except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the prophets, even if a long time passes between them, come only with revelation from Allah. When much time passes, people forget the covenant, it fades and is effaced. But if it is by revelation from Allah, it is renewed according to the renewal of that revelation, because between Abraham and Noah there were long periods.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: praise of Abraham. Its basis is that he was a follower of one who calls to the Oneness of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Everyone who follows one who calls to Allah is, without doubt, worthy of praise.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse in His saying: ﴿When he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾: praise of Abraham again, in that he came to Allah the Glorified and Exalted with a sound heart. This quality, although negative in form, includes perfection, because when the heart is free from doubts and desires, it becomes purely for Allah in intention, will and action. So in it is praise of Abraham for the soundness of his heart.

* Among its benefits: Allah the Glorified and Exalted's care for Abraham, shown by attributing lordship to him: "when he came to his Lord." Is this lordship specific or general? Specific. Specific lordship implies more care than general lordship, because those nurtured by general lordship are covered by general mercy, but those with specific lordship have specific mercy.

* Among the benefits of His saying: ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾: the demonstration of Abraham's strength, upon him be peace, and that the blame of no blamer took him in matters of Allah. A man who addresses his father and people with this expression is strong for the sake of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because it is customary for a person to favour his father and his people, but Abraham, upon him be peace, did not favour them. Rather, he denounced them and said: ﴿What do you worship?﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that nearness by lineage to the people of good does not benefit a person at all. Abraham was, in relation to his father, the nearest thing, because he was a part of him. Yet his father did not benefit from him, rather he was a polytheist, and he even argued with his son about it. This is supported by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (to be good) to his parents. His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years. Give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the destination. And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them﴾ [Luqman 14–15]. This indicates the difference between the son and the parents, to the point that they strive with him to make him associate partners with Allah, and yet Allah the Exalted said: Do not obey them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the correctness of attributing a people to a messenger even if they denied him, because of His saying: ﴿When he said to his father and his people﴾. Attribution by lineage does not mean disavowal of the religion. A person may be attributed to his father who is a disbeliever, and it is not said that this is an act of loyalty; rather, this is a matter of reality. Lineage never ceases to exist because of a difference in religion. Look at the saying of Allah the Exalted to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And your people denied it, though it is the truth﴾ [al-An'am 66]. He attributed them to him while attributing the denial to them. This shows that a person may come from a disbelieving people and be attributed to them, and that this does not harm his religion.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the foolishness of these people, in that they worshipped something besides Allah. For this reason, the most intelligent of creation, Abraham, denounced them, saying: ﴿What do you worship?﴾. Allah has guided to this in His saying: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ [al-Baqarah 130]. The religion of Abraham is the *hanifiyyah*, based on sincerity. Whoever opposes that has made a fool of himself, that is, has put himself into foolishness, which is the opposite of guidance and reason.

* Among the benefits of the noble verses in His saying: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than Allah that you desire?﴾: that everyone who claims that there is a god besides Allah whom he worships is a liar and deceiver, because of His saying: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than Allah that you desire?﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the claim that these are gods does not give them the attribute of divinity, because falsehood does not turn realities from their origin. If you say, for example: "Zayd arrived," and he did not arrive, he was not an arrival. These gods, even if they made them gods, will not be gods, as Allah the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿They are only names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ [al-Najm 23].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that those who worship gods besides Allah intend them with a true intention in their hearts, as they turn to them with their limbs. Therefore He said: ﴿Besides Allah you desire﴾. They do not worship them merely out of habit, but they worship them with intention and devotion, to the point that they forgot Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of the noble verses in His saying: ﴿So what is your assumption about the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Saffat 87]: the severe denunciation by Abraham, upon him be peace, of his people, when he asked them in rebuke: What do you suppose about the Lord of the worlds if you worship other than Him? Do you suppose Him deficient, not deserving to be worshipped alone? Do you suppose Him heedless of your deeds, so that He leaves you without punishment? Do you suppose He is pleased that another be worshipped along with Him? None of this is so. Your assumption is a mistaken assumption.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of the lordship of Allah the Glorified and Exalted, because of His saying: ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾.

* Among its benefits: the establishment of proof against the opponent by means of something he cannot deny, because of His saying: ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾. "The worlds" includes even the gods they worship. If their gods are things that are lorded over, how could they be worshipped? This is a contradiction! It has already passed us during the lesson that whoever acknowledges Allah's sole lordship must acknowledge His sole divinity, or else he is contradictory, since only the Lord, the Creator, the Owner, the Governor deserves worship. Whoever is not like this does not deserve to be worshipped.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that creation is a sign of its Creator, a token and a proof. Creation, insofar as it is a sign of the existence of Allah, His power, the perfection of His authority and His governance, is a known matter. But it may also be a sign of a specific meaning. For example, the falling of rain is a sign of mercy, and calamities, fear, and loss of wealth, and of souls, are signs of His punishment, His jealousy, and His vengeance against those who disobey Him. The essential point is that there is a general meaning in which all signs share, which is that they indicate the existence of the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic, the perfection of His lordship and authority, and that nothing among these created things opposes Him. There is also a specific meaning to each sign and what it indicates by itself, such as the indication of rain for mercy, and the indication of drought for vengeance against those who disobey Him.

Among the benefits of the verses, in His saying ﴿So he cast a glance at the stars﴾ [al-Saffat 88]: the permissibility of tawriya (a speaker conveying to the addressee something other than what he intends, such that the addressee understands a meaning other than the one meant). Tawriya may be obligatory, recommended, permissible, disliked, or forbidden, so the five legal categories apply to it. If tawriya becomes the means of rescuing an innocent person from destruction, for example, it becomes obligatory. Such as when a wrongdoer comes asking about a person he wants to kill, while you know where that person is; here you must use tawriya, because it saves an innocent person from destruction. It may be recommended, as when someone asks you about a righteous deed you performed and you fear falling into showing off (riya') if you tell him about it; what then? Here tawriya is recommended. It may be permissible, as when you use tawriya with someone who wants to wrong you, or who wants from you something you do not wish to give, such as saying: "O brother, lend me a hundred thousand riyals," while you know this man is destitute or a procrastinator who will not fulfil his obligation; here tawriya is permissible. It may be disliked, as when it is used without a reason.

The correct view is that it is disliked, because of the risk that a person is attributed to lying: if a person uses tawriya and then the matter turns out to be contrary to what the listener understood, he is attributed to lying. This is disliked, and only a reason makes it permissible. It may be forbidden, as when two men dispute before a judge, one claims a right against the other, the defendant bears the burden of denial and the oath falls on him. If the defendant swears before the judge, saying: "By God, he has nothing with me," the judge understands from such a phrase the defendant's innocence, while the defendant intended by "ma" (what) to be a relative pronoun, meaning: "By God, the one who has something with me [is nothing]." We say that this tawriya is forbidden, because it includes denying a right that he is obliged to discharge. In short, the five categories apply to tawriya.

If someone asks: what is the default ruling regarding it, permissibility or disliking? The closer view is that the default is disliking, but it may be permissible, recommended, obligatory, or forbidden.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of attributing a description to a person with regard to the future, derived from His saying ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾. He is not sick at present, but every person is liable to fall sick. It is also possible that by his saying ﴿I am sick﴾ he meant "weak," in view of His saying ﴿and man was created weak﴾ [al-Nisa' 28]. Then is the description here present or future? It is present.

Among the benefits of His saying ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating﴾ [al-Saffat 90]: when he said this statement to them, and after he had cast a glance at the stars, they were convinced. It follows from this that a person in error may be convinced of something even if it is false in reality, and that is so: when a person in error is deceived with his falsehood, he thinks it is true, adopts it, and regards it.

Among the benefits of His saying ﴿Then he turned to their gods and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ up to the end [al-Saffat 91-92]: the demonstration of Ibrahim's strength, as previously mentioned, in that he went swiftly and secretly to these gods to break them. But he, peace be upon him, did not break them until he had established proof against those who were with them, that these gods are not fit to be gods, because they do not reason, do not speak, do not know what benefits them, and do not bring benefit to themselves; so how much more so to others. Therefore he said: ﴿He said, "Will you not eat? What is wrong with you that you do not speak?"﴾

Among the benefits of this noble verse also: the permissibility of tawriya as already mentioned, because he, peace be upon him, knew that these idols neither eat nor speak, but by this question he intended to establish the proof against those who were guarding them and defending them, that these idols are not fit for worship, because they do not know what benefits or harms them, and do not bring benefit to themselves, nor ward off harm from themselves.

Among the benefits of His saying ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking them with the right hand﴾: again, the demonstration of the strength of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Among its benefits also: a person, when he does an action, should be earnest and resolute in it, doing it with strength, not with laziness and sluggishness, unlike what some people do, for you find them facing their work with weakness, laziness and sloth. A person is in reality with himself as he is accustomed: if he is accustomed to resolution and strength, and not to postponing work to a future time, he becomes resolute in his actions and aware of them. But if he is lazy and negligent, saying: "I will leave this until tomorrow," then the tasks will pile up on him, and in the end he will find himself unable to do them, isn't that so? For if he postpones one day's work to tomorrow, two tasks gather on him tomorrow: yesterday's work and today's work. If he postpones it again, three tasks gather on him, and so on until he becomes incapable and weary. This is why a person who has to make up the fasts of Ramadan is forbidden to delay them until after the next Ramadan. Why? Because if he delays them until the next year, debts pile up on him, and then he becomes unable to make up these debts. The point is that His saying ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking them with the right hand﴾ teaches that a person should meet his tasks with strength and resolution, so that he discharges them with complete ease.

Among the benefits of the noble verse in His saying ﴿So they came hastening to him﴾ [al-Saffat 94]: the demonstration of the intensity of these people's defence of their gods. For His saying ﴿So they came﴾ indicates sequence, immediacy, and also causation: that is, because of what was done with this implement, they came to him hastening. The fa' (then), as you know, indicates sequence and immediacy. In it is evidence of the intensity of these people's defence of their gods, despite the falsehood of these gods.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: that gathering has an effect even in falsehood; His saying ﴿So they came to him﴾ means all of them together. When people gather, some become support for others, and it is well known that a person gains victory and strength through others.

From this benefit it follows: when a person wants an important task and fears he will be unable to accomplish it alone, it is better that he seek help from others, and he should not say that this is seeking help from other than God. For God said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿He it is who supported you with His help and with the believers, and joined their hearts together﴾ [al-Anfal 62-63]. This is not regarded as a deficiency in trust in God, the Mighty and Majestic, because the Prophet, peace be upon him, was the master of those who trust in God, and yet God said: ﴿He it is who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾, and He said: ﴿And consult them in the affair; then when you have resolved, put your trust in God﴾ [Al 'Imran 159].

This is a point some people overlook: you find one who is about to undertake a great matter but does not take supporters for it. This is open to question; that is, this conduct is questionable. Yet wisdom must be observed regarding these supporters: is the wise course that they all go, or that they agree on a view even if they separate in going? I say: wisdom must be used here, because it may be wise for them all to go, and it may be wise for them to go separately but agree on one view. This in reality depends on the work they want to agree upon and the confrontation they want to face. Some people are affected by a large group and submit to them, while others are seized by pride in sin and think that this is an attack upon them, so they accept from them neither repentance nor ransom.

The point is that gathering around a matter is a cause of strength and victory, but how is the matter on which we have gathered to be handled? Is it handled individually or collectively? This depends on what the circumstances require, and a person should use wisdom in that. (...)

Student: ﴿And when he reached with him the age of exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am slaughtering you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, God willing, among the steadfast"﴾ [al-Saffat 102].

Shaykh: I seek refuge with God from the accursed Satan. God the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "Build for him a structure and throw him into the blaze."﴾ [al-Saffat 97].

God the Exalted said: ﴿So they came hastening to him. He said, "Do you worship what you carve?"﴾ up to the end [al-Saffat 94-95].

* Among the benefits of this verse and what follows: that the people of falsehood hasten to attain their aim, as in His saying ﴿So they came hastening to him﴾ [al-Saffat 94]. If the people of falsehood hasten to attain their aim, the people of truth should be swifter than them, because the people of truth are helped and the people of falsehood are forsaken.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: gathering around a matter is among the causes of attaining the desired end. That is, whenever people gather around a matter, that is closer to attaining their aim, as in His saying ﴿So they came to him﴾, meaning they did not come one by one, and this is stronger in power. It follows from this that when a person wants a matter, he should gather with his brothers for it. But is it wise that they come all together, or that they come individually yet agree on a matter? We have mentioned that this depends on what the circumstances require, so whatever is more beneficial is followed. Sometimes gathering together is better, and sometimes the reverse.

* Among the benefits of this verse also: these people defend their idols and objects of worship although they are false. So the people of truth who defend God, the Mighty and Majestic, should be far more zealous in defending the religion of God, glorified and exalted be He. When you look at the present reality of the Muslims, you find them divided: every scholar does not take refuge in another scholar, nor consult him, nor follow his opinion; rather, regrettably, he may even oppose him in his view while knowing he is right. This bears a resemblance to the Jews, who envied the Arabs for the great prophethood God had given them, for the Jews used to seek victory against those who disbelieved and prevail over them; that is, they hoped for victory over them by following Muhammad ﷺ. But when Muhammad came, they disbelieved in him, because they supposed that he would come from the Children of Israel, and he came from the Arabs. They thought this out of wishful thinking; otherwise they know the Prophet ﷺ as they know their own sons.

* Among the benefits of His saying ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ [al-Saffat 95]: rebuking the people of falsehood for their falsehood by way of reason, and arguing against them by their falsehood through reason. How so? ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ That is, how do you carve it yourselves and make it yourselves, and then worship it? Is it not more fitting, rationally, that this carved thing should be the one to worship you, since you are the ones who carved it and brought it into being? But their minds are inverted, so the matter became reversed: they worship what they carve.

* Among the benefits of the verse in His saying ﴿And God created you and what you do﴾ [al-Saffat 96]: establishing the proof that God alone deserves to be worshipped, from His saying "who created you." The Creator is the one who must be worshipped. How can you worship one who did not create you and abandon the one who created you, or worship one who did not create you, associating him with the one who created you? For this reason God established the proof that it is not valid for anything other than Him to be worshipped, in His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21]. He said: ﴿worship your Lord who created you﴾ and did not say "worship God," establishing the evidence against them through lordship.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the deeds of servants are created by God. This follows from His saying ﴿created you and what you do﴾, whether we take "ma" as a verbal-source particle or as a relative pronoun. If we take it as a verbal-source particle, the matter is clear: He created you and created your action. If we take it as a relative pronoun, then because the creation of the thing done is a branch of the creation of the act: if the object of your work, which you yourself performed, is created by God, how much more so your action which came from God?!

In this verse there is a refutation of whom? Of the Qadariyya, who deny that God, glorified and exalted be He, has any role in the actions of the children of Adam, and who say: a person is independent in his action, with no will or creation from God in it.

In the verse there is also a refutation of the Jabriyya, who say that a person is compelled in his action, by His saying ﴿you do﴾, where He attributed the action to them; and attributing the action to a person requires that he is the doer and the agent in reality. And that is so: in reality the person is the one who acts, does, wills and chooses. If the verse contains a refutation of the two deviant groups, which group does it support? It supports the People of the Sunnah and the Community, who say: a person has capacity and choice, and brings his action into existence; but the one who created him and created this capacity and will is God. So his act is attributed to God in creation and decree, and attributed to him in bringing into being and direct performance. It is attributed to the servant in one respect, and to God in another respect.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse also: what was previously alluded to, namely establishing the proof against the people of falsehood by their falsehood through reason. If God created them and created what they do, how can they worship this creature alongside God and make it a partner with God in worship?

He said: ﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham﴾ [al-Saffat 83], meaning among those who followed him in the fundamentals of the religion.

﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham﴾. This sentence consists of "inna" (indeed) with its noun and predicate. Its noun is delayed: ﴿Abraham﴾ is the noun, and the predicate is advanced: ﴿among his followers﴾. The lam here is the lam of emphasis. The meaning is that Abraham, peace be upon him, was among the followers (shi'ah) of Noah, peace be upon him. In the language, "shi'ah" applies to everyone who supports a person, follows him, helps him and aids him. So Abraham, peace be upon him, was among Noah's followers, that is, among his adherents, those of like kind, and those who support what he brought of the sharia. Whoever supports the sharia at any time and in any place is a supporter of all the sharias, because backing the law that came from God at any time and in any place is backing the whole of God's law. For this reason, for example, we rejoice in the victory of the messengers and their followers, even if they lived in a distant time and were not those sent specifically to us. So Abraham, peace be upon him, was among Noah's followers, that is, among his supporters and followers in what he brought, not in the very same sharia but in the category of revelation. That is, he backs and supports the revelation which is of the same kind as the revelation Noah, peace be upon him, brought.

For this reason the author said: "that is, among those who followed him in the fundamentals of the religion," and this is accepting the revelation of God, Mighty and Majestic, acting upon it, and calling to it. Thus all the messengers are followers of one another, meaning they all support one another and believe in the entire revelation.

As for his saying: "﴿Abraham﴾ even though a long time passed between them, and it was two thousand six hundred and forty years": his statement "even though a long time passed between them" is correct. There is no doubt that a long period of time lay between Noah, peace be upon him, and Abraham. But specifying it with the figure the author mentioned requires a sound proof, either from the Book of God or from the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and we know of no basis for this in the Qur'an or the Sunnah.

If it is said: this only comes from what was transmitted from the Children of Israel, which we neither believe nor disbelieve.

(And between them were Hud and Salih.) The evidence for this is that God, glorified and exalted, always links the story of Hud with the story of Noah, and after it the story of Salih. This indicates that these three came before Abraham. As for Idris, some historians mentioned that he was before Noah, but this is a very weak opinion, because we have already noted that Noah, peace be upon him, was the first messenger God sent to the people of the earth. The view that Idris came before him is weak, indeed false in reality. So Noah is the first of the messengers, and Idris appears, God knows best, to have been one of the prophets of the Children of Israel.

He said: ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾. The author said: "that is, he followed him at the time of his coming." This may be what the author said, that ﴿when﴾ is connected to his saying ﴿followers﴾, meaning: and among those who followed him when he came to his Lord with a sound heart was Abraham. It may also be that ﴿when﴾ is resumptive (isti'nafiyyah), and the sentence is to be read as: remember ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾. This is the more correct view. The correct view is that it is not connected to that, and that he was among his followers at the time of coming and at other times. But God wished to draw attention to this great quality of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾. The author said: "free from doubt and other things." When does his coming to his Lord take place? Is it meant that he came to his Lord when he met Him after death, or that he came to his Lord when his people harmed him and threatened him with burning? Or do we leave it as God left it? The better course is to leave it as God left it, and to say: ﴿he came to his Lord﴾ at a time that God alone knows, ﴿with a sound heart﴾. The author said: "free from doubt and other things." The correct view is that soundness is broader than what the author said. He was sound from doubts and sound from desires. Sound from doubts: there was no doubt in him in any respect; rather he had knowledge and certainty of what he believed. Sound from desires: there was in his heart no inclination contrary to what the revelation brought. This is the soundness of the heart: that it is free from the doubts that come to it and from uncertainties, so that the person is a true believer, and that it is free from desires.

And what are the desires?

The desires are the wills that oppose what the revelation brought. Does every heart desire what the revelation brought? No. Hearts turn right and left. At times a person's own heart wanders; sometimes it is fully turned toward the revelation, loving it and applying it, and at other times it finds coolness in turning to the revelation and coolness in applying what it brought. For this reason a person should always ask God, glorified and exalted, for steadfastness in the matter and steadfastness of the heart, because the heart is between two fingers of the Most Merciful, who turns it however He wills. So a person should not be deceived by himself or be pleased with his creed. He must always ask God for steadfastness, because the heart, as I have said, is affected by doubts and affected by desires. Sometimes a person is truly a believer, then Satan casts a doubt into his heart and he becomes blind, God forbid, and goes astray. Sometimes a person is righteous and upright in obedience to God, then Satan casts a desire into his heart and he goes astray and follows desires. So the sound heart is the one that is safe from what? From doubts and desires. And when it is safe from these, it remains upright in obedience to God, glorified and exalted.

﴿when he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾.

(﴿when he said to his father and his people﴾ in this continuing state) This we say about it, as we said about ﴿when he came to his Lord﴾, that it is a resumptive sentence explaining Abraham's condition, peace be upon him. His heart was sound and righteous in itself, and yet he tried to reform others: ﴿when he said to his father and his people﴾ (rebuking them) ﴿what do you worship?﴾. ﴿when he said to his father and his people, what do you worship?﴾. The author said: "rebuking them." So the interrogation here means rebuke, and rebuke implies disapproval of them and something more, because you may disapprove of a person without rebuking him, but when you rebuke him, your rebuke implies disapproval of him.

As for his saying ﴿when he said to his father﴾: God named this father in Surah al-An'am, saying: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, do you take idols as gods?﴾ [al-An'am 74]. His father was a polytheist, and Abraham, peace be upon him, promised to ask forgiveness for him: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord; indeed He is ever gracious to me﴾ [Maryam 47]. He did ask forgiveness for him, but when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disowned him. His dialogue with his father in Surah Maryam is clear: how he addressed him with gentleness and kindness, while the father addressed him with severity and harshness. He said to him: ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you, and leave me alone﴾, that is, leave me and abandon me ﴿for a long time﴾ [Maryam 46], that is, for a long period.

﴿when he said to his father and his people, what do you worship?﴾ [al-Saffat 85]. ﴿What do you worship?﴾ This is an interrogative sentence. But is "dha" (this) redundant, or is it a relative noun? Both possibilities are allowed. If we make it a relative noun, we parse "ma" as the subject and "dha" as its predicate, and we take the returning pronoun as omitted, the meaning being: what is it that you worship? This is if we make it a relative noun. If we make it redundant, we parse "madha" as a whole, and say: "madha" is an interrogative noun, a fronted object of "ta'budun" (you worship). Or we say "ma" is a fronted interrogative noun and "dha" has no grammatical position, being a particle or like a particle, with no place in the sentence. In any case, the grammatical analysis is not our concern. What matters is the meaning: he disapproved of them and said: what is it that you worship? Do you worship a true god, or do you worship a false god?

﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾ [al-Saffat 86]. Regarding its two hamzas, the same discussion applies as before: the readings are realization (tahqiq) and facilitation (tashil) of the second, and inserting an alif between them in both realization and facilitation, so the readings become four.

He says: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire?﴾. He says: ("ifkan" is an object of purpose, "alihah" is a direct object of "turidun" [you desire]. "Ifk" is the worst of lies, meaning: do you worship other than God?) The author, may God have mercy on him, parsed this sentence for us, saying that "ifkan" is an object of purpose, that is, an object of cause, and that his saying "alihah" is the object of "turidun," and "dun Allah" is an adjective of "alihah." The interrogation in his saying "a-ifkan alihah" is like that before it: for what? For rebuke. That is, do you desire gods other than God for the sake of falsehood and lies, which drives you to this falsehood, which is the worst of lies? The meaning is: do you desire gods besides God to worship them? Here "irada" means intention, and "alihah" means "ma'lubah," that is, the worshipped ones. You desire this because of the falsehood you have invented, which is the worst of lies. There is no doubt that the worst and most wicked lie is to make another god alongside God, for he is the greatest liar and the most wicked liar. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, associating others with God is a tremendous wrong﴾ [Luqman 13]. Here He said "dun Allah," meaning other than Him and besides Him, and this may suggest a lower rank, that is, that they are not equal to God, Mighty and Majestic. How then do you take them as gods and intend them?

He says: (﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Saffat 87], if you worship other than Him, that He will leave you without punishment) and so on to the end.

His saying ﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾: the interrogation here, according to the author's words, is an interrogation of threat. That is, what do you think God will do to you if you worship other than Him? Do you think He will leave you alone? The answer is no. It may also mean: if you take another god alongside God, what is your opinion of Him? Do you think He will accept this partnership? God, Mighty and Majestic, will not accept it. God, the Exalted, said: "Whoever does a deed in which he associates another with Me, I will abandon him and his association" [recorded by Muslim (2985/46) from Abu Hurayrah]. Or it may mean: ﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾: what is your opinion of His greatness and majesty? If you had magnified Him as He deserves, you would not have associated another with Him. So the interrogation in his saying ﴿So what is your opinion﴾ includes all these meanings: what do you think of Him, that He would leave you aimless without punishment? What do you think of Him, if you take another with Him, that you have belittled Him? What do you think of Him, that He would be pleased for you to worship another with Him? If they merely held these assumptions, they would have wronged God in their assumptions and not measured God with His due measure. But these assumptions are binding upon them if they take another with God; they cannot escape them. And his saying ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾: we have already noted that "the worlds" here means everything other than God, Mighty and Majestic. Everything other than God is a "world," and they were called a world because they are a sign pointing to God, by which He is known through His creation, glorified and exalted, as He said: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day and the sun and the moon﴾ [Fussilat 37]; ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust, then behold, you are human beings spreading out﴾ [al-Rum 20]; ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the diversity of your languages and your colors. Indeed in that are signs for those who know﴾ [al-Rum 22], and so on through what God cites as evidence of Himself from His signs. So his saying ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾: who are meant by "the worlds"? Everything other than God. They were called "worlds" because they are a sign and proof of their Creator. And his saying ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾: is His lordship here general or specific? It is general, and for this reason He said "the worlds," inclusive of everyone.

The author said: (They were astrologers. They went out to a festival of theirs and left their food by their idols, claiming it would be blessed, and when they returned they would eat it. They said to the master Abraham: come out with us. ﴿So he glanced at the stars﴾.) This statement which the author supposes to be omitted for the sake of brevity: by what? By omission, it requires proof that these people prepared food, placed it by these idols for blessing, intended to eat it after their return, and asked Abraham to come out with them. All of this requires evidence. We noted earlier that the stories of the earlier prophets are known only to God: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you, the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows but God?﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. If that is the case, we do not receive the reports of these people except from revelation, either from the Book or from the Sunnah. Whatever reports of them come by another route, namely not the route of revelation, we suspend judgment on, unless we know that they contradict the sharias. If we know they contradict the sharias, we are obliged to reject them.

So in this story we should limit ourselves to what God, Mighty and Majestic, has mentioned: that Abraham, one day, glanced at the stars in order to argue with his people and show their inability. This is like His saying in Surah al-An'am about Abraham's argument with his people: ﴿When the night covered him, he saw a star and said, this is my lord. But when it set, he said, I do not love those that set﴾ [al-An'am 76], that is, that disappeared, ﴿for a lord cannot disappear from what he lords over.﴾ Since this star disappeared, he knew it was not a lord, because a lord must have complete care for those he lords over.

﴿So when he saw the moon rising, he said, this is my lord﴾ [al-An'am 77]. The moon is clearer and more evident than the star. ﴿But when it set, he said: unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people﴾ [al-An'am 77]. This is an allusion to his people, saying they are misguided. Notice the progression: first he said ﴿I do not love those that set﴾, meaning he disowned that. The second was an implication that his people were misguided: ﴿unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the misguided people﴾ (77). ﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said: this is my lord, this is greater﴾ [al-An'am 77–78]. Indeed the sun is greater than the moon. ﴿But when it set, he said: O my people, I am free from what you associate﴾ [al-An'am 78]. He declared their polytheism and his disassociation from them, and this is from the perfection of his argument. So it is not far-fetched that this verse ﴿So he glanced at the stars﴾ [al-Saffat 88] is of the kind of argument mentioned in Surah al-An'am.

* Student: May God be good to you, Shaykh. (...) His Lord's saying, glorified: ﴿came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾, that this is after death (...) In Surah al-Shu'ara: ﴿And do not disgrace me on the day they are resurrected. The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara 87–89]. We say: this supports (...) after death.

* Shaykh: This perhaps supports that it is after death, but ﴿when he said to his father and his people﴾ is in life, and this is what prevents a firm judgment that it is after death. For this reason we leave ﴿came to his Lord﴾ open: God knows best whether it was after death or during life.

* Student: It seems they confirm this statement, as if they accept it?
* Shaykh: Yes, because this (...) by calculation, and something past, known by calculation. And in it is evidence that the historians, do you know when the historians say? They say: Ibrahim, may Allah be pleased with him, died on the tenth of Rabi' al-Awwal. Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet ﷺ, on the tenth of Rabi' al-Awwal. And this is not possible, the sun can never be eclipsed on the tenth day.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Because the cause of a solar eclipse is the moon coming between it and the earth. On the tenth of Rabi' it is not possible, this is never possible.
* Student: And the moon, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: And the moon is only in the nights of full moon.
* Student: (...) meaning the fifteenth night.
* Shaykh: The fourteenth, the fifteenth, the sixteenth, meaning the nights of full moon are possible; because the cause of its eclipse, the natural cause, is the earth coming between it and the sun. For this reason, when the scholars assumed: if the sun rises while the moon is eclipsed, the eclipse prayer is not prayed. We say: this is an impossible assumption; because it is not possible for the sun and the moon to meet at a horizon so that an eclipse occurs, ever, or not? Because the eclipse requires that the moon be beneath the earth so that the earth comes between it and the sun.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: I have never heard that (...).

* Shaykh: No, it was eclipsed, but since it was not clear, what (...) no, it was eclipsed here, how we put a mirror, because you cannot see it with the eye, but we put a mirror and saw it eclipsed, perhaps about between an eighth and a quarter.
* Student: But it was announced many times, Shaykh (...) it was announced more than once (...).
* Shaykh: No, I have no doubt about it, and this is something mentioned by the scholars among the verifiers, such as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and others, and Ibn Hazm (...) it is not possible. This is something known by calculation, it is not knowledge of the unseen.
* Student: The view of the jurists when they said: if an eclipse coincides with a festival.
* Shaykh: It is never possible.
* Student: So they assumed.
* Shaykh: If an eclipse coincided with a festival, we say this in Shawwal, meaning on the Festival of Fitr: if an eclipse coincided with a festival, it is known that the day is not a festival, and that the witnesses erred in their testimony; because the illusion of the observer is a possible matter, but the change of the custom which Allah established is an impossible matter. Even the scholars also said: if an eclipse occurred while he was standing at Arafat (a lunar eclipse), he prays and then departs, so that the prayer is not missed. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah says: this is a hypothetical matter that can never occur. But the scholars, the jurists, assume things for training in the legal rulings, such as when they say: they assumed twenty grandmothers in the wills and inheritances, twenty grandmothers. When are there twenty grandmothers? Setting aside the one connected with two parents, or three, or four, or five, twenty grandmothers, where? Who will have twenty grandmothers inheriting? In any case, these are arithmetical problems with no difficulty in them (...).
