He said: ﴿while he was sick﴾. As for the author's statement that it was on that day, or after three days, or four days, or seven days, or twenty days, or forty days, these are opinions, and none of them has evidence. But there is no doubt that Allah, glorified and exalted, kept him in the belly of the fish as long as Allah willed. As for specifying that, there must be evidence from one whose word is a proof, namely the Messenger (ﷺ). Anything other than that in such matters is not accepted.

He said: (﴿while he was sick﴾, weak, like a featherless chick). His saying "weak" is an explanation of "sick", and "sakam" means illness and ailment. As for his saying "like a featherless chick", meaning one whose hair has been plucked, there is nothing in the verse indicating that. But there is no doubt that the sick person is weak in body and has no capacity to withstand the sun and the wind. And His saying ﴿while he was sick﴾ indicates, on its apparent meaning, that Jonah remained in the belly of the fish for a period that led to his sickness.

He says: ﴿And We caused to grow over him a gourd vine﴾ [As-Saffat 146] (it is the squash, which shades him with its stem, contrary to the custom of squash, as a miracle for him). "We caused to grow over him", and He did not say "We caused to grow for him", because he now needed shade, so Allah caused to grow over him a shade, this tree ﴿a tree of gourd﴾. The "min" here is explanatory of kind, as one says "a ring of iron". And "yaqtin" is squash. Squash has kinds in reality: among them is a squash called here "Najdi squash", which has a tree, and its branches are soft like silk. It is said that flies do not settle on it. As for the second kind of squash, its leaves are rough, so that when a person touches it with his hand he senses roughness. The apparent meaning is that what Allah caused to grow over him was of the first kind, the soft one that is like silk, and it also gives cool shade. Allah caused this tree to grow over him. As for the author's statement that it had a stem contrary to custom, this needs evidence, but there is no doubt that Allah caused to grow over him a tree that shaded him, and it must have some height.

﴿And We sent him﴾. He said: (And a doe would come to him morning and evening, and he would drink from her milk until he grew strong). The "waʿla" is the female of the wild goats, i.e., the female of the wild goats; she would come to him and he would drink from her milk until he grew strong. This report needs evidence from an infallible source, and there is no evidence from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So it is an Israelite report about which we suspend judgment: we neither affirm nor deny it. If Allah arranged that for him, then Allah is over all things capable. This is a sensory means that a person needs; he needs food. And if Allah strengthened him to bear hunger and thirst, that is also not far-fetched, and then we would take the verse to mean that Allah strengthened him contrary to custom. But if we take it as the doe, then his survival and nourishment would be according to custom in one respect, and a miracle in another respect, according to custom: he was nourished by what? By milk, like other humans. Contrary to custom: Allah arranged for him this doe, which is not of his kind, to come so that he could drink from her milk. But if we say that Allah strengthened him to bear hunger and thirst, this becomes a pure sign, and this is not far-fetched; for when the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade continuous fasting, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, you are continuing." Continuous fasting means a fasting person joins two days without breaking the fast between them. They said: "You are continuing," and he said: «Indeed I am not like your state; indeed I spend the night with my Lord, who feeds me and gives me drink»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1965) and Muslim (1103/57) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], meaning without eating or drinking. And he is content with what Allah has deposited in his heart of love for Allah and remembrance of Him, instead of physical food; that is, he is content with spiritual nourishment in place of physical nourishment. Allah is over all things capable.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verses 139–148 (part 2 of 3):

A similar example in some respects is that Allah, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿If you do not help him, Allah has already helped him when those who disbelieved expelled him, the second of two. When they were in the cave, he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us."﴾ [At-Tawbah 40]. Here Allah did not mention how He helped him against Quraysh while he was in the cave. So what is this to be understood as? Weak narrations have come down that a spider spun its web over him, that a dove perched at the mouth of the cave, and that Allah caused a tree to grow that blocked the sight of the polytheists from the Messenger ﷺ and his companion Abu Bakr.[[Narrated by al-Bazzar in his Musnad (4344), and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (1082), from the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam, al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, and Anas ibn Malik.]] These three things are sensory matters that prevent seeing the Prophet ﷺ and his companion in the cave. They are ordinary sensory matters. But is their existence at that moment a sign or not? It is a sign: that Allah caused this tree to grow and subjected this dove to stand at the entrance of the cave, and subjected the spider to weave over its door. This is undoubtedly a sign. But there is a greater sign than this, a pure sign: that Allah, exalted, blinded their eyes from seeing the Prophet ﷺ and his companion, because they stood at the cave, standing on their feet, until Abu Bakr said: "If one of them had looked at his feet, he would have seen us."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3653) and Muslim (2381/1), from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.]] This is established in al-Bukhari and Muslim and others. This indicates the weakness of the story of the spider, the dove, and the tree, because the second is a clearer sign than the first. Abu Bakr's statement indicates that there was no sensory barrier preventing sight, neither a tree nor a spider's web. Nor is there anything to rule out that a dove could land at its door while someone was inside the cave, just as a dove may land at the door of a room even when someone is inside, as is frequently observed.

The conclusion is that some people bring up such signs without considering that they weaken the aspect of the sign. For the sign that Allah blinded the eyes of Quraysh from seeing the Messenger ﷺ and Abu Bakr, although they were standing right at the cave, is far greater than the spider, the tree, or the dove. Moreover, the best of these narrations in terms of chain is the spider's web narration.[[Narrated by Ahmad (3251) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]] Nevertheless, it is weak. And if a narration is weak in its chain and anomalous (shadh) in its text, because it contradicts what came in the two Sahihs, it is not acceptable.

Now we return to the story of Yunus. The author mentioned that the mountain goat would come to him and he would suckle from it until he became strong. What did we say about this report? We said: this report is not established from an infallible source. Our position regarding it is to suspend judgment and say: this is not definitive, and perhaps Allah helped Yunus to endure hunger and thirst.

He (the author) said: (﴿And We sent him﴾ afterward, as before, to the people of Nineveh, in the land of Mosul in Iraq, ﴿to a hundred thousand, or more﴾ — rather, ﴿they were more﴾, twenty or thirty or seventy thousand more, ﴿and they believed﴾ at the sight of the punishment they had been promised, ﴿so We let them enjoy for a time﴾, meaning We let them remain, enjoying, ﴿for a time﴾.) Allah, exalted, sent him after that to his people, meaning He completed his mission, ﴿to a hundred thousand or more﴾. ﴿To a hundred thousand﴾ is explicit regarding the number. As for His saying, ﴿or more﴾, the scholars differed concerning the (or) here. It was said that it means (rather), as the author said, meaning: rather, more than a hundred thousand. As for specifying this as an increase of twenty or thirty or seventy thousand, there is no evidence for it, and the increase cannot be seventy thousand. For if the increase were seventy thousand, it would not be correct to say: ﴿to a hundred thousand or more﴾; rather, it would be said: "to a hundred and seventy thousand," because the difference between the first number and the second would be large. So according to the author's statement, Allah sent him to more than a hundred thousand, and (or) here would mean (rather). What is meant by it, namely by (rather) that is or has the same meaning, is the transitional idrab (change of subject, al-idrab al-intiqali, "a shift to a new point"), not the cancelling idrab (al-idrab al-ibtali, "a retraction of what came before"), because they say: idrab is either to cancel what preceded, or to move from it to what follows.

Some scholars held that (or) here is for confirmation (tahqiq) and not for idrab. That is: if they did not exceed a hundred thousand, they did not fall below it. So what follows (or) is to confirm what precedes it, not to add to it. This is like when someone asks you about your people: "How many are they?" and you say: "A hundred thousand or more," meaning that if they are not more, they are not fewer. The intention is not to affirm a majority or an increase over this number, but to confirm this number.

There is a possibility, but it does not arise in this context, that (or) is for doubt. This possibility is not valid here. Why? Because doubt can never apply to the report of Allah, given the completeness of His knowledge of everything. Accordingly, (or) here is either in the sense of (rather), or for confirmation, namely confirming the earlier number. On the first view, those sent to were more than a hundred thousand. On the second, those sent to were a hundred thousand, but this was emphasized by His saying: ﴿or more﴾.

If Allah wills, the rest of the discussion on the verse and its benefits will come later.

* Student: When Allah mentioned the story of Yunus and that he fled on the ship, he mentioned Yunus's state, then (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, in Surah Yunus Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed and whose faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy for a time.﴾ [Yunus 98]. There is in this some praise of them. In reality, they had a fault on one side, and on the other side their blame is averted.
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you, the infallibility of the prophets (...) how is the report about Yunus, peace be upon him, here?
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: That is, he did not seek permission and went out in anger...
* Shaykh: We will discuss that in the benefits.
* Student: The author's statement that the stopping of the ship was because of Yunus, what is its basis, shaykh? Because Allah, exalted, decreed the stopping of the ship in order to make clear that Yunus was in this trial. That is, how can there be a basis for attributing it to Yunus?
* Shaykh: We should take a rule: that which goes beyond the normal course needs evidence. Otherwise, matters remain according to what is customary.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿So ask them: "Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons? Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses? Is it not that they say, out of their own falsehood, 'Allah has begotten,' and they are indeed liars? Did He choose daughters over sons? What is the matter with you? How do you judge? Will you not remember?"﴾ [As-Saffat 149–155].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And indeed Yunus was among the messengers.﴾ This sentence is emphasized with how many emphases?
* Student: Two.
* Shaykh: ﴿And indeed Yunus was among the messengers.﴾ What are they?
* Student: Inna and the lam.
* Shaykh: Inna and the lam, good. What is the wisdom in its being emphasized with two emphases? Why was it not limited to a mere statement?
* Student: Because the message may reach someone who believes, and someone who is in doubt about it, or who denies it.
* Shaykh: Because some people deny the message. That is one?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: And the second?
* Student: Because the messengers, peace be upon them, were emphasized with moral matters, so they were also emphasized...
* Shaykh: No, let us leave the ways of emphasis. And because of the importance of the establishment of his messengership, so that we believe in him. Good. His saying: ﴿when he fled to the laden ship﴾, Muhammad, ﴿when he fled﴾: (idh) here is an adverb related to what?
* Student: Related to "the messengers."
* Shaykh: To "the messengers."
* Student: Related to ﴿Remember﴾.
* Shaykh: To an omitted verb.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Correct.
* Student: (...) related to ﴿Remember﴾.
* Shaykh: Well done, correct. Because there is no basis for praising him at the time of his fleeing. His saying: ﴿So he was among those cast off﴾: the author took a course contrary to the apparent meaning. What is it?
* Student: That the people of the ship, when...
* Shaykh: No, only ﴿among those cast off﴾.
* Student: That is, he was a slave who fled from his master (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (Min) here is partitive.
* Shaykh: No. What did the author take, which we then refuted?
* Student: That he said: the people of the ship said: a slave fled from his master.
* Shaykh: No, yes.
* Student: He said that they said: Yunus was thrown into the sea because of his situation.
* Shaykh: Alone?
* Student: Alone.
* Shaykh: Correct.
* Student: And (min) is partitive, meaning there were others with him.
* Shaykh: Correct. The author took the view that the one who was thrown was Yunus alone, and this contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse, because the verse indicates that there was someone else with him. Good. The clause ﴿while he was blameworthy﴾: what is its grammatical position (i'rab)?
* Student: The accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).
* Shaykh: Its position is the accusative as a circumstantial clause, from the subject of "swallowed" or from the object.
* Student: From the verb, shaykh?
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: From the object.
* Shaykh: From the object. (...) Does the verse not allow it to be from the subject? The one blamed: the fish that swallowed, or Yunus who was swallowed?
* Student: Yunus.
* Shaykh: Yunus. Then it is a circumstantial clause from the object. What is the meaning of ﴿blameworthy﴾?
* Student: That is: one who comes with what he deserves blame for.
* Shaykh: One who comes with what he deserves blame for. Correct. His saying: ﴿So had he not been among those who glorify Allah﴾: (law-la) here is a particle.
* Student: Prohibition of something because of the existence of something else.
* Shaykh: Prohibition of something because of the existence of something else. What is the prohibited thing and what is the existing thing?
* Student: The prohibited thing is his remaining in the belly of the fish.
* Shaykh: His remaining in the belly of the fish until the Day of Resurrection. And the existing thing?
* Student: The glorification.
* Shaykh: The glorification. What is the glorification that became the cause of his coming out of the belly of the fish?
* Student: His saying: "There is no god but You, glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."
* Shaykh: His saying: "There is no god but You, glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾. (or)?
* Student: The scholars differed. Some of them said it means (rather), and some of them said...
* Shaykh: It is for idrab.
* Student: (...) rather they are more than that.
* Shaykh: That is, according to this, the ones sent to them were more than a hundred thousand. And the second view.
* Student: The second view is that it is for confirmation, meaning if they were not two hundred thousand, they do not fall below that number.
* Shaykh: They do not fall below that number, like His saying, exalted: ﴿Then your hearts became hard after that, so they were like stones or even harder in hardness.﴾ [Al-Baqarah 74].

His saying: ﴿So We let them enjoy for a time﴾. What is the meaning of "let them enjoy"?
* Student: We stopped at it.
* Shaykh: That does not contradict it. If Allah wills, we will take it now. ﴿So We let them enjoy for a time﴾ means We let them remain until a time, and this time is the time of their appointed terms which Allah decreed for them. That is, they were not destroyed by this punishment that befell them, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed and whose faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy for a time.﴾ [Yunus 98].

* There are several benefits in these verses. First: the establishment of the messengership of Yunus, peace and blessings be upon him. Following from this benefit is the obligation to believe in him as a messenger. That is, it is obligatory upon us to believe that Yunus is a messenger from Allah.
* Among its benefits: praise of Yunus, from His saying: ﴿among the messengers﴾, because there is no doubt that the station of messengership is the highest station of humankind, as Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and the Messenger, those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [An-Nisa' 69]. This is what the Muslim nation holds: that the station of messengership is superior to every other station, and is the highest station of humankind. This is contrary to those who claim that the highest station of humankind is sainthood (wilayah), then prophethood, then messengership, and who said in this a reprehensible statement, saying:
  "The station of prophethood is in an isthmus, above the Messenger and below the saint."
These people, a group among the Sufis, say: the station of prophethood is in an isthmus, above the Messenger, and below the saint, meaning far below. So sainthood is then the highest thing. They lied in this. The station of messengership is the highest of stations. Every messenger is a saint, but not vice versa. Then prophethood, then sainthood.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: it is not permitted to disparage Yunus because of what occurred from him of impatience. For Allah said: ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish﴾. But it is not permitted for us to disparage him for that, because he is one of the messengers, and disparaging the messengers is disbelief. Indeed the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta."[[I have not found it with this wording. In al-Bukhari (3395) and Muslim (2377/167), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, with the wording: "No servant should say, I am better than Yunus ibn Matta."]] He forbade us to prefer him over Yunus, out of humility on his part, ﴿and so that preference (of the Messenger ﷺ) does not lead to contempt for Yunus.
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: the establishment of a group of messengers, from His saying: ﴿among the messengers﴾. But how many messengers are there? Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24]. There is no nation among the nations but that a messenger came to it, establishing the proof against it, as Allah said: ﴿Messengers as bearers of good news and as warners, so that people will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [An-Nisa' 165].
* Among the benefits of the noble verses: that the station of prophethood does not prevent doing some things that are not beloved to Allah. That is, a messenger may commit some sins or do something he was not commanded to do. The proof of this is His saying: ﴿when he fled to the laden ship﴾. Ibaq (fleeing) means running away: a slave fleeing from his master. When a slave flees from his master, he has run away from him in rebellion against him. But there is no doubt that this description applies only to a slave owned by a human being, not to Yunus, peace and blessings be upon him. Yet Allah expressed his departure as ibaq because he departed in a manner he had not been commanded to.

This matter, namely the question of the infallibility of the messengers, is a subject of long and broad disagreement among the scholars, and we have previously explained it in detail. We mentioned that they are infallible from everything that would injure or contradict the messengership, such as lying, betrayal, shirk, and the like. They are certainly infallible from these, because they came to destroy shirk, and it is impossible that lying or betrayal should come from them, since that would lead to doubt about what they brought.

Second: they are infallible from what? 
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: We mentioned it. They are also infallible from everything that undermines honour, such as theft and similar things that are regarded as baseness and vileness. This is because prophethood is the highest station of humankind, so those who are characterized by it should not adopt the most despicable morals of humankind.

The third point: they are protected from persisting in sin. They cannot be left to continue in it. Rather, they must be alerted to it, and repentance is granted to them. This differs from other people, who may commit sin and persist in it without being granted repentance. As for the claim that they have no sins at all, this view contradicts the Book and the Sunnah. God Most High said to the noblest of messengers, ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin, and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad 19], and He said to him, ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear conquest, that Allah may forgive for you what preceded of your sin and what will follow and complete His favor upon you and guide you to a straight path﴾ [al-Fath 1-2]. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "O Allah, forgive me all my sins, the small and the great, the open and the secret, the first and the last. O Allah, forgive me what I have done in advance and what I have left behind, what I have concealed and what I have made public" [Narrated by Muslim (483/216) from Abu Hurayrah]. All of this clearly shows that the Messenger (ﷺ) may commit a sin, but the crucial matter is that he does not persist in it.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: Allah, glorified and exalted, may facilitate for the servant what he never expected. This is seen in His words, ﴿when he fled to the loaded ship﴾, where He decreed that he board this filled ship in order to accomplish the purpose Allah intended, which was that the fish swallow him, hide him, and confine him until it became clear to him that there is no escape from the decree of Allah. As Allah, the Exalted, said, ﴿And [mention] Dhu al-Nun, when he went off in anger and thought that We would not decree [anything] upon him. But he called out within the darknesses, "There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Anbiya' 87].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of al-musahamah (drawing lots), meaning al-qur'ah (casting lots), based on His words, ﴿and he drew lots﴾.

If someone says: "This is from the law of those before us?"

The answer: the law of those before us is law for us as long as our law does not reveal something contrary to it. How much more so when our law has come in agreement with it? The Prophet (ﷺ) "used to draw lots among his wives when he intended to travel, and whichever wife's lot came out, he would take her with him" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2593) and Muslim (2445/88) from 'Aishah].

Therefore, what is derived from this is the permissibility of al-musahamah, meaning al-qur'ah.

If someone says: "Drawing lots involves risk, and it is a form of gambling (maysir), because a person may be a gainer (ghanim) or a loser (gharim)?"

The answer to this is one of two ways: either prohibition or acceptance. However, because necessity called for it, we accept it. Either we prohibit it, by saying that in a lottery a person cannot be a gainer or a loser, but is either a gainer or safe, and never loses anything; or we say that it involves uncertainty (gharar), but necessity calls for it, since distinguishing between co-owners in a right is impossible except through lots. Therefore, when distinction can be made without lots, it is obligatory to distinguish without them. For example, the Prophet's (ﷺ) drawing lots among his wives when he wished to travel: we say that he could not take all of them, because if he could, he would have taken them all. So he must distinguish who deserves to go out. How do we distinguish? We say: the last of them, the youngest of them, the eldest of them. We do not know, since they are equal in rights, and there is no way to specify except by lots. So when the lot comes out for one of them, the others have lost nothing; the only thing that happens is that they miss what they desired. For this reason, if the lot shifts from this purpose to gambling, it becomes prohibited.

An example of this: two partners in wheat wished to divide the wheat between them, and they were partners in equal shares, each owning half. They divided the wheat into thirds, meaning two-thirds were placed on one side and one-third on the other, and they wanted to draw lots as to which of them would take the two-thirds. The lot here is prohibited, because one of them is either a gainer or a loser: either he receives more than his right, or his right is reduced. This becomes prohibited because it has clearly become gambling. But if we divided the wheat into halves and wanted to distinguish each one's right, what is the way if neither yields to the other, allowing him to choose and saying, "Choose whatever you wish"? There is no way to distinguish between them except by lots.

Now, has the lot been mentioned in the Qur'an in any place other than this? Yes, in Al 'Imran: ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens [to determine] which of them should be entrusted with Maryam, nor were you with them when they disputed﴾ [Al 'Imran 44].

* From the benefits of the verse: there is no specific method for the lot or for al-musahamah. Whatever achieves the distinction may be used, whether by writing slips, or using stones, or rolls of cloth, or any other method. The essential point is to distinguish the one who has the right by any means, because al-musahamah is mentioned in the texts without specifying a particular method for it. So whatever method leads us to it is permissible.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: committing the lesser of two harms to avert the greater. The reasoning is that this lot would result in the destruction of some passengers, which is less severe than the destruction of all.

Therefore, if one of two harms is unavoidable, it is obligatory to commit the lesser, because committing the lesser removes from us committing the greater corruption, and avoiding the greater corruption is obligatory. For this reason we say: it is obligatory to commit the lesser of two harms to avert the greater.

These verses are evidence for acting upon such a principle. That is, if people were in a ship, and the ship was loaded, and it was necessary either to throw some passengers overboard or for all to perish, then it is permissible to throw some passengers overboard, but by way of lot, so that the rest may survive.

If someone says: "How can we throw this man into the sea to his destruction? Is this not killing a soul?" What is the answer? We take the man, knowing that he will die, and throw him into the sea. Is this not killing a soul?

We say: Yes, it is killing a soul, but to preserve souls. Which is preferable: that all be killed or that some be saved? The second is undoubtedly preferable, and this is a matter that cannot be avoided. Because if we preserved everyone, we would have caused the destruction of everyone. Causing the destruction of some is less serious than causing the destruction of all. However, this is on condition that there is no possibility, even a weak one, of rescue. If there is such a possibility, then such an act is not permissible. Now, if the ship is loaded with goods, food, sheep, and people, with whom do we begin throwing? The goods, which have no soul. If that is not enough, we throw the food. If that is not enough, we throw the animals. If that is still not enough, we cast lots among the people.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the occurrence of one of the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, namely that this fish was subjected to Yunus so that it swallowed him without chewing. There is no doubt that this is from the signs of Allah, because such a thing is rare according to custom. Normally, a creature chews and then swallows, but this one swallowed him whole without breaking any of his bones or crushing any part of his ribs or other parts.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the love of excuse from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He loves to be given excuses by His creatures. That is, to establish a justification for what He, Mighty and Majestic, does, so that His act is not attributed to injustice or foolishness. This is derived from His words, ﴿So the fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy﴾, meaning he was not in a state for which he would not be blamed, so that it could be said that this involved injustice to him or foolishness on His part. Rather, the fish swallowed him in a state in which he deserved that, and for this reason He said, ﴿while he was blameworthy﴾.

* From the benefits of the verses: prophets may commit something for which they are blamed, but Allah facilitates their escape from it. This is based on His words, ﴿while he was blameworthy﴾.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: previous acts of obedience are a cause of deliverance from later destructions. This is based on His words, ﴿And had he not been of those who exalt [Allah], he would have remained within its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾. This provides evidence for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Become acquainted with Allah in prosperity, and He will know you in adversity" [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3382) from Abu Hurayrah, and Ahmad (2803) from Ibn 'Abbas]. This is as much the implication of verbal texts as it is of actual events. The three men in the cave, whom the cave closed upon [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2272) and Muslim (2743/99) from Ibn 'Umar], were delivered by Allah through what? Through their righteous deeds that had preceded. So when you perform a righteous deed, this deed may be a cause of your deliverance from great hardships. "Become acquainted with Allah in prosperity, and He will know you in adversity." And here He said, ﴿And had he not been of those who exalt [Allah], he would have remained within its belly until the Day they are resurrected﴾.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: if he had remained in its belly, that would have been a sign from the signs of Allah, that this fish would remain from that time until the Day of Resurrection, because this is the apparent meaning of the wording: he would remain in its belly until resurrection.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: the actions of created beings are attributed to Allah, but they are attributed to Him in terms of decree and predestination, and they are attributed to the doer directly in terms of acquisition (kasb). This is derived from His words, ﴿So We threw him onto the open land﴾, since it is well known that the one who expelled him was the fish. Nevertheless, we do not affirm this definitively, because perhaps the fish expelled him and Allah facilitated for him a wind that carried him until he reached dry land. It is also possible that the fish expelled him onto dry land. Allah knows best. The essential point is that Allah facilitated for him the means of reaching dry land until He brought him to it.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: a person should never despair of recovery, even if his illness reaches its utmost extent. This is based on His words, ﴿while he was ill﴾, through to His words, ﴿and We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat 147]. This sick man who remained in the belly of the fish for as long as Allah willed came out sick, and Allah granted him health and healing. So do not despair of the mercy of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, because of the illness that befalls you. Allah may facilitate for you what becomes a cause of your recovery.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: affirming the effect of causes. This is based on His words, ﴿And We caused to grow over him a gourd vine﴾ [al-Saffat 146], because this plant shaded him and cooled him. As we have previously mentioned, it is soft to the touch, and it is said that flies do not settle on it. Allah is capable of shading him with a cloud, for example, and capable of leaving him in the sun in the open without being affected. But Allah, Mighty and Majestic, makes clear to His servants that things occur through their causes. Yesterday, in usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence), we went over the explanation that causes are effective, but not by themselves; rather, through what Allah has placed in them of the power to produce effects.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: Allah, Glorified and Exalted, sends earlier messengers to particular peoples. This is based on His words, ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾. Some later scholars used this verse as evidence for establishing a census of population, because He said, ﴿to a hundred thousand or more﴾, thus counting them numerically, even though He could have said, "We sent him to his people," which would have sufficed. Instead, He counted them. We know of no benefit for this except enumeration. There is no doubt that if enumeration has a benefit, it falls under the general texts that indicate the existence of what is beneficial. But if it has no benefit, and is merely prolonging the period, wasting time, and squandering money on what is spent upon it, then it is like anything else that has no benefit and is not sought.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: Allah, Glorified and Exalted, saved the people of Yunus after they witnessed the punishment. This is based on His words, ﴿Then they believed, so We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾.

If someone says: "What is the wisdom in Allah singling out the people of Yunus for this, by accepting their repentance after the punishment had descended?" The answer is that the wisdom behind this is that their prophet did not remain patient until the establishment of proof against them was complete. Rather, he left them in anger before he was permitted, so the establishment of proof was not completed. Therefore, they had a kind of excuse for the delay of punishment from them.

* From the benefits of the noble verse: even if a person is saved from the destructive causes, he will not escape death. Rather, it is inevitable, whether the time is long or short. This is based on His words, ﴿so We gave them enjoyment for a time﴾.

* From its benefits: faith is a cause of a long life. This is based on His words, ﴿Then they believed, so We gave them enjoyment﴾. There is no doubt that faith is a cause of a long life, because Nuh said to his people, ﴿He will forgive you of your sins and give you respite until a specified term﴾ [Nuh 4]. So he made clear to them that if faith and repentance occurred from them, Allah would forgive them and delay them until a specified term, and if they did not do so, Allah would destroy them.

* From the benefits of all the verses: the affirmation of the greatness of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, because He attributes actions to Himself, by means of what? By the plural pronoun. It is well known that Allah is one. This has been confused for the Christians, may the curse of Allah be upon them. It became confusing for them, so they affirmed a plurality of gods because of the plural pronoun attributed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is following the ambiguous (mutashabih), for they followed this ambiguity and turned away from the clear statement in His words, ﴿And your God is one God; there is no deity except Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah 163].

The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿So ask them, "Has your Lord got daughters while they have sons? Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses? Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, 'Allah has begotten,' and indeed they are liars. Has He chosen daughters over sons? What is the matter with you? How do you judge? Will you not then take heed? Or do you have a clear authority? Then bring your Book, if you are truthful. And they have made a kinship between Him and the jinn, but the jinn know that they will be brought forth. Glory be to Allah above what they describe, except for the sincere servants of Allah.﴾ [Al-Saffat 149–160].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿So ask them, "Has your Lord got daughters while they have sons?"﴾ The command in His words ﴿So ask them﴾ refers to the Messenger of Allah ﴿ﷺ﴾, and the pronoun in His words ﴿ask them﴾ refers to the polytheists who attributed daughters to Allah while they themselves have sons.

His words ﴿ask them﴾ mean: request from them that they give you a ruling. The *iftaa* (issuing of a legal ruling) originally means the explanation of a legal ruling. Directing the request for a ruling to them is by way of mockery, as if they had appointed themselves judges who rule as they wish. This is like His words, ﴿Taste! Indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 49], according to one of the two opinions regarding its interpretation. Otherwise, these people are not qualified to be asked for a ruling, let alone to be asked about this grave matter. But this is by way of mockery.

Then He stated the matter asked about, saying: ﴿Has your Lord got daughters while they have sons?﴾ The interrogative here is for rebuke, meaning He rebukes them for this ruling, which is already known, since they attributed daughters to Allah and attributed sons to themselves.

For this reason He says: ﴿So ask them﴾ (inquire of the Makkan disbelievers as a rebuke to them). This refers to the interrogation. As for the mockery, it is the directing of the request for a ruling to them. He said: ﴿Has your Lord got daughters﴾ (according to their claim that the angels are the daughters of Allah) ﴿while they have sons﴾, so they take the best for themselves, meaning the most excellent. That is, is this a sound and just ruling, or a false and unjust ruling? The answer is known to everyone: this is a false and unjust ruling. For this reason Allah, Exalted, said in Surat An-Najm: ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female? That, then, is an unfair division﴾ [An-Najm 21–22], meaning unjust. His words ﴿while they have sons﴾ are not a circumstantial clause (*hal*); rather, the clause is conjoined to the clause before it (*ma'tuf*), so it falls within the scope of the interrogation, meaning: how can Allah have daughters while they have sons? This is an unjust ruling. For this reason He said: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾

The particle ﴿or﴾ here (*am*) is *munqati'a* (disjunctive), and the disjunctive *am* is the one used for transition (*li-l-idrab*); for this reason it is estimated as ﴿bal﴾ ("rather") together with the interrogative hamza. For example, ﴿Or did We create the angels﴾: the sense of the sentence is "Rather, did We create the angels as females?" The *am* may be conjunctive (*muttasila*) and may be disjunctive (*munqati'a*). When it can be replaced by ﴿bal﴾ and the interrogative hamza, it is disjunctive; and when it means ﴿aw﴾ ("or"), it is conjunctive. You say: "Is Zayd with you or 'Amr?" meaning "or 'Amr?"

﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [Al-Munafiqun 6], meaning: "or you do not ask forgiveness for them," and the conjunctive form generally follows the equalizing hamza (*hamzat al-taswiyah*). ﴿Or did We create the angels as females?﴾ His words ﴿We created the angels as females﴾ mean: "We made them females." Accordingly, ﴿females﴾ is the second object of ﴿created﴾. It is also permissible to keep ﴿created﴾ in its original sense, meaning: "Or did We make the angels into females?" It is also permissible to keep ﴿created﴾ in its own sense, and ﴿females﴾ is then in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "Or did We create the angels in a state of being females?" The answer: No, did Allah create the angels as females? No, Allah did not create the angels as females, nor even as males. For this reason we do not describe the angels as female or as male, because the angels do not reproduce, do not eat, and do not drink. But they said that the angels are the daughters of Allah, so they made the angels females.

﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ (We created them, so they say that). The clause in His words ﴿while they were witnesses﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. The meaning: Did We create the angels as females while these people were witnessing Our creating them as females? The answer: No. Allah did not create the angels as females, and they did not witness their creation. This is like His statement in the second verse: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, into females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded and they will be questioned﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 19].

The summary is that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has explained to these people two states:

The first state: the unjust ruling they pronounced among themselves and between them and Allah, when they attributed the angels to Allah while attributing sons to themselves. This is injustice, as the Surat An-Najm indicates.

The second state: their making the angels females. Whether they had assigned sons to themselves or not, this is also a lie and a fabrication, because they did not witness the creation of the angels so as to judge them to be females. For this reason He said: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ And who are the angels?

The angels are an unseen world (*'alam ghaybi*); they are absent from us and we do not see them, except when Allah shows them to us as an honour, or as a sign. Otherwise they are an unseen world, because there is no human being except that he has two angels on his right and on his left, seated, and angels who guard him from before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah. We do not see them. And there are angels who attend gatherings of remembrance, and we do not see them, because they belong to the unseen world. The angels were created from light, as established from the Messenger of Allah ﴿ﷺ﴾ [Reported by Muslim (1827/18) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr]. They were created as *samad* (i.e., they do not eat and do not drink), because they glorify Allah night and day without respite.

Among the angels are those whose identities we know and those whose identities we do not know. Among those whose identities we know are Jibril, Mika'il, and Israfil, whom the Prophet ﴿ﷺ﴾ used to name at the beginning of the night prayer, saying: "O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mika'il, and Israfil, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that in which they differed. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth in what has been disputed, for You guide whom You will to a straight path." [Reported by Muslim (770/200) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]

* * *

* Student: (...) ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [As-Saffat 182].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿And Our word had already preceded to Our servants, the messengers﴾ [As-Saffat 171] (...). Mika'il (is over) that which gives life to the earth, which is rain and vegetation, and Israfil (is over) that which gives life to bodies at the blowing of the Trumpet, for he has put the Trumpet to his mouth, waiting for when he will be commanded. The point is that it is obligatory for us to believe in the angels in general regarding those whose names we do not know, and specifically regarding those whose names we know. We also believe in what we know of their attributes; for example, Jibril has six hundred wings which fill the horizon [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3232) and Muslim (174/280) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud], and in what we know of their states and their worship, because this is among the foundations of faith which the Messenger ﴿ﷺ﴾ explained to Jibril when he asked him about faith. He said: "That you believe in Allah and His angels" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. It is also incumbent upon us to love these angels, to honour them and to exalt them, because they are servants of Allah: ﴿honoured servants﴾ [Al-Anbiya 26], obedient to the command of Allah, so we love them for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It is also incumbent upon us to honour them, so we hate whoever is hostile to them, such as the Jews, for example, who were hostile to Jibril. We also hate everyone who reviles them or harms them, because they are among the most noble servants of Allah. The scholars have differed as to whether the angels are better or the righteous among mankind are better. The disagreement on this is well known and widespread, and most of it is a dialectical dispute, because the station and rank with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, indicate that mankind is better, for humans enter Paradise and are provided therein without reckoning: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you because you were patient"﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 23–24]. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Mankind is better in terms of the end, and the angels are better in terms of the beginning, because humans were created from clay and the angels were created from light, and light is nobler than clay."

Then He said: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ [As-Saffat 150]. Allah, Exalted, said, explaining their false ruling which was known in advance, before they were asked: ﴿Unquestionably, it is of their own falsehood that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾ [As-Saffat 151]. ...

[The text repeats here from the start of the passage.]

Their statement: ﴿Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾ ... Let us seek refuge in Allah. ﴿Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾. As you can see, this sentence is emphasized with three emphatics: (ألا) *alā*, (إن) *inna*, and (اللام) *al-lām*. How many? *Alā*, what else?

* Student: (And) *inna*.

* The Shaykh: And *inna*.

* Students: And the *lām*.

* The Shaykh: And the *lām*. As for *alā*, it definitely comes for emphasis, as it also comes for alerting and opening speech. For this reason it is said that *alā* is an opening particle, intended to alert, emphasize, and affirm, meaning it confirms what follows it.

﴿Surely they﴾ means those who made the angels females, and those who attributed daughters to Allah while they have what they desire. ﴿Surely it is of their own fabrication﴾ means of their own (lying), ﴿that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾ [As-Saffat 151–152]. Here the cause is placed before the effect: the cause is the fabrication, and the effect is the saying. The fabrication is placed before the saying because of its importance, and so that a person may recognize its falsehood before it is stated. Otherwise, the normal order would be: "Surely they say, Allah has begotten," because ﴿they say﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. The expected construction would have the noun come directly after *inna*, but it was delayed to show that this saying is false, so that it arrives in the mind already known to be false.

The ﴿min﴾ here is causal, meaning: they say it because of their fabrication. It is also permissible for it to be partitive, meaning that this vile saying is part of their fabrications, because their fabrications are many. They attributed a son to Allah, they attributed a partner to Allah, and they attributed a wife to Allah. All of this is fabrication. In sum, ﴿min﴾ may be partitive and may be causal.

His words ﴿of their own fabrication﴾ mean of their own (lying), because *ifk* is lying, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander are a group among you﴾ [An-Nur 11], meaning with the lie.

﴿They say﴾: the clause is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. The object of the saying is ﴿Allah has begotten﴾ [As-Saffat 152]. Accordingly, ﴿Allah has begotten﴾ is in the accusative position as the object of the saying: "Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, 'Allah has begotten.'" How did they say "Allah has begotten"? In what form? The author said: (by their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah). It is known that a daughter is a child, since in the Arabic language *walad* (child) applies to both a daughter and a son. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ [An-Nisa 11].

(﴿Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾ [As-Saffat 151–152] by their saying: the angels are the daughters of Allah; ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾.) This sentence is emphasized with two emphatics, and its purpose is to refute this saying. Allah refuted this saying before mentioning what is said and after mentioning it: before mentioning it in His words ﴿of their own fabrication﴾, and after it in His words ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾. We too bear witness that they are liars in this, for Allah is One, the Eternal Refuge, the Self-Sufficient. He neither begets nor is begotten, and there is none comparable to Him.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has proven the falsity of this in Surat Al-An'am. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And they have attributed to Allah partners from among the jinn, although He created them; and they have fabricated for Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Exalted is He and high above what they describe. The Originator of the heavens and the earth — how could He have a son when He has no companion and He created all things, and He is, of all things, Knowing?﴾ [Al-An'am 100–101]. He said: ﴿How could He have a son when He has no companion?﴾ How can He have a son when He has no wife? This is impossible. The second point: He created all things, and the Creator of all things cannot have a son, because a son is a part of his father, and if he were part of Him he would not be a created thing, since the part of the Creator would be a creator like Him. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And they have attributed to Him a portion from His servants. Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 15]. ﴿And He created all things, and He is, of all things, Knowing﴾ [Al-An'am 101]. He has informed us that He has no son. How then could their report be contrary to reality? Thus Allah has proven the impossibility of a son from three aspects: the impossibility of a consort, that He created all things, and the third: that He is Knowing of all things. His knowledge of all things requires that what He has told us, that He has not begotten, is true. This report must correspond to His knowledge.

He said: (﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ [As-Saffat 152] in it), meaning in their saying "Allah has begotten."

Then He said: ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ [As-Saffat 153]. ﴿Has He chosen﴾: the original form is (*istafa*), derived from (*safwa*), and the choicest part of a thing is its *safwa*. Accordingly, the meaning of ﴿iṣṭafā﴾ is "chose." Here it says ﴿iṣṭafā﴾, and it is well known that the hamza of *iṣṭafā* is a connecting hamza (*hamzat al-wasl*), not a cutting hamza (*hamzat al-qat'*). So why is it a cutting hamza here?

Listen to the author's words: (with a fatha on the hamza for interrogation). The hamza here is not the connecting hamza that is used to make it possible to pronounce the following consonant; therefore what follows it is not necessarily vowelless. The hamza here is not a connecting hamza, but an interrogative hamza. (So it is sufficient with it), meaning with the interrogative hamza, (from the connecting hamza). How is it sufficient from the connecting hamza? Because the interrogative hamza is vowelled with a fatha, so pronouncing the consonant after it is easy. The connecting hamza was introduced in order to make pronunciation of a consonant possible, and when there is a cutting hamza we dispense with the connecting hamza by means of it. Yet another possibility exists in other verses, such as ﴿iṣṭafā al-banāt﴾, where the connecting hamza is changed into a long vowel (*madd*). Among examples of this is His words, ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾ [An-Naml 59], and ﴿Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?﴾ [Yunus 59].

(And he said, "He chose" — this is the explanation of the verb "isṭafā" (chose).) Meaning: would Allah, Mighty and Majestic, choose daughters over sons? That is, even if we supposed, as a utterly impossible supposition, that Allah took a son, would He choose daughters over sons? No, because sons are nobler than daughters, and it is not possible for Allah to choose daughters over sons. Even if one supposed the absolutely impossible supposition that Allah chose a son, He would not have chosen daughters over sons, just as you yourselves do not choose daughters over sons: you assign sons to yourselves and daughters to Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 153]. What is the answer? It is: it is impossible.

﴿What is wrong with you?﴾ I want one of the brothers to parse ﴿مَا لَكُمْ﴾?

* Student: ﴿مَا لَكُمْ﴾: ﴿مَا﴾ is an interrogative, a mubtada' (subject), and ﴿لَكُمْ﴾ is the khabar (predicate).

* The Shaykh: Excellent. Do not think that ﴿مَا﴾ is a negative particle; rather it is interrogative, as the brother said. It is the subject, and the prepositional phrase ﴿لَكُمْ﴾ is the predicate. Meaning: what is it for you, that you pass this judgment and say that Allah has daughters, namely the angels?! This interrogation is for rebuke and denunciation, like the one after it: how can you pass this corrupt judgment?

This judgment, as the author said, is corrupt ("fāsid"), and also an unjust judgment: ﴿That is then an unfair division﴾ [al-Najm 22]. So it is a corrupt and unjust judgment.

Then He said: ﴿Will you not remember?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 155]. The interrogation here is also for rebuke. All the interrogations here serve rebuke and reproach, with another benefit when the context indicates it.

﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 155] He said: (with the assimilation of the tā' into the dhāl). Its original form is (تتذكرون), so the tā' was assimilated into the dhāl and it became ﴿تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾.

There is a reading ﴿تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾, so? This is the reading of the seven, and it is what is present in our mushaf: ﴿تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾.

It has passed with us that when two readings come in one verse, the better course is to recite with this one once and with that one once, so that you preserve what came in the Noble Qur'an, because all of it is from Allah. However, we said that this is not appropriate for the common people, because it causes fitnah: the layman does not know, and perhaps he is an emotional, zealous layman. If you say to him, for example, ﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾, he will say to you: ﴿أَفَلَا تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 155]. If you then go back and say ﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾, he says: ﴿أَفَلَا تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾. If you go back again and say ﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾, he may take the biggest thing he has and strike you, because he sees that you are now distorting the Qur'an.

In any case, the student of knowledge who knows that this is a reading of the seven should recite it once and what is in the mushaf once, so that he brings the Qur'an in the modes in which it was revealed.

He said: ﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 155]. The meaning of ﴿﴿تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾ is tadhakkur, i.e., admonition: will you not be admonished, so that you realize that what you have judged is an unjust judgment not acceptable from you?

He said: ﴿أَفَلَا تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ (that He, glorified is He, is exalted above having offspring). Yes, Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is exalted above having offspring, by evidence from reason and evidence from transmitted text. As for transmitted evidence, there are many verses in which Allah denies that He took a son, among them His saying: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born. Nor is there to Him any equivalent﴾ [al-Ikhlāṣ 1–4].

As for rational evidence: we say, if Allah had a son, he would be a part of Him, and would deserve worship just as his father deserves it.

Second: we say, if Allah had taken a son, this son would be created, and createdness cannot be a part of Allah, since Allah has always been and always will be, existing by His own essence, Glorified and Exalted. If it is supposed that He took a son, this son would be created; how could he be created and yet be a part of Allah? Because the son is a part of the father, as Allah said: ﴿And they have made for Him a portion from His servants﴾ [al-Zukhruf 15], and as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Fāṭimah is a part of me" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (3714), Muslim (2449/94), from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah].

It is also impossible for Allah to have a son, because a son must resemble his father. This is the third point: that he would resemble his father, and Allah, Glorified is He, has no likeness; nothing is equal to Him.

Fourth: a son is taken only by one who needs him to preserve the species, and Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has need of no one. For this reason, when a person is barren, his trace ends in this world; but when he is fertile and children follow one after another, his trace remains in the world. Therefore procreation among humans is the sole cause of the survival of the human species. These are four rational points showing the impossibility of offspring for Allah, Glorified and Exalted.

He said: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 156]. This is also a transitional idrāb (إضراب انتقالي), "rather," and here the idrāb is transitional: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, moved from rebuking them for what they judged regarding Allah having a son to demanding proof. He said: "Rather, do you have a clear authority?" The word "sulṭān" here means that by which one has authority, and authority varies according to the context. In the matter of governorships, authority is by what? By office: the ruler has authority. In the matter of actions, authority is by strength: the strong and capable one has authority over the act. In the matter of argument and seeking evidence, authority is by what? By evidence. So here ﴿سُلْطَانٌ مُبِينٌ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 156] means evidence: do you have proof? Because by proof the one who argues gains authority: if a person argues with you and has proof, he has authority over you, i.e., power. For this reason He said: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾. The word ﴿مُبِينٌ﴾ here may be from (abāna) intransitive or from (abāna) transitive. Because the quadriliteral (abāna) may be intransitive or transitive. If you say: abāna al-ṣubḥ (the dawn became clear), is it intransitive or transitive?

* Students: Intransitive.

* The Shaykh: Intransitive. And if you say: abāna fulān al-ḥaqq (so-and-so made the truth clear), that is transitive. So the word (mubīn) here: is it intransitive, meaning "do you have a clear authority," or transitive, meaning "do you have an authority that makes clear what you say, or makes the proof clear for you"? Yes, the transitive is better here, why? Because the transitive includes the intransitive; for whatever makes others clear is itself clear.

﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 156]. The author said: (a clear proof that Allah has a son). The author's phrasing "clear" indicates that he took ﴿مُبِينٌ﴾ as intransitive, i.e., "clear." But the more correct view is that it is from transitive (abāna), i.e., "making clear"; because if we take it as transitive, it necessarily implies the existence of (...), meaning the intransitive, but not the reverse.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: And (bāna) is intransitive, and (abāna) is intransitive; both are intransitive (...).

* Student: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority? Then bring your book, if you are truthful. And they have made between Him and the jinn a lineage. And the jinn certainly know that they will be brought forth. Glory be to Allah above what they describe, except the sincere servants of Allah. Indeed, you and what you worship, you cannot lead astray except one who will burn in Hellfire﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 156–163].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah says: ﴿So ask them: Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 149]. What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So ask them﴾?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Meaning, ask them.
What does the expression "istaftā" (asking for a ruling) convey to you?

* Student: Mockery of them.

* The Shaykh: It conveys mockery of them, as if He made them the judges in this.

His saying: ﴿Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 149]. The interrogation here is meant for what?

* Student: Rebuke.

* The Shaykh: Rebuke. How is His saying ﴿Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 149]? Explain this.

* Student: They claim that the angels are daughters of Allah, so this interrogation is to rebuke them.

* The Shaykh: And they assign sons to themselves: ﴿And when one of them is given good news of a female, his face becomes dark, and he suppresses grief﴾ [al-Naḥl 58], and they are content to attribute this to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

His saying: ﴿Or did We create the angels﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 150]. Is ﴿أَمْ﴾ here connected (muttaṣilah) or disconnected (munqaṭi'ah)?

* Student: Disconnected.

* The Shaykh: Disconnected. What is the sign of disconnected ʾam?

* Student: That it means "bal" and the hamzah.

* The Shaykh: Yes, it means "bal" and the hamzah. And the connected one means?

* Student: "aw" (or).

* The Shaykh: It means "aw."

His saying: ﴿Surely they say, out of their own lie﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 151]. This sentence is emphasized by several emphatics?

* Student: ﴿أَلَا﴾, the opening particle, and the energetic nūn.

* The Shaykh: That is not the energetic nūn!!

* Student: ﴿إِنَّهُمْ﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes, but it is not the energetic nūn!!

* Student: It is ﴿إِنَّهُمْ﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes, but it is not called the energetic nūn. The energetic nūn is the one that comes with the verb, like...

* Student: The emphatic.

* The Shaykh: The (inna) of emphasis.

* Student: The emphatic (inna) and the lām in ﴿لَيَقُولُونَ﴾.

* The Shaykh: Yes. And His saying: ﴿Surely they say, out of their own lie﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 151]. The ﴿مِنْ﴾ here means what?

* Student: Partitive.

* The Shaykh: Partitive. Does it not bear a second meaning?

* Student: It does not.

* The Shaykh: It does not.

* Student: It could be causal.

* The Shaykh: How causal?

* Student: The cause of (...).

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: Either it is causal (...).

* The Shaykh: Did we not say explanatory?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What does "ifk" mean?

* Student: Lie.

* The Shaykh: Lie. Where is the content of the saying in His words ﴿لَيَقُولُونَ﴾? Every saying has a content: when you say "I said," you must say what? So every saying has its content?

* Student: ﴿وَلَدَ اللَّهُ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 152].

* The Shaykh: The clause ﴿Allah has begotten﴾.

His saying: ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 153]. Why was the hamzah here cut (qaṭ') while with ṣṭafā it is a hamzat al-waṣl?

* Student: Here it is the hamzat al-istifhām.

* The Shaykh: And not the hamzat al-waṣl?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Where is the hamzat al-waṣl?

* Student: It was deleted.

* The Shaykh: It was deleted, being dispensed with because of the interrogative hamzah.
And the meaning of iṣṭafā?

* Student: Chose.

* The Shaykh: And the interrogation here means?

* Student: Rebuke.

* The Shaykh: Rebuke and negation: He rebukes them and negates that He chose daughters over sons.

His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you?﴾. The interrogation here?

* Student: The interrogation here is also for rebuke.

* The Shaykh: Also for rebuke, well done. And ﴿How do you judge?﴾?

* Student: For wonder and rebuke.

* The Shaykh: And also for rebuke.
Where is the predicate of the subject in ﴿مَا لَكُمْ﴾?

* Student: ﴿لَكُمْ﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿لَكُمْ﴾, the prepositional phrase.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verses 149–163 (part 3 of 5):

Then he said: ("And they have made" — i.e., the polytheists — "between Him" (Exalted is He) "and the jinn" — i.e., the angels, because they are hidden from sight — "a kinship" by their saying that they are the daughters of God. "And the jinn have certainly known that they will be brought forth [to punishment]" [al-Saffat 158].) "And they have made": the pronoun refers to the polytheists who said that the angels are the daughters of God.

If someone says: How can the pronoun refer to something not previously mentioned?

We say: It is mentioned by context; that is, the context determines the referent of the pronoun. It is not required that the referent of a pronoun be an explicit, clear noun; this is not a necessary condition. When the context indicates what is meant, it is treated accordingly. God Most High said: "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good [things] over the remembrance of my Lord until [the sun] disappeared behind the veil" [Sad 32]. The subject in His saying "disappeared" refers to the sun, even though it was not previously mentioned, because it is well known. And He Most High said: "Everyone upon it is perishing" [al-Rahman 26]. "Upon it" — what? Upon the earth, even though no nearby mention of it had preceded, but the context indicates it. Thus the referent of a pronoun may be determined by context.

"And they have made between Him" — i.e., between God, glory be to Him, "and the jinn a kinship" [al-Saffat 158]. It is said: al-jinna, al-janna, and al-junna (with a dhamma), and all of them revolve around concealment and hiddenness, because this root (j-n-n) all revolves around this meaning: concealment and hiddenness. From it comes janan, the heart; from it comes janin, the fetus; from it comes jinna, the jinn; from it comes jannah, a garden with many trees; from it comes junna, that which a combatant hides behind against arrows, such as a shield. So this root all revolves around the meaning of hiddenness. What, then, is meant by al-jinna here? The author says: it means "the angels." How are angels called jinn? He said: Yes, because they are concealed from the eyes; they are the world of the unseen, like the jinn who are the offspring of Satan. This is what the author adopted, but this view is very weak, because al-jinna is a name for the jinn, not for the angels. God Most High said: "[the whisperer] who whispers in the breasts of mankind, of the jinn and of mankind" [al-Nas 5–6], meaning the jinn. And He Most High said: "Or do they say there is madness in him [jinnah]?" [al-Mu'minun 70], that is, a jinn has afflicted him with possession.

It is not possible to express by the jinn, who are among the most distinctive of God's creatures and were created from fire, the angels who were created from light and are among the most noble of God's creation, glory be to Him. God Most High said: "Rather, they are honored servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command. He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not intercede except for those whom He approves, and they are, out of fear of Him, apprehensive" [al-Anbiya' 26–28]. So what is meant by al-jinna here is the jinn, who are an unseen creation created from fire. But how were they made into a kinship? The meaning of kinship here is mere connection, not the kinship of blood relation but the kinship of connection. This is because when the polytheists said that the angels are the daughters of God, it was said to them: there are no daughters except by a wife. They said: Yes, God — exalted is He, glory be to Him above what they describe — married a female jinn, and she bore the angels. May God destroy them! This is the kinship that they made between God and the jinn. So what is meant by kinship here? Mere connection, not only blood relation. This is the meaning indicated by the use of "jinn" in the speech of God, and the meaning of "jinn" is the jinn. The aspect of kinship as connection is that they said, when it was asked of them: How can you say the angels are the daughters of God? Where did the daughters come from? They said: He married a female jinn, and she bore him the angels.

God Most High said: "And the jinn have certainly known" [al-Saffat 158].

The author, directing what he adopted — that the jinn means the angels — said: "because they are concealed from sight." This does not justify calling the angels jinn.

He says: ("a kinship" [al-Saffat 158] by their saying that they are the daughters of God), thus making kinship here mean blood relation, but this view is not correct.

God Most High said: ("And the jinn have certainly known that they" — i.e., those who said that — "will be brought forth" — "to the Fire, where they will be tormented.")

"And the jinn have certainly known": this sentence is emphasized with three emphatics: the lam, qad, both apparent, and the implied oath; the meaning being: "By God, the jinn have certainly known that they will be brought forth." Emphasis here is undoubtedly of the highest rhetorical degree. That is, these jinn who were made a kinship between themselves and God know, by God's ruling, what these people do not know: they know that those who lied against God will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection, and will be raised, and will be punished according to what their crime requires. Hence He said: ("And the jinn have certainly known that they" — i.e., those who said that — "will be brought forth" — "to the Fire, where they will be tormented.")

God Most High said: ("Glory be to God" — exalting Him — "above what they describe" [al-Saffat 159] — by claiming that God has a son.)

"Glory be to God" is a verbal noun (ism masdar) of "sabbaha" (to glorify). The meaning of our saying "ism masdar of sabbaha" is that it is a verbal noun whose verb is sabbaha. What is the infinitive of sabbaha? Tasbihan. But subhan means tasbih, so it is an ism masdar, because every word that contains the meaning of the infinitive without its letters is an ism masdar. Examples are many: kalam meaning takleem, salam meaning taslim.

Regarding "Subhan Allah," the author, may God have mercy on him, said: (tanzihan lahu, "exalting Him"). So what is it that God is exalted above?

What God is exalted above revolves around two matters: deficiency, and resemblance to created beings. Deficiency in what He has affirmed for Himself of perfection; and second, resemblance to created beings. God Most High said regarding the first: "And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days" [Qaf 38] — this indicates what? Perfection of power and strength. "And no fatigue touched Us" [Qaf 38] is a negation of deficiency of strength; that is, despite the greatness of these great creations and the brevity of the time in creating them, no weariness touched God, glory be to Him; that is, no fatigue or exhaustion. This is exaltation above deficiency. And He Most High said: "There is nothing like Him" [al-Shura 11] — exaltation above resemblance to created beings.

So we say: the exaltation by which God is described revolves around two things: exaltation above deficiency in His perfection, that is, in what He has affirmed for Himself of perfection, which has no deficiency; and second, resemblance to created beings. You have understood from the evidences we mentioned.

His saying: "above what they describe" [al-Saffat 159] — that is, of deficiency and resemblance also — by their claim that God has a son. This is a description that is not fitting for God, glory be to Him, because the existence of a son entails resemblance and also entails deficiency. By claiming a son for God, they described God with deficiency and described Him with resemblance to created beings.

He said: "Glory be to God above what they describe, except the sincere servants of God" [al-Saffat 159–160]. "Servants of God": servitude (ubudiyyah) is derived from humiliation; so the 'abid means the humble one, and ta'abbud means self-abasement.

Servitude is of two kinds: servitude to decree (qadar), and servitude to the Law (shar'). That is, submission to decree and submission to the Law. As for servitude to decree, it is general to everyone; there is no person except that he is submissive to God's decree, and he cannot escape it at all. Do you understand? This is servitude to decree: every worshipper is subject to God's decree, humbled before it. The evidence for this is His saying: "There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant" [Maryam 93]. Everyone in the heavens and earth is a worshipper of God, humbled to Him. No one can leave this humility to His decree, even the most arrogant and tyrannical of people are servants of God in this sense. Pharaoh was a servant of God in this sense, was he not? And for this he was overtaken by drowning.

The second: servitude to the Law, that is, devotion to God's law. This is specific to believers, because the disbelievers did not devote themselves to God's law, but are arrogant. Among the examples and evidences of this is His saying: "And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility" [al-Furqan 63]. The meaning of servitude here is servitude to the Law, that is, those who devoted themselves to God's law, and this is specific to Muslims who submit to God's command. This too is divided into two parts: one more specific than the other. The servitude of messengerhood and prophethood is more specific than the general servitude of Islam. For example, His saying: "And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant" [al-Baqarah 23] — this is servitude of messengerhood, so it is more specific than His saying: "And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility" [al-Furqan 63]. "Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant" [al-Furqan 1] — this is also servitude of a special kind, in reality the special of the special; that is, servitude of messengerhood, which is more specific than His saying: "And the servants of the Most Merciful..." [al-Furqan 63].

His saying, Exalted: "Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them, except those of the deviators who follow you" [al-Hijr 42]. From which of the two categories?

* Students: General... the specific and the specific of the specific.
* The Shaykh: No, there is no "specific of the specific" here. If He says: "Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them except those who follow you," then if we take the exception as disjunctive (munqati'), the servitude is specifically servitude to the Law; and if we take the exception as connected (muttasil), it is servitude to decree. That is why the scholars differed about it: is the exception disjunctive or connected? This verse is similar to "except the sincere servants of God" [al-Saffat 160], that is, the believers whom God has purified for Himself.

The author said: ("disjunctive exception"). The sign of a disjunctive exception is that what follows "illa" is not of the same kind as what precedes it, and the second sign is that "illa" carries the meaning of "lakin" (but). That is why we call it a disjunctive exception, as if what follows it has been cut off from what precedes it. Accordingly, if the exception is disjunctive, as the author said, we say: "except the sincere servants of God" [al-Saffat 160] means what? "But the sincere servants of God" — that is, they did not describe Him with this description. He, may God Most High have mercy on him, said: ("a disjunctive exception; that is, they exalt God above what these people describe").

Some scholars held that the exception here is connected; it is an exception from the waw in His saying: "Glory be to God above what they describe" [al-Saffat 159], and the meaning would be: "Glory be to God above what all people describe, except what the sincere servants of God describe Him with, for He is characterized by it." This is a possibility, but the apparent context supports what the author adopted, that His saying "Glory be to God above what they describe" refers to whom? To the polytheists who described Him as having daughters, and believers are not included among them. The believers are not of the same kind as what was excepted from, and then the exception is disjunctive. The benefit of this disjunctive exception is the praise of the sincere servants of God, in that they did not describe Him with what those others described Him with.
