Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verses 149–163 (part 3 of 5):

Then he said: ("And they have made" — i.e., the polytheists — "between Him" (Exalted is He) "and the jinn" — i.e., the angels, because they are hidden from sight — "a kinship" by their saying that they are the daughters of God. "And the jinn have certainly known that they will be brought forth [to punishment]" [al-Saffat 158].) "And they have made": the pronoun refers to the polytheists who said that the angels are the daughters of God.

If someone says: How can the pronoun refer to something not previously mentioned?

We say: It is mentioned by context; that is, the context determines the referent of the pronoun. It is not required that the referent of a pronoun be an explicit, clear noun; this is not a necessary condition. When the context indicates what is meant, it is treated accordingly. God Most High said: "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good [things] over the remembrance of my Lord until [the sun] disappeared behind the veil" [Sad 32]. The subject in His saying "disappeared" refers to the sun, even though it was not previously mentioned, because it is well known. And He Most High said: "Everyone upon it is perishing" [al-Rahman 26]. "Upon it" — what? Upon the earth, even though no nearby mention of it had preceded, but the context indicates it. Thus the referent of a pronoun may be determined by context.

"And they have made between Him" — i.e., between God, glory be to Him, "and the jinn a kinship" [al-Saffat 158]. It is said: al-jinna, al-janna, and al-junna (with a dhamma), and all of them revolve around concealment and hiddenness, because this root (j-n-n) all revolves around this meaning: concealment and hiddenness. From it comes janan, the heart; from it comes janin, the fetus; from it comes jinna, the jinn; from it comes jannah, a garden with many trees; from it comes junna, that which a combatant hides behind against arrows, such as a shield. So this root all revolves around the meaning of hiddenness. What, then, is meant by al-jinna here? The author says: it means "the angels." How are angels called jinn? He said: Yes, because they are concealed from the eyes; they are the world of the unseen, like the jinn who are the offspring of Satan. This is what the author adopted, but this view is very weak, because al-jinna is a name for the jinn, not for the angels. God Most High said: "[the whisperer] who whispers in the breasts of mankind, of the jinn and of mankind" [al-Nas 5–6], meaning the jinn. And He Most High said: "Or do they say there is madness in him [jinnah]?" [al-Mu'minun 70], that is, a jinn has afflicted him with possession.

It is not possible to express by the jinn, who are among the most distinctive of God's creatures and were created from fire, the angels who were created from light and are among the most noble of God's creation, glory be to Him. God Most High said: "Rather, they are honored servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command. He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not intercede except for those whom He approves, and they are, out of fear of Him, apprehensive" [al-Anbiya' 26–28]. So what is meant by al-jinna here is the jinn, who are an unseen creation created from fire. But how were they made into a kinship? The meaning of kinship here is mere connection, not the kinship of blood relation but the kinship of connection. This is because when the polytheists said that the angels are the daughters of God, it was said to them: there are no daughters except by a wife. They said: Yes, God — exalted is He, glory be to Him above what they describe — married a female jinn, and she bore the angels. May God destroy them! This is the kinship that they made between God and the jinn. So what is meant by kinship here? Mere connection, not only blood relation. This is the meaning indicated by the use of "jinn" in the speech of God, and the meaning of "jinn" is the jinn. The aspect of kinship as connection is that they said, when it was asked of them: How can you say the angels are the daughters of God? Where did the daughters come from? They said: He married a female jinn, and she bore him the angels.

God Most High said: "And the jinn have certainly known" [al-Saffat 158].

The author, directing what he adopted — that the jinn means the angels — said: "because they are concealed from sight." This does not justify calling the angels jinn.

He says: ("a kinship" [al-Saffat 158] by their saying that they are the daughters of God), thus making kinship here mean blood relation, but this view is not correct.

God Most High said: ("And the jinn have certainly known that they" — i.e., those who said that — "will be brought forth" — "to the Fire, where they will be tormented.")

"And the jinn have certainly known": this sentence is emphasized with three emphatics: the lam, qad, both apparent, and the implied oath; the meaning being: "By God, the jinn have certainly known that they will be brought forth." Emphasis here is undoubtedly of the highest rhetorical degree. That is, these jinn who were made a kinship between themselves and God know, by God's ruling, what these people do not know: they know that those who lied against God will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection, and will be raised, and will be punished according to what their crime requires. Hence He said: ("And the jinn have certainly known that they" — i.e., those who said that — "will be brought forth" — "to the Fire, where they will be tormented.")

God Most High said: ("Glory be to God" — exalting Him — "above what they describe" [al-Saffat 159] — by claiming that God has a son.)

"Glory be to God" is a verbal noun (ism masdar) of "sabbaha" (to glorify). The meaning of our saying "ism masdar of sabbaha" is that it is a verbal noun whose verb is sabbaha. What is the infinitive of sabbaha? Tasbihan. But subhan means tasbih, so it is an ism masdar, because every word that contains the meaning of the infinitive without its letters is an ism masdar. Examples are many: kalam meaning takleem, salam meaning taslim.

Regarding "Subhan Allah," the author, may God have mercy on him, said: (tanzihan lahu, "exalting Him"). So what is it that God is exalted above?

What God is exalted above revolves around two matters: deficiency, and resemblance to created beings. Deficiency in what He has affirmed for Himself of perfection; and second, resemblance to created beings. God Most High said regarding the first: "And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days" [Qaf 38] — this indicates what? Perfection of power and strength. "And no fatigue touched Us" [Qaf 38] is a negation of deficiency of strength; that is, despite the greatness of these great creations and the brevity of the time in creating them, no weariness touched God, glory be to Him; that is, no fatigue or exhaustion. This is exaltation above deficiency. And He Most High said: "There is nothing like Him" [al-Shura 11] — exaltation above resemblance to created beings.

So we say: the exaltation by which God is described revolves around two things: exaltation above deficiency in His perfection, that is, in what He has affirmed for Himself of perfection, which has no deficiency; and second, resemblance to created beings. You have understood from the evidences we mentioned.

His saying: "above what they describe" [al-Saffat 159] — that is, of deficiency and resemblance also — by their claim that God has a son. This is a description that is not fitting for God, glory be to Him, because the existence of a son entails resemblance and also entails deficiency. By claiming a son for God, they described God with deficiency and described Him with resemblance to created beings.

He said: "Glory be to God above what they describe, except the sincere servants of God" [al-Saffat 159–160]. "Servants of God": servitude (ubudiyyah) is derived from humiliation; so the 'abid means the humble one, and ta'abbud means self-abasement.

Servitude is of two kinds: servitude to decree (qadar), and servitude to the Law (shar'). That is, submission to decree and submission to the Law. As for servitude to decree, it is general to everyone; there is no person except that he is submissive to God's decree, and he cannot escape it at all. Do you understand? This is servitude to decree: every worshipper is subject to God's decree, humbled before it. The evidence for this is His saying: "There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant" [Maryam 93]. Everyone in the heavens and earth is a worshipper of God, humbled to Him. No one can leave this humility to His decree, even the most arrogant and tyrannical of people are servants of God in this sense. Pharaoh was a servant of God in this sense, was he not? And for this he was overtaken by drowning.

The second: servitude to the Law, that is, devotion to God's law. This is specific to believers, because the disbelievers did not devote themselves to God's law, but are arrogant. Among the examples and evidences of this is His saying: "And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility" [al-Furqan 63]. The meaning of servitude here is servitude to the Law, that is, those who devoted themselves to God's law, and this is specific to Muslims who submit to God's command. This too is divided into two parts: one more specific than the other. The servitude of messengerhood and prophethood is more specific than the general servitude of Islam. For example, His saying: "And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant" [al-Baqarah 23] — this is servitude of messengerhood, so it is more specific than His saying: "And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility" [al-Furqan 63]. "Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant" [al-Furqan 1] — this is also servitude of a special kind, in reality the special of the special; that is, servitude of messengerhood, which is more specific than His saying: "And the servants of the Most Merciful..." [al-Furqan 63].

His saying, Exalted: "Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them, except those of the deviators who follow you" [al-Hijr 42]. From which of the two categories?

* Students: General... the specific and the specific of the specific.
* The Shaykh: No, there is no "specific of the specific" here. If He says: "Indeed, My servants — you have no authority over them except those who follow you," then if we take the exception as disjunctive (munqati'), the servitude is specifically servitude to the Law; and if we take the exception as connected (muttasil), it is servitude to decree. That is why the scholars differed about it: is the exception disjunctive or connected? This verse is similar to "except the sincere servants of God" [al-Saffat 160], that is, the believers whom God has purified for Himself.

The author said: ("disjunctive exception"). The sign of a disjunctive exception is that what follows "illa" is not of the same kind as what precedes it, and the second sign is that "illa" carries the meaning of "lakin" (but). That is why we call it a disjunctive exception, as if what follows it has been cut off from what precedes it. Accordingly, if the exception is disjunctive, as the author said, we say: "except the sincere servants of God" [al-Saffat 160] means what? "But the sincere servants of God" — that is, they did not describe Him with this description. He, may God Most High have mercy on him, said: ("a disjunctive exception; that is, they exalt God above what these people describe").

Some scholars held that the exception here is connected; it is an exception from the waw in His saying: "Glory be to God above what they describe" [al-Saffat 159], and the meaning would be: "Glory be to God above what all people describe, except what the sincere servants of God describe Him with, for He is characterized by it." This is a possibility, but the apparent context supports what the author adopted, that His saying "Glory be to God above what they describe" refers to whom? To the polytheists who described Him as having daughters, and believers are not included among them. The believers are not of the same kind as what was excepted from, and then the exception is disjunctive. The benefit of this disjunctive exception is the praise of the sincere servants of God, in that they did not describe Him with what those others described Him with.

* * *

* The student: "And there is none of us but has a known station. And indeed, we are those who line up. And indeed, we are those who glorify. And indeed, they used to say, 'If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been sincere servants of God.'" [al-Saffat 164–169].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God, blessed and exalted, said: "Then bring your scripture, if you are truthful" [al-Saffat 157]. Who is meant by the command here?

* A student: "Then bring your scripture, if you are truthful" [al-Saffat 157] — the polytheists are meant.

* The Shaykh: But what is meant by the command?

* The student: The command is for rebuke; the miraculousness and challenge.

* The Shaykh: The challenge and the miraculousness.

And what is the position of the clause "if you are truthful" in relation to what precedes it, in meaning?

* A student: A circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya).

* The Shaykh: No, in meaning, not in grammar.

* The student: The meaning is determined by the context.

* The Shaykh: That is, but it is not meant in grammar.

* The student: "If you are truthful" [al-Saffat 157] — that God has daughters, that the angels are the daughters of God.

* Another student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It is an emphasis of the challenge and miraculousness; its position relative to what precedes it is an emphasis of the challenge and miraculousness.

There remains a point needing to be known which we did not explain yesterday: "Then bring your scripture, if you are truthful" [al-Saffat 157]. It is known that "in" here is conditional, and that it requires a protasis and an apodosis. Is that so? The protasis is present: "if you are truthful." Where is its apodosis? It is said: its apodosis is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, which is "then bring your scripture," and the estimate is: "then bring your scripture if you are truthful, then bring your scripture," so it is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, and it is not necessary to mention it, because mentioning it is superfluous. It was also said: the conditional "in" in such a construction requires no apodosis at all; it is without an apodosis. On this view, there is no estimate in such a construction, and since this omitted element was known, there is no need to mention it, and if we have no need to mention it we have no need to estimate it.

Then God, Mighty and Majestic, said: "Indeed, you and what you worship, you cannot tempt [anyone] concerning Him, except one who is to burn in Hell" [al-Saffat 161–163]. "Indeed, you" — the address here is to the disbelievers, and there is an iltifat (shift) from third person to second person, because the kaf is for the addressee, and the addressee is present, whereas what preceded had pronouns referring to an absent party: "And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship. And the jinn have certainly known that they will be brought forth. Glory be to God above what they describe" [al-Saffat 158–159], all with third-person pronouns.

The shift has a consistent benefit: a shift from address to third person, or the reverse, has a consistent benefit, namely alerting the addressee. The reason is that when the address is in one uniform manner, there is nothing prompting attention; when the style changes, a person pays attention. This benefit is consistent in every place where there is a shift. There is another benefit that depends on the context and is not consistent in every place, and the benefit here in "Indeed, you and what you worship" [al-Saffat 161] is that when God, glory be to Him, spoke of them in the third-person form, and what follows the third-person pronouns concerned a matter whose possessor thinks he is able to do it, He addressed him directly, to humiliate him and to show his weakness and inability to do ... (...).

The disbelievers try to tempt people away from their religion by every means: sometimes by promoting their deities, sometimes by disparaging the worship of God, sometimes by disparaging the Muslims, and so on, thinking they stand on something. So God Most High addressed them with explicit address, as a humiliation, saying: "Indeed, you" — O polytheists — "and what you worship" — of idols. He used "ma" (what), which is generally used for non-rational beings, because most of what the polytheists worship is non-rational.

It is possible that "ma" is a verbal (masdariyya) particle; that is, "indeed, you and your worship; you cannot tempt anyone to it." The meaning in both readings is one: you and your idols do not tempt people except those who are to burn in Hell; or you and your worship do not tempt people to it except those who are to burn in Hell.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 149–163 (part 4 of 5):

His saying: "﴿وَمَا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ [al-Saffat 161] — from the idols." Do they worship idols? The answer: Yes, they worship idols. They make vows to them, they bow and prostrate to them, they seek help from them, and they consider them equal to God. Yet their minds have deceived them, and indeed their devils have deceived them, as they say: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to God in closeness﴾ [al-Zumar 3]. The reality is that their worship of them distances them from God and does not bring them near to Him.

He says: "﴿So indeed you and what you worship (161) are not ones who can lead astray concerning it﴾, i.e., concerning your deity, and 'concerning it' is connected to His saying ﴿bi-fatinin﴾ (those who lead astray), meaning anyone."

His saying: ﴿So indeed you and what you worship (161) concerning it are not ones who can lead astray﴾ [al-Saffat 161, 162]. It is well known that this "inna" (indeed) requires a noun and a predicate. Its noun is the kaf in "innakum" (you), and ﴿wa-ma taʿbudūn﴾ (and what you worship) is conjoined to it, and the clause ﴿ma antum ʿalayhi bi-fatinin﴾ (you are not those who can lead astray concerning it) is the predicate. The meaning: you and your deities cannot lead anyone away from the religion of God, except one who is destined for the blazing fire.

As for His saying ﴿ma antum ʿalayhi bi-fatinin﴾, the author said: "i.e., concerning your deity," and did not say "concerning them" (i.e., your deities), so that it includes each one individually; that is, none of these deities can cause any person to be led astray concerning it.

As for His saying ﴿bi-fatinin﴾, it means "those who turn away," because fitnah (trial, seduction) can mean turning away, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Buruj 10], i.e., they turned them away. It also comes in the sense of testing, as in: ﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah 102], and it has other meanings, but what is intended here is "those who turn away." The author's statement "concerning it is connected to ﴿bi-fatinin﴾" means the estimated sense is: "you are not those who lead astray concerning it." The word fatin is an active participle from fatana, which is a transitive verb, so where is its object? The author estimated it in his saying "i.e., anyone." The meaning of the verse in general terms is that God addressed these polytheists: that they and their deities, however much they employ schemes and propaganda, will never lead anyone astray so that he worships these idols.

﴿Except for him who is destined for the blazing fire﴾ [al-Saffat 163] means: except for the one who is destined for the blazing fire. ﴿Ṣāli﴾ is an active participle, and the yā' at the end of the verb was deleted because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Where are the two unvocalized letters? The yā' and the hamzat al-wasl: ﴿illa man huwa ṣāli al-jaḥīm﴾. According to the author's view, ﴿man﴾ is in the accusative position as a substitute for the omitted object ("anyone"): "you are not those who lead anyone astray, except him who is..."

Some grammarians held that ﴿man﴾ is the object of "fatinin," on the basis that it is an exceptive construction that is "emptied" (istithna' mufarragh). Do you know the emptied exception? It is where what follows "illa" (except) is a complement of what precedes it. This emptied exception, whether it is the subject, object, or genitive, is such that when you say: "Ma qama illa Zayd" (no one stood except Zayd), this is an emptied exception, because you have emptied the governing verb of its complement, leaving only what follows illa. So you say: "ma" is a negation particle, "qama" is a past-tense verb, "illa" is a particle of restriction (not an exception particle here), and "Zayd" is the subject. And you say: "Ma ra'aytu illa 'Amran" (I did not see except 'Amr): "ra'aytu" is a verb and subject, "illa" is a particle of restriction, and "'Amran" is the object of "ra'aytu." And you say: "Ma marartu illa bi-Zayd" (I did not pass except by Zayd): "illa" is a particle of restriction, and "bi-Zayd" is a prepositional phrase attached to "marartu."

Accordingly, the verse before us is like the example we have given, namely "Ma ra'aytu illa Zaydan," and this view of some grammarians is more correct than that of the author; that is, the exception is emptied, and therefore we do not need to estimate the object, so the "anyone" the author estimated is unnecessary, because the exception is emptied. Just as if you say "Ma ra'aytu illa Zaydan," you do not need to estimate "Ma ra'aytu aḥadan illa Zaydan," you do not need this estimate, so likewise: ﴿ma antum ʿalayhi bi-fatinin (162) illa man huwa ṣāli al-jaḥīm﴾ [al-Saffat 162, 163].

The summary of the matter: we say, ﴿ma antum ʿalayhi bi-fatinin﴾ [al-Saffat 162]: "ma" is a negation particle, "antum" is its noun, and "bi-fatinin" is its predicate. "Fatin" is an active participle that requires an object, and the object is "man" in His saying ﴿illa man huwa ṣāli al-jaḥīm﴾ [al-Saffat 163].

As for His saying ﴿ṣāli al-jaḥīm﴾, the author said: "in the knowledge of God." He needed to estimate "in the knowledge of God" because ﴿ṣāli﴾ is an active participle, and they have not yet entered it, why? Because they have not died. The one being led astray is alive, so how can one say "destined for the blazing fire" when he has not yet died? The author said: the intended meaning is "destined for the blazing fire in God's knowledge"; that is, whoever God knows will enter the blazing fire is the one you lead astray, whereas whoever God knows to be a believer, you will not lead astray. This is like His saying: ﴿Whomever God guides, he is the one rightly guided, and whomever He leaves astray, those are the losers﴾ [al-A'raf 178].

God, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So ask them: Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?﴾ [al-Saffat 149].

* Among the benefits of this: challenging the people of disbelief and polytheism by presenting evidence against what they say of lies and fabrication.
* Also among its benefits: mockery of these polytheists, in that He made them like scholars who are consulted, while they are, without doubt, the most ignorant of people.
* And among its benefits: clarifying the injustice of these polytheists, in that they attributed daughters to God while they themselves dislike daughters: ﴿When one of them is given good news of a female, his face becomes darkened, and he suppresses his anger﴾ [al-Nahl 58], yet they attribute daughters to God, although both sons and daughters are impossible for God, since God neither begets nor is begotten.
* And among the benefits of the noble verses, all of them: a rebuke of those who said that the angels are God's daughters, based on His saying: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ [al-Saffat 150].
* And among its benefits also: challenging those who claimed that God, glorified and exalted, made the angels His daughters, since it is said to them: Did you witness God's creation of daughters so that you know they are God's daughters? The answer: did they witness it or not? They did not witness it; therefore He said: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ [al-Saffat 150].
* And among its benefits: affirming the angels, and belief in the angels is one of the six pillars of faith, as is well known.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that whoever makes a claim is required to provide proof for it, based on His saying: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ [al-Saffat 150]. So were they witnesses, that they could make such a claim?
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: affirming the fabrication of these liars who claimed that God has a son, based on His saying: ﴿Surely they say, out of their own fabrication (151), "God has begotten"﴾ [al-Saffat 151, 152].
* And among its benefits: that these people have multiple fabrications, based on the view that "min" is partitive: ﴿Surely they say, out of their own fabrication, "God has begotten"﴾ [al-Saffat 151, 152].
* And among the benefits of the verses: that God, exalted, is free from having offspring, because God made this claim a fabrication and a lie, and God affirmed this by His saying: ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾.
* And among the benefits of the verses also: proving against these people through the evidence of reason, which is to say: how could God prefer daughters over sons? This is not reasonable, not rational; yet they regard this thing as a reasonable and necessary matter: that God should have daughters and they should have sons.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that these people who passed this judgment are most like madmen; therefore they were addressed in the manner of addressing a madman, when it was said to them: ﴿What is wrong with you?﴾, i.e., what is this action? Is this the action of a sane person?!
* And among its benefits: denouncing every false judgment, based on His saying: ﴿How do you judge?﴾ [al-Saffat 154], for this is a denunciation of them for this judgment whose falsehood is known by necessity of reason and transmitted text.
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: declaring the foolishness of these people and that they do not benefit from the signs, based on His saying: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ [al-Saffat 155].
* And among its benefits also: rebuking whoever does not remember, since the rhetorical question here is meant as a rebuke; so whoever does not reflect upon God's signs is undoubtedly deserving of blame and rebuke.
* And among its benefits: showing the justice of God, mighty and majestic, in debating an enemy and opponent, in His saying: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [al-Saffat 156]. God did not limit Himself to denying them, meaning merely calling them liars, but demanded from them proof if they were truthful in their claim. It is known that they will not establish proof; therefore He said: ﴿Then bring your book, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Saffat 157].
* And among its benefits also: the permissibility of challenging the opponent with something he cannot achieve, and that this is one of the methods of silencing him.

For in a debate, the opponent's argument can be refuted in several ways; among them is the challenge. But the challenge must be with something that he cannot establish proof and evidence for, because if you challenge him with something he can establish proof and evidence for, and he does so, he will defeat you and weaken your position. So beware of challenging in a debate except with something you know cannot be done.

This is why God, the Exalted, mentioned in the debate of Abraham with the man, when Abraham said: ﴿My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. The man said to him: "I give life and cause death." Abraham said: ﴿Indeed God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. Abraham, peace be upon him, first challenged him by saying that God gives life and causes death, while you, O debater, neither give life nor cause death. When he falsely claimed that he gives life and causes death, and this was a deception upon the common people, because he said: "I give life and cause death": I bring a man deserving of execution and I do not kill him; this, by his claim, is giving life. The reality is that this is not giving life, but sparing a life; and it is not even sparing a life, but removing a cause by which death would occur, and this man whose cause of death we removed may survive or may not. And he said: I bring an innocent man and I kill him; this, by his claim, is causing death. But this is not causing death; it is merely doing an act that may cause death, and it may not cause death.

The conclusion is that Abraham, peace be upon him, wanted to shorten the path and cut it short, saying: ﴿Indeed God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾ [al-Baqarah 258], and the disbeliever was defeated (﴿so the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾). This is one of the etiquettes of debate: silencing the opponent with what he cannot establish as proof and evidence. But, as I said, you must observe that if you silence him, or challenge him with something he can do, and he does it, this weakens your position, and it will be one of the means of your defeat; therefore He said: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [al-Saffat 156].

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that proof is an authority for its holder, because by it he holds power over his opponent whom he debates.

* Student: ﴿ṣāli al-jaḥīm﴾, the yā' is deleted (...).
* Shaykh: Because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters.
* Student: Which ones?
* Shaykh: The jaḥīm — is it not a hamzat al-wasl?
* Student: In the case of "qāḍin," the yā' was deleted from it.
* Shaykh: That is also because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters, since the tanwīn is unvocalized.
* Student: And here, if that is so (...).
* Shaykh: This is due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, but it differs, because here there is no tanwīn; the reason is that what has tanwīn is not construct, and the construct does not take tanwīn. Did you not hear the poet's saying:
"As if I am tanwīn, and you are an idāfa (construct), so where do you see me, may the place not be lowered for me."
* Student: And you do not combine the definite article with tanwīn.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: God said in the verse: ﴿So indeed you and what you worship (161) concerning it are not ones who can lead astray﴾ [al-Saffat 161, 162]. Does this mean that among them are rational and non-rational beings?
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. But what is predominant?
* Student: The predominant is that it refers to non-rational beings.
* Shaykh: Non-rational; therefore He used "ma" by way of predominance (taghlīb).
* Student: Is this by way of predominance?
* Shaykh: Yes, like: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens glorifies God﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 1].
* Student: Can we take from the verses as a whole God's preference of the male child over the female child?
* Shaykh: Of the son over the daughter? It is well known that the son is better.
* Student: So it is included in His saying: ﴿Men are the protectors of women﴾ [al-Nisa' 34]?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station (164). And indeed we are those who stand in rows (165). And indeed we are those who glorify (166). And indeed they used to say (167): If only we had a reminder from the former peoples (168), we would surely have been the sincere servants of God (169). But they disbelieved in it, so they will soon know﴾ [al-Saffat 164–170].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan. God the Exalted said: ﴿So bring your book, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Saffat 157].
* From the benefits of this verse: that whoever challenges another is entitled to demand proof for what that other says, by His saying: ﴿So bring your book﴾ [al-Saffat 157].
* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that the proof of the Qur'an is a decisive, binding proof that cannot be escaped; therefore it always comes in the form of a challenge, to demonstrate the incapacity of the opponent and his inability to counter it.
* And among the benefits of this noble verse: that these people are lying in what they claim and unable to establish proof for it, by His saying: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ [al-Saffat 157].
* And among the benefits of His saying: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ [al-Saffat 158] and onward: a clarification of the arrogance and transgression of these people, in that they described God, glorified and exalted, with what does not befit Him, making between Him and the jinn a kinship.
* And among its benefits: that these people who made between Him and the jinn a kinship know that they are punished for what they said, and that they will be brought forth into the Fire, by His saying: ﴿And the jinn certainly know that they will be brought forth﴾ [al-Saffat 158].
* And among its benefits: that this jinn is disassociated from what these people claim concerning it, because when it knows that they will be brought forth into punishment, it did not approve of what they claimed for God, glorified and exalted, of offspring.
* And among the benefits of the noble verses: the glorification of God above what the wrongdoers and transgressors describe, by His saying: ﴿Glory be to God above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat 159].
* And among its benefits: that God's attributes are negative, meaning indicating negation, and affirmative, meaning indicating affirmation. His saying ﴿Glory be to God﴾ is among the negative attributes, because it is exaltation. The negative attributes by which God describes Himself do not indicate bare negation, because bare negation is nothing, let alone praise; rather they indicate the affirmation of His perfection, free from this defect. So glorifying God above what is not fitting for Him implies His perfection in what is specific to Him, glorified and exalted. This is a rule for all negative attributes: they are not meant as bare negation, because bare negation is nothing, being a negation, let alone praise; rather they are meant to affirm His perfection, glorified and exalted, in His attributes, such that every attribute of deficiency is negated from Him.
* And among the benefits of the noble verses: that among the servants of God, glorified and exalted, are those upon whom He bestowed favour, purifying them, and they purified their sincerity to Him, by His saying: ﴿except the sincere servants of God﴾ [al-Saffat 160], those whom God purified from what afflicted others, and those who were sincere to God in what they describe Him with.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: this noble Qur'an is *mathani* (oft-repeated pairs), in which things are paired. When it mentions the blameworthy attribute of a people, it then mentions the praiseworthy attributes of other peoples. So when Allah mentioned what these wrongdoing transgressors were described as, He made clear that there are people who are not in this state: they are the servants of Allah whom Allah has purified for Himself, and who have purified for Him what is due to Him.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So indeed you and what you worship, / you cannot tempt [anyone] against Him, / except one who is destined for the Blazing Fire.﴾ [As-Saffat 161–163] In this verse is a clarification that these criminals, who describe Allah with what does not befit Him and who turn people away from the path of Allah, will never be able to lead astray those whom Allah has guided. They only lead astray the one who is *salin al-Jahim* (destined to burn in the Hellfire); that is, the one who follows them in their misguidance, until he enters the Hellfire.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: it points out that whoever follows the people of evil in their evil is feared to be among those for whom it has been decreed that they are companions of the Hellfire, based on His saying: ﴿You cannot tempt [anyone] against Him, except one who is destined for the Blazing Fire﴾ [As-Saffat 162–163].

* Another of its benefits: people of insight cannot be among the companions of the Fire, because they know the truth and know falsehood, so they take hold of the truth and avoid falsehood. The reasoning for this is that Allah informed us that these criminal, misguided, misguiding people will never be able to tempt anyone away from his religion except one who is destined for the Blazing Fire. So a person should beware of the temptation of the people of evil and corruption, lest he be among those destined for the Blazing Fire.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of punishment in the Hereafter, based on His saying: ﴿except one who is destined for the Blazing Fire﴾ [As-Saffat 163]. What is meant is the Hellfire of the Hereafter and its fire, not the hellfire of this world.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: that people are divided into two categories: those destined for the Hellfire and those saved from it. This is because the exception in His saying ﴿except one who is destined for the Blazing Fire﴾ indicates that there is something excepted from it, namely the second category, for whom Allah has decreed salvation.

The student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿So ask them, "Has your Lord got daughters while they have sons? Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses? Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, 'Allah has begotten,' and indeed they are liars. Has He chosen daughters over sons? What is the matter with you? How do you judge? Will you not then take heed? Or do you have a clear authority? Then bring your Book, if you are truthful. And they have made a kinship between Him and the jinn, but the jinn know that they will be brought forth. Glory be to Allah above what they describe, except for the sincere servants of Allah.﴾ [Al-Saffat 149–160].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿So ask them, "Has your Lord got daughters while they have sons?"﴾ The command in His words ﴿So ask them﴾ refers to the Messenger of Allah ﴿ﷺ﴾, and the pronoun in His words ﴿ask them﴾ refers to the polytheists who attributed daughters to Allah while they themselves have sons.

His words ﴿ask them﴾ mean: request from them that they give you a ruling. The *iftaa* (issuing of a legal ruling) originally means the explanation of a legal ruling. Directing the request for a ruling to them is by way of mockery, as if they had appointed themselves judges who rule as they wish. This is like His words, ﴿Taste! Indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [Ad-Dukhan 49], according to one of the two opinions regarding its interpretation. Otherwise, these people are not qualified to be asked for a ruling, let alone to be asked about this grave matter. But this is by way of mockery.

Then He stated the matter asked about, saying: ﴿Has your Lord got daughters while they have sons?﴾ The interrogative here is for rebuke, meaning He rebukes them for this ruling, which is already known, since they attributed daughters to Allah and attributed sons to themselves.

For this reason He says: ﴿So ask them﴾ (inquire of the Makkan disbelievers as a rebuke to them). This refers to the interrogation. As for the mockery, it is the directing of the request for a ruling to them. He said: ﴿Has your Lord got daughters﴾ (according to their claim that the angels are the daughters of Allah) ﴿while they have sons﴾, so they take the best for themselves, meaning the most excellent. That is, is this a sound and just ruling, or a false and unjust ruling? The answer is known to everyone: this is a false and unjust ruling. For this reason Allah, Exalted, said in Surat An-Najm: ﴿Is for you the male and for Him the female? That, then, is an unfair division﴾ [An-Najm 21–22], meaning unjust. His words ﴿while they have sons﴾ are not a circumstantial clause (*hal*); rather, the clause is conjoined to the clause before it (*ma'tuf*), so it falls within the scope of the interrogation, meaning: how can Allah have daughters while they have sons? This is an unjust ruling. For this reason He said: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾

The particle ﴿or﴾ here (*am*) is *munqati'a* (disjunctive), and the disjunctive *am* is the one used for transition (*li-l-idrab*); for this reason it is estimated as ﴿bal﴾ ("rather") together with the interrogative hamza. For example, ﴿Or did We create the angels﴾: the sense of the sentence is "Rather, did We create the angels as females?" The *am* may be conjunctive (*muttasila*) and may be disjunctive (*munqati'a*). When it can be replaced by ﴿bal﴾ and the interrogative hamza, it is disjunctive; and when it means ﴿aw﴾ ("or"), it is conjunctive. You say: "Is Zayd with you or 'Amr?" meaning "or 'Amr?"

﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [Al-Munafiqun 6], meaning: "or you do not ask forgiveness for them," and the conjunctive form generally follows the equalizing hamza (*hamzat al-taswiyah*). ﴿Or did We create the angels as females?﴾ His words ﴿We created the angels as females﴾ mean: "We made them females." Accordingly, ﴿females﴾ is the second object of ﴿created﴾. It is also permissible to keep ﴿created﴾ in its original sense, meaning: "Or did We make the angels into females?" It is also permissible to keep ﴿created﴾ in its own sense, and ﴿females﴾ is then in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "Or did We create the angels in a state of being females?" The answer: No, did Allah create the angels as females? No, Allah did not create the angels as females, nor even as males. For this reason we do not describe the angels as female or as male, because the angels do not reproduce, do not eat, and do not drink. But they said that the angels are the daughters of Allah, so they made the angels females.

﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ (We created them, so they say that). The clause in His words ﴿while they were witnesses﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. The meaning: Did We create the angels as females while these people were witnessing Our creating them as females? The answer: No. Allah did not create the angels as females, and they did not witness their creation. This is like His statement in the second verse: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, into females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded and they will be questioned﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 19].

The summary is that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has explained to these people two states:

The first state: the unjust ruling they pronounced among themselves and between them and Allah, when they attributed the angels to Allah while attributing sons to themselves. This is injustice, as the Surat An-Najm indicates.

The second state: their making the angels females. Whether they had assigned sons to themselves or not, this is also a lie and a fabrication, because they did not witness the creation of the angels so as to judge them to be females. For this reason He said: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ And who are the angels?

The angels are an unseen world (*'alam ghaybi*); they are absent from us and we do not see them, except when Allah shows them to us as an honour, or as a sign. Otherwise they are an unseen world, because there is no human being except that he has two angels on his right and on his left, seated, and angels who guard him from before him and behind him, guarding him by the command of Allah. We do not see them. And there are angels who attend gatherings of remembrance, and we do not see them, because they belong to the unseen world. The angels were created from light, as established from the Messenger of Allah ﴿ﷺ﴾ [Reported by Muslim (1827/18) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr]. They were created as *samad* (i.e., they do not eat and do not drink), because they glorify Allah night and day without respite.

Among the angels are those whose identities we know and those whose identities we do not know. Among those whose identities we know are Jibril, Mika'il, and Israfil, whom the Prophet ﴿ﷺ﴾ used to name at the beginning of the night prayer, saying: "O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mika'il, and Israfil, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that in which they differed. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth in what has been disputed, for You guide whom You will to a straight path." [Reported by Muslim (770/200) from the hadith of 'A'ishah.]

* * *

* Student: (...) ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [As-Saffat 182].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: ﴿And Our word had already preceded to Our servants, the messengers﴾ [As-Saffat 171] (...). Mika'il (is over) that which gives life to the earth, which is rain and vegetation, and Israfil (is over) that which gives life to bodies at the blowing of the Trumpet, for he has put the Trumpet to his mouth, waiting for when he will be commanded. The point is that it is obligatory for us to believe in the angels in general regarding those whose names we do not know, and specifically regarding those whose names we know. We also believe in what we know of their attributes; for example, Jibril has six hundred wings which fill the horizon [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3232) and Muslim (174/280) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud], and in what we know of their states and their worship, because this is among the foundations of faith which the Messenger ﴿ﷺ﴾ explained to Jibril when he asked him about faith. He said: "That you believe in Allah and His angels" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9/5) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. It is also incumbent upon us to love these angels, to honour them and to exalt them, because they are servants of Allah: ﴿honoured servants﴾ [Al-Anbiya 26], obedient to the command of Allah, so we love them for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It is also incumbent upon us to honour them, so we hate whoever is hostile to them, such as the Jews, for example, who were hostile to Jibril. We also hate everyone who reviles them or harms them, because they are among the most noble servants of Allah. The scholars have differed as to whether the angels are better or the righteous among mankind are better. The disagreement on this is well known and widespread, and most of it is a dialectical dispute, because the station and rank with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, indicate that mankind is better, for humans enter Paradise and are provided therein without reckoning: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you because you were patient"﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 23–24]. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Mankind is better in terms of the end, and the angels are better in terms of the beginning, because humans were created from clay and the angels were created from light, and light is nobler than clay."

Then He said: ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾ [As-Saffat 150]. Allah, Exalted, said, explaining their false ruling which was known in advance, before they were asked: ﴿Unquestionably, it is of their own falsehood that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾ [As-Saffat 151]. ...

[The text repeats here from the start of the passage.]

Their statement: ﴿Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾ ... Let us seek refuge in Allah. ﴿Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾. As you can see, this sentence is emphasized with three emphatics: (ألا) *alā*, (إن) *inna*, and (اللام) *al-lām*. How many? *Alā*, what else?

* Student: (And) *inna*.

* The Shaykh: And *inna*.

* Students: And the *lām*.

* The Shaykh: And the *lām*. As for *alā*, it definitely comes for emphasis, as it also comes for alerting and opening speech. For this reason it is said that *alā* is an opening particle, intended to alert, emphasize, and affirm, meaning it confirms what follows it.

﴿Surely they﴾ means those who made the angels females, and those who attributed daughters to Allah while they have what they desire. ﴿Surely it is of their own fabrication﴾ means of their own (lying), ﴿that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾ [As-Saffat 151–152]. Here the cause is placed before the effect: the cause is the fabrication, and the effect is the saying. The fabrication is placed before the saying because of its importance, and so that a person may recognize its falsehood before it is stated. Otherwise, the normal order would be: "Surely they say, Allah has begotten," because ﴿they say﴾ is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. The expected construction would have the noun come directly after *inna*, but it was delayed to show that this saying is false, so that it arrives in the mind already known to be false.

The ﴿min﴾ here is causal, meaning: they say it because of their fabrication. It is also permissible for it to be partitive, meaning that this vile saying is part of their fabrications, because their fabrications are many. They attributed a son to Allah, they attributed a partner to Allah, and they attributed a wife to Allah. All of this is fabrication. In sum, ﴿min﴾ may be partitive and may be causal.

His words ﴿of their own fabrication﴾ mean of their own (lying), because *ifk* is lying, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who came with the slander are a group among you﴾ [An-Nur 11], meaning with the lie.

﴿They say﴾: the clause is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾. The object of the saying is ﴿Allah has begotten﴾ [As-Saffat 152]. Accordingly, ﴿Allah has begotten﴾ is in the accusative position as the object of the saying: "Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, 'Allah has begotten.'" How did they say "Allah has begotten"? In what form? The author said: (by their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah). It is known that a daughter is a child, since in the Arabic language *walad* (child) applies to both a daughter and a son. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ [An-Nisa 11].

(﴿Surely it is of their own fabrication that they say, "Allah has begotten"﴾ [As-Saffat 151–152] by their saying: the angels are the daughters of Allah; ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾.) This sentence is emphasized with two emphatics, and its purpose is to refute this saying. Allah refuted this saying before mentioning what is said and after mentioning it: before mentioning it in His words ﴿of their own fabrication﴾, and after it in His words ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾. We too bear witness that they are liars in this, for Allah is One, the Eternal Refuge, the Self-Sufficient. He neither begets nor is begotten, and there is none comparable to Him.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has proven the falsity of this in Surat Al-An'am. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And they have attributed to Allah partners from among the jinn, although He created them; and they have fabricated for Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Exalted is He and high above what they describe. The Originator of the heavens and the earth — how could He have a son when He has no companion and He created all things, and He is, of all things, Knowing?﴾ [Al-An'am 100–101]. He said: ﴿How could He have a son when He has no companion?﴾ How can He have a son when He has no wife? This is impossible. The second point: He created all things, and the Creator of all things cannot have a son, because a son is a part of his father, and if he were part of Him he would not be a created thing, since the part of the Creator would be a creator like Him. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And they have attributed to Him a portion from His servants. Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 15]. ﴿And He created all things, and He is, of all things, Knowing﴾ [Al-An'am 101]. He has informed us that He has no son. How then could their report be contrary to reality? Thus Allah has proven the impossibility of a son from three aspects: the impossibility of a consort, that He created all things, and the third: that He is Knowing of all things. His knowledge of all things requires that what He has told us, that He has not begotten, is true. This report must correspond to His knowledge.

He said: (﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ [As-Saffat 152] in it), meaning in their saying "Allah has begotten."

Then He said: ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ [As-Saffat 153]. ﴿Has He chosen﴾: the original form is (*istafa*), derived from (*safwa*), and the choicest part of a thing is its *safwa*. Accordingly, the meaning of ﴿iṣṭafā﴾ is "chose." Here it says ﴿iṣṭafā﴾, and it is well known that the hamza of *iṣṭafā* is a connecting hamza (*hamzat al-wasl*), not a cutting hamza (*hamzat al-qat'*). So why is it a cutting hamza here?

Listen to the author's words: (with a fatha on the hamza for interrogation). The hamza here is not the connecting hamza that is used to make it possible to pronounce the following consonant; therefore what follows it is not necessarily vowelless. The hamza here is not a connecting hamza, but an interrogative hamza. (So it is sufficient with it), meaning with the interrogative hamza, (from the connecting hamza). How is it sufficient from the connecting hamza? Because the interrogative hamza is vowelled with a fatha, so pronouncing the consonant after it is easy. The connecting hamza was introduced in order to make pronunciation of a consonant possible, and when there is a cutting hamza we dispense with the connecting hamza by means of it. Yet another possibility exists in other verses, such as ﴿iṣṭafā al-banāt﴾, where the connecting hamza is changed into a long vowel (*madd*). Among examples of this is His words, ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾ [An-Naml 59], and ﴿Has Allah permitted you, or do you fabricate against Allah?﴾ [Yunus 59].

(And he said, "He chose" — this is the explanation of the verb "isṭafā" (chose).) Meaning: would Allah, Mighty and Majestic, choose daughters over sons? That is, even if we supposed, as a utterly impossible supposition, that Allah took a son, would He choose daughters over sons? No, because sons are nobler than daughters, and it is not possible for Allah to choose daughters over sons. Even if one supposed the absolutely impossible supposition that Allah chose a son, He would not have chosen daughters over sons, just as you yourselves do not choose daughters over sons: you assign sons to yourselves and daughters to Allah. For this reason He said: ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 153]. What is the answer? It is: it is impossible.

﴿What is wrong with you?﴾ I want one of the brothers to parse ﴿مَا لَكُمْ﴾?

* Student: ﴿مَا لَكُمْ﴾: ﴿مَا﴾ is an interrogative, a mubtada' (subject), and ﴿لَكُمْ﴾ is the khabar (predicate).

* The Shaykh: Excellent. Do not think that ﴿مَا﴾ is a negative particle; rather it is interrogative, as the brother said. It is the subject, and the prepositional phrase ﴿لَكُمْ﴾ is the predicate. Meaning: what is it for you, that you pass this judgment and say that Allah has daughters, namely the angels?! This interrogation is for rebuke and denunciation, like the one after it: how can you pass this corrupt judgment?

This judgment, as the author said, is corrupt ("fāsid"), and also an unjust judgment: ﴿That is then an unfair division﴾ [al-Najm 22]. So it is a corrupt and unjust judgment.

Then He said: ﴿Will you not remember?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 155]. The interrogation here is also for rebuke. All the interrogations here serve rebuke and reproach, with another benefit when the context indicates it.

﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 155] He said: (with the assimilation of the tā' into the dhāl). Its original form is (تتذكرون), so the tā' was assimilated into the dhāl and it became ﴿تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾.

There is a reading ﴿تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾, so? This is the reading of the seven, and it is what is present in our mushaf: ﴿تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾.

It has passed with us that when two readings come in one verse, the better course is to recite with this one once and with that one once, so that you preserve what came in the Noble Qur'an, because all of it is from Allah. However, we said that this is not appropriate for the common people, because it causes fitnah: the layman does not know, and perhaps he is an emotional, zealous layman. If you say to him, for example, ﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾, he will say to you: ﴿أَفَلَا تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 155]. If you then go back and say ﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾, he says: ﴿أَفَلَا تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾. If you go back again and say ﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾, he may take the biggest thing he has and strike you, because he sees that you are now distorting the Qur'an.

In any case, the student of knowledge who knows that this is a reading of the seven should recite it once and what is in the mushaf once, so that he brings the Qur'an in the modes in which it was revealed.

He said: ﴿﴿أَفَلَا تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 155]. The meaning of ﴿﴿تَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ ﴾ is tadhakkur, i.e., admonition: will you not be admonished, so that you realize that what you have judged is an unjust judgment not acceptable from you?

He said: ﴿أَفَلَا تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾ (that He, glorified is He, is exalted above having offspring). Yes, Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is exalted above having offspring, by evidence from reason and evidence from transmitted text. As for transmitted evidence, there are many verses in which Allah denies that He took a son, among them His saying: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born. Nor is there to Him any equivalent﴾ [al-Ikhlāṣ 1–4].

As for rational evidence: we say, if Allah had a son, he would be a part of Him, and would deserve worship just as his father deserves it.

Second: we say, if Allah had taken a son, this son would be created, and createdness cannot be a part of Allah, since Allah has always been and always will be, existing by His own essence, Glorified and Exalted. If it is supposed that He took a son, this son would be created; how could he be created and yet be a part of Allah? Because the son is a part of the father, as Allah said: ﴿And they have made for Him a portion from His servants﴾ [al-Zukhruf 15], and as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Fāṭimah is a part of me" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (3714), Muslim (2449/94), from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah].

It is also impossible for Allah to have a son, because a son must resemble his father. This is the third point: that he would resemble his father, and Allah, Glorified is He, has no likeness; nothing is equal to Him.

Fourth: a son is taken only by one who needs him to preserve the species, and Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has need of no one. For this reason, when a person is barren, his trace ends in this world; but when he is fertile and children follow one after another, his trace remains in the world. Therefore procreation among humans is the sole cause of the survival of the human species. These are four rational points showing the impossibility of offspring for Allah, Glorified and Exalted.

He said: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 156]. This is also a transitional idrāb (إضراب انتقالي), "rather," and here the idrāb is transitional: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, moved from rebuking them for what they judged regarding Allah having a son to demanding proof. He said: "Rather, do you have a clear authority?" The word "sulṭān" here means that by which one has authority, and authority varies according to the context. In the matter of governorships, authority is by what? By office: the ruler has authority. In the matter of actions, authority is by strength: the strong and capable one has authority over the act. In the matter of argument and seeking evidence, authority is by what? By evidence. So here ﴿سُلْطَانٌ مُبِينٌ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 156] means evidence: do you have proof? Because by proof the one who argues gains authority: if a person argues with you and has proof, he has authority over you, i.e., power. For this reason He said: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾. The word ﴿مُبِينٌ﴾ here may be from (abāna) intransitive or from (abāna) transitive. Because the quadriliteral (abāna) may be intransitive or transitive. If you say: abāna al-ṣubḥ (the dawn became clear), is it intransitive or transitive?

* Students: Intransitive.

* The Shaykh: Intransitive. And if you say: abāna fulān al-ḥaqq (so-and-so made the truth clear), that is transitive. So the word (mubīn) here: is it intransitive, meaning "do you have a clear authority," or transitive, meaning "do you have an authority that makes clear what you say, or makes the proof clear for you"? Yes, the transitive is better here, why? Because the transitive includes the intransitive; for whatever makes others clear is itself clear.

﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 156]. The author said: (a clear proof that Allah has a son). The author's phrasing "clear" indicates that he took ﴿مُبِينٌ﴾ as intransitive, i.e., "clear." But the more correct view is that it is from transitive (abāna), i.e., "making clear"; because if we take it as transitive, it necessarily implies the existence of (...), meaning the intransitive, but not the reverse.

* The Shaykh: And (bāna) is intransitive, and (abāna) is intransitive; both are intransitive (...).

And the jinn certainly know that they will be brought forth. Glory be to Allah above what they describe, except the sincere servants of Allah. Indeed, you and what you worship, you cannot lead astray except one who will burn in Hellfire﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 156–163].

* Student: (...).

Which is better: that we make ﴿مُبِينٌ﴾ here mean (clear, bayyin), or mean (making clear, mubdin) something manifest?

* Student: Meaning transitive or intransitive?

* The Shaykh: I said that: the one meaning clear, or the one meaning making something clear?

* Student: (...) transitive.

* The Shaykh: I am asking: which is better?

* The Shaykh: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾?

* Student: Making clear, because it is transitive.

* The Shaykh: How so?

So if it is possible for it to be from transitive (abāna), that is, whenever ﴿مُبِين﴾ appears and it can be transitive, it is better; but sometimes that is not possible, as in ﴿in manifest error﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 164]: it cannot mean (abāna), but only (bayyin). But if (mubīn) can mean (abāna) and is clearer, then it is preferable.

Allah says: ﴿Then bring your book﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 157]. This is a consequence of His saying: ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 156]; that is, if you have a clear authority, then bring your book in which is the authority. The command here is for challenge and demonstration of inimitability, like His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then bring a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah 23]. This is a challenge and demonstration of inimitability. So His saying ﴿your book﴾ means: your book in which is the proof and authority.

The author's statement "the Torah" is undoubtedly a mistake, because this verse is not disputing with the Jews, so that we could say the intended meaning is the Torah. Rather, whom does it dispute with? The polytheists who made the angels daughters of Allah. For this reason it is absent in some copies, that is, absent in some copies of the author's text, and the copy from which it was dropped is more accurate than this copy.

He said: (Show us that in it), i.e., show us that Allah has daughters in that book you bring.

Then He demonstrated their inability through His saying: (﴿if you are truthful﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 157] in your claim), and this shows that it is impossible for them to bring a book in which Allah made the angels His daughters; this is an impossible thing.
