* Shaykh: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us﴾ [Qaf 50:38].

Good. He said ﴿And indeed we are the glorifiers﴾. The two clauses, as you know, are nominal sentences. The scholars said: a nominal sentence indicates stability and continuity; that is, this is their constant practice. This is supported by His saying, Exalted is He, describing them: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain His worship, nor do they tire. They glorify Him night and day; they never slacken﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:19–20]. So the angels are always in continuous worship, unlike humans who have heedlessness, amusement and forgetfulness; rather they are always in the worship of Allah. Here there are three categories of creation: devils, who are always in disobedience; angels, who are always in obedience; and humans, who are sometimes in obedience, sometimes in disobedience, and sometimes in heedlessness.

He said: ﴿And indeed they used to say: "If only we had a reminder from the former peoples"﴾ [al-Saffat 37:167–168] and so on to the end. ﴿And indeed they used to say﴾ — is (in) here conditional? No, because there is no condition and consequence in it. Is it negating? No, because the lam in His saying ﴿la-yaqūlūn﴾ prevents it from being negating, since the lam is for emphasis and negation is the opposite of emphasis. Is it superfluous? No, because it has a meaning, and a superfluous element is one whose removal does not disturb the meaning. So what is it? We say: it is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), its origin being: "wa-innahum kānū" (and indeed they were). Its origin is thus, but it was lightened, so it became ﴿wa-in kānū la-yaqūlūn﴾. On this occasion we wish to review the meanings of (in). (In) comes as a negation, as in: —
* Student: ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near or whether my Lord will appoint for it a term﴾ [al-Jinn 72:25].
* Shaykh: ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near﴾; i.e., I do not know whether what you are promised is near. And it comes as a conditional; give an example.
* Student: From the verses?
* Shaykh: From the verses. Better from the verses, if you have one.
* Student: ﴿If you are truthful﴾ [al-Saffat 37:157].
* Shaykh: What? ﴿If you are truthful﴾ ... (...) it comes as a conditional (in) with a condition and a consequence.
* Student: ﴿And if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:24].
* Shaykh: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it, then fear the Fire﴾; and ﴿And if you are in doubt concerning what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:23]. And it comes as superfluous?
* Student:
*"Banī Ghudānah, mā in antum dhahab / wa-lā ṣarīf, wa-lākin antumu al-kharaf"*
* Shaykh: Correct.
*"Banī Ghudānah, mā in antum dhahab..................."*
i.e., silver. "But you are clay": pottery. The evidence is his saying "mā in antum" (what you are); if "in" were removed and he said "mā antum dhahaban," the sentence would still be sound.

And it comes as a lightened form, as in this verse, a lightened form of the heavy (inna). The lightened form of the heavy has, as they say, a noun that is omitted, called the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). The pronoun of the matter, they say, is singular masculine, because the word sha'n (matter) is singular masculine. The estimate is: ﴿And indeed they used to say﴾, i.e., "and indeed it (the matter) — i.e., their matter — they were indeed saying." It has also been said that the pronoun of the matter is estimated according to the context: if it is singular masculine it is singular masculine, if it is plural it is plural. On this basis the estimate of the verse here is: "wa-innahum kānū la-yaqūlūn."

He said: ﴿And if they used to say﴾: "kānū" is a defective verb with its subject; the waw is the subject. The lam in His saying ﴿la-yaqūlūn﴾ is the lam of emphasis, and the clause "yaqūlūn" is the predicate of what? The predicate of kāna. Kāna with its subject and predicate is the predicate of the lightened (in), from the heavy. ("And if" is lightened from the heavy; "kānū" means the Quraysh of Makkah; "la-yaqūlūn") — what? ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 37:168–169]; i.e., if a book had been sent down to us like the books of the former peoples, we would be the servants of Allah, submitting to His law and sincere to Him. But this argument is rejected by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down, so follow it and fear Allah that you may receive mercy. [That you may] not say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and indeed we were unaware of their study." Or [that] you may say: "If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they." But there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord and guidance and mercy﴾ [al-An'am 6:155–157].

So this claim from them is obstinacy. Why was it obstinacy? Because there was sent down to them a Book that is the most guiding and most upright of books, yet they disbelieved in it.

﴿And if they used to say: "If only we had a reminder"﴾ (a book), ﴿from the former peoples﴾, i.e., from the books of past nations, ﴿we would certainly have been servants of Allah, the sincere ones﴾ devoted to His worship.

Note that ﴿if only we had a reminder﴾ means: that which would remind us; and what reminds is the Book. Allah said: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:50]. So the meaning of "reminder" here is that by which a person remembers, which is the Book.

As for His saying ﴿from the former peoples﴾, the author said: (from the books of the former peoples). So it is with an omitted noun: ﴿from the former peoples⟩, i.e., from their books, not from themselves, but from the books that were sent down to them. "If we had any of this, we would be the sincere servants of Allah." The lam in ﴿we would have been﴾ is the answer to "if" (law), and "law" here is conditional, or is it verbal? Conditional. Now, ﴿law anna 'indanā﴾: they say the conditional particle is followed only by a verb, yet here it is followed by (anna). Even the definitive conditional is followed only by a verb, yet here it is followed by (anna). They said: yes, but it is on an estimated verb; that is, "if it were established that 'indanā dhikran..."; ﴿we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾, like His saying: ﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:5]; i.e., if it were established that they were patient.

﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾ — are they the servants of Allah in the legal or in the predestined sense? In the legal sense, because in the predestined sense they are already servants of Allah by decree, and cannot deviate from Allah's decree and destiny. But ﴿we would have been servants of Allah﴾ is legal. He said: (the ones sincere in worship to Him). "Sincere" (mukhlisīn) with a kasra on the lam, so the author explained it: "sincere in worship to Him." And "sincere" (mukhlaṣīn) with a fatha on the lam means those whom Allah has made sincere and chosen. So "al-mukhlisīn" has two readings: with a fatha and with a kasra on the lam. On the reading with a fatha, the meaning is: those whom Allah has made sincere for Himself and chosen. On the reading with a kasra, the meaning is: those who made worship sincere for Him. The two meanings are interrelated, because whoever makes worship sincere for Allah, Allah has made him sincere for Himself: ﴿we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾.

Allah said: (﴿So they disbelieved in it﴾; i.e., in the Book that came to them, which is the Qur'an, the most noble of those books; ﴿so they will come to know﴾ the consequence of their disbelief). The structure of the verse: a book came to them; they said ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been servants of Allah﴾; then the Book came to them, the reminder came to them, but they did not accept this reminder; they disbelieved in it, denying the report and being arrogant toward the command. They denied the Messenger, peace be upon him. He said: "You will indeed be resurrected," and they said: "There is no resurrection." He said: "It is true," and they said: "He is a liar." He said: "Worship Allah alone, with no partner," and they worshipped idols. So they disbelieved in this Book, denying its report and being arrogant toward its command. They did not believe what Allah informed of in His Book, nor did they comply with the command and submit to it; rather they combined the disbelief of denial and arrogance, may Allah protect us. They disbelieved in it although the Qur'an is more noble than those books which they claimed, if it had come to them of their kind, they would have been the sincere servants of Allah. Yet they disbelieved in this Book, and this shows that their claim was among the most false of claims. ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been servants of Allah﴾: it was said to them, "This is a reminder; there has come to you a reminder more noble than the reminders and greater than the earlier books, yet you disbelieved in it."

Allah said: ﴿So they will come to know﴾. The fa' in ﴿so they disbelieved﴾ is for sequence, and the fa' in ﴿so they will come to know﴾ is for sequence and causation; that is, because of their disbelief they will come to know. What will they come to know? They will come to know the outcome of their affair: humiliation in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. This has occurred, praise be to Allah. Allah humbled them in the greatest battle in which they used to take pride and imagine honor and victory, the Battle of Badr. They set out with their champions, nobles and great men, to the extent that Abu Jahl, when he was advised to turn back, said: "By Allah, we will not return until we reach Badr, where we will slaughter camels, drink wine, have singing girls play for us, and the Arabs will hear of us, and they will forever stand in awe of us."

Look at the arrogance and pride! Then it passed, and what happened? He was killed, praise be to Allah, along with the leaders and nobles who were with him. The Arabs heard of them, and the Arabs spoke of them, but of what? Of what brings them awe, or of what brings shame and disgrace? The latter. The Arabs spoke of their news, praise be to Allah, with what brings shame and disgrace until the Day of Resurrection. These are among the grievous consequences.

In their own town of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ had left it in fear, hidden, and entered it victorious and triumphant, adorned. The banner was raised at the entrance of Makkah at al-Hajun. He entered the House and broke the idols, and stood at the door while the Quraysh were below waiting to see what he would do. He said: «What do you think I will do with you, O assembly of Quraysh?» They said: "Good. A noble brother and the son of a noble brother."[[Narrated by al-Tabari in al-Tarikh (3/61).]] So he, peace be upon him, pardoned them, and they were called "the freed ones" (al-Tulaqa'), meaning freed from killing and captivity.

Look at how this outcome turned out. This Prophet ﷺ, Allah protected him from them. They plotted to kill him, or to imprison him, or to expel him, but the plot turned back against them. They were the very people whom the Messenger ﷺ pardoned and released. Yet what is in the Hereafter is harsher and greater. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, for those who did wrong there is a punishment short of that, but most of them do not know﴾ [al-Tur 47]. ﴿And We will surely make them taste the nearer punishment before the greater punishment﴾ [al-Sajdah 21]. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ [al-Ra'd 34]. We seek refuge in Allah.

The purpose of this sentence, i.e., His saying ﴿So they will soon know﴾, is a warning (tahdid): a threat to these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ.

* Student: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya' 20], said of the angels. Does this not indicate that by His saying ﴿maqam﴾ (station) is meant a place?
* Shaykh: A place? No, even a time.
* Student: All night and day in worship?
* Shaykh: Yes, but night and day in their entirety. Then we say: general glorification may also be different from specific glorification. Specific glorification is in a specific station, correct or not? They are still (...) even in the place they are in, but this specific station has a specific glorification.
* Student: We mentioned ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks (al-saffun)﴾ [al-Saffat 165]. Regarding the angels, they line up before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in nearness...
* Shaykh: Whether the near is near and the far is far.
* Student: And the qidam (antiquity) in terms of creation?
* Shaykh: It is not qidam, it is qadam (foot). Qadam means the foot, the leg. The author says: "ṣāffūn aqdāmanā", i.e., our feet.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And certainly has Our word preceded for Our servants, the messengers, that they would indeed be helped, and that Our soldiers would indeed be the victorious. So turn away from them for a time, and watch them, and they will soon see. Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment? And when it descends upon their courtyard, then evil will be the morning of those who were warned. And turn away from them for a time, and watch, and they will soon see. Exalted is your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace upon the messengers. And praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat 171–182].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat 164]. The starting point of the discussion is His saying ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾. Where is the subject (mubtada') here?
* Student: "Ma'lum" (known).
* Shaykh: What is the estimated (taqdir) form?
* Student: The estimate is: "And there is none of us [any one]."
* Shaykh: "And there is none of us [any one] but has a known station." Well done. The sentence "illa lahu maqam ma'lum" (but has a known station): what is its grammatical position (mahall)?
* Student: The predicate (khabar) of the subject.
* Shaykh: How the predicate of the subject? You said the subject is "ahad" (any one) and its predicate is "minna" (of us). Then "illa lahu maqam ma'lum"?
* Student: An exception (istithna') from "ahad".
* Shaykh: An exception from "ahad". So its position is in the nominative (raf'), or it is a substitute (badal) from "ahad", and its position is nominative.
* Student: Here, "minna ahad" here, now we said...
* Shaykh: Is the speech before it complete or incomplete?
* Student: No, now it is complete.
* Shaykh: Complete. Affirmative or negative?
* Student: Negative.
* Shaykh: If what precedes "illa" (except) is complete and negative, what is the ruling on what follows it?
* Student: What follows may either be parsed according to its position, or it is parsed as a substitute (badal).
* Shaykh: Substitute, good. Or?
* Student: Or according to its position.
* Shaykh: Even if it is a substitute, according to its position?
* Student: An exception (mustathna).
* Shaykh: Or in the accusative (nasb) as an exception.
* Student: In the accusative as an exception, yes.
* Shaykh: So it is permissible that ﴿lahu maqam ma'lum﴾ is in the accusative position as an exception, or?
* Student: A substitute from ﴿ahad﴾.
* Shaykh: In the nominative position as a substitute from ﴿ahad﴾.
Good. Here, does the "maqam" refer to a place, or to place and time?
* Student: The "maqam" here includes the station of time and place.
* Shaykh: Includes?
* Student: Because the sentence allows both, and if it allows both, then the rule is...
* Shaykh: Because "maqam" is suitable for both time and place, so it includes both.

His saying: ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks﴾ [al-Saffat 165]. What is the meaning of ﴿al-saffun﴾?
* Student: They arrange the rows. The author says: "muṣṭafūn", i.e., aligned, shoulder to shoulder in their feet.
* Shaykh: Equal in their feet.
* Student: (...) the first, then the first.
* Shaykh: The ranks are in what? In worship, or in what else?
* Student: In worship.
* Shaykh: In worship. Good. How are their rows, brother?
* Student: The rows of the angels: they join the first to the first (...) Mighty and Majestic.
* Shaykh: They complete them first to first and they align tightly. This is how the Prophet ﷺ explained it.
Good. What is the meaning of al-musabbihun?
* Student: Those who declare Allah far above every deficiency.
* Shaykh: Above every deficiency, or above what is not befitting to Him?
* Student: Above what is not befitting to Him.
* Shaykh: Above what is not befitting to Him. The declaration of Allah's transcendence (tanzih). How many things do we say Allah is exempt from?
* Student: Two: exemption from likeness, the likeness of created beings, and from deficiency.
* Shaykh: In?
* Student: In His perfection.
* Shaykh: From deficiency in His perfection. An example of the first?
* Student: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Qaf 38].
* Shaykh: That is exemption from likeness to created beings.
* Student: ﴿There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura 11].
* Shaykh: And an example of exemption from deficiency in His perfection?
* Student: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf 38].
* Shaykh: Well done. His saying ﴿And if they indeed used to say﴾ [al-Saffat 167]: is the sentence here negated or affirmed?
* Student: Negated.
* Shaykh: Then "in" (إنْ) here is negating.
* Student: No, affirmed.
* Shaykh: Here "in", what is it when it is affirmative?
* Student: Emphasis.
* Shaykh: Emphasis. What do the grammarians call it?
* Student: Lightened from the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah).
* Shaykh: Lightened from the heavy, well done. Now where is its noun (ism), ﴿And if they indeed used to say﴾?
* Student: The angels.
* Shaykh: No, the angels do not say it.
* Student: A pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-sha'n).
* Shaykh: Is its noun omitted or present?
* Student: Omitted.
* Shaykh: Omitted. The pronoun of the matter, what is its estimate?
* Student: "Innahum kanu" (indeed they were).
* Shaykh: "Innahum" (indeed they): is there another estimate?
* Student: "Innahu kana" (indeed it was).
* Shaykh: "Innahu", i.e., the matter; meaning that their matter is that they say such and such. The second view is that the pronoun of the matter is estimated according to context. Good. Where is the object of the saying (maqul al-qawl)?
* Student: ﴿Layaqulun﴾.
* Shaykh: No, "yaqulun" is the saying itself. But where is the object of the saying?
* Student: Omitted.
* Shaykh: Read the verse.
* Student: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾.
* Shaykh: The object of the saying is His saying: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 168–169]. Good. Is their saying correct according to reality?
* Student: No, it is not correct.
* Shaykh: Not correct, because the reminder came to them but they disbelieved.
His saying ﴿layaqulun﴾: what is its position in the grammar (i'rab)?
* Student: Noun of "kana".
* Shaykh: Noun of "kana"! Is the noun of "kana" a whole sentence?! Read the verse.
* Student: ﴿And if they indeed used to say﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿And if they indeed used to say﴾.
* Student: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾.
* Shaykh: What do you say now? The waw in ﴿kanu﴾ is not the noun of "kana"?
* Student: The noun of "kana", and this is its predicate.
* Shaykh: So then.
* Student: ﴿Layaqulun﴾ is the predicate of "kana".
* Shaykh: Its position is accusative, as the predicate of "kana".
Now ﴿If that we had a reminder﴾: what is the estimate of the sentence?
* Student: Object of the saying.
* Shaykh: The sentence, no. We want the estimate of the sentence.
* Student: "If we had a reminder."
* Shaykh: No, that is not suitable.
* Student: The estimate: "If we had a book from the former peoples."
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: "If that we had a reminder from it, from the books of the former peoples."
* Another student: "If it is established that we have a reminder."
* Shaykh: This is the estimate: "If it is established that we have a reminder from the former peoples." We estimated it this way because the conditional "law" (if) only enters upon a verb.
Now His saying ﴿al-mukhlasin﴾ has two readings.
* Student: ﴿al-mukhlasin﴾ and ﴿al-mukhlisin﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿al-mukhlasin﴾ and ﴿al-mukhlisin﴾. ﴿al-mukhlasin﴾: is it an active participle (ism fa'il) or a passive participle (ism maf'ul)?
* Student: Passive.
* Shaykh: ﴿al-mukhlisin﴾?
* Student: No, active.
* Shaykh: If you say "mukhlis", is it active or passive? "So-and-so is mukhlis."
* Student: Active.
* Shaykh: And "so-and-so is mukhlas"?
* Student: Passive.
* Shaykh: Passive. So "al-mukhlisin" is an active participle and "al-mukhlasin" is a passive participle. On the reading "mukhlasin", what does it mean?
* Student: They are those whom Allah, glory be to Him, made sincere for Himself.
* Shaykh: Allah made them sincere for Himself, so He chose them over creation by the blessing of worship that Allah bestowed upon them. And "al-mukhlasin"?
* Student: And "al-mukhlasin" are those whom Allah, glory be to Him, made sincere for worship.
* Shaykh: What is meant by His saying ﴿So they will soon know﴾?
* Student: "They will soon know" by the one who denied.
* Shaykh: But what is meant by it? What is meant by this sentence?
* Student: The "fa" is consequential and causal: because of their disbelief, "so they will soon", i.e., their knowledge.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Causal.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Warning.
* Shaykh: The intention is warning. You threaten your child, you say: "You will soon find out what I will do to you," right? You threaten him. Shall we take the lessons from His saying?
* Student: ﴿And there is none of us﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ and so on to the end.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: showing that the angels are exempt from what these people claim, that they are the daughters of Allah. The reason is that they are charged with worship at a known limit, and whoever is charged with worship cannot be a son of the one worshipped.
* And among the lessons of the verse: the perfect order of the angels, peace be upon them, in that they keep to the known stations that Allah appointed for them: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾.
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: an indication that a person should have an organized schedule, assigning a known task to each thing, so that time is not wasted for him, because a person who uses time haphazardly does not benefit from it. But our saying this does not mean that a person continues in one fixed state, for what is less excellent may sometimes become better than what is more excellent. That is, if you organize yourself and then something arises that requires departing from this system, there is no blame upon you for breaking this system, because the Messenger ﷺ used to fast until it was said, "He never breaks his fast," and used to pray at night until it was said, "He never sleeps," or the reverse, according to what the public interest requires.
* And among the lessons of the noble verses in general: the angels, peace be upon them, are among the most perfect people in worship, in that they gather in the worship of Allah and form rows in glorifying Him. This is based on His saying: ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks﴾.
* And among its lessons: it is appropriate to emphasize speech when the addressee is denying or doubtful, or when the meaning is important and needs emphasis. This is based on His saying ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks﴾, to establish the truth for these deniers who claim that the angels are daughters of Allah. They say: "We stand in rows in worship and glorification of Him."
* And among the lessons of the noble verses: the perfect declaration of the angels' transcendence of Allah in His saying ﴿And indeed, we are the ones who glorify﴾.
* And among its lessons: their habit is also glorification, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya' 20]. We derive this from this verse, because the sentence came as a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), and a nominal sentence indicates establishment and continuity.
* And among its lessons: the transcendence of Allah, glory be to Him, is expressed on the tongues of the angels from everything not befitting to Him, and He, glory be to Him, is exempt from everything not befitting to Him. For this reason, many verses came negating likeness from Allah, negating deficiency, affirming wisdom, and negating play and falsehood concerning Him, Exalted: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in falsehood. That is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾ [Sad 27]. ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Anbiya' 16]. ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 36], and many other verses that indicate His perfection, glory be to Him, and the absence of play and falsehood from His acts.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they indeed used to say, "If that we had a reminder from the former peoples"﴾ and so on to the end.
* Among the lessons of these verses: these deniers of the Messenger, peace be upon him, claim that no reminder came to them through which they could be reminded. For this reason they raise this objection, saying: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾.
* And among its lessons: the arguments of the disbelievers are arguments of obstinacy, not based on truth. For example, their saying ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾: what do we say to them? We say: "Rather, you have a reminder from the former peoples; rather, you have the best of remembrances absolutely."
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: people cannot be upright except through books sent down from heaven. Even the polytheist disbelievers acknowledge this, by their saying: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾. This lesson is confirmed by reality: you find the nations to whom no books were revealed in constant chaos, their affairs do not become upright, and they do not walk on a straight path, unlike the People of the Book, and unlike the nations to whom books were revealed, which are upright to the extent they hold fast to these books.
* And among the lessons of these verses: revealed books are a reminder for those to whom they were sent. We have previously mentioned that its being a reminder has two aspects or three? It is a reminder, i.e., an honor for those to whom it was sent; it is a reminder through which they remember and are admonished; and it is a reminder through which they draw near to Allah, Exalted, because it is the best kind of remembrance.
* And among the lessons of these verses: those who claimed that if they had a reminder from the former peoples they would be sincere servants of Allah were liars, as evidenced by the fact that they did have a reminder from the former peoples but disbelieved in it. We have previously mentioned that their disbelief includes both types of disbelief: ignorance and arrogance.
* And among the lessons of the verses: the warning to disbelievers, by His saying ﴿So they will soon know﴾. The warning of disbelievers is undoubtedly consistent with wisdom, because the proof has been established against them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and warners, so that people will not have an argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa' 165].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 164–170 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat 37:164]. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, made clear that this is the speech of Jibril, peace be upon him. The author said: (Jibril said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾).

When Allah mentioned that these criminal wrongdoers said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah," He, glorified and exalted is He, explained through the tongue of the angels what their condition is, what their station is, and what their deeds toward Allah, glorified and exalted is He, are. So He said: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾. The author said: (﴿And there is none of us﴾ O assembly of angels) — "assembly" meaning group — (anyone ﴿but has a known station﴾). The author supplied "anyone" (aḥad) because the context indicates it; it is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the preceding ﴿minna﴾ ("of us"), a prepositional phrase.

As for His saying: ﴿but has a known station﴾ (in the heavens), this exception is an exception from "anyone." It is a sentence that can be taken to indicate the state of these angels.

His saying: ﴿but has a station﴾ means a place of standing, because maqam (maf'al) can be a noun of time and a noun of place. Here the apparent meaning is a noun of place: a place of standing in which he stands to worship Allah. It is also permissible to take it as a noun of time: a time in which he stands before Allah and a place in which he stands before Allah. Thus the worship of the angels is restricted to a time and confined to a place, and there is no contradiction between the two views. The principle in tafsir is that if a verse is capable of two meanings that do not contradict each other, both are adopted, because taking both is broader in meaning than restricting it to one of them. If one of them contradicts the other, weighing (tarjih) is sought; what the one who weighs prefers is taken, and the other is left.

He says here: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾, meaning: a place and also a time in which he worships Allah, Exalted is He, and he does not worship Allah in anything else, neither in a time nor in a place.

(﴿And indeed we are the ranked ones﴾ [al-Saffat 37:165], our feet in prayer.) The pronoun in ﴿indeed we﴾ refers to whom? To the angels. ﴿We are the ranked ones﴾ means those who line up before Allah, glorified and exalted is He, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: «Will you not line up as the angels line up before their Lord?» They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how is that?" He said: «They complete the first rows, then the next, and they press close together»[[Narrated by Muslim (430/119) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Samurah.]]. This is the condition of the angels before Allah in their station of worship: they line up in glorification of Him, completing the first row after the first. The foremost and earliest of them is the nearest to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Likewise in the rows of prayer, whoever is earlier and nearer to the imam is better.

﴿And indeed we are the ranked ones﴾ [al-Saffat 37:165]. The author said: (our feet in prayer). The phrase "our feet in prayer" requires evidence, because the apparent description ﴿we are the ranked ones﴾ refers to the angels themselves, not to their feet. Moreover, if we say "our feet," we need to establish that the angels have feet, whereas Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has described the angels as possessing wings; so this requires evidence.

His saying: ﴿And indeed we are the ranked ones﴾ contains two emphases. The first emphasis?
* Student: (inna).
* Shaykh: And the second?
* Student: The second is (the lam).
* Shaykh: The lam in His saying: ﴿lanahnu al-ṣāffūn﴾.
It contains two emphases. The first emphasis?
* Student: (...) (inna).
* Shaykh: And the second?
* Student: The second is the lam.
* Shaykh: The lam in His saying: ﴿lanahnu al-ṣāffūn﴾ [al-Saffat 37:165].

﴿And indeed we are the glorifiers﴾ [al-Saffat 37:166]. The sentence is emphasized in the same way as the first: that is, "and indeed we, the assembly of angels, are surely the glorifiers." The author said: (those who declare Allah free of what is not befitting to Him), because tasbih means tanzih (declaring Allah free of imperfection), and the declaring of Allah free means declaring Him free of what is not befitting to Him. It rests on two matters. The first: that He is declared free of resemblance to created beings, and its evidence is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura 42:11]. The second: that He is declared free of any deficiency in His perfection, and among its examples is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us﴾ [Qaf 50:38]. When He mentioned His creation of these great heavens and the earth in this brief period, He made clear that no fatigue or exhaustion reached Him in that. This is declaring Allah free of deficiency in His perfection. So the declaring free rests on what?
* Student: On two attributes.
* Shaykh: On two attributes? No.
* Student: On two matters: first, the resemblance of Allah to created beings.
* Shaykh: And its evidence?
* Student: ﴿There is nothing like Him.﴾ The second: declaring Allah free of deficiency in His perfection.
* Shaykh: And an example of it? Give an example.
* Student: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat 37:159].
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿And We created the heavens...﴾
* Shaykh: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us﴾ [Qaf 50:38].

Good. He said ﴿And indeed we are the glorifiers﴾. The two clauses, as you know, are nominal sentences. The scholars said: a nominal sentence indicates stability and continuity; that is, this is their constant practice. This is supported by His saying, Exalted is He, describing them: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain His worship, nor do they tire. They glorify Him night and day; they never slacken﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:19–20]. So the angels are always in continuous worship, unlike humans who have heedlessness, amusement and forgetfulness; rather they are always in the worship of Allah. Here there are three categories of creation: devils, who are always in disobedience; angels, who are always in obedience; and humans, who are sometimes in obedience, sometimes in disobedience, and sometimes in heedlessness.

He said: ﴿And indeed they used to say: "If only we had a reminder from the former peoples"﴾ [al-Saffat 37:167–168] and so on to the end. ﴿And indeed they used to say﴾ — is (in) here conditional? No, because there is no condition and consequence in it. Is it negating? No, because the lam in His saying ﴿la-yaqūlūn﴾ prevents it from being negating, since the lam is for emphasis and negation is the opposite of emphasis. Is it superfluous? No, because it has a meaning, and a superfluous element is one whose removal does not disturb the meaning. So what is it? We say: it is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), its origin being: "wa-innahum kānū" (and indeed they were). Its origin is thus, but it was lightened, so it became ﴿wa-in kānū la-yaqūlūn﴾. On this occasion we wish to review the meanings of (in). (In) comes as a negation, as in: —
* Student: ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near or whether my Lord will appoint for it a term﴾ [al-Jinn 72:25].
* Shaykh: ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near﴾; i.e., I do not know whether what you are promised is near. And it comes as a conditional; give an example.
* Student: From the verses?
* Shaykh: From the verses. Better from the verses, if you have one.
* Student: ﴿If you are truthful﴾ [al-Saffat 37:157].
* Shaykh: What? ﴿If you are truthful﴾ ... (...) it comes as a conditional (in) with a condition and a consequence.
* Student: ﴿And if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:24].
* Shaykh: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it, then fear the Fire﴾; and ﴿And if you are in doubt concerning what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:23]. And it comes as superfluous?
* Student:
*"Banī Ghudānah, mā in antum dhahab / wa-lā ṣarīf, wa-lākin antumu al-kharaf"*
* Shaykh: Correct.
*"Banī Ghudānah, mā in antum dhahab..................."*
i.e., silver. "But you are clay": pottery. The evidence is his saying "mā in antum" (what you are); if "in" were removed and he said "mā antum dhahaban," the sentence would still be sound.

And it comes as a lightened form, as in this verse, a lightened form of the heavy (inna). The lightened form of the heavy has, as they say, a noun that is omitted, called the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). The pronoun of the matter, they say, is singular masculine, because the word sha'n (matter) is singular masculine. The estimate is: ﴿And indeed they used to say﴾, i.e., "and indeed it (the matter) — i.e., their matter — they were indeed saying." It has also been said that the pronoun of the matter is estimated according to the context: if it is singular masculine it is singular masculine, if it is plural it is plural. On this basis the estimate of the verse here is: "wa-innahum kānū la-yaqūlūn."

He said: ﴿And if they used to say﴾: "kānū" is a defective verb with its subject; the waw is the subject. The lam in His saying ﴿la-yaqūlūn﴾ is the lam of emphasis, and the clause "yaqūlūn" is the predicate of what? The predicate of kāna. Kāna with its subject and predicate is the predicate of the lightened (in), from the heavy. ("And if" is lightened from the heavy; "kānū" means the Quraysh of Makkah; "la-yaqūlūn") — what? ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 37:168–169]; i.e., if a book had been sent down to us like the books of the former peoples, we would be the servants of Allah, submitting to His law and sincere to Him. But this argument is rejected by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down, so follow it and fear Allah that you may receive mercy. [That you may] not say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and indeed we were unaware of their study." Or [that] you may say: "If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they." But there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord and guidance and mercy﴾ [al-An'am 6:155–157].

So this claim from them is obstinacy. Why was it obstinacy? Because there was sent down to them a Book that is the most guiding and most upright of books, yet they disbelieved in it.

﴿And if they used to say: "If only we had a reminder"﴾ (a book), ﴿from the former peoples﴾, i.e., from the books of past nations, ﴿we would certainly have been servants of Allah, the sincere ones﴾ devoted to His worship.

Note that ﴿if only we had a reminder﴾ means: that which would remind us; and what reminds is the Book. Allah said: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:50]. So the meaning of "reminder" here is that by which a person remembers, which is the Book.

As for His saying ﴿from the former peoples﴾, the author said: (from the books of the former peoples). So it is with an omitted noun: ﴿from the former peoples⟩, i.e., from their books, not from themselves, but from the books that were sent down to them. "If we had any of this, we would be the sincere servants of Allah." The lam in ﴿we would have been﴾ is the answer to "if" (law), and "law" here is conditional, or is it verbal? Conditional. Now, ﴿law anna 'indanā﴾: they say the conditional particle is followed only by a verb, yet here it is followed by (anna). Even the definitive conditional is followed only by a verb, yet here it is followed by (anna). They said: yes, but it is on an estimated verb; that is, "if it were established that 'indanā dhikran..."; ﴿we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾, like His saying: ﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:5]; i.e., if it were established that they were patient.

﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾ — are they the servants of Allah in the legal or in the predestined sense? In the legal sense, because in the predestined sense they are already servants of Allah by decree, and cannot deviate from Allah's decree and destiny. But ﴿we would have been servants of Allah﴾ is legal. He said: (the ones sincere in worship to Him). "Sincere" (mukhlisīn) with a kasra on the lam, so the author explained it: "sincere in worship to Him." And "sincere" (mukhlaṣīn) with a fatha on the lam means those whom Allah has made sincere and chosen. So "al-mukhlisīn" has two readings: with a fatha and with a kasra on the lam. On the reading with a fatha, the meaning is: those whom Allah has made sincere for Himself and chosen. On the reading with a kasra, the meaning is: those who made worship sincere for Him. The two meanings are interrelated, because whoever makes worship sincere for Allah, Allah has made him sincere for Himself: ﴿we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾.

Allah said: (﴿So they disbelieved in it﴾; i.e., in the Book that came to them, which is the Qur'an, the most noble of those books; ﴿so they will come to know﴾ the consequence of their disbelief). The structure of the verse: a book came to them; they said ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been servants of Allah﴾; then the Book came to them, the reminder came to them, but they did not accept this reminder; they disbelieved in it, denying the report and being arrogant toward the command. They denied the Messenger, peace be upon him. He said: "You will indeed be resurrected," and they said: "There is no resurrection." He said: "It is true," and they said: "He is a liar." He said: "Worship Allah alone, with no partner," and they worshipped idols. So they disbelieved in this Book, denying its report and being arrogant toward its command. They did not believe what Allah informed of in His Book, nor did they comply with the command and submit to it; rather they combined the disbelief of denial and arrogance, may Allah protect us. They disbelieved in it although the Qur'an is more noble than those books which they claimed, if it had come to them of their kind, they would have been the sincere servants of Allah. Yet they disbelieved in this Book, and this shows that their claim was among the most false of claims. ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been servants of Allah﴾: it was said to them, "This is a reminder; there has come to you a reminder more noble than the reminders and greater than the earlier books, yet you disbelieved in it."

Allah said: ﴿So they will come to know﴾. The fa' in ﴿so they disbelieved﴾ is for sequence, and the fa' in ﴿so they will come to know﴾ is for sequence and causation; that is, because of their disbelief they will come to know. What will they come to know? They will come to know the outcome of their affair: humiliation in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. This has occurred, praise be to Allah. Allah humbled them in the greatest battle in which they used to take pride and imagine honor and victory, the Battle of Badr. They set out with their champions, nobles and great men, to the extent that Abu Jahl, when he was advised to turn back, said: "By Allah, we will not return until we reach Badr, where we will slaughter camels, drink wine, have singing girls play for us, and the Arabs will hear of us, and they will forever stand in awe of us."

Look at the arrogance and pride! Then it passed, and what happened? He was killed, praise be to Allah, along with the leaders and nobles who were with him. The Arabs heard of them, and the Arabs spoke of them, but of what? Of what brings them awe, or of what brings shame and disgrace? The latter. The Arabs spoke of their news, praise be to Allah, with what brings shame and disgrace until the Day of Resurrection. These are among the grievous consequences.

In their own town of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ had left it in fear, hidden, and entered it victorious and triumphant, adorned. The banner was raised at the entrance of Makkah at al-Hajun. He entered the House and broke the idols, and stood at the door while the Quraysh were below waiting to see what he would do. He said: «What do you think I will do with you, O assembly of Quraysh?» They said: "Good. A noble brother and the son of a noble brother."[[Narrated by al-Tabari in al-Tarikh (3/61).]] So he, peace be upon him, pardoned them, and they were called "the freed ones" (al-Tulaqa'), meaning freed from killing and captivity.

Look at how this outcome turned out. This Prophet ﷺ, Allah protected him from them. They plotted to kill him, or to imprison him, or to expel him, but the plot turned back against them. They were the very people whom the Messenger ﷺ pardoned and released. Yet what is in the Hereafter is harsher and greater. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, for those who did wrong there is a punishment short of that, but most of them do not know﴾ [al-Tur 47]. ﴿And We will surely make them taste the nearer punishment before the greater punishment﴾ [al-Sajdah 21]. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ [al-Ra'd 34]. We seek refuge in Allah.

The purpose of this sentence, i.e., His saying ﴿So they will soon know﴾, is a warning (tahdid): a threat to these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ.

* Student: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya' 20], said of the angels. Does this not indicate that by His saying ﴿maqam﴾ (station) is meant a place?
* Shaykh: A place? No, even a time.
* Student: All night and day in worship?
* Shaykh: Yes, but night and day in their entirety. Then we say: general glorification may also be different from specific glorification. Specific glorification is in a specific station, correct or not? They are still (...) even in the place they are in, but this specific station has a specific glorification.
* Student: We mentioned ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks (al-saffun)﴾ [al-Saffat 165]. Regarding the angels, they line up before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in nearness...
* Shaykh: Whether the near is near and the far is far.
* Student: And the qidam (antiquity) in terms of creation?
* Shaykh: It is not qidam, it is qadam (foot). Qadam means the foot, the leg. The author says: "ṣāffūn aqdāmanā", i.e., our feet.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And certainly has Our word preceded for Our servants, the messengers, that they would indeed be helped, and that Our soldiers would indeed be the victorious. So turn away from them for a time, and watch them, and they will soon see. Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment? And when it descends upon their courtyard, then evil will be the morning of those who were warned. And turn away from them for a time, and watch, and they will soon see. Exalted is your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe. And peace upon the messengers. And praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat 171–182].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat 164]. The starting point of the discussion is His saying ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾. Where is the subject (mubtada') here?
* Student: "Ma'lum" (known).
* Shaykh: What is the estimated (taqdir) form?
* Student: The estimate is: "And there is none of us [any one]."
* Shaykh: "And there is none of us [any one] but has a known station." Well done. The sentence "illa lahu maqam ma'lum" (but has a known station): what is its grammatical position (mahall)?
* Student: The predicate (khabar) of the subject.
* Shaykh: How the predicate of the subject? You said the subject is "ahad" (any one) and its predicate is "minna" (of us). Then "illa lahu maqam ma'lum"?
* Student: An exception (istithna') from "ahad".
* Shaykh: An exception from "ahad". So its position is in the nominative (raf'), or it is a substitute (badal) from "ahad", and its position is nominative.
* Student: Here, "minna ahad" here, now we said...
* Shaykh: Is the speech before it complete or incomplete?
* Student: No, now it is complete.
* Shaykh: Complete. Affirmative or negative?
* Student: Negative.
* Shaykh: If what precedes "illa" (except) is complete and negative, what is the ruling on what follows it?
* Student: What follows may either be parsed according to its position, or it is parsed as a substitute (badal).
* Shaykh: Substitute, good. Or?
* Student: Or according to its position.
* Shaykh: Even if it is a substitute, according to its position?
* Student: An exception (mustathna).
* Shaykh: Or in the accusative (nasb) as an exception.
* Student: In the accusative as an exception, yes.
* Shaykh: So it is permissible that ﴿lahu maqam ma'lum﴾ is in the accusative position as an exception, or?
* Student: A substitute from ﴿ahad﴾.
* Shaykh: In the nominative position as a substitute from ﴿ahad﴾.
Good. Here, does the "maqam" refer to a place, or to place and time?
* Student: The "maqam" here includes the station of time and place.
* Shaykh: Includes?
* Student: Because the sentence allows both, and if it allows both, then the rule is...
* Shaykh: Because "maqam" is suitable for both time and place, so it includes both.

His saying: ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks﴾ [al-Saffat 165]. What is the meaning of ﴿al-saffun﴾?
* Student: They arrange the rows. The author says: "muṣṭafūn", i.e., aligned, shoulder to shoulder in their feet.
* Shaykh: Equal in their feet.
* Student: (...) the first, then the first.
* Shaykh: The ranks are in what? In worship, or in what else?
* Student: In worship.
* Shaykh: In worship. Good. How are their rows, brother?
* Student: The rows of the angels: they join the first to the first (...) Mighty and Majestic.
* Shaykh: They complete them first to first and they align tightly. This is how the Prophet ﷺ explained it.
Good. What is the meaning of al-musabbihun?
* Student: Those who declare Allah far above every deficiency.
* Shaykh: Above every deficiency, or above what is not befitting to Him?
* Student: Above what is not befitting to Him.
* Shaykh: Above what is not befitting to Him. The declaration of Allah's transcendence (tanzih). How many things do we say Allah is exempt from?
* Student: Two: exemption from likeness, the likeness of created beings, and from deficiency.
* Shaykh: In?
* Student: In His perfection.
* Shaykh: From deficiency in His perfection. An example of the first?
* Student: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth﴾ [Qaf 38].
* Shaykh: That is exemption from likeness to created beings.
* Student: ﴿There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura 11].
* Shaykh: And an example of exemption from deficiency in His perfection?
* Student: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf 38].
* Shaykh: Well done. His saying ﴿And if they indeed used to say﴾ [al-Saffat 167]: is the sentence here negated or affirmed?
* Student: Negated.
* Shaykh: Then "in" (إنْ) here is negating.
* Student: No, affirmed.
* Shaykh: Here "in", what is it when it is affirmative?
* Student: Emphasis.
* Shaykh: Emphasis. What do the grammarians call it?
* Student: Lightened from the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah).
* Shaykh: Lightened from the heavy, well done. Now where is its noun (ism), ﴿And if they indeed used to say﴾?
* Student: The angels.
* Shaykh: No, the angels do not say it.
* Student: A pronoun of the matter (ḍamir al-sha'n).
* Shaykh: Is its noun omitted or present?
* Student: Omitted.
* Shaykh: Omitted. The pronoun of the matter, what is its estimate?
* Student: "Innahum kanu" (indeed they were).
* Shaykh: "Innahum" (indeed they): is there another estimate?
* Student: "Innahu kana" (indeed it was).
* Shaykh: "Innahu", i.e., the matter; meaning that their matter is that they say such and such. The second view is that the pronoun of the matter is estimated according to context. Good. Where is the object of the saying (maqul al-qawl)?
* Student: ﴿Layaqulun﴾.
* Shaykh: No, "yaqulun" is the saying itself. But where is the object of the saying?
* Student: Omitted.
* Shaykh: Read the verse.
* Student: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾.
* Shaykh: The object of the saying is His saying: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 168–169]. Good. Is their saying correct according to reality?
* Student: No, it is not correct.
* Shaykh: Not correct, because the reminder came to them but they disbelieved.
His saying ﴿layaqulun﴾: what is its position in the grammar (i'rab)?
* Student: Noun of "kana".
* Shaykh: Noun of "kana"! Is the noun of "kana" a whole sentence?! Read the verse.
* Student: ﴿And if they indeed used to say﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿And if they indeed used to say﴾.
* Student: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾.
* Shaykh: What do you say now? The waw in ﴿kanu﴾ is not the noun of "kana"?
* Student: The noun of "kana", and this is its predicate.
* Shaykh: So then.
* Student: ﴿Layaqulun﴾ is the predicate of "kana".
* Shaykh: Its position is accusative, as the predicate of "kana".
Now ﴿If that we had a reminder﴾: what is the estimate of the sentence?
* Student: Object of the saying.
* Shaykh: The sentence, no. We want the estimate of the sentence.
* Student: "If we had a reminder."
* Shaykh: No, that is not suitable.
* Student: The estimate: "If we had a book from the former peoples."
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: "If that we had a reminder from it, from the books of the former peoples."
* Another student: "If it is established that we have a reminder."
* Shaykh: This is the estimate: "If it is established that we have a reminder from the former peoples." We estimated it this way because the conditional "law" (if) only enters upon a verb.
Now His saying ﴿al-mukhlasin﴾ has two readings.
* Student: ﴿al-mukhlasin﴾ and ﴿al-mukhlisin﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿al-mukhlasin﴾ and ﴿al-mukhlisin﴾. ﴿al-mukhlasin﴾: is it an active participle (ism fa'il) or a passive participle (ism maf'ul)?
* Student: Passive.
* Shaykh: ﴿al-mukhlisin﴾?
* Student: No, active.
* Shaykh: If you say "mukhlis", is it active or passive? "So-and-so is mukhlis."
* Student: Active.
* Shaykh: And "so-and-so is mukhlas"?
* Student: Passive.
* Shaykh: Passive. So "al-mukhlisin" is an active participle and "al-mukhlasin" is a passive participle. On the reading "mukhlasin", what does it mean?
* Student: They are those whom Allah, glory be to Him, made sincere for Himself.
* Shaykh: Allah made them sincere for Himself, so He chose them over creation by the blessing of worship that Allah bestowed upon them. And "al-mukhlasin"?
* Student: And "al-mukhlasin" are those whom Allah, glory be to Him, made sincere for worship.
* Shaykh: What is meant by His saying ﴿So they will soon know﴾?
* Student: "They will soon know" by the one who denied.
* Shaykh: But what is meant by it? What is meant by this sentence?
* Student: The "fa" is consequential and causal: because of their disbelief, "so they will soon", i.e., their knowledge.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Causal.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: Warning.
* Shaykh: The intention is warning. You threaten your child, you say: "You will soon find out what I will do to you," right? You threaten him. Shall we take the lessons from His saying?
* Student: ﴿And there is none of us﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ and so on to the end.
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: showing that the angels are exempt from what these people claim, that they are the daughters of Allah. The reason is that they are charged with worship at a known limit, and whoever is charged with worship cannot be a son of the one worshipped.
* And among the lessons of the verse: the perfect order of the angels, peace be upon them, in that they keep to the known stations that Allah appointed for them: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾.
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: an indication that a person should have an organized schedule, assigning a known task to each thing, so that time is not wasted for him, because a person who uses time haphazardly does not benefit from it. But our saying this does not mean that a person continues in one fixed state, for what is less excellent may sometimes become better than what is more excellent. That is, if you organize yourself and then something arises that requires departing from this system, there is no blame upon you for breaking this system, because the Messenger ﷺ used to fast until it was said, "He never breaks his fast," and used to pray at night until it was said, "He never sleeps," or the reverse, according to what the public interest requires.
* And among the lessons of the noble verses in general: the angels, peace be upon them, are among the most perfect people in worship, in that they gather in the worship of Allah and form rows in glorifying Him. This is based on His saying: ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks﴾.
* And among its lessons: it is appropriate to emphasize speech when the addressee is denying or doubtful, or when the meaning is important and needs emphasis. This is based on His saying ﴿And indeed, we are the ranks﴾, to establish the truth for these deniers who claim that the angels are daughters of Allah. They say: "We stand in rows in worship and glorification of Him."
* And among the lessons of the noble verses: the perfect declaration of the angels' transcendence of Allah in His saying ﴿And indeed, we are the ones who glorify﴾.
* And among its lessons: their habit is also glorification, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya' 20]. We derive this from this verse, because the sentence came as a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), and a nominal sentence indicates establishment and continuity.
* And among its lessons: the transcendence of Allah, glory be to Him, is expressed on the tongues of the angels from everything not befitting to Him, and He, glory be to Him, is exempt from everything not befitting to Him. For this reason, many verses came negating likeness from Allah, negating deficiency, affirming wisdom, and negating play and falsehood concerning Him, Exalted: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in falsehood. That is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾ [Sad 27]. ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Anbiya' 16]. ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 36], and many other verses that indicate His perfection, glory be to Him, and the absence of play and falsehood from His acts.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they indeed used to say, "If that we had a reminder from the former peoples"﴾ and so on to the end.
* Among the lessons of these verses: these deniers of the Messenger, peace be upon him, claim that no reminder came to them through which they could be reminded. For this reason they raise this objection, saying: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾.
* And among its lessons: the arguments of the disbelievers are arguments of obstinacy, not based on truth. For example, their saying ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾: what do we say to them? We say: "Rather, you have a reminder from the former peoples; rather, you have the best of remembrances absolutely."
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: people cannot be upright except through books sent down from heaven. Even the polytheist disbelievers acknowledge this, by their saying: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾. This lesson is confirmed by reality: you find the nations to whom no books were revealed in constant chaos, their affairs do not become upright, and they do not walk on a straight path, unlike the People of the Book, and unlike the nations to whom books were revealed, which are upright to the extent they hold fast to these books.
* And among the lessons of these verses: revealed books are a reminder for those to whom they were sent. We have previously mentioned that its being a reminder has two aspects or three? It is a reminder, i.e., an honor for those to whom it was sent; it is a reminder through which they remember and are admonished; and it is a reminder through which they draw near to Allah, Exalted, because it is the best kind of remembrance.
* And among the lessons of these verses: those who claimed that if they had a reminder from the former peoples they would be sincere servants of Allah were liars, as evidenced by the fact that they did have a reminder from the former peoples but disbelieved in it. We have previously mentioned that their disbelief includes both types of disbelief: ignorance and arrogance.
* And among the lessons of the verses: the warning to disbelievers, by His saying ﴿So they will soon know﴾. The warning of disbelievers is undoubtedly consistent with wisdom, because the proof has been established against them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and warners, so that people will not have an argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa' 165].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 164–170 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat 37:164]. The author, may Allah have mercy on him, made clear that this is the speech of Jibril, peace be upon him. The author said: (Jibril said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾).

When Allah mentioned that these criminal wrongdoers said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah," He, glorified and exalted is He, explained through the tongue of the angels what their condition is, what their station is, and what their deeds toward Allah, glorified and exalted is He, are. So He said: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾. The author said: (﴿And there is none of us﴾ O assembly of angels) — "assembly" meaning group — (anyone ﴿but has a known station﴾). The author supplied "anyone" (aḥad) because the context indicates it; it is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the preceding ﴿minna﴾ ("of us"), a prepositional phrase.

As for His saying: ﴿but has a known station﴾ (in the heavens), this exception is an exception from "anyone." It is a sentence that can be taken to indicate the state of these angels.

His saying: ﴿but has a station﴾ means a place of standing, because maqam (maf'al) can be a noun of time and a noun of place. Here the apparent meaning is a noun of place: a place of standing in which he stands to worship Allah. It is also permissible to take it as a noun of time: a time in which he stands before Allah and a place in which he stands before Allah. Thus the worship of the angels is restricted to a time and confined to a place, and there is no contradiction between the two views. The principle in tafsir is that if a verse is capable of two meanings that do not contradict each other, both are adopted, because taking both is broader in meaning than restricting it to one of them. If one of them contradicts the other, weighing (tarjih) is sought; what the one who weighs prefers is taken, and the other is left.

He says here: ﴿There is none of us but has a known station﴾, meaning: a place and also a time in which he worships Allah, Exalted is He, and he does not worship Allah in anything else, neither in a time nor in a place.

(﴿And indeed we are the ranked ones﴾ [al-Saffat 37:165], our feet in prayer.) The pronoun in ﴿indeed we﴾ refers to whom? To the angels. ﴿We are the ranked ones﴾ means those who line up before Allah, glorified and exalted is He, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: «Will you not line up as the angels line up before their Lord?» They said: "O Messenger of Allah, how is that?" He said: «They complete the first rows, then the next, and they press close together»[[Narrated by Muslim (430/119) from the hadith of Jabir ibn Samurah.]]. This is the condition of the angels before Allah in their station of worship: they line up in glorification of Him, completing the first row after the first. The foremost and earliest of them is the nearest to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Likewise in the rows of prayer, whoever is earlier and nearer to the imam is better.

﴿And indeed we are the ranked ones﴾ [al-Saffat 37:165]. The author said: (our feet in prayer). The phrase "our feet in prayer" requires evidence, because the apparent description ﴿we are the ranked ones﴾ refers to the angels themselves, not to their feet. Moreover, if we say "our feet," we need to establish that the angels have feet, whereas Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has described the angels as possessing wings; so this requires evidence.

His saying: ﴿And indeed we are the ranked ones﴾ contains two emphases. The first emphasis?
* Student: (inna).
* Shaykh: And the second?
* Student: The second is (the lam).
* Shaykh: The lam in His saying: ﴿lanahnu al-ṣāffūn﴾.
It contains two emphases. The first emphasis?
* Student: (...) (inna).
* Shaykh: And the second?
* Student: The second is the lam.
* Shaykh: The lam in His saying: ﴿lanahnu al-ṣāffūn﴾ [al-Saffat 37:165].

﴿And indeed we are the glorifiers﴾ [al-Saffat 37:166]. The sentence is emphasized in the same way as the first: that is, "and indeed we, the assembly of angels, are surely the glorifiers." The author said: (those who declare Allah free of what is not befitting to Him), because tasbih means tanzih (declaring Allah free of imperfection), and the declaring of Allah free means declaring Him free of what is not befitting to Him. It rests on two matters. The first: that He is declared free of resemblance to created beings, and its evidence is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura 42:11]. The second: that He is declared free of any deficiency in His perfection, and among its examples is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us﴾ [Qaf 50:38]. When He mentioned His creation of these great heavens and the earth in this brief period, He made clear that no fatigue or exhaustion reached Him in that. This is declaring Allah free of deficiency in His perfection. So the declaring free rests on what?
* Student: On two attributes.
* Shaykh: On two attributes? No.
* Student: On two matters: first, the resemblance of Allah to created beings.
* Shaykh: And its evidence?
* Student: ﴿There is nothing like Him.﴾ The second: declaring Allah free of deficiency in His perfection.
* Shaykh: And an example of it? Give an example.
* Student: ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat 37:159].
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿And We created the heavens...﴾
* Shaykh: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us﴾ [Qaf 50:38].

Good. He said ﴿And indeed we are the glorifiers﴾. The two clauses, as you know, are nominal sentences. The scholars said: a nominal sentence indicates stability and continuity; that is, this is their constant practice. This is supported by His saying, Exalted is He, describing them: ﴿And those who are with Him do not disdain His worship, nor do they tire. They glorify Him night and day; they never slacken﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:19–20]. So the angels are always in continuous worship, unlike humans who have heedlessness, amusement and forgetfulness; rather they are always in the worship of Allah. Here there are three categories of creation: devils, who are always in disobedience; angels, who are always in obedience; and humans, who are sometimes in obedience, sometimes in disobedience, and sometimes in heedlessness.

He said: ﴿And indeed they used to say: "If only we had a reminder from the former peoples"﴾ [al-Saffat 37:167–168] and so on to the end. ﴿And indeed they used to say﴾ — is (in) here conditional? No, because there is no condition and consequence in it. Is it negating? No, because the lam in His saying ﴿la-yaqūlūn﴾ prevents it from being negating, since the lam is for emphasis and negation is the opposite of emphasis. Is it superfluous? No, because it has a meaning, and a superfluous element is one whose removal does not disturb the meaning. So what is it? We say: it is a lightened form of the heavy (inna), its origin being: "wa-innahum kānū" (and indeed they were). Its origin is thus, but it was lightened, so it became ﴿wa-in kānū la-yaqūlūn﴾. On this occasion we wish to review the meanings of (in). (In) comes as a negation, as in: —
* Student: ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near or whether my Lord will appoint for it a term﴾ [al-Jinn 72:25].
* Shaykh: ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near﴾; i.e., I do not know whether what you are promised is near. And it comes as a conditional; give an example.
* Student: From the verses?
* Shaykh: From the verses. Better from the verses, if you have one.
* Student: ﴿If you are truthful﴾ [al-Saffat 37:157].
* Shaykh: What? ﴿If you are truthful﴾ ... (...) it comes as a conditional (in) with a condition and a consequence.
* Student: ﴿And if you do not, and you will never do it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:24].
* Shaykh: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it, then fear the Fire﴾; and ﴿And if you are in doubt concerning what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:23]. And it comes as superfluous?
* Student:
*"Banī Ghudānah, mā in antum dhahab / wa-lā ṣarīf, wa-lākin antumu al-kharaf"*
* Shaykh: Correct.
*"Banī Ghudānah, mā in antum dhahab..................."*
i.e., silver. "But you are clay": pottery. The evidence is his saying "mā in antum" (what you are); if "in" were removed and he said "mā antum dhahaban," the sentence would still be sound.

And it comes as a lightened form, as in this verse, a lightened form of the heavy (inna). The lightened form of the heavy has, as they say, a noun that is omitted, called the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). The pronoun of the matter, they say, is singular masculine, because the word sha'n (matter) is singular masculine. The estimate is: ﴿And indeed they used to say﴾, i.e., "and indeed it (the matter) — i.e., their matter — they were indeed saying." It has also been said that the pronoun of the matter is estimated according to the context: if it is singular masculine it is singular masculine, if it is plural it is plural. On this basis the estimate of the verse here is: "wa-innahum kānū la-yaqūlūn."

He said: ﴿And if they used to say﴾: "kānū" is a defective verb with its subject; the waw is the subject. The lam in His saying ﴿la-yaqūlūn﴾ is the lam of emphasis, and the clause "yaqūlūn" is the predicate of what? The predicate of kāna. Kāna with its subject and predicate is the predicate of the lightened (in), from the heavy. ("And if" is lightened from the heavy; "kānū" means the Quraysh of Makkah; "la-yaqūlūn") — what? ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾ [al-Saffat 37:168–169]; i.e., if a book had been sent down to us like the books of the former peoples, we would be the servants of Allah, submitting to His law and sincere to Him. But this argument is rejected by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down, so follow it and fear Allah that you may receive mercy. [That you may] not say: "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and indeed we were unaware of their study." Or [that] you may say: "If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they." But there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord and guidance and mercy﴾ [al-An'am 6:155–157].

So this claim from them is obstinacy. Why was it obstinacy? Because there was sent down to them a Book that is the most guiding and most upright of books, yet they disbelieved in it.

﴿And if they used to say: "If only we had a reminder"﴾ (a book), ﴿from the former peoples﴾, i.e., from the books of past nations, ﴿we would certainly have been servants of Allah, the sincere ones﴾ devoted to His worship.

Note that ﴿if only we had a reminder﴾ means: that which would remind us; and what reminds is the Book. Allah said: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya 21:50]. So the meaning of "reminder" here is that by which a person remembers, which is the Book.

As for His saying ﴿from the former peoples﴾, the author said: (from the books of the former peoples). So it is with an omitted noun: ﴿from the former peoples⟩, i.e., from their books, not from themselves, but from the books that were sent down to them. "If we had any of this, we would be the sincere servants of Allah." The lam in ﴿we would have been﴾ is the answer to "if" (law), and "law" here is conditional, or is it verbal? Conditional. Now, ﴿law anna 'indanā﴾: they say the conditional particle is followed only by a verb, yet here it is followed by (anna). Even the definitive conditional is followed only by a verb, yet here it is followed by (anna). They said: yes, but it is on an estimated verb; that is, "if it were established that 'indanā dhikran..."; ﴿we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾, like His saying: ﴿And if they had been patient until you came out to them, it would have been better for them﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:5]; i.e., if it were established that they were patient.

﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾ — are they the servants of Allah in the legal or in the predestined sense? In the legal sense, because in the predestined sense they are already servants of Allah by decree, and cannot deviate from Allah's decree and destiny. But ﴿we would have been servants of Allah﴾ is legal. He said: (the ones sincere in worship to Him). "Sincere" (mukhlisīn) with a kasra on the lam, so the author explained it: "sincere in worship to Him." And "sincere" (mukhlaṣīn) with a fatha on the lam means those whom Allah has made sincere and chosen. So "al-mukhlisīn" has two readings: with a fatha and with a kasra on the lam. On the reading with a fatha, the meaning is: those whom Allah has made sincere for Himself and chosen. On the reading with a kasra, the meaning is: those who made worship sincere for Him. The two meanings are interrelated, because whoever makes worship sincere for Allah, Allah has made him sincere for Himself: ﴿we would have been the sincere servants of Allah﴾.

Allah said: (﴿So they disbelieved in it﴾; i.e., in the Book that came to them, which is the Qur'an, the most noble of those books; ﴿so they will come to know﴾ the consequence of their disbelief). The structure of the verse: a book came to them; they said ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been servants of Allah﴾; then the Book came to them, the reminder came to them, but they did not accept this reminder; they disbelieved in it, denying the report and being arrogant toward the command. They denied the Messenger, peace be upon him. He said: "You will indeed be resurrected," and they said: "There is no resurrection." He said: "It is true," and they said: "He is a liar." He said: "Worship Allah alone, with no partner," and they worshipped idols. So they disbelieved in this Book, denying its report and being arrogant toward its command. They did not believe what Allah informed of in His Book, nor did they comply with the command and submit to it; rather they combined the disbelief of denial and arrogance, may Allah protect us. They disbelieved in it although the Qur'an is more noble than those books which they claimed, if it had come to them of their kind, they would have been the sincere servants of Allah. Yet they disbelieved in this Book, and this shows that their claim was among the most false of claims. ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been servants of Allah﴾: it was said to them, "This is a reminder; there has come to you a reminder more noble than the reminders and greater than the earlier books, yet you disbelieved in it."

Allah said: ﴿So they will come to know﴾. The fa' in ﴿so they disbelieved﴾ is for sequence, and the fa' in ﴿so they will come to know﴾ is for sequence and causation; that is, because of their disbelief they will come to know. What will they come to know? They will come to know the outcome of their affair: humiliation in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. This has occurred, praise be to Allah. Allah humbled them in the greatest battle in which they used to take pride and imagine honor and victory, the Battle of Badr. They set out with their champions, nobles and great men, to the extent that Abu Jahl, when he was advised to turn back, said: "By Allah, we will not return until we reach Badr, where we will slaughter camels, drink wine, have singing girls play for us, and the Arabs will hear of us, and they will forever stand in awe of us."

Look at the arrogance and pride! Then it passed, and what happened? He was killed, praise be to Allah, along with the leaders and nobles who were with him. The Arabs heard of them, and the Arabs spoke of them, but of what? Of what brings them awe, or of what brings shame and disgrace? The latter. The Arabs spoke of their news, praise be to Allah, with what brings shame and disgrace until the Day of Resurrection. These are among the grievous consequences.

In their own town of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ had left it in fear, hidden, and entered it victorious and triumphant, adorned. The banner was raised at the entrance of Makkah at al-Hajun. He entered the House and broke the idols, and stood at the door while the Quraysh were below waiting to see what he would do. He said: «What do you think I will do with you, O assembly of Quraysh?» They said: "Good. A noble brother and the son of a noble brother."[[Narrated by al-Tabari in al-Tarikh (3/61).]] So he, peace be upon him, pardoned them, and they were called "the freed ones" (al-Tulaqa'), meaning freed from killing and captivity.

Look at how this outcome turned out. This Prophet ﷺ, Allah protected him from them. They plotted to kill him, or to imprison him, or to expel him, but the plot turned back against them. They were the very people whom the Messenger ﷺ pardoned and released. Yet what is in the Hereafter is harsher and greater. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, for those who did wrong there is a punishment short of that, but most of them do not know﴾ [al-Tur 47]. ﴿And We will surely make them taste the nearer punishment before the greater punishment﴾ [al-Sajdah 21]. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is harder﴾ [al-Ra'd 34]. We seek refuge in Allah.

The purpose of this sentence, i.e., His saying ﴿So they will soon know﴾, is a warning (tahdid): a threat to these deniers of the Messenger ﷺ.

* Student: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya' 20], said of the angels. Does this not indicate that by His saying ﴿maqam﴾ (station) is meant a place?
* Shaykh: A place? No, even a time.
* Student: All night and day in worship?
