* And among its lessons: the transcendence of Allah, glory be to Him, is expressed on the tongues of the angels from everything not befitting to Him, and He, glory be to Him, is exempt from everything not befitting to Him. For this reason, many verses came negating likeness from Allah, negating deficiency, affirming wisdom, and negating play and falsehood concerning Him, Exalted: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in falsehood. That is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾ [Sad 27]. ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Anbiya' 16]. ﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah 36], and many other verses that indicate His perfection, glory be to Him, and the absence of play and falsehood from His acts.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they indeed used to say, "If that we had a reminder from the former peoples"﴾ and so on to the end.
* Among the lessons of these verses: these deniers of the Messenger, peace be upon him, claim that no reminder came to them through which they could be reminded. For this reason they raise this objection, saying: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾.
* And among its lessons: the arguments of the disbelievers are arguments of obstinacy, not based on truth. For example, their saying ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples﴾: what do we say to them? We say: "Rather, you have a reminder from the former peoples; rather, you have the best of remembrances absolutely."
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: people cannot be upright except through books sent down from heaven. Even the polytheist disbelievers acknowledge this, by their saying: ﴿If that we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would certainly have been sincere servants of Allah﴾. This lesson is confirmed by reality: you find the nations to whom no books were revealed in constant chaos, their affairs do not become upright, and they do not walk on a straight path, unlike the People of the Book, and unlike the nations to whom books were revealed, which are upright to the extent they hold fast to these books.
* And among the lessons of these verses: revealed books are a reminder for those to whom they were sent. We have previously mentioned that its being a reminder has two aspects or three? It is a reminder, i.e., an honor for those to whom it was sent; it is a reminder through which they remember and are admonished; and it is a reminder through which they draw near to Allah, Exalted, because it is the best kind of remembrance.
* And among the lessons of these verses: those who claimed that if they had a reminder from the former peoples they would be sincere servants of Allah were liars, as evidenced by the fact that they did have a reminder from the former peoples but disbelieved in it. We have previously mentioned that their disbelief includes both types of disbelief: ignorance and arrogance.
* And among the lessons of the verses: the warning to disbelievers, by His saying ﴿So they will soon know﴾. The warning of disbelievers is undoubtedly consistent with wisdom, because the proof has been established against them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and warners, so that people will not have an argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa' 165].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verse 171–182 (part 1 of 5):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And certainly Our word had preceded to Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they would be the ones given victory.﴾ "And Our word had preceded": i.e., it had gone forth in eternity (al-azal). The word of Allah is explained here in His saying: ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory.﴾ This is the preceding word which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, decreed in eternity.

As for His saying: ﴿And certainly Our word had preceded﴾, the sentence here contains several emphasizers. What are they?
* Student: The lam of oath, and (qad).
* Shaykh: The lam of oath, and (qad)?
* Student: Emphasis: "to Our servants, the messengers."
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: The separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: The implied oath (al-qasam al-muqaddar).
* Shaykh: And the implied oath. Since you say "the lam of oath," it necessarily means there is an oath. So the implied sense is: "By Allah, indeed Our word had preceded," or "By Allah, certainly Our word had preceded." Every sentence that comes in this form contains these emphasizers: the oath, the lam, and (qad).

As for His saying: ﴿Our word to Our servants, the messengers﴾, the word "servants" here refers to a special servanthood, indeed the most special of the special: the servanthood of messengerhood (ʿubūdiyyat al-risāla). Servanthood is of two kinds. The first is the servanthood of creation to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which is cosmic servanthood (ʿubūdiyya kawniyya); this is general and encompasses all creation, for there is no created being except that it is subject to Allah's decree. The second is legislative servanthood (ʿubūdiyya sharʿiyya), which is specific to those who obey Allah; and the most distinguished type of this is the servanthood of messengerhood, because the messengers are charged with what others are not charged with: they are charged with bearing the message, conveying it to creation, and calling people to it. For this reason, Allah does not send a messenger except while knowing that he is fit for messengerhood, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-Anʿām 124]. And Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an in gradual revelation. So be patient for the decision of your Lord﴾ [al-Insān 23–24]. When He mentioned that He had sent down the Qur'an to him, He did not say: "Then thank Allah for this blessing," but said: ﴿so be patient for the decision of your Lord﴾, indicating that the sending down of the Qur'an to him is a matter that requires patience, because it requires enduring hardship and confronting people.

Whoever reflects on what the Messenger ﷺ encountered from his people, their opposition to him and their harm to him, will see the wisdom in His saying ﴿so be patient for the decision of your Lord﴾.

﴿Our word had preceded to Our servants, the messengers﴾. The author (al-Mufassir) said: (﴿And certainly Our word had preceded﴾ concerning victory, ﴿to Our servants, the messengers﴾, and it is ﴿I and My messengers will surely prevail﴾, or it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾). Here, "or" (aw) is used for uncertainty (li-l-tardīd); meaning: is the word His saying ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾ [al-Mujādila 21], or is the word His saying: ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾? The second possibility is preferable, because the second possibility makes the explanation of the statement lie within the statement, whereas the first makes the explanation separate from it, and when the explanation is connected, it is better. On this basis, the word is: ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾, which is part of His saying: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail."﴾

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾, this sentence is emphasized with three emphasizers: the first is (inna), the second is the lam in ﴿lahum﴾, and the third is (hum), because (hum) is a separating pronoun. So this sentence is emphasized with three emphasizers.
* Student: (Inna), the lam, and (hum), the separating pronoun.
* Shaykh: And (hum) is the separating pronoun.

Furthermore, in its structure it is a sentence of ta'kīd, or rather tawkīdiyya; tawkīdiyya is better than ta'kīdiyya, because it is the language of the Qur'an: ﴿and do not break oaths after their confirmation (tawkīdihā)﴾ [al-Naḥl 91]. It is a tawkīdiyya sentence because it is a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), and the nominal sentence conveys establishment and continuity.

Now, we have mentioned that (inna) is for emphasis, and this is clear; the lam is for emphasis, which is also clear; (hum), the separating pronoun, is for emphasis. As for the separating pronoun, grammatically it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical position), and semantically it conveys three things: emphasis, restriction (ḥaṣr), and separation between the attribute and the predicate. How many is this? Three. Count them for us, you.
* Student: Restriction.
* Shaykh: Yes, it conveys restriction.
* Student: And the attribute.
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: And the separation (...).
* Shaykh: I want you to listen.
* Student: It conveys emphasis, restriction, and separation.
* Shaykh: Emphasis, restriction, and separation between the predicate and the attribute. This is why it is called a separating pronoun.

An example that clarifies the matter: if you say, "Zayd al-fāḍil," then the word (al-fāḍil) in this context may be an attribute, so a person looks for the predicate: "Zayd the virtuous, what about him?" You say, "standing," for example: "Zayd the virtuous is standing." Here, "the virtuous" is what? An attribute. But if you say, "Zayd the virtuous," and you omit "standing," the sentence becomes open to the possibility that (al-fāḍil) is an attribute with the predicate still to come, or that (al-fāḍil) is the predicate. If you say, "Zayd is (the) virtuous," then it is determined that (al-fāḍil) is the predicate of the subject.

Thus, the insertion of the pronoun (huwa) between the attribute and the predicate, where it is determined that what follows is a predicate and not an attribute. Likewise, if you say, "Zayd huwa al-fāḍil," it becomes more emphatic than your saying "Zayd al-fāḍil," because you say (huwa) for emphasis.

Third: when you say, "Zayd huwa al-fāḍil," you mean "not anyone else," so it restricts virtue to him.

Thus, the separating pronoun grammatically has no place in i'rab: it is neither a subject nor a predicate nor anything at all. Semantically it conveys three things: emphasis, restriction, and separation between the predicate and the attribute.

Now here, ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾: we say, the hā' is the noun of (inna), the lam is for emphasis, (hum) is a separating pronoun with no place in i'rab, and ﴿al-manṣūrūn﴾ is the predicate of (inna).

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾. ﴿Lahum﴾ means: not others. ﴿Al-manṣūrūn﴾ are given victory by whom? By Allah, those whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gives victory through the signs He decrees or through the armies He sends. At Badr, Allah sent the angels, and they fought alongside the Prophet ﷺ. At the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb), Allah sent a fierce wind against their enemies along with armies: ﴿So We sent upon them a wind and armies you did not see﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 9]. Thus, at the Confederates, Allah combined the angels, who cast terror into the hearts of these enemies, with the wind that shook them, until they had no place to settle, so they fled. So, they are given victory by Allah through the signs He sends or through the angels.

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed Our army﴾: al-jund are the defenders. Defenders of whom? They are an army for Him, those who support Him and defend Him. From this comes the usage: the soldiers of the emir and the sultan and the like. Here He says: ﴿And indeed Our army﴾, meaning the army of Allah. These soldiers are not an army of Allah because Allah has need of them, but because they defend His law, and so they became His army. These soldiers are the victorious, because they are the army of Allah, and Allah, Glorified and Exalted, holds victory: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail."﴾ So the army of Allah, who defend His law, must have victory. For this reason He said: ﴿they are the ones who will be victorious﴾, and the sentence, like the first, is emphasized with three emphasizers: (inna), the lam, and the separating pronoun.

Now, ﴿al-ghālibūn﴾, as you know, is the active participle of ghalaba. Is ghalaba transitive or intransitive? Transitive. A transitive verb necessarily has an agent and an object. The participle (al-ghālib) here is an active participle from a transitive verb, so it necessarily has an agent and an object. Who is the agent?
* Students: Allah.
* Shaykh: No, the army; ﴿And indeed Our army, they are the victorious﴾. But they are victorious by Allah's command, without doubt. The object is omitted; the implied meaning, as the author said, is: (victorious over the disbelievers by argument and by being given victory over them in this world, and if some of them are not victorious in this world, then in the Hereafter).

The author pointed to a difficulty that we wanted to postpone to the benefits, but now it is necessary to speak about it. ﴿And indeed Our army, they are the victorious﴾: Allah has made clear, with three emphasizers, that His army, the believers who defend His religion, are the victorious. And previously He emphasized that the messengers are the ones given victory.

If someone says: is this emphasized statement from the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, consistent with reality, or does reality contradict it?

If you say: it is consistent with reality, then it was refuted by Uhud, when the victory went to the polytheists. Among the prophets, some were killed: ﴿and they killed the prophets without right﴾ [al-Baqara 61]. Among the people of good, some were killed: ﴿and they kill those who enjoin justice among people﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 21]. So what is the answer to this?

The answer is that we say: either the victory that Allah promised the messengers is based on the predominant majority; indeed, the predominant majority is without doubt the victory of the messengers over their enemies, and read the verses about the messengers and you will find that Allah says: ﴿So We saved him and those with him﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 64], and He destroyed the others. This is victory without doubt.

Or it is said: the intended victory is the victory of those who were commanded to fight. Those who were commanded to fight, Allah has guaranteed them victory. As for those who were not commanded to fight, there was no contest between them and their enemies such that it could be said they were victorious, and their killing does not contradict the verse.

The third aspect is that the intended victory is absolute victory, which is the victory of the Hereafter; as for the victory of this world, it is not guaranteed. So the answers now are three.

There is a fourth aspect: that the intended victory is the victory of their argument, not of their persons; that is, the victory of what they brought and its prevalence, without sensible dominance, since that is not of great importance compared with the dominance of the law they brought.

These are four aspects in answering the reality that may appear to contradict the apparent meaning of the verse. We must know that there is nothing explicit in the Qur'an that contradicts reality at all; that is impossible. Nor is there anything authentic and explicit in the Sunnah that contradicts reality. I say: there is nothing explicit in the Qur'an that contradicts reality, and there is nothing authentic and explicit in the Sunnah that contradicts reality. Brother, what is the difference between the two statements?
* Student: Is it "from the Book and from the Sunnah"?
* Shaykh: Yes, what is the difference between them? I said: there is nothing explicit in the Qur'an that contradicts reality, and there is nothing authentic and explicit in the Sunnah that contradicts reality.
* Student: Because there may be non-authentic hadiths in the Sunnah.
* Shaykh: Non-authentic. That is why we needed to say "authentic." In the Qur'an we do not need to say "authentic." Why? Because it is all transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur), and it is all authentic, with no difficulty.

Thus, it is impossible that there be in the Qur'an anything explicit that contradicts reality, and there is nothing in the authentic Sunnah that explicitly contradicts reality. If there is found something whose apparent meaning contradicts reality, know that either there is no contradiction, but the contradiction is from your own assumption, meaning that reality does not contradict the apparent meaning of the Qur'an; or what you thought was explicit in the Qur'an is not explicit.

For example, many scholars, though not most scholars, say that the earth is not spherical, because Allah says: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created? And at the sky, how it was raised? And at the mountains, how they were set up? And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾ [al-Ghāshiya 17–20]. And flatness (al-saṭḥiyya) contradicts sphericity. So whoever says the earth is spherical has contradicted the explicit Qur'an, because Allah says: ﴿how it was spread out (suṭiḥat)﴾. They denied that the earth is spherical on the basis of what? On their understanding that the Qur'an is explicit in this.

Among the scholars are those who say it is spherical, and reality testifies to the view of these people, for it is not possible now to say that it is not spherical at all: if you left Jeddah airport in a plane heading west, where would your destination be? You would return to Jeddah.

So it is spherical, and where do you go? The evidence of perceived reality testifies to this. We say: then the Qur'an that they claimed is explicit in saying it is not spherical must be contrary to what they understood. Could someone say: the perceived reality must be false? It is impossible.

If someone said that perceived reality is false, people would throw stones at him, not to mention stones of the mouth; that is, not merely insulting him with the tongue, but with stones. He would be called insane. Then what becomes necessary for us? To say that the Qur'an is not explicit in this, so the flatness in it is understood as what a person needs from the earth. Whatever you need from the earth is flat: that is, He did not make the earth flat like the back of a mountain or the slope of a mountain, meaning ascending; not at all. Whatever you need is flat: you settle on it, pour water on it, and plant on it, flat.

Then we say: there is in the Qur'an what indicates that it is spherical, such as His saying: ﴿When the sky is split open, and it listens to its Lord and it is obligated; and when the earth is stretched out, and it throws out what is within it and empties itself﴾ [al-Inshiqāq 1–4]. From His saying ﴿and when the earth is stretched out﴾ it is understood that it is not now stretched out, and therefore a hadith says: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will stretch out the earth like a leather hide (adīm)"[[Narrated by Ibn Māja (4081), Aḥmad (3556), and al-Ḥākim in al-Mustadrak (3489), from the hadith of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd.]]: the adīm is the skin; it is stretched like this and becomes one flat surface.

There is also another proof, such as His saying: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾ [al-Zumar 5]. Takwīr means tadwīr (turning around), and it is known that night and day turn around the earth; if this turns, then that around which it turns must be spherical, necessarily.

In any case, the principle we hold is: it is impossible that there be in perceived reality anything that contradicts explicit transmitted text, never; just as there is nothing in explicit reason that contradicts authentic transmitted text. We address the first sentence to the materialists, and the second to the people of reason who claim to be people of intellect, such as the theologians (mutakallimūn) and others. We say: there is nothing in the explicit Qur'an or the explicit authentic Sunnah that contradicts reason. To whom do we address this? To the people of kalām and others who speak about creed with rational arguments.

Now, there is nothing in the explicit Qur'an or the explicit authentic Sunnah that contradicts what is perceived. We address this to the proponents of matter, that is, the materialists who have nothing but what they see with their eyes or hear with their ears.

Accordingly, His saying ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory (172). And indeed Our army, they are the victorious﴾ is to be understood as one of the four interpretations you have heard, and the discussion of them will be completed, God willing, tomorrow.

* Student: In such (...) ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾ ﴿Indeed, we are surely those who glorify﴾ ﴿Indeed, we are surely those who line up﴾. And these pronouns, if it is not a separating pronoun, and the pronoun is not described and does not describe, and if the separating pronoun is described it allows description; likewise, does the separating pronoun abbreviate another separating pronoun?
* Shaykh: It is not described by them. Now, (those who line up) is not an attribute of the separating pronoun; (those who line up) is the predicate.
* Student: And if the predicate (...) ﴿Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾.
* Shaykh: Good. (Hum) is a separating pronoun with no place in i'rab.
* Student: And (hum) is the subject?
* Shaykh: No, it is not the subject; this is a separating pronoun that has no place in i'rab.
* Student: A separating pronoun, so that it separates the predicate from the subject?
* Shaykh: Yes. However, here there is also another reason that distinguishes the attribute from the predicate, namely the lam of emphasis, because the lam of emphasis only enters upon the predicate. So we now have two things: the lam of emphasis and the separating pronoun, both of which confirm that what follows them is the predicate.
* Student: Is it not possible that "the victorious" is an attribute, because (...)?
* Shaykh: No, it is not possible, and how could it be an attribute when it is in the nominative while the pronoun in (inna) is in the accusative?! It cannot be an attribute; there is no problem with this.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verses 171–182 (part 2 of 5):**

* Student: May Allah pardon you. Some of them interpret "And indeed, Our soldiers – they will be the victorious" to mean that, in the final analysis, the messengers who were tested and tortured were in the middle of their mission, while at the end of their mission victory was with them.
* The Shaykh: God willing, we will complete the discussion of this tomorrow.

Question: Is this sentence, ﴿وَلَقَدْ سَبَقَتْ﴾ ("And indeed, Our word has already preceded"), emphasized, and with how many emphasizers was it emphasized?

* Student: It is emphasized with three emphasizers. First: the oath (...), and (qad), and the lam.
* The Shaykh: What informed you that there is an oath in it?
* Student: The waw in ﴿وَلَقَدْ﴾.
* The Shaykh: The waw. So the waw is then a particle of oath. Fine, what is the object of the oath? It was covered in the Ajurrumiyya that the particles of oath only enter upon a noun, and here (laqad) is not a noun.
* Student: It is omitted (...), "By Allah, indeed."
* The Shaykh: The waw of oath cannot be used with the thing sworn by omitted.
* Student: The oath is implied.
* The Shaykh: Implied.
* Student: "By Allah, indeed."
* The Shaykh: "By Allah, indeed, it has preceded."

His saying: ﴿إِنَّهُمْ لَهُمُ الْمَنْصُورُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, they will surely be the victorious"). How do we reconcile this with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَيَقْتُلُونَ النَّبِيِّينَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ﴾ ("and kill the prophets without right") [Ali 'Imran 21]?

* Student: Is it a condition that the victory be...?
* The Shaykh: We have mentioned answers to this.
* Student: Either the victory is by divine support, so that the means are cut off, or the victory is for some of them over others, even if it is not permanent.
* The Shaykh: How would some of them be victorious over others? The messengers do not defeat one another; they are all upon one aim.
* Student: Some of them are victorious through others.
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: We said that victory depends on four situations.
* The Shaykh: Either the victory is by proof and evidence. That is one.
* Student: And either it is by majority.
* The Shaykh: Or, based on what is most common, as a third.
* Student: Third: for those who were commanded to fight.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Fourth: that the victory is absolute, and it is the victory of the Hereafter.
* The Shaykh: The victory of the Hereafter. These are four aspects.

His saying: ﴿وَإِنَّ جُنْدَنَا لَهُمُ الْغَالِبُونَ﴾ ("And indeed, Our soldiers – they will be the victorious"). What is meant by the soldiers of Allah?

* Student: The soldiers of Allah are the angels.
* The Shaykh: The angels? No.
* Student: The prophets are those who defend His law and His religion.
* The Shaykh: Correct. Those who defend His law and His religion.

Now, His saying: ﴿لَهُمُ الْغَالِبُونَ﴾. Is the dominance here a dominance by the sword and weapons, or by some of the signs of Allah, or what?

* Student: First, it is by proof and evidence.
* The Shaykh: No, dominance is other than victory.
* Student: Or it is by signs.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Or it is by angels.
* The Shaykh: By angels. Like what?
* Student: In the Battle of Badr.
* The Shaykh: Allah, Exalted is He, supported them with angels, so they prevailed by what He supported them with of angels. And in the Confederates...
* Student: By the wind.
* The Shaykh: By the wind, and likewise the angels.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿فَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ حَتَّى حِينٍ﴾ ("So turn away from them for a time") [as-Saffat 174]. (Tawalla) is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the pronoun in ﴿عَنْهُمْ﴾ returns to the people of Makkah. The meaning of turning away is what the author explained with his words: (i.e., turn away from the disbelievers of Makkah). ﴿حَتَّى حِينٍ﴾ means: until an unspecified time, but its knowledge is with Allah. For this reason the author said: (until a time when you will be commanded to fight them). On this basis, the verse is abrogated (naskh, i.e., superseded by a later ruling) by the verses of the sword, for the Messenger (ﷺ) was not commanded to fight until he had strength and power, and that was after his migration to Madinah. As for in Makkah, he was not commanded to fight, because wisdom did not require it. On this basis, the time to which the turning away was limited is the command to fight them.

﴿فَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ حَتَّى حِينٍ (١٧٤) وَأَبْصِرْهُمْ﴾ ("So turn away from them for a time, and observe them") [as-Saffat 174–175]. (When the punishment descends upon them, they will see the consequence of their disbelief.) (Absir-hum) means: look at them when the punishment descends upon them. On this basis, seeing is sight by vision; meaning you will see them when the punishment descends upon them. So it is a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to look when the punishment descends upon them. The meaning of His saying (observe them) is consolation and reassurance for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, that these people will see their recompense.

It has also been said that seeing here means giving respite. (Absir-hum) means: give them respite, i.e., grant them time, as in His saying: ﴿فَمَهِّلِ الْكَافِرِينَ أَمْهِلْهُمْ رُوَيْدًا﴾ ("So give respite to the disbelievers; give them time, a little") [at-Tariq 17], and as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿قُلْ يَوْمَ الْفَتْحِ لَا يَنْفَعُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إِيمَانُهُمْ وَلَا هُمْ يُنْظَرُونَ﴾ ("Say, 'On the day of victory, the faith of those who disbelieved will not benefit them, nor will they be reprieved'") [as-Sajdah 29]. The end result of both views is one: whether we say, "Look at them with your eye when the punishment descends upon them," or "Give them respite until the punishment comes to them."

His saying: ﴿فَسَوْفَ يُبْصِرُونَ﴾ ("and they will see"). This sentence is intended as a threat: a threat to these people that they will see the consequence of their affair, by humiliation, disgrace and shame in this world, and likewise by punishment in the Hereafter.

The author said: (They said mockingly: When is the descent of this punishment? Allah, Exalted is He, said as a threat to them: ﴿أَفَبِعَذَابِنَا يَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾ ("Then, is it Our punishment they seek to hasten?") [as-Saffat 176]). The hamza in ﴿أَفَبِعَذَابِنَا﴾ is the interrogative, and the fa' is conjunctive. The people of knowledge have mentioned that when the interrogative hamza enters upon a conjunctive particle, two possibilities are allowed in its i'rab (grammatical analysis):

The first possibility: that the item conjoined-to is implied between the hamza and the conjunctive particle, and it is implied with what suits the context.

The second: that the sentence is conjoined to what precedes without an implied element, and the position of the hamza is after the conjunctive particle.

On this basis, the implied form is: "So is it for Our punishment that they seek to hasten?" According to the first possibility, we imply what suits the context, so we say: "Have they mocked, so is it for Our punishment that they seek to hasten?"

Their seeking to hasten the punishment is of two kinds:

The first: that it be by speech, so they say: "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"

The second: that it be by action, which is by persisting in disobedience, because one who persists in disobedience is, in reality, seeking to hasten the punishment, since sins are a cause of punishment, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَلَوْ أَنَّ أَهْلَ الْقُرَى آمَنُوا وَاتَّقَوْا لَفَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ بَرَكَاتٍ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَلَكِنْ كَذَّبُوا فَأَخَذْنَاهُمْ بِمَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ ("And if the people of the cities had believed and feared Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they had been earning") [al-A'raf 96]. On this basis, the seeking of punishment by people is of two kinds. What is the first kind? What is it?

* Student: It is by action, which is by persisting in disobedience, and it is by speech.
* The Shaykh: Like their saying what? An example by speech?
* Student: They said.
* The Shaykh: "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" They say to the Messenger: "When is this promise, if you are truthful? When is this victory, if you are truthful?" This is seeking by speech.

Seeking by action is persisting in disobedience, because sins are a cause for the occurrence of punishment. So the continuation of these people in denying the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, requires that punishment be hastened for them, and this is seeking by action. Seeking by speech is that they say: "When is this promise? Where is the punishment you threaten us with?" So these people combined both forms, seeking by action and by speech.

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿أَفَبِعَذَابِنَا يَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾ [as-Saffat 176]. The (na) here is for glorification and is not for plurality, because Allah, Exalted is He, is one. Every pronoun that Allah attributes to Himself in the plural form is intended as glorification.

﴿أَفَبِعَذَابِنَا يَسْتَعْجِلُونَ (١٧٦) فَإِذَا نَزَلَ بِسَاحَتِهِمْ فَسَاءَ صَبَاحُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾ ("Then, is it Our punishment they seek to hasten? But when it descends upon their courtyard, evil will be the morning for those who were warned") [as-Saffat 176–177]. (When it descends): the subject returns to the punishment; that is, when the punishment descends upon their courtyard. The courtyard (sahah) is the courtyard of the people, that is, their open area, which is what is near their houses and land. This is expressed as a threat and warning, as one says: "The enemy descended upon their courtyard," as in the authentic hadith about the story of Khaybar: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) approached them, they began running to their hiding places, saying: 'This is Muhammad, or Muhammad has come with the army.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, when we descend upon the courtyard of a people, evil is the morning of those who were warned.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (371) and Muslim (1365/84), from the hadith of Anas.]]

Here Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿فَإِذَا نَزَلَ بِسَاحَتِهِمْ﴾ ("But when it descends upon their courtyard"). ﴿نَزَلَ﴾ means what? The punishment; that is, it befell them. And (﴿بِسَاحَتِهِمْ﴾ means: in their open area). This is a phrase the Arabs use for threat.

(Al-Farra' said: The Arabs suffice with mentioning the courtyard instead of the people.) Al-Farra' is one of the scholars of the Arabic language, and he is an authority in what he says: that the Arabs suffice with mentioning the courtyard instead of the people, as though he is saying: "When it descends upon them." According to al-Farra's statement, the implied meaning of the verse would be: "When it descends upon them." But there is no need to say this, because it is well known that when an enemy descends upon a people, he does not enter their homes from the first moment; rather, he descends upon their courtyard and open area, then attacks them and raids them.

In this there is a metaphor (istiʿara), as the rhetoricians say: where the punishment is likened to an enemy that descends upon them, that is, upon their courtyard. Then the likened-to element (the enemy) is omitted, and it is indicated by one of its attributes, which is descending upon the courtyard. This type of metaphor they call an implicit metaphor (istiʿara makniyya), because in it the likened-to element is omitted and indicated by one of its necessary features.

He said: ﴿فَإِذَا نَزَلَ بِسَاحَتِهِمْ فَسَاءَ صَبَاحُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾. The author said regarding (sa'a): (bi'sa, "was evil"). Then he said: (morning), then he said: ﴿صَبَاحُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾. This is because (sa'a) is a verb of dispraise, and verbs of dispraise require two things: a subject (fa'il) and a specification (tamyiz). So the author supplied the specification in his saying: (morning). As for the subject, it is in the verse, which is His saying: ﴿صَبَاحُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾, meaning: evil is the morning of those who were warned, a morning that is evil; or: evil is the morning of those who were warned, a morning.

The main point is that verbs of dispraise, as well as verbs of praise such as (ni'ma), (habbadha), and similar ones, require a subject and a specification. The author supplied the specification, but is this supply obligatory? The correct view is that it is not obligatory, and that the subject fills its place, as in this verse and in many other verses also, such as: ﴿نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ إِنَّهُ أَوَّابٌ﴾ ("An excellent servant; indeed, he was one who often turned back") [Sad 30], and He did not say "excellent servant as a servant."

Now, ﴿فَسَاءَ صَبَاحُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾. Is ﴿الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾ an active participle or a passive participle? A passive participle, meaning: evil is the morning of the people who were warned, because they were warned and the proof was established against them, so they have no excuse. He said: ﴿فَسَاءَ صَبَاحُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾, which contains the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, because the requirement of the context would be for him to say: "When it descends upon their courtyard, evil will be their morning." But he said: ﴿فَسَاءَ صَبَاحُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾, placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. Explain this expression for me.

* Student: The meaning of the speech is that...
* The Shaykh: The requirement of the context is that he would say...
* Student: That he would say: "When it descends upon their courtyard, evil will be their morning." But here he mentioned "those who were warned"...
* The Shaykh: He placed the apparent noun, because (those who were warned) is an apparent noun in the position of?
* Student: In the position of the pronoun that is implied.
* The Shaykh: In the position of the pronoun, or the implied pronoun. Placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun must have a benefit: either verbal, or meaningful, or both verbal and meaningful. Let us look here: placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun has a verbal benefit, which is observing the rhyme endings (fawasil) of the verses, because Allah, Exalted is He, expresses a word, and the apparent form differs from the expression with it for the sake of observing the rhyme endings. ﴿قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِرَبِّ هَارُونَ وَمُوسَى﴾ ("They said, 'We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses'") [Ta-Ha 70] in Surah Ta-Ha. It is known that Musa is better than Harun, and in the Book of Allah he is mentioned first, but in this verse "the Lord of Harun and Musa," he placed Harun before Musa for the sake of the rhyme endings, because the rhyme endings of Surah Ta-Ha are mostly ending in alif.

Here we say: "evil is their morning." If he had said "evil is their morning," the rhyme ending would not have harmonized with the one before it and the one after it, so he said: ﴿فَسَاءَ صَبَاحُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾. This is a verbal benefit, or a verbal and meaningful benefit. The meaningful benefit is establishing the proof against those upon whose courtyard the punishment descended: that they had been warned, had no excuse, and deserved the punishment by the justice of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿فَسَاءَ صَبَاحُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ﴾. Now, what is warning (inedhar)? The scholars say: warning is informing accompanied by intimidation, and glad tidings is informing accompanied by joy in what delights and gladdens. So glad tidings concern what is pleasing, and warning is its opposite. Thus (al-mundharin) are those who were warned, by establishing the proof against them; that is, they were informed of what would frighten them if they opposed the command of Allah.

He said: (﴿وَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ حَتَّى حِينٍ (١٧٨) وَأَبْصِرْ فَسَوْفَ يُبْصِرُونَ﴾ ("And turn away from them for a time, and observe, and they will see") [as-Saffat 178–179]. He repeated it for emphasis of their threat and for consolation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)). This verse, as you see, is the same as the verse before it. The verse before it says: ﴿فَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ حَتَّى حِينٍ (١٧٤) وَأَبْصِرْهُمْ فَسَوْفَ يُبْصِرُونَ﴾, and here he said: ﴿وَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ حَتَّى حِينٍ (١٧٨) وَأَبْصِرْ فَسَوْفَ يُبْصِرُونَ﴾. It differs only in the conjunction: the first is ﴿فَتَوَلَّ﴾, and the second is ﴿وَتَوَلَّ﴾. Also, in the first he said (observe them), and here he said (observe), so he left it absolute; otherwise, it is the same. The benefit of repetition is repeating their warning, by threatening them, and consoling the Messenger (ﷺ), because whenever speech is repeated it becomes more emphatic.

Then he said: ﴿سُبْحَانَ رَبِّكَ رَبِّ الْعِزَّةِ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ (١٨٠) وَسَلَامٌ عَلَى الْمُرْسَلِينَ﴾ ("Exalted is your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe. And peace upon the messengers") [as-Saffat 180–181]. ﴿سُبْحَانَ رَبِّكَ﴾: we want its i'rab from the brother.

* Student: (Subhana) is a verbal noun of (sabbaha).
* The Shaykh: That is in terms of morphology. The i'rab, and it is in the accusative case.
* Student: It is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq).
* The Shaykh: As an absolute object, whose verb is obligatorily omitted. So (subhana), in terms of morphology, is a verbal noun of (sabbaha); in terms of i'rab, it is in the accusative as an absolute object for an omitted verb that is obligatorily omitted. For this reason one does not combine (subhana) and (sabbih); one does not say "sabbih subhan."

Now, ﴿سُبْحَانَ رَبِّكَ﴾: that is, glorification (tanzih) of Him. We have already gone over what Allah is glorified from. What is it that Allah is glorified from? We want you, as a student of knowledge and an alert, recording listener, to answer.

* Student: From what does not befit Him.
* The Shaykh: And it revolves around...
* Student: Around resemblance, and... deficiency.
* The Shaykh: Around two things: glorification from resemblance (to creation), and from deficiency in the attributes of perfection.

His saying: ﴿سُبْحَانَ رَبِّكَ﴾ attributes lordship to the Messenger (ﷺ), so the meaning is a particular lordship, because lordship is divided into two kinds: general, which is for all creation, and this is the lordship of authority and management; and particular, which is the lordship of nurture and care. Both kinds came together in His saying, about the sorcerers of Pharaoh: ﴿قَالُوا آمَنَّا بِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ (١٢١) رَبِّ مُوسَى وَهَارُونَ﴾ ("They said, 'We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun'") [al-A'raf 121–122]. The first is general (Lord of the worlds), and the second is particular (the Lord of Musa and Harun). For this reason, one of the requirements of this lordship was that Allah, Exalted is He, said to them both: ﴿لَا تَخَافَا إِنَّنِي مَعَكُمَا أَسْمَعُ وَأَرَى﴾ ("Do not fear; indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see") [Ta-Ha 46].

He said: ﴿سُبْحَانَ رَبِّكَ﴾, and the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ); that is, glorification of your Lord who has enveloped you with His care and concern.

Then he said: ﴿رَبِّ الْعِزَّةِ﴾, that is, the might, the dominance. (Rabb) here means "owner," not "creator." In the Qur'an it comes meaning creator, owner, and manager, except in this place, so its meaning here is only "owner." It cannot mean "creator," because might is one of the attributes of Allah, and the attributes of Allah are uncreated. Therefore the meaning of "Lord" in His saying ﴿رَبِّ الْعِزَّةِ﴾ must be "owner of might," not "creator," because the attributes of the Lord are uncreated.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 37, verses 171–182 (part 3 of 5):**

Allah's words, ﴿Your Lord, the Lord of Might﴾, attribute the Lord (rabb) here to might ('izza) rather than to any of His other attributes, because the context requires it. The context concerns the outcome of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the outcome of those who denied him: that Allah will support him, that victory will be his, and that humiliation and abandonment will befall his enemies. So the context calls for the attribute by which victory is achieved, which is might. Allah says in surah al-Munafiqun: ﴿They say, "If we return to Madinah, the more honourable will surely expel therefrom the more humble."﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. In reality it is the more honourable who will expel the more humble, but who is the more honourable? ﴿And might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾. As for the hypocrites, they have no might.

Accordingly, we say: Allah mentions the attribute of might here rather than any other, because the context requires it, since it is in the setting of victory for the Messenger (ﷺ) and humiliation for his enemies.

Among the names of Allah is al-'Aziz (the Mighty), and it occurs very frequently in the Noble Book. The scholars said: "Might ('izza) has three meanings: the might of dominance (ghalaba), the might of rank (qadr), and the might of invulnerability (imtina')." Three categories. Recite them for us.

* Student: The might of dominance, the might of rank, and the might of invulnerability.

* The Shaykh: Three. The might of dominance means that Allah is dominant over everything. The might of rank means that Allah is above everything in rank. The might of invulnerability means that Allah is inaccessible, so that no one can reach Him with harm. From this third sense comes the expression "ard 'azzaz", meaning land that is hard and firm, on which the pickaxes leave no mark.

(﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might﴾: dominance; ﴿above what they describe﴾: by ascribing to Him a son.) The phrase ﴿above what they describe﴾ may have the ma (what) as a verbal-masdar particle, so the sentence would read: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above their description." And the 'izza has three meanings: the might of dominance, the might of rank, and the might of invulnerability. Three categories. Recite them for us.

* Student: The might of dominance, the might of rank, and the might of invulnerability.

* The Shaykh: Three. The might of dominance means that Allah is dominant over every thing.
The might of rank means that Allah is above everything in rank.
The might of invulnerability means that Allah cannot be reached by anyone with harm.
From the third comes their saying "ard 'azzaz", meaning what? It means hard and firm, on which the pickaxes leave no mark.

(﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might﴾: the dominance; ﴿above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat 180]: by ascribing to Him a son.)

The phrase ﴿above what they describe﴾ may have the ma (what) as a verbal-masdar particle, and the sentence would then mean: "Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above their description." It may also be a relative pronoun, with the returning pronoun omitted, and the sense would be: "above what they describe Him with."

The author's words, "by ascribing to Him a son," are an example of what they ascribe to Allah from which He is exempt. Otherwise, they say that Allah has a son, a wife, a partner, a helper, and so on. Every attribute unbefitting Allah is one from which He is exempt, however those lying liars ascribe it to Him.

He says: ﴿And peace be upon the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat 181]. (Peace) is the subject, and (upon the messengers) is its predicate.

Here "peace" (salam) means "greeting" (taslim). It is a masdar-type noun from the verb sallama, like kalam meaning "speech" from kallama.

The meaning of "peace be upon them" is that what they said about the Essence and Attributes of Allah is free of every deficiency. So Allah has glorified Himself above what the opponents of the messengers ascribed to Him, and then He gave peace to the messengers because what they said was free of deficiency and flaw. There is no falsehood in it and no defect. This is why He says: ﴿And peace be upon the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat 181] (those who conveyed from Allah the Tawhid and the sharia).

Having mentioned the exaltation of Allah in what He described Himself with, and in what His messengers described Him with, He then mentioned praise (hamd), which is the ascription of perfection to the one praised. So the verses combine the exaltation of Allah above attributes of deficiency with the affirmation of attributes of perfection. The affirmation of perfection comes after the exaltation, because it is said: "adornment comes after clearing away", that is, decoration after removing what is harmful.

He says: ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat 182]. I said that praise (hamd) is the ascription of perfection to the one praised, and the perfection of Allah, glory be to Him, revolves around two matters: essential perfection and active perfection.

As for essential perfection, He, glory be to Him, is perfect in His Essence, which is characterised by every attribute of perfection.

Active perfection: Allah is perfect in His actions. He has favour over His servants by bringing what benefits them and averting what harms them. For this reason, the sharia prescribes that a person, when he finishes eating and drinking, should praise Allah for the food and drink He has provided. If you wish, you may go further and praise Allah who does not need what you need of food and drink.

He says: ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat 182]. Lord of the worlds means: their Creator, their Owner, and the Manager of their affairs.

"Alam" (world) means everything other than Allah, and they are called 'alam because they are a sign (ʿalam) pointing to their Creator, mighty and majestic is He. In every created thing of Allah there is a sign pointing to His oneness and perfection.

He says: ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat 182]. The author said: "(for their victory)," that is, the victory of the messengers, "and the destruction of the disbelievers."

Had the author made it unrestricted, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, for everything," including what He decrees at times, such as the domination of His enemies over His allies, then He is praised for that too, because of the great benefits that follow from it. This is as in the battle of Uhud, in which Allah mentioned many wisdoms. Ibn al-Qayyim (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned a large part of them in Zad al-Ma'ad. With this, this surah ends.

* Student: (...) ﴿And a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾ [al-Baqarah 221] (...). Likewise it is permissible when the predicate precedes the subject (...). So this is from (…)?

* The Shaykh: It is not restricted to five. It is not restricted to five, nor to fifty. Ibn Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) stated a rule, saying:

"The beginning with an indefinite noun is not permitted unless it conveys a benefit..."

You know it. So whenever a benefit is conveyed, it is permissible to begin with it. And Ibn Hisham in al-Qatr says: "Beginning with an indefinite noun is permitted if it is general or specific." That is, whether it is general or a particular, specified noun. But Ibn Malik's wording is better:

"The beginning with an indefinite noun is not permitted unless it conveys a benefit, such as 'at Zayd there is a striped cloak.'"

* Student: As long as it conveys a benefit, that is enough.

* The Shaykh: That is enough; it has no restriction (...).

* * *

* Student: ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an, full of reminder. Rather, those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition. How many generations We destroyed before them, and they cried out when there was no longer any escape. And they wondered that a warner from among them had come to them, and the disbelievers said, "This is a magician, a liar. Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing."﴾ [Sad 1–5].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿So turn away from them for a time﴾ [al-Saffat 174]. What is this "time" (hin) to which the period of turning away is set?

* Student: Until their term.

* The Shaykh: Until their term?

* Student: Until he is commanded to fight.

* The Shaykh: Until he is commanded to fight. On this interpretation, what is the verse?

* Student: Abrogated (naskh). That is, this verse is abrogated.

* The Shaykh: Abrogated by verses.

* Student: The command to fight.

* The Shaykh: The command to fight. Does ﴿turn away from them for a time﴾ admit of what your brother said, that it means until their death?

* Student: The verse does not admit it. It does not admit "until their death." No, it does not admit it.

* The Shaykh: Why?

* Student: What is the benefit of turning away until their death? They will not go astray until death.

* Another student: I say yes, it admits it, because it is not turning away from fighting, but turning away from them, not allying with them, until they die as long as they remain in disbelief.

* The Shaykh: Does it not conflict with His words: ﴿See them, and they will see﴾ [al-Saffat 175]?

* Student: No, this does not conflict with it.

* The Shaykh: Why not?

* Student: Because he will not ally with them. Some of them will die while he has not allied with them.

* The Shaykh: No, he is the one who turned away. He turned away, meaning (...).

* Student: Yes, that is right, meaning he does not lean toward them.

* The Shaykh: So this admits that "for a time" means until they die, and you will see that they died, whether by fighting or otherwise. On this, the verse is not abrogated.

His words: ﴿but they will see﴾ [al-Saffat 175]. What is the purpose of this clause?

* Student: ﴿but they will see﴾ is a threat.

* The Shaykh: Its purpose is a threat.

His words: ﴿Do they seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ [al-Saffat 176]. This is a response to what?

* Student: Their haste.

* The Shaykh: To their haste for punishment. What did they say in hastening the punishment?

* Student: They said: "Indeed..."

* The Shaykh: What did they say in asking for the punishment to be hastened? That is, what is the expression indicating that they sought to hasten the punishment?

* Student: Their saying: ﴿Bring us a punishment﴾ [al-Anfal 32].

* Another student: They said: ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ [Yunus 48].

* The Shaykh: They said: ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾, ﴿When is this victory, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-Sajdah 28], and ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal 32], and similar.

His words: ﴿When it descends into their courtyard﴾ [al-Saffat 177]. What is the meaning of "when it descends into their courtyard"?

* Student: It means that when punishment descends upon the people, in their courtyard, that is, in their houses (...).

* The Shaykh: It is as if He is saying: "When punishment comes upon them."

His words: ﴿Evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾ [al-Saffat 177]. This "sa'a" (evil is) is a verb of what kind?

* Student: Of blame, the nasikh.

* The Shaykh: Of blame. What does it require?

* Student: It requires a specification (tamyiz) and a subject (fa'il).

* The Shaykh: It requires a specification and a subject. Where is the subject?

* Student: "Sa'a sabah al-mundharin": the subject is elided, and the phrase "sabah al-mundharin" is the specification.

* The Shaykh: "Sabah al-mundharin" is the specification.

* Student: The subject is "sabah."

* The Shaykh: The subject is "sabah." And where is the specification?

* Student: The specification is elided.

* The Shaykh: What is the estimate (taqdir)?

* Student: "Fa-sa'a sabah al-mundharin sabahan."

* The Shaykh: "Fa-sa'a sabahan sabah al-mundharin."

In His words: ﴿the morning of those who were warned﴾ [al-Saffat 177], your brother has a rhetorical point. What is it?

* Student: A change from the pronoun to the explicit noun.

* The Shaykh: To the explicit noun. "Explicit" is not a pronoun; the explicit is the counterpart of the pronominal. You understand the meaning, but you did not express it well. I want the expression to be good.

* Student: Placing the explicit noun in place of the pronoun.

* The Shaykh: There is placing the explicit noun in place of the pronoun. The explicit noun cannot be made a pronoun (...). Do you know what the rhetorical benefit is of placing the explicit noun in place of the pronoun?

* Student: Two benefits. The first benefit: to show the consequence, that is, that they were warned and the proof was established.

* The Shaykh: That is, establishing the proof against them, that the warning reached them.

* Student: Second, so that the rhymed endings (fawasil) correspond.

* The Shaykh: Observing the rhymed endings.

* Student: I say: there is a verbal benefit and a semantic benefit. The verbal benefit is the verses' rhymed endings, observing the fawasil.

* The Shaykh: Observing the fawasil. And the semantic one?

* Student: It has three benefits. First, generalisation. Second, that the description applies to them. Third, emphasis upon these people.

* The Shaykh: Establishing the proof against them that they were warned: ﴿Evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾ [al-Saffat 177].

His words: ﴿So turn away from them for a time. And see, and they will see﴾ [al-Saffat 178–179]. How does it relate to what precedes it in meaning?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It is conjoined to what precedes it, and in meaning it is an emphasis. That is why we said "in meaning."

﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat 180]. Your brother, what does it mean?

* Student: Exaltation (tanzih).

* The Shaykh: Exaltation, what kind? From where did you take the tanzih?

* Student: From "subhan" (glory be).

* The Shaykh: From "subhan." And what is it that Allah is exalted above?

* Student: Likeness and deficiency.

* The Shaykh: Likeness and deficiency: the likeness of created things, and deficiency in His perfection.

His words: ﴿Lord of Might﴾ [al-Saffat 180]. What does "rabb" mean here?

* Student: Owner.

* The Shaykh: In the sense of owner. Could it not be in the sense of creator?

* Student: It can.

* The Shaykh: It can mean creator?

* Student: It cannot mean creator.

* The Shaykh: Why?

* Student: Because the attributes of Allah are not created.

* The Shaykh: Because the attributes of Allah are not created. If you say "Lord of creation," meaning the Creator, Allah, that is fine. But "Lord of Might" is the might of Allah. It cannot mean creator, because that would entail that the attribute of Allah is created. Do you understand?

His words: ﴿Peace be upon the messengers﴾ [al-Saffat 181]. Is the sentence declarative or performative?

* Student: Declarative.

* The Shaykh: Declarative. That is, Allah informs that peace is upon the messengers?

* Student: Peace.

* The Shaykh: Peace. Why did He give peace to them?

* Student: Because of the soundness of what they said.

* The Shaykh: Because what they said is free of deficiency and flaw, unlike what those people ascribed to Him.

What is the benefit of His words after: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might﴾ [al-Saffat 180], and His words: ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Saffat 182]?

* Student: On the perfection, that is, the favour of Allah in granting victory to...

* The Shaykh: (...) ﴿Glory be to your Lord﴾ and between ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. What is the benefit of that?

* Student: The benefit is that, along with the exaltation of Allah, glory be to Him, above deficiency, for example, praise belongs to Him.

* The Shaykh: That is not clear.

* Student: When Allah mentioned what the disbelievers said, ascribing deficiency to Allah, He mentioned the attributes of perfection by which He is described, glory be to Him. Then He said: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾.

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: Allah, mighty and majestic, affirms perfection for Himself after exalting Himself above deficiency. That is, adornment after clearing away.

* The Shaykh: The complete answer is that He affirms for Himself the attributes of perfection after exalting Himself above the attributes of deficiency, so that what He describes Himself with combines negation and affirmation.

Now let us take the benefits.

Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿So turn away from them for a time﴾ [al-Saffat 174].

This is the beginning of the lesson. Have the benefits before it been taken?

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We had already preceded in Our word to Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they would be the ones given victory﴾ [al-Saffat 171–172].

* From the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, mighty and majestic, decreed victory for His servants the messengers, as shown by His words: ﴿And Our word had already preceded﴾ [al-Saffat 171]. The cosmic word of Allah, mighty and majestic, does not change.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), and steadfastness upon the message he carried.

* From its benefits: a threat to the enemies of the messengers, and that they are forsaken, because when victory is decreed for the messengers, it will be humiliation for their enemies.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the victory of the messengers comes from Allah and from what He facilitates of His creation and signs. This is why He said: ﴿They are the ones given victory﴾ [al-Saffat 172], without specifying who the helper is, so that it is more comprehensive. Allah says: ﴿He it is who supported you with His help and with the believers﴾ [al-Anfal 62].

* From the benefits of this noble verse: dominance belongs to the soldiers of Allah who stand to support His law and defend it, as shown by His words: ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers will be the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat 173].

* From its benefits: the strengthening of those who call to Allah, mighty and majestic, among the followers of the messengers, by assuring them that dominance belongs to them, as Allah says: ﴿And might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8].

If someone asks: How do you reconcile this verse with what happened to some messengers and some of their followers, which seems to contradict the apparent meaning of the verse? The answer to this has already been given to us from several angles, so let it be known to you.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So turn away from them for a time﴾ [37:174] ﴿And watch them, and they will see﴾ [37:175], to the end of the verses.

In this noble verse there is a warning to these deniers of the Messenger (ﷺ), and that their tyranny will not last, as He says: ﴿for a time﴾ [37:174]. So this tyranny will come to an end, either at the hands of the Messenger (ﷺ) when he is commanded to fight, or by death through the decree of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Their affair must end, and their tyranny cannot continue.

Among its benefits: consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ), for he was informed that his enemies' affair would end after a time.

Among them: a warning to these enemies who had reached such heights of tyranny and aggression against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Among the benefits of these verses: confirmation of this matter, namely their destruction and removal; as He says: ﴿And watch them﴾ [37:175], meaning: when the punishment descends upon them, you will see and witness it with your own eyes.

Among its benefits also: repeating the warning a second time in a different style, in His saying: ﴿but they will see﴾ [37:175].

Among its benefits: emphasizing the meaning through varied expressions, so that it is more forceful and so that these threatened people await the punishment from every direction; as He says: ﴿but they will see﴾ [37:175].

Among the benefits of the noble verses: showing the foolishness of these deniers and their tyranny, in that they used to seek to hasten the punishment. The reason for this is that if they had been wise, they would have feared the punishment and not sought to hasten it; and if they had possessed any measure of moderation, they would not have challenged the messengers, saying: "Bring us the punishment if you are truthful." So they have foolishness and an exaggerated tyranny and aggression. And the verse we pointed to earlier, His saying: ﴿And when they said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment"﴾ [8:32], indicates the foolishness of the Quraysh, and that they were among the utmost in foolishness; for if they had been forbearing and rightly guided, they would have said: "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then [what?] guide us to it." This is the correct stance. As for "rain down upon us stones from the sky," this is among the most foolish things a human being could say.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, glorified and exalted, speaks of Himself in the context of threat using the plural of majesty, to terrify and unsettle those who are threatened; as He says: ﴿Then do they seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ [37:176], and He did not say "My punishment." That is why, when mention of the punishment came in the form of information, He said: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [15:49], and "And that My punishment is the painful punishment" [15:50], and He did not say "Our punishment."

Among the benefits of the noble verses: that when punishment descends upon a people, it will not let them escape; as He says: ﴿So when it descends upon their courtyard, evil will be the morning of those who were warned﴾ [37:177].

Among its benefits: that if they believed at this time, it would not benefit them; for if belief had benefited them, this statement, His saying: ﴿evil will be the morning of those who were warned﴾ [37:177], would not be fully true of them; for if belief had benefited them, this evil would have been removed from them. But belief will not benefit them. This is the sunnah of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, concerning His servants: when punishment descends upon them and they then believe, belief does not benefit them. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone, and we disbelieve in what we used to associate with Him." But their belief did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾ [40:84–85]. Pharaoh, when drowning overtook him, said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims﴾ [10:90], and it was said to him: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾ [10:91], meaning: it will not benefit you. And Allah the Exalted said in Surah an-Nisa': ﴿And repentance is not accepted from those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says: "Indeed, I repent now"﴾ [4:18]. All of this obliges the sensible person to hasten to repentance, not to delay, and not to neglect, for he does not know when death will overtake him; and if death comes upon him, repentance will not benefit him. Repentance must be at a time when it is accepted.

An exception is made from this: one town whose belief after the descent of the punishment upon it benefited it. And who are they?

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: A town that believed after the punishment descended upon it, and its belief benefited it. Did you not attend yesterday?
* Student: No.
* The Shaykh: Alright.
* Student: The people of Yunus.
* The Shaykh: The people of Yunus. What is the evidence that their belief benefited them after the punishment had descended upon them?
* Student: The verses in the surah..
* The Shaykh: (...) Is it valid for one to say: the evidence is a verse of the Qur'an?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Leave this.
* Another student: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its belief benefited it—except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy for a time﴾ [10:98].
* The Shaykh: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its belief benefited it—except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment﴾ [10:98]. So the punishment had descended upon them, but when they believed, Allah removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world.

What is the wisdom in the fact that these people's belief benefited them after the punishment had descended upon them?

* Student: Because their prophet Yunus, peace be upon him, left in anger before he was commanded to leave.
* The Shaykh: Before he was commanded to leave, so this was an excuse for them. Correct.

* Among the benefits of these verses: that Allah, glorified and exalted, will not destroy a people until He establishes the proof against them through warning. What is the evidence from the verse?
* Student: ﴿evil will be the morning of those who were warned﴾ [37:177].
* The Shaykh: ﴿evil will be the morning of those who were warned﴾, and this indicates that the punishment will not befall them except after the warning. This is found in the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [17:15], and Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And Allah would never misguide a people after He has guided them until He makes clear to them what they should avoid. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ [9:115].

The correct view is that this is general regarding tawhid and what is below it, so it includes the branches of Islam, such as prayer, zakat, purification, and so on. A person is not bound by any of them except after the establishment of the proof and the arrival of the message. For this reason the preponderant view is that whoever lived in the desert, far from people, and did not fast, did not pray, did not pay zakat, while being ignorant, has no obligation to make up for it, even if he remained for years.

The evidence for this is many texts from the Sunnah indicating that whoever was ignorant, raised in a remote desert, not knowing the Shariah, has no obligation to make up for it. For example, the man who did not settle in his prayer remained upon this for a period known only to Allah. But he remained for a period in which he did not do better than this, a prayer in which he did not settle. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not command him to repeat what had passed of his prayers, but commanded him to repeat the prayer of the present time, because the demand for it at this time was in force; so he commanded him to repeat it so that his prayer would be valid. As for what was before, he did not command him to repeat it.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (757) and Muslim (397 / 45), from Abu Hurayrah.]] And he did not tell the woman who said that she menstruates a heavy, severe menstruation that prevents her from praying to repeat the prayers, even though she was istihadah, and the istihadah woman prays.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (228) and Muslim (333 / 62), from 'A'ishah.]] Examples of this are many.

And there is no difference, as I have said, between tawhid and what is below it. Suppose a Muslim man was raised in a distant land and did not know that he was worshipping this grave, not knowing that it was disbelief. He is not judged a disbeliever, because he is a Muslim who committed this error and did not intend it in his heart, so there is nothing upon him. Likewise, whoever commits a forbidden act of shirk or something less, interpreting it and finding no one to clarify for him, is not a disbeliever, because intention is necessary. Consider the man whose camel was lost in a barren wilderness; he searched for it and did not find it, despaired of it, lay down in the shade of a tree awaiting death. While he was in that state, suddenly the rope of his camel was hanging from the tree; he took hold of its rope and said: "O Allah, You are my servant and I am Your lord!"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6309) and Muslim (2747 / 7), with its wording, from Anas ibn Malik.]] He made himself a lord and made the Lord of the worlds a servant. This is undoubtedly a word of disbelief. If someone were to say: "I am greater than Allah, I am His lord, and He is my servant," he would undoubtedly be a disbeliever. But this man erred and did not intend the speech; he erred from excessive joy. So he was not a disbeliever, because he did not intend disbelief. Likewise the man who was extravagant against himself in sins said to his family: "When I die, burn me and scatter me in the sea, thinking that if he does this he will be saved from the punishment of Allah. But Allah, by His power, said to him: 'Be!' and he was. He was gathered, and his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, asked him: 'Why did you do this?' He said: 'Out of fear of Your punishment, O Lord.' He said to him words meaning: 'Your fear of My punishment has saved you from My punishment.'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3481) and Muslim (2756 / 24), from Abu Hurayrah.]] So Allah saved him from the punishment, although this man had doubt about Allah's power, but not with deliberate, interpreted intent, so he was not a disbeliever.

It is not permissible for a person to be hasty in such matters, I mean the matter of declaring someone a disbeliever or a wrongdoer (fisq). For some brothers hasten to declare takfir and look at the statement without the speaker, and look at the act without the doer. If this statement is disbelief, he says: "Whoever says it is an absolute disbeliever." And if this act is disbelief, he says: "Whoever does it is an absolute disbeliever," and does not consider the impediments. For this statement, if it is takfir-worthy, is undoubtedly a cause of disbelief; this act, if it is takfir-worthy, is a cause of disbelief. But do causes have impediments that affect them, or not?

Yes, every cause has an impediment. There may be an impediment in this specific person that prevents judging him a disbeliever. Among these impediments are ignorance, coercion, forgetfulness, and being overcome by one's self so that one cannot control it. For this reason, if someone slipped and said a word of disbelief, do we say he is a disbeliever? No. Forgetfulness and ignorance are twins in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and in the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ).

Therefore the seeker of knowledge must distinguish between the statement and the speaker, and between the act and the doer. A statement may be disbelief while the speaker is not a disbeliever, and an act may be disbelief while the doer is not a disbeliever. Consider: if a man were coerced into prostrating to an idol, and it was said to him: "Either you prostrate or the sword": he prostrated under coercion, not drawn near to the idol. Is he a disbeliever? He is not a disbeliever, because Allah says: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief—except one who is forced while his heart remains firm in faith; but whoever opens his breast to disbelief—upon them is wrath from Allah﴾ [16:106]. Look at the words: ﴿except one who is forced while his heart remains firm in faith, but whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, meaning he chooses it with his breast expanded to it. This is the one who is given its ruling. As for one who is not like that, no. Therefore, O brothers, we must not be hasty in declaring takfir and fisq. Some people, out of zeal, hasten to judge: "This is a disbeliever!" O son of the lawful, fear Allah! If you declare a person a disbeliever who is not a disbeliever, the disbelief returns upon you, as established in the authentic hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6104) and Muslim (60 / 111), from Ibn 'Umar.]] Do you want to be a disbeliever? Do not declare takfir except upon one against whom the proof has been established. That is, for the establishment of the proof against someone's disbelief, two matters are needed:

The establishment that this thing is disbelief, and the fulfilment of the conditions of disbelief in this doer or this speaker. That is, the proof against a person's disbelief is not established except by two matters:

The establishment that this thing is takfir-worthy.

And the second: the realization of disbelief with respect to this particular person. For a thing may be takfir-worthy, yet disbelief is not realized in this doer or this speaker.

I repeat this matter because of its importance, for it reaches me that some people, as soon as they are told that so-and-so did such-and-such, say: "I seek refuge in Allah, this is a disbeliever, we disassociate from him to Allah; we disassociate from him to Allah?!" This is an error.

What do you say about killing a soul? It is among the major sins. When Usama ibn Zayd killed the man who said "There is no god but Allah," interpreting it, did the Messenger kill him? He did not kill him, nor did he impose blood money on him. The most that he said to him was: «Did you kill him after he said: There is no god but Allah?» And Usama said: "He said it, O Messenger of Allah, as a seeking of refuge."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4269) and Muslim (96 / 158), from Usama ibn Zayd.]] The story is well known, I think.

The story: a man from the disbelievers fled, and Usama ibn Zayd pursued him. When he caught up with him, the man said: "There is no god but Allah," and Usama killed him, thinking he had said it as a seeking of refuge, meaning out of fear of being killed. The indication was with Usama, for when a disbelieving man is overtaken by a Muslim with his sword and says "There is no god but Allah," the evidence that he said it to seek refuge is very strong. But the Messenger (ﷺ) does not want us to judge by what we suspect; he wants us to judge by the outward: «I only judge by what I hear.»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6967) and Muslim (1713 / 4), from Umm Salamah.]] He said: «Did you kill him after he said: There is no god but Allah?» He said: "O Messenger of Allah, he only said it as a seeking of refuge." He said: «Did you kill him after he said: There is no god but Allah?» He said: "He only said it as a seeking of refuge." He said: «Did you kill him after he said: There is no god but Allah?» Notice the repetition: he kept repeating it until I wished I had not yet become Muslim. Allahu Akbar.

The conclusion is that we must be gentle with ourselves and with people. We must not declare anyone a disbeliever until it becomes clear to us that this thing is disbelief and that what he said or did meets the conditions of takfir, so that we do not bring disbelief or wrongdoing upon ourselves.

And praise be to Allah. Is the judgment with Allah or with us? With Allah. If Allah has not declared this person a disbeliever, why should we declare him one? If we declare disbelief what Allah has not declared, it is as if we have forbidden what Allah has permitted, or permitted what Allah has forbidden. So we must fear Allah. And the default regarding a Muslim is what? Islam. As long as he professes Islam, but he does an act of disbelief or says a word of disbelief while being ignorant, not raised in a land where Islam is established, how can we say he is a disbeliever? A Bedouin raised in a distant land far from the Shariah sciences, but a poor man who every morning sets up a stone and prostrates to it, not knowing it; do we say he is a disbeliever while he testifies that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah?!

For this reason the scholars stated in their books: if a man denied the obligation of prayer, he would be a disbeliever. But they said: if he denied the obligation of prayer while being raised in a land far from religious knowledge, or being recently converted to Islam, he would not be a disbeliever, because he is ignorant.

So His saying: ﴿evil will be the morning of those who were warned﴾ [37:177] indicates that no one can be punished except after the warning.

Is the arrival of the proof sufficient, or is it necessary to understand the proof?

* Students: There is a difference of opinion.

The Sheikh: The second point: it is necessary to understand it. This is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And had We sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs, and he had recited it to them, they would not have believed in it﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 198-199]. Why? Because they would not understand it, and if they do not believe in it because they do not understand it, then they are excused. Allah the Exalted also said: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people﴾ [Ibrahim 4], in their language, so that he could make it clear to them. So understanding the proof is necessary. If you said to a non-Arab person, "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," while he does not know what it means, would the proof be established against him? It would not be established. If you said to him, "O so-and-so, did you divorce your wife?" and he said, "Yes, three times," and he said, "Yes, four and five," and by "you divorced your wife" he understood that you had made her a divorcee who goes and comes, and the non-Arab does not know, we would say, "Finished, she has separated from you; she is not lawful to you unless she marries another husband!" How he would shout: "O people, how is this speech?" We would say: "We asked you whether you divorced your wife?" You said, "Yes." We said, "Three times?" You said, "Three and four." Then the wife has separated from him. Does she become separated from him or not? She does not become separated, why? Because he does not know the meaning.

But if he said: "Bahashtam," meaning, "I divorced her three times."

A student: What is its meaning?

The Sheikh: Thus the jurists said: if he says "bahashtam," meaning "I divorced her three times." If I say to you: an Arab says to his wife, "Bahashtam, bahashtam, bahashtam," she is not divorced even once, because he does not know it.

The point is that these are important matters which a person should take care of, and not put himself into ruin or put others into ruin, and show loyalty or enmity in a manner not prescribed by the Sharia. Judgment on people belongs to Allah the Mighty and Majestic.
